q: Gonzo tells a sporting-goods dealer that he needs a tent that will survive a Himalayan blizzard, and asks the dealer to pick one. The dealer picks a summer tent. Gonzo's reliance on this dealer was arguably unreasonable because the dealer obviously knew little about mountaineering. Does that defeat a fitness claim?
o: No, because reliance must be actual but need not be reasonable.
Yes, because the dealer is no mountaineering expert.
No, because the dealer is a merchant in sporting goods.
Yes, because the buyer's reliance must be reasonable.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The outline's fitness elements: seller need not be a merchant, and reliance need not be reasonable.
The dealer had reason to know Gonzo relied on its selection.
Merchant status is not the reason.
§ 2-315 doesn't require the buyer's reliance to be reasonable, only actual.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fitness: reasonable reliance

q: On March 1, Scooter orders a sound mixer by phone, and the store agrees to sell it. The mixer arrives on March 10 in a box with a printed card inside: "SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY." Scooter never signs or agrees to anything else. The mixer fails in ordinary use. Is the disclaimer effective?
o: No, because merchantability can never be disclaimed in a sale to a consumer.
No, because it came after the contract was formed and Scooter never agreed to it.
Yes, because by keeping the mixer, Scooter assented to the terms on the card.
Yes, because the card mentions merchantability and is printed in capital letters.
Yes, because a modification of a sales contract needs no consideration under § 2-209.
oe: Article 2 allows consumer disclaimers that meet § 2-316. The problem here is timing.
Correct. A disclaimer is effective only if it's part of the contract. Terms delivered after formation are at most a proposal to modify, which needs the buyer's assent (§ 2-209). See Problem 5-4.
Keeping goods bought under an existing contract doesn't show assent to new terms.
It meets the form requirements of § 2-316(2), but it never became part of the deal.
A modification needs no consideration, but it does need agreement.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer delivered with the goods

q: When does a lessor's insurable interest end?
o: When the goods are delivered.
When the lease is signed.
When a purchase option is exercised and risk has passed.
It never ends while the goods exist.
When the lessee buys its own policy.
oe: It continues through the lease.
The lessor still has its residual.
Correct. Section 2A-218(3). The lessee gets one on identification (§§ 2A-217, 2A-218(1)-(2)), and the parties may agree who insures and who gets proceeds (5).
Section 2A-218(3) says when it ends.
Both may hold interests.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Insurable interest in leases

q: Prairie Dawn hires Speedy Print to print and bind 500 copies of her art book. Most of the price reflects Speedy Print's labor. When the books arrive with smeared pages, does Article 2 govern Prairie Dawn's claim?
o: No, because most of the price is for services.
Yes, because services that manufacture goods count on the goods side.
Yes, but that is because Speedy Print is a merchant printer.
No, because a book is intellectual property, not goods.
No, because hybrid transactions fall outside Article 2 altogether.
oe: Services that manufacture the goods count toward the goods side of the predominance test (§ 2-102(2) cmt. 3).
Correct. That is Problem 1-2. And because the claim concerns the conformity of the books, Article 2's warranty rules would apply even if services predominated.
Scope never depends on merchant status.
The buyer is purchasing printed books, which are movable things, not a license of the copyright.
Under the 2022 amendments, Article 2 applies fully to a hybrid transaction in which goods predominate, and in part even when they don't.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: manufacturing services

q: Big Bird's contract for wheat requires it to be GMO-free. Big Bird wants to hold the delivered wheat for a two-week lab test before deciding whether to accept. Is that allowed?
o: Yes, but Big Bird must pay for the wheat first.
Likely yes, if two weeks is a reasonable time and manner to inspect.
Likely not, because holding the wheat for two weeks is an acceptance.
Yes, and the seller must pay for the lab test whatever the result.
No, because a buyer must inspect immediately on delivery.
oe: Inspection comes before payment unless otherwise agreed.
Correct. Problem 4-5(b). Big Bird may hold the wheat without accepting it, and pays the test costs unless the wheat fails and is rejected. The parties would do well to agree on a testing protocol.
Possession during a reasonable inspection is not acceptance.
The buyer bears inspection costs unless the goods are nonconforming and rejected (§ 2-513(2)).
Inspection must be at a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner, which may be longer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — GMO lab test

q: Barbara rejects a new car because a side mirror fell off during the test drive. The dealer offers to reattach it properly, at no charge, the same afternoon. Is that a cure?
o: No, because cure requires her written consent.
Yes, but only if the dealer also pays her a money allowance.
Yes, because the repair fully negates this trivial defect.
No, because any repair turns a new car into a used car.
No, because a new car must be replaced, never repaired.
oe: Cure is the seller's right, so her consent isn't needed.
A money allowance isn't required for cure.
Correct. Cure means negating the breach and putting the buyer where proper performance would have, whether by repair or replacement.
A trivial repair doesn't change the car's character.
Repair can be cure when it truly fixes the problem.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Mirror and starter

q: Under a two-year contract for monthly shipments of printer paper, payment is due on the 1st of each month. For the first eight months, the buyer pays on the 10th, and the seller cashes every check without objecting. What best describes the pattern of late payments?
o: An express term of the contract.
A course of dealing.
A course of performance.
A modification that requires a signed writing.
A usage of trade.
oe: Express terms are what the parties stated, not their later conduct.
A course of dealing concerns conduct in previous transactions between the parties (§ 1-303(b)), not repeated performance under this contract.

Correct. A course of performance is a sequence of conduct between the parties to a particular transaction that involves repeated occasions for performance, which the other party accepted or acquiesced in without objection (§ 1-303(a)).
Conduct can show waiver or modification, and § 2-209 needs no writing unless a clause or the statute of frauds requires one. In any event the pattern itself is a course of performance.
A usage of trade is a practice regularly observed in a trade or place (§ 1-303(c)), not the parties' own conduct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Identifying a course of performance

q: A buyer accepted goods and won't pay. The seller has no security interest. What is the seller's main remedy?
o: The price plus incidental damages, subject to offsets.
Consequential damages for lost use of the money.
Resale damages under § 2-706.
Repossession of the goods by self-help.
Market damages under § 2-708(1).
oe: Correct. Sections 2-709, 2-607(1), with offsets under §§ 2-714, 2-717. Withholding, stopping, and resale fit goods the seller or a carrier still holds.
Sellers get no consequential damages.
The buyer has the goods, so the seller can't resell them.
A seller with no security interest can't repossess.
The price is the proper remedy for accepted goods.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Which remedy fits

q: What may the parties do to the § 2-725 period by agreement?
o: Waive it entirely.
Extend it up to six years.
Extend it, but only for consumers.
Shorten it to 30 days.
Shorten it to as little as one year, but not extend it.
oe: A waiver would be an extension.
They can't extend it.
There's no consumer exception.
The floor is one year.
Correct. Section 2-725(1).
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Changing limitations

q: Which of the following best illustrates a "particular purpose" under § 2-315?
o: Buying a toaster to make toast for a large family each morning.
Buying a pencil to write with at work.
Buying shoes for ordinary walking around town.
Buying shoes for mountain climbing on the store's advice.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary purpose.
Ordinary purpose.
That is an ordinary purpose (cmt. 2).
Correct. This is Comment 2's example.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Ordinary vs. particular

q: Fozzie Fabrication sends Gonzo Greenhouses a written proposal to sell two irrigation pumps; its attached terms require any warranty suit within 9 months of delivery. Gonzo accepts with its own purchase order, whose back-page boilerplate "reserves all rights and remedies available at law" and says "acceptance is expressly limited to the terms of this order." The pumps sit in storage for a year and prove defective. Gonzo sues 14 months after delivery. What is the most likely result?
o: The suit is timely, because the conflicting terms knock out and the Code's four-year period applies.
The suit is barred, because Gonzo's purchase order was a counteroffer that Fozzie accepted by shipping.
The suit is timely, because the last form sent always controls.
The suit is barred, because Fozzie's offer controls and its 9-month limit governs.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Daitom, the PO was an acceptance, the shortened period and the reservation of remedies are different terms that drop out (cmt. 6), and § 2-725's four years applies.

"Expressly limited to the terms of this order" is not "expressly conditional" on assent (Daitom), so the PO was an acceptance. And even as a counteroffer, Gonzo's terms would not include the 9-month limit.
§ 2-207 abolished the "last shot" rule.
The offeror's terms don't automatically win. Gonzo's reservation of its legal remedies conflicts with the 9-month limit.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Knockout: limitations period

q: A buyer prepaid $1,000 on a $10,000 contract. The seller never delivers. The market has fallen to $8,000, and the buyer has no other loss. What can the buyer recover?
o: Nothing, because the falling market left it better off.
$2,000, the difference between contract and market.
$3,000, the $1,000 plus the $2,000 market drop.
$1,000 less the $2,000 savings, so nothing at all.
The $1,000 it paid, and no market damages.
oe: The refund under § 2-711(1) is available regardless of the market.
That also reverses the formula.
The formula is market minus contract, never the reverse.
The Code doesn't offset a price drop against the refund.
Correct. Section 2-711(1) gives back any price paid even with no other damages. Market minus contract is negative, so no direct-damage award follows.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Refund without damages

q: A student groups mistake, fraud and impracticability together as "excuses." How does the text sort them?
o: All three arise only at formation.
Article 2 fully codifies fraud and mistake.
All three arise only after a contract is formed.
Mistake and fraud arise at formation; impracticability arises later.
Impracticability arises at formation; mistake arises later.
oe: Impracticability arises later.
Those come in through § 1-103(b).
Fraud and mistake go to formation.

Correct. Formation-time doctrines include incapacity, fraud, mistake, duress, illegality, unconscionability and the statute of frauds. Later events include death of a promisor of personal performance, destruction of the subject matter, impracticability and frustration. Article 2 addresses only unconscionability at formation, leaving the rest to § 1-103(b).
That's reversed.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Formation vs. later events

q: Kermit, a seller, "assigns all my rights under this contract" to Fozzie, who accepts the assignment. Nothing indicates the parties meant to transfer only rights. Fozzie never delivers the goods. Whom may the buyer sue for nondelivery?
o: Neither, because the buyer didn't consent to the assignment.
Only Kermit, because the buyer never contracted with Fozzie.
Only Fozzie, because Kermit transferred the contract to him.
Either Kermit or Fozzie, because both are now bound to deliver the goods.
Only Kermit, because an assignment of "rights" never transfers duties.
oe: Consent isn't required for an assignment and delegation that is otherwise permitted.
The assignee's acceptance creates a promise the other party may enforce (§ 2-210(5)).
Delegation never relieves the delegating party (§ 2-210(1)).

Correct. A general assignment of "all my rights under the contract" is also a delegation of performance unless the language or circumstances indicate otherwise, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform that the other party can enforce (§ 2-210(5)). Kermit stays liable (§ 2-210(1)).
Section 2-210(5) treats a general assignment as a delegation too.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform

q: A seller fails to deliver 1,000 widgets priced at $10 each. The buyer promptly and reasonably buys substitutes for $13 each, spending $200 to arrange the purchase, and saves $100 in freight it would have paid under the original contract. Ignoring consequential damages, what can the buyer recover under § 2-712?
oe: That's the cost of cover, not damages.
That leaves out the incidental expenses and the savings.
That subtracts the $200 instead of adding it.
That forgets to subtract the $100 saved.
Correct. Cover minus contract price ($3,000) plus incidental damages ($200) minus expenses saved ($100).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Cover damages

q: To secure a business loan, Rosita's Rugs assigns to Sesame Bank "all of Rosita's rights under" her contract to sell 300 rugs to a hotel. Rosita then fails to deliver the rugs. The hotel sues Sesame Bank for breach. What is the most likely result?
o: The hotel wins, but only if the bank received notice of the hotel's claim before the loan.
The hotel wins, because an assignment of "all rights" always includes a delegation of duties.
The hotel wins, because the bank holds the right to the price and must therefore deliver the goods.
The bank wins, because a hotel cannot sue anyone except the original seller in any case.
The bank wins, because an assignment for security doesn't delegate the assignor's duties.
oe: Notice doesn't turn a security assignment into a promise to perform.
Not always. § 2-210(5) names an assignment for security as the standard example of circumstances showing no delegation.
Holding the right to payment as collateral doesn't make the bank a delegate. Rosita alone owes the rugs.
An assignee who accepts a delegation can be sued by the other party (§ 2-210(5)). The bank wins only because there was no delegation.

Correct. § 2-210(5) treats a general assignment of rights as a delegation of duties unless the language or the circumstances, as in an assignment for security, indicate otherwise. The bank never promised to deliver rugs.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Assignment for security

q: A supplier allocates a shortage and gives a non-consumer finance lessee half its order. The lessee wants half the goods at half the rent. Under § 2A-406, what can it do?
o: It may sue the lessor for breach.
It must take all goods at full rent.
It has 60 days to decide.
It can terminate, but can't take the quota at reduced rent.
It can take the quota at half rent.
oe: Excuse covers the delay.
It may terminate.
The period is a reasonable time, up to 30 days.
Correct. The rent allowance is excluded in a non-consumer finance lease, to stay in line with § 2A-407.
That's the rule outside non-consumer finance leases.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Quota in a finance lease

q: A laundry detergent cleans clothes but damages washing machines in ordinary use. A pencil writes, but its eraser tears paper with ordinary effort. Are the goods merchantable?
o: Only the pencil fails, because it's a simple good.
No, because neither is fit for its ordinary purposes.
Yes, unless a particular purpose was stated.
No, because goods must be the best available.
Yes, because each does its main job.
oe: Both fail.

Correct. Slide examples: detergent must clean without damaging fabric or the washer and match its label; a pencil must write and erase with ordinary effort. The standard is fitness for ordinary use, not perfection.
Merchantability doesn't need a stated purpose.
The standard is ordinary, not the best.
Ordinary purposes include use without damage.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Slide examples of merchantability

q: A seller repudiates in July. Fuel will be needed on October 1. The buyer calmly watches prices for six weeks, as a prudent buyer in this market would do, then covers on Sept. 1 at $4.20, while the market on the repudiation date was $3.90 and the contract price is $3.50. The seller argues damages are capped at 40 cents. Which is the best response?
o: The seller's argument wins because the price rose after repudiation.
Cover must occur on the repudiation date itself.
Cover needs only no unreasonable delay; a prudent six weeks is allowed.
The buyer may wait until any time before Oct. 1 without limit.
The market date always caps cover damages.
oe: A rise doesn't automatically fall on the buyer.
The statute doesn't say that.
Correct. Section 2-712 gives a reasonable time, and § 2-610 lets a buyer await performance for a commercially reasonable time. The test is reasonableness, so 70 cents may stand.
The delay must still be reasonable.
Cover has its own measure.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Repudiation, then wait and cover

q: Gobo receives a delivery of 50 cans of paint and promptly uses 10 cans to paint his barn before discovering that the paint is the wrong color. Has Gobo accepted the paint?
o: No, because the paint did not conform to the contract.
Yes, as to the 10 cans he used, but not the other 40.
Yes, because using it is inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
No, because he hadn't finished inspecting the paint when he used it.
None of the above.
oe: A buyer can accept nonconforming goods.
If the cans are a commercial unit, acceptance of part is acceptance of the whole unit.
Use, not inspection, is the problem.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Acts inconsistent with ownership

q: After rightfully rejecting a machine, a buyer that paid $30,000 down refuses to let the seller collect it until the $30,000 is refunded. The seller says the buyer must hold the goods at its disposition. Who is right?
o: The buyer, which has a lien for the money paid.
The seller, because rejection ends all buyer's rights.
The buyer, but only for damages, not the price.
The seller, because the buyer is only a bailee.
Neither; a court must take custody.
oe: Correct. Section 2-711(3) gives a security interest in rejected goods in its possession for payments made, and it may hold and resell. Its bailee duty is subject to that interest.
Rejection preserves them.
The lien covers the price paid and expenses, not other damages.
Its duties are subject to the security interest.
The Code gives the buyer the lien directly.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Buyer's lien vs. seller's demand

q: Abby contracts to buy a custom storefront sign for $12,000 and prepays $4,000. The contract validly liquidates the seller's damages for Abby's breach at $1,000. Abby repudiates, and the sign maker justifiably stops work and withholds delivery. Abby has received no benefit from the contract. How much is Abby entitled to get back?
oe: That keeps 20% of the price ($2,400). The 20% figure belongs to the default rule, which a valid liquidated damages term displaces.
A valid liquidated damages term lets the seller keep the liquidated amount out of the prepayment.
Keeping the whole $4,000 would exceed the agreed liquidated amount, a forfeiture § 2-718(2) forbids.

Correct. When the seller justifiably withholds delivery because of the buyer's breach, the buyer gets restitution of the amount by which its payments exceed the valid liquidated amount (§ 2-718(2)(a)): $4,000 - $1,000 = $3,000.
The smaller-of-20%-or-$500 rule applies only when there is no liquidated damages term (§ 2-718(2)(b)).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Prepayment over the LD amount

q: Statler's purchase order (the offer) says: "Seller's acceptance is limited to the terms of this order." Waldorf's acknowledgment accepts but adds a modest, customary force-majeure clause. Both are merchants, and Statler never objects. Is the force-majeure clause part of the contract?
o: No, because force-majeure clauses are not allowed in sales contracts.
No, because the offer expressly limited acceptance to its own terms.
Yes, because a reasonable force-majeure clause is not a material alteration.
Yes, because Statler never objected to it.
None of the above.
oe: They are allowed, and § 2-615 even assumes such allocations.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(a). An offer that expressly limits acceptance to its terms keeps added terms out, however reasonable.
True of the clause (cmt. 5), but the offer itself shut out added terms.
An objection isn't needed when the offer already limits acceptance to its terms.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Offer limits acceptance

q: A seller accepts a check post-dated 30 days at delivery, and it bounces. Why does § 2-507 reclamation likely fail?
o: Checks can't ever support reclamation.
The seller had to give 10 days' notice first.
The goods had already been identified to the contract.
Section 2-507 applies only between merchants.
A post-dated check is a credit term, so it isn't a cash sale.
oe: A check given at delivery can (§ 2-511 cmts. 4-6).
The problem is the credit term, not a notice requirement.
Identification isn't relevant.
Section 2-507 applies to any seller, merchant or not.
Correct. A credit sale or post-dated check doesn't count. Look to § 2-702 if the buyer is insolvent.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Post-dated check

q: A sale contract signed in 2020 says suits must be filed "within eight months." Goods were tendered June 2021. A plain defect is found in June 2023. Suit is filed in July 2023. Which is correct?
o: The suit is untimely, as a period can't exceed one year.
The suit is untimely under the eight-month clause.
The suit is timely, because discovery starts the clock.
The clause fails, as the period can't be under one year.
The suit is timely, because the contract was signed in 2020.
oe: The cap is four years.
A period that short is ineffective.
Article 2 runs from tender, not discovery.
Correct. Section 2-725(1). With the clause gone, four years from tender applies, and the suit is timely.
Tender, not signing, triggers accrual for warranties.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Limitation clause and warranty

q: Under § 2-616, after receiving a seller's notice of allocation, a buyer says nothing for 30 days. What happens?
o: The seller must deliver the full contract quantity.
The contract is reinstated in full as originally written.
The buyer is deemed to accept the allocation.
The buyer is in breach for failing to respond in time.
The contract lapses with respect to the affected deliveries.
oe: The contract lapses as to the affected deliveries.
No.
Silence for 30 days leads to lapse.
Silence isn't a breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Buyer silence

q: Which statement about whether a disclaimer is "conspicuous" is correct?
o: Fine print is conspicuous if the buyer signs directly below it.
The jury decides, based on how a reasonable buyer would read it.
It is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to have noticed it.
It is conspicuous whenever it appears in the signed contract.
None of the above.
oe: Not by itself.
It is a question for the court.
Correct. § 1-201(b)(10): for example, capitals, larger type, or contrasting type. Conspicuousness is a question for the court.
It must stand out.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Conspicuous

q: Ernie's restaurant-supply company in Delaware contracts to buy espresso machines from a manufacturer in Italy. The contract says nothing about governing law. Which body of law most likely governs the sale?
o: The CISG, because the parties are in different countries, unless they agree otherwise.
UCC Article 2, because the buyer is located in Delaware.
Italian law, because the seller makes the goods.
Article 2A, because the machines are commercial equipment.
The common law of contracts, because Article 2 cannot reach a seller located outside the United States.
oe: Correct. The third factor is the parties' location; an international sale of goods falls under the CISG unless the parties' agreement (the fourth factor) displaces it.
The location factor points the other way: the parties are in different countries.
Where the goods are made doesn't decide it.
Article 2A governs leases. This is a sale.
The CISG, not the common law, fills that role for international sales.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — International sale

q: A hardware store sells a ladder that has a hidden manufacturing defect. The store had no way to discover the defect. The ladder collapses on ordinary use. Is the store liable for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because the store was not negligent in selling it.
Yes, because the seller's lack of knowledge is no defense.
Yes, provided the store knew or should have known of it.
No, because the store didn't manufacture the ladder.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability is strict liability, not negligence-based.
Correct. Merchantability is a form of strict liability: the warranty is breached if the goods were defective at the time of sale.
Knowledge is not required.
A retailer that deals in ladders makes the warranty even if it didn't make the goods.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Strict liability

q: A restaurant-supply company's preprinted sales form says: "This agreement may be modified only by a writing signed by both parties." A restaurant, also a merchant, signs the form only at the bottom. Later, the supplier's sales manager orally agrees to cut the price by 10%. When the supplier bills the full price, the restaurant argues that the oral price cut is binding because it never separately signed the clause. What is the most likely result?
o: The clause binds the restaurant, so the oral cut fails as a modification but may operate as a waiver.
The oral price cut is binding, because the sales manager had actual authority to set the prices.
The oral price cut is binding, because a modification under Article 2 needs no new consideration.
The oral price cut is binding, because the restaurant never separately signed the no-oral-modification clause.
The clause is unenforceable, because a merchant can't bind another party with terms on its own form.
oe: Correct. A signed agreement excluding modification except by a signed writing can't be otherwise modified, and the requirement that the other party separately sign it applies only "except as between merchants" (§ 2-209(2)). The failed modification can still work as a waiver (§ 2-209(4)).
Authority doesn't overcome a valid no-oral-modification clause.
Consideration isn't the problem. The no-oral-modification clause is.
Separate signature is required only when the other party is a non-merchant.
Between merchants, the clause on one party's form binds a party that signed the form.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — No-oral-modification clause between merchants

q: After repeated electrical failures, a dealer offers yet another repair. The buyer demands a brand-new car. Which is the best statement?
o: She must accept every repair the dealer offers.
She lost her rights by allowing the earlier repairs.
The offer likely isn't cure, but she can't force a new car.
She is limited to a value claim under § 2-714.
She may compel a replacement car under § 2-508.
oe: Repeated failure ends the seller's right to keep trying.
Allowing repairs doesn't forfeit them; see § 2-608(1)(a).
Correct. She gets her money back with damages. Section 2-508 gives her no right to compel replacement.
Rejection or revocation may still be available.
Cure is the seller's right; she can't compel it.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Repeated failed repairs

q: A dealer's Picasso, identified at contracting, is destroyed by a fire with no one at fault before pickup. In a second sale a town cancels the sewer project for which a plumber bought special fittings, and his bank freezes his account. Which is correct?
o: The dealer owes damages for the Picasso.
The first is avoided; the plumber may be excused, but must find equivalent payment.
Both contracts stay fully in force.
The plumber is excused by the frozen account alone.
Frustration never applies under Article 2.
oe: A no-fault casualty avoids the contract.
Correct. Section 2-613 avoids the first. Frustration may excuse the plumber on the special fittings; a frozen account means he must offer an equivalent (§ 2-614(2)).
The first is avoided.
An equivalent means of payment is required.
It comes in through § 1-103(b).
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Problem 6-6 mix

q: A seller asks whether it may use every remedy listed in § 2-703 at once. Which is the best answer?
o: It may combine them, but § 1-305 bars overcompensation.
The list is complete, and the common law adds nothing.
It must elect a single remedy immediately.
It may use only those the buyer agreed to in the contract.
It may combine them even if that gives double recovery.
oe: Correct. Comment 1 says the remedies are cumulative in the sense of not electing, but § 1-305 forbids overcompensation. Like the buyer's list, it is an incomplete catalog.
Section 2-703 is an incomplete catalog.
The Code rejects election of remedies (§ 2-703 cmt. 1).
The remedies are statutory.
Section 1-305 forbids that.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — § 2-703 is incomplete

q: A buyer's purchase order for 1,000 valves says nothing about warranties. The seller's acknowledgment form, which doesn't make its acceptance conditional on anything, adds a conspicuous clause: "SELLER DISCLAIMS THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY." Both parties are merchants, and neither objects. The valves leak. Is merchantability disclaimed?
o: No, because a form that adds new terms can't be an acceptance of the purchase order.
Yes, because between merchants an additional term is part of the contract unless the buyer objects.
Yes, because the clause mentions merchantability and is conspicuous, as § 2-316 requires.
No, because a warranty disclaimer materially alters the deal, so it isn't part of it.
Yes, because the seller's acknowledgment was the last form sent before performance.
oe: A definite acceptance with additional terms is still an acceptance under § 2-207(1).
That's true only for terms that don't materially alter the contract.
Meeting § 2-316's form rules doesn't help if § 2-207 keeps the term out of the contract.

Correct. Before applying § 2-316, ask whether the disclaimer is part of the contract. Between merchants, additional terms become part of the contract unless they materially alter it, and a clause negating standard warranties is the classic example of a material alteration (§ 2-207 cmt. 4).
Article 2 rejects the common-law "last shot" rule.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer added in an acceptance form

q: Which of the following statements about unconscionability under § 2-302 is NOT accurate?
o: A court may refuse to enforce the entire contract.
The jury decides whether a clause is unconscionable, judged as of the time of the breach.
The parties must be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence of the clause's commercial setting, purpose, and effect.
A court may limit the application of an unconscionable clause to avoid an unconscionable result.
A court may enforce the rest of the contract without the unconscionable clause.
oe: This is one option under § 2-302(1).
Correct. Unconscionability is decided by the court "as a matter of law" and is judged "at the time it was made," not at the time of breach (§ 2-302(1)).
This is required by § 2-302(2).
This is one option under § 2-302(1).
This is one option under § 2-302(1).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Unconscionability: which is NOT accurate

q: A brewery orders custom fermentation tanks for a new taproom it plans to open on May 1, and tells the seller that time is of the essence. After negotiating, they agree on liquidated damages of $1,500 for each day of inexcusable delay, a figure that fairly estimated the brewery's expected lost profits. The tanks arrive 20 days late. As it turns out, May was unusually slow, and the brewery's actual lost profits were about $5,000. What can the brewery most likely recover?
o: $30,000, because the clause was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
Nothing, because Article 2 treats liquidated damages clauses as void penalties.
$5,000, because the liquidated damages clause wasn't printed conspicuously.
$5,000, because liquidated damages can never exceed the buyer's actual damages.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Section 2-718(1) allows liquidated damages "at an amount which is reasonable in the light of the anticipated or actual harm caused by the breach." A clause that was reasonable when made doesn't fail because actual harm turned out lower. See Problem 5-6.
Article 2 enforces reasonable liquidated damages clauses.
Nothing requires a liquidated damages clause to be conspicuous.
The test is reasonableness in light of anticipated or actual harm, not a cap at actual harm.
One of the other choices is correct: $30,000, because the clause was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Liquidated damages: reasonable in light of anticipated harm

q: A contract says "Buyer shall inspect at Seller's plant in Akron," but delivery is at Buyer's plant in Tulsa. Which statement is correct under § 2-513(4)?
o: It's presumed exclusive, but it doesn't move delivery or risk.
It bars any later claim for breach of warranty.
It shifts risk of loss to the buyer in Akron.
It moves the place of delivery to Akron.
It's void, because inspection is mandatory at delivery.
oe: Correct. An agreed place or method of inspection is presumed exclusive. It doesn't shift the place for delivery or the passing of risk of loss, and if compliance becomes impossible, inspection follows the statute.
Inspection doesn't waive hidden defects.
The statute says it doesn't.
The statute says it doesn't.
The parties may fix the place and method.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection place clause

q: In each of eight earlier sales of pressure gauges to a refinery, a supplier included a certificate showing that each gauge had been calibrated before shipment. The ninth order says nothing about certificates, and the supplier ships uncalibrated gauges without them. The refinery's strongest argument is that the supplier breached:
o: The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
No warranty, because the ninth order was silent about calibration.
An express warranty by sample, because earlier gauges were calibrated.
An implied warranty arising from course of dealing under § 2-314(3).
An implied warranty arising from course of performance under this contract.
oe: Nothing shows a particular purpose or the refinery's reliance on the supplier's selection.
Course of dealing supplements an agreement that is silent on a point (§ 1-303(d)).
Earlier deliveries under other contracts weren't samples for this one.

Correct. Section 2-314(3) recognizes "other implied warranties" that "arise from course of dealing or usage of trade." Eight earlier sales with calibration certificates are a course of dealing (§ 1-303(b)) that gives meaning to and supplements the ninth contract.
Course of performance is repeated performance under one contract. The earlier sales were separate transactions, which makes them a course of dealing.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Implied warranty from course of dealing

q: Elmo orally agrees to buy a used guitar from Grover for $450. Grover later refuses to deliver, claiming the contract is unenforceable because it is not in writing. Is Grover right?
o: No, because Elmo can prove the contract by his own testimony.
Yes, because Grover is not a merchant who deals in guitars.
No, because the statute applies only at $500 or more.
Yes, because the guitar is used goods sold privately.
Yes, because contracts for the sale of goods must be in writing.
oe: Testimony would not get around § 2-201 if it applied. The point is that it doesn't apply.
Merchant status does not affect the $500 threshold.
Correct. § 2-201(1) applies only to sales for $500 or more, so at $450 the oral contract is enforceable without a record.
Used goods are covered by the same rule.
Only contracts for $500 or more fall within § 2-201(1).
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — $500 threshold

q: Bunsen signs a contract to buy a used forklift from a dealer. The contract says nothing about delivery, the parties have never dealt before, and no trade usage applies. The dealer tells Bunsen to come get it; Bunsen insists the dealer deliver it. If neither budges, who is in breach?
o: The dealer, because sellers must bring the goods to the buyer.
Bunsen, because unless otherwise agreed, the place for delivery is the seller's place of business.
The dealer, because unless the parties agree otherwise, the default place for delivery is the buyer's place of business.
Neither, because the contract fails without a delivery term.
Neither, because a court will split the cost of delivery.
oe: Not by default.
Correct. § 2-308(a). Problem 3-8(A): with no course of dealing or usage to fill the gap, the buyer who refuses to pick up is in breach.
It's the seller's place.
Open terms don't defeat a contract; gap fillers apply.
No such rule.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Place of delivery gap filler

q: In a finance lease with no agreed time, and a merchant supplier delivering at the lessee's plant by its own truck, when does risk pass?
o: When the lessor pays the supplier.
Never, because the lessor always keeps the risk.
On tender, because the supplier is a merchant.
On the lessee's receipt of the goods.
When the lease is signed.
oe: Payment isn't a trigger.
Risk passes in a finance lease.
A merchant's goods need receipt.
Correct. Section 2A-219(2)(c): otherwise on receipt if the lessor or, in a finance lease, the supplier is a merchant; if not, on tender.
Signing isn't a statutory trigger.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — When risk passes in a finance lease

q: A hotel contracts with a celebrated glass artist, Camilla, to create and sell it a one-of-a-kind chandelier designed and made by Camilla herself. Short on time, Camilla delegates the job to a skilled apprentice. The hotel objects. May Camilla delegate?
o: Yes, because both buyers and sellers are generally free to delegate their duties.
Yes, because the contract between Camilla and the hotel doesn't prohibit delegation.
Yes, as long as Camilla remains liable to the hotel if the apprentice's work is defective.
No, because any delegation of a duty requires the other party's consent.
No, because the hotel has a substantial interest in Camilla's own performance.
oe: That's the general rule, but it gives way when the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
Even without a prohibition, delegation is barred when the other party has a substantial interest in the original performance.
Continued liability is the consequence of a permitted delegation. It doesn't make this delegation permissible.
Delegation generally needs no consent. The bar here comes from the hotel's substantial interest.

Correct. A party may perform through a delegate "unless otherwise agreed or unless the other party has a substantial interest in having his original promisor perform or control the acts required by the contract" (§ 2-210(1)). A commission for an artist's own work is the classic example.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Substantial interest in personal performance

q: Which group states the risk-of-loss principles the text recalls?
o: The party holding title always bears it.
The party who suffered the loss bears it.
Wealth, merchant status, and ownership decide.
The party who paid first bears it.
Control, likely insurance, and breach decide who should bear it.
oe: Title doesn't control.
That restates the question.
Those aren't the principles.
Payment order isn't relevant.
Correct. See Section IX.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Risk principles

q: A seller supplies a boiler and installs it. The buyer's lawyer wants Article 2 applied to the boiler and the common law to the installation. Which is the best statement?
o: A buyer's promise of services makes the deal a hybrid.
A hybrid is defined as any sale made on credit.
Article 2 can never reach any transaction involving services.
Bifurcation is the required approach under § 2-102(2).
A few courts bifurcate like that, but courts generally pick one law for the deal.
oe: Services by the buyer are just the price.
Credit has nothing to do with a hybrid transaction.
Article 2 reaches hybrids where goods predominate.
The 2022 text doesn't require it; only a few courts did it.

Correct. Section 2-106(5) defines a hybrid transaction as goods plus services, a lease of other goods, or non-goods property from the seller. Most courts look to the predominant purpose, and only a few have split the deal. A buyer paying in services is just paying a price.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid defined; bifurcation

q: After a seller's breach, the buyer sends a one-line email: "We cancel." Which statement correctly describes the effect?
o: The cancellation is ineffective without 30 days' notice.
The cancellation is ineffective without a court order.
The buyer's duty ends, and it keeps its damages claim.
The buyer gives up damages unless it expressly reserves them.
The contract is treated as if it had never existed.
oe: Cancellation for breach has no notice period; the 30 days belongs to § 2-609.
Cancellation is self-help under § 2-711(1).
Correct. Section 2-106(3)-(4). No procedure or notice is prescribed, but word it carefully so it doesn't look like a discharge or waiver (§ 1-306; § 2-720).
Under § 2-720, cancellation language doesn't renounce a claim unless a contrary intention clearly appears.
Cancellation ends future duties; it doesn't erase rights arising from the breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Effect of cancelling

q: A coin collector agrees to buy a rare 1909-S VDB penny from a dealer for $2,000. Is the penny "goods" under Article 2?
o: No, because money is excluded from the definition of goods in every case.
No, because rare coins bought as collectibles are investment securities.
Yes, because money sold as a commodity, rather than used to pay, is goods.
No, because a coin is a thing in action, which § 2-105 excludes.
Yes, but only because the price exceeds the coin's face value by more than $500.
oe: Only money used to pay the price is excluded.
Investment securities are Article 8 interests such as stock, not physical collectibles.
Correct. Section 2-105(1) excludes only "the money in which the price is to be paid." Comment 1 explains that money treated as a commodity, such as a rare coin, is goods. See Problem 1-1(B).
A thing in action is a right to sue, such as a debt. A physical coin isn't one.
The amount of the markup doesn't determine whether it's goods.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Money as goods

q: Waldorf contracts to buy a used printing press from Statler's Supply for $30,000. Before delivery, Waldorf assigns "all my rights under the contract" to Pepe, who accepts. Statler delivers the press to Pepe, who never pays. From whom may Statler recover the price?
o: Only from Pepe, because Waldorf transferred his duty to pay along with his rights.
Only from Pepe, and only if Statler consented to the assignment in advance.
Only from Waldorf, because Statler never made a contract with Pepe.
From neither, because an assignment of rights transfers no duties to the assignee.
From either Pepe or Waldorf, though Statler may collect only once.
oe: Delegation never relieves the delegating party of liability (§ 2-210(1)). Waldorf is still on the hook.
Statler's consent isn't needed for the assignment, and Waldorf remains liable either way.
Statler doesn't need a contract with Pepe. § 2-210(5) makes Pepe's acceptance a promise to perform that Statler may enforce.
An assignment of "all my rights" is presumptively a delegation as well (§ 2-210(5)).

Correct. A general assignment of "all my rights" is also a delegation of the assignor's duties, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform that the other original party can enforce (§ 2-210(5)). Waldorf, the delegator, remains liable too (§ 2-210(1)).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — "All my rights" accepted

q: A hardware store sells Ernie a can of paint labeled "Eggshell White." The paint inside is bright yellow but otherwise high quality. Which merchantability requirement does the paint most clearly fail?
o: Fitness for Ernie's particular purpose.
Fair average quality for fungible goods.
Fitness for the ordinary purposes for which paint is used.
Conformity to the promises or affirmations of fact on the container or label.
None of the above.
oe: That's § 2-315, not merchantability, and no particular purpose appears.
The quality is high.
It paints well.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Merchantability: label

q: A buyer repudiates; goods identified and conforming are destroyed a commercially reasonable time later, before risk would otherwise pass. The seller's full insurance pays the loss. What may the seller claim from the buyer for the goods?
o: The insurer's premiums.
Nothing, as § 2-510(3) reaches only the insurance deficiency.
Consequential damages.
Half the loss.
The full price, as the buyer breached.
oe: That isn't a shifted loss.
Correct. The seller may still have other damages for the repudiation, but with full coverage nothing shifts for the goods' loss.
Sellers don't get them.
There's no split.
Risk shifts only for a deficiency.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Casualty after repudiation, seller's insurance

q: A lease says, "Any sublease is an event of default." The lessee subleases anyway. What may the lessor do?
o: Treat the sublease as void.
Use its default remedies, as the lease made it a default.
Nothing, as anti-assignment clauses are void.
Only sue for damages it couldn't prevent.
Recover double rent.
oe: It's otherwise effective.
Correct. Section 2A-303(4)(a). See also § 9-407(b), which allows a default clause for a lessee's transfer of possession or use.
That's for payment rights, not possession.
That's (4)(b), for a mere prohibition.
There's no such remedy.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Lease default clause on transfer

q: A law office receives a new copier that keeps jamming. The office promptly emails the seller that it rejects the copier and asks the seller to pick it up. While waiting, the office keeps using the copier for all its daily work for three weeks. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The seller may treat the office's continued use as an acceptance of the copier.
The rejection stands, because the office notified the seller promptly after delivery.
The office has revoked its rejection, so it must pay the full price and loses its damages claim.
The office has accepted only the copies it made, not the copier itself.
The rejection stands, because the copier was defective, so the office had a right to reject.
oe: Correct. After rejection, any exercise of ownership by the buyer is wrongful (§ 2-602(2)(a)), and doing any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership is an acceptance, at the seller's option if it's wrongful against the seller (§ 2-606(1)(c)).
A timely notice doesn't protect a buyer who then treats the goods as its own.
If the use is treated as acceptance, the office must pay the price (§ 2-607(1)) but keeps its claim for damages for the defect if it gives notice (§§ 2-607(3), 2-714).
Acceptance under § 2-606 is of the goods, and part of a commercial unit can't be accepted alone (§ 2-606(2)).
A rightful reason to reject doesn't permit the buyer to keep using the goods.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Use after rejection

q: Rowlf's signed letter to Scooter says: "Per the attached order sheet, I confirm our agreement." The attached, unsigned order sheet lists 400 microphone stands at $30 each. Scooter sues Rowlf to enforce the deal. Is there a sufficient record?
o: No, because the letter and the order sheet were never stapled together.
No, because the letter itself states no price.
No, because the quantity appears only on an unsigned page.
Yes, but only if Scooter also signed the order sheet.
None of the above.
oe: Physical attachment isn't the test. The signed letter expressly refers to the sheet.
Price isn't required, and the sheet states one anyway.
The signed letter incorporates the attached sheet, so the papers are read together.
Only the party to be charged (Rowlf) must sign.
Correct. Yes: several papers can be read together if they are connected, and Rowlf's signed letter refers to the order sheet, which supplies the quantity. No choice gives that answer.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Several writings read together

q: Which statement correctly separates §§ 2-605 and 2-607(3)(a)?
o: Both concern only goods that have been accepted.
Section 2-605 concerns accepted goods; § 2-607(3)(a) concerns rejected goods.
Section 2-605 concerns rejected goods; § 2-607(3)(a) concerns accepted goods.
Both concern only goods that have been rejected.
Section 2-605 bars all remedies; § 2-607(3)(a) bars one defect.
oe: Section 2-605 follows rejection.
That reverses them.
Correct. The first is about stating defects when rejecting. The second is about notifying of breach after accepting.
Section 2-607(3)(a) applies after acceptance.
That's the other way round.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — § 2-605 vs. § 2-607

q: A signed record calls for delivery of 100 units on June 1. The parties later orally agree to move delivery to July 1. There is no no-oral-modification clause. Does the statute of frauds bar the modification?
o: Yes, because any change to a written contract must be in writing.
Yes, because the contract as modified is for $500 or more.
No, because § 2-209 exempts modifications from the statute of frauds.
No, because the quantity term did not change.
None of the above.
oe: That would be true only with a NOM clause, and there isn't one.
The record already satisfies § 2-201. Only the quantity must appear in it.
§ 2-209(3) says they are when the modified contract is within § 2-201.
Correct. Problem 3-4(e). A NOM clause would be a separate barrier.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Delivery date: no SOF problem

q: Which fact pattern raises the conflict between § 2-712 or § 2-713 and § 1-305's expectation principle?
o: A buyer that passed the whole extra cost to its own customer.
A broker with a fixed-price resale far below the market.
A buyer that never wanted the goods anyway.
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: A pattern from Problem 7-9, but not the only one.
A pattern from Problem 7-10.
Seller's argument in Problem 7-6(C).
Correct. In each, the formula could give the buyer more than it truly lost, testing § 1-305(a).
All three raise the conflict.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Overcompensation pattern

q: Directed Decorating locates antique furniture for luxury hotels. It introduces the hotel to the antique's owner, the owner sells directly to the hotel, and the hotel pays Directed Decorating a finder's fee. A chair it located collapses because of rot that was present when it was sold. Is Directed Decorating liable for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because Directed Decorating only located the chair and never sold it to the hotel.
Yes, but only if the chair's owner who sold it was not a merchant.
Yes, because it holds itself out as having special knowledge and skill regarding antiques.
No, because antiques are used goods, and used goods carry no implied warranties.
Yes, because it received money in the transaction in the form of a finder's fee.
oe: Correct. Section 2-314(1) implies the warranty in a contract for sale by a seller who is a merchant. A finder or broker that never sells the goods doesn't make the warranty, though the actual seller might. See Problem 3-9(d).
Liability doesn't shift to the finder because the actual seller isn't a merchant.
Knowledge or skill can make someone a merchant, but merchantability still requires that person to be the seller.
Used goods can carry the warranty when sold by a merchant seller. The problem here is that Directed Decorating sold nothing.
A finder's fee from the buyer doesn't make the finder a seller.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Finder isn't a seller

q: A spice importer contracts to sell saffron from a single named region to three restaurants. A government embargo unexpectedly cuts off that region, leaving the importer only 40% of what it needs. Which statement best describes the importer's obligations?
o: It is not excused, because embargoes are always foreseeable.
It is excused only to the extent of the shortfall, must allocate fairly among customers, and must notify them seasonably.
It is fully excused and may deliver nothing to anyone.
It must fill one restaurant's order completely before the others.
None of the above.
oe: An unexpected embargo cutting off the agreed source can excuse.
Correct. § 2-615(b)-(c). Each buyer may then take its share or terminate (§ 2-616).
Only to the extent of the shortfall.
It must allocate fairly.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Embargo: allocation

q: A contract for a commercial ice-cream freezer limits the buyer's remedy to repair or replacement of defective parts, which the contract says is exclusive. The freezer fails repeatedly, and after six repair attempts over four months it still won't hold temperature. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The limitation was void from the start, because remedy limits aren't allowed in commercial sales.
The failure of the remedy automatically voids any separate exclusion of consequential damages.
The remedy has failed of its essential purpose, so other Article 2 remedies are available.
The buyer is limited to more repair attempts, because it agreed to an exclusive remedy.
The buyer may now recover only the price of the freezer, and no other damages.
oe: Section 2-719(1) expressly permits limited remedies.
Many courts, as in Razor v. Hyundai, treat the consequential-damages exclusion separately, judged by unconscionability.

Correct. "Where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in this Act" (§ 2-719(2)). A repair remedy that can't produce a working machine within a reasonable time fails of its essential purpose.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose no longer limits the buyer.
Once the remedy fails, the buyer may seek its full Article 2 remedies, subject to any separate valid exclusion.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Repair remedy fails of its essential purpose

q: A furniture dealer sells Abby a dining set. During the sale, the dealer says aloud, "I'm not giving you any warranty of merchantability on this set." Nothing is put in writing. Abby told the dealer she needed a table that could seat twelve and relied on his pick. Which implied warranties survive?
o: Only the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
Neither, because a consumer can never receive a fitness warranty.
Both merchantability and fitness, because disclaimers must always be written.
Neither, because the dealer clearly disclaimed implied warranties.
Only merchantability, because a merchantability disclaimer must be in writing.
oe: Correct. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability (§ 2-316(2)). Fitness can be excluded only by a writing, so the oral statement leaves it intact.
Consumers routinely receive fitness warranties when § 2-315's elements are met.
Only the fitness disclaimer must be written. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral.
The dealer mentioned only merchantability, and orally. That can't exclude fitness.
Backwards. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability; it's the fitness disclaimer that must be written.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Oral merchantability disclaimer

q: Two months before delivery, a buyer gave this seller a false written financial statement showing solvency. The seller first demands return 40 days after receipt. Is the demand too late?
o: Yes, unless the statement went to all of the buyer's creditors.
Yes, unless the misrepresentation was made orally.
No, because reclamation has no time limit.
Yes, because the 10-day limit is absolute.
No, because a written misrepresentation lifts the 10-day limit.
oe: It must be to the particular seller.
It must be in writing, and it was.
The limit is lifted only by the exception.
The exception applies on these facts.
Correct. Section 2-702(2).
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Written misrepresentation

q: In § 2-714(2), the value formula is measured:
o: At the time of trial, at the buyer's location.
At the time and place of acceptance, unless special circumstances exist.
At the time of tender, with no possible exceptions.
At the time of contracting, at the seller's location.
At the time the buyer discovered the defect.
oe: Neither the time nor the place fits § 2-714(2).
Correct. The measure is the value difference, and special circumstances can vary it.
Special circumstances are an express exception.
Neither fits the statute.
The statute says acceptance, not discovery.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Special circumstances

q: A seller delivered goods on 60-day credit with no security interest. The buyer doesn't pay and is solvent. Can the seller take the goods back?
o: No, because its right is to the price, not the goods.
Yes, if it acts without breach of the peace.
Yes, within ten days after the due date.
Yes, but only by court order under § 2-716.
Yes, since title stays with an unpaid seller.
oe: Correct. The general rule surprises people. A credit seller should take a security interest, since reclamation is too narrow to rely on.
That's a secured party's right; this seller isn't one.
The ten days run from receipt, and require insolvency.
Section 2-716 is a buyer's remedy.
Title passes on delivery, whatever the payment terms.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Unpaid seller and the goods

q: A lessee rightfully revokes acceptance of a press, then a fire destroys it at the lessee's plant before the lessor collects it. The lessee's insurance pays half. The lease is one where risk had passed to the lessee. Who bears the rest?
o: The lessor, for the entire loss.
The lessee, as it had possession.
The lessor, to the extent of the lessee's insurance shortfall.
The lessee, as revocation doesn't affect risk.
The two share it equally.
oe: Only for the shortfall.
The revocation lets it treat risk as the lessor's.
Correct. Section 2A-220(1)(b), the analog of § 2-510(2).
Section 2A-220 says it does.
There's no split.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Rightful revocation and risk

q: A contract calls for 500 folding tables and says nothing about delivery in lots. The seller arrives with 250 tables and promises the rest next week. The buyer refuses to take any. Is the buyer in breach?
o: No, because all must come in one delivery.
Yes, because the shortfall is minor and curable.
Yes, because a buyer must accept partial deliveries.
No, because the seller had to deliver to the buyer's place of business.
Yes, unless the buyer pays for the 250 tables.
oe: Correct. § 2-307.
The buyer may still insist on a single delivery.
Not unless the contract provides for them.
Place isn't the issue.
The buyer need not take or pay for a partial tender.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Single delivery

q: Bert, a guitar dealer, contracts to sell Ernie a specific 1959 guitar, to be picked up Saturday. On Friday night, Bert leaves a space heater running next to the guitar, and the guitar is destroyed in the resulting fire. Is Bert excused?
o: No, because Bert must deliver a substitute guitar.
Yes, because a fire is beyond the parties' control.
Yes, because the guitar was unique and identified.
No, because Bert's negligence is fault.
None of the above.
oe: Bert can't, and the remedy is damages.
Bert's negligence caused this fire.
The loss must also be without fault.
Correct. § 2-613 requires the loss to occur without fault; negligence is fault (Problem 6-6(a)'s coffee pot).
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Casualty caused by negligence

q: Which of the following circumstances is most likely to exclude the warranty of title without any express disclaimer?
o: A sheriff's sale of seized goods.
A sale between two consumers at a yard sale.
A sale by a used-car dealer.
A sale at a discount price.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Circumstances that give the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title, like sheriff's, executor's, or police auctions, exclude the warranty (§ 2-312(2)).
Every seller makes the title warranty.
An ordinary dealer makes the warranty.
A low price alone isn't enough.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer by circumstances

q: Best Car Rental rents cars by the day and week. Every four months, as a regular part of its business, it sells the oldest cars in its fleet to the public from a lot at its main office. Telly buys a two-year-old sedan from that lot. Nothing is said about warranties, and the transmission fails a week later in ordinary driving. Did Best Car Rental give an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because the merchantability warranty doesn't apply to used cars sold at a low price.
Most likely yes, because it regularly sells used cars, so it deals in goods of that kind.
No, because the company never said anything to Telly about the car's mechanical condition.
No, because the company is in the rental business, not the business of selling cars.
Yes, but only if the company knew about the transmission problem when it sold the car.
oe: Used goods sold by a merchant carry the warranty, adjusted for their age and condition.

Correct. The warranty arises when the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind (§ 2-314(1)), meaning one who deals in them (§ 2-104(1)). A company that sells off its fleet on a regular schedule from a sales lot deals in used cars, unlike someone making an isolated sale. The warranty applies to used goods, measured by what's ordinary for a car of that age. See Problem 3-9(b).
The merchantability warranty is implied. No statement is needed.
A business can deal in goods of a kind even if selling them isn't its main line. Regular, scheduled sales from a sales lot are dealing.
Implied warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fleet seller as merchant

q: Kermit and Fozzie, both merchants, orally agree that Fozzie will buy 600 rubber chickens from Kermit for $3,000. The next day Kermit sends Fozzie a signed letter: "This confirms our deal: 600 rubber chickens at $5 each." Fozzie reads the letter but never responds. Three weeks later, Fozzie refuses to perform. Can Kermit enforce the contract against Fozzie?
o: Yes, because Fozzie admitted the deal by staying silent.
No, because the confirmation was sent after the oral deal.
Yes, because Fozzie failed to object to the confirmation in time.
No, because Fozzie never signed anything himself.
No, because Fozzie had 30 days to object and only three weeks passed.
oe: The admission exception requires an admission in court (§ 2-201(3)(b)). Silence works only through § 2-201(2).
A confirmation is supposed to follow the oral deal.

Correct. § 2-201(2): between merchants, a confirmation sent within a reasonable time, sufficient against the sender, received by a recipient with reason to know its contents, binds the recipient unless written objection is given within 10 days.
The merchant's confirmation exception lets the sender's signed confirmation bind the recipient.
The objection period is 10 days.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Merchant's confirmation

q: A buyer repudiates in 2022 a contract for delivery in 2023. The seller waits until 2026, past a commercially reasonable time, and sues. Which is the safest advice the text gives?
o: Sue any time before the buyer's next breach.
Wait for the buyer to retract.
Sue within four years after the delivery date.
Sue within one year.
Sue within four years of the repudiation.
oe: A later breach doesn't extend the period for this one.
Waiting risks the claim.
That risks being late.
The period is four years.
Correct. The text notes that the commercially reasonable wait is uncertain.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Repudiation and limitations

q: Broker buys 100,000 gallons at $2.50 F.O.B. New Orleans, with a fixed resale at $2.70 to Customer in St. Louis. Seller repudiates when the market is $4.50 in New Orleans and $4.70 in St. Louis, and Customer holds Broker liable. Broker's lost profit on the resale is about $14,500. Which is the best statement?
o: Only the $14,500 lost profit.
Nothing, as Customer's claim wasn't foreseeable.
Exactly $200,000, the market formula.
$414,500, adding market damages to the liability.
About $214,500, its liability plus lost profit, if foreseeable.
oe: That would leave Broker bearing Customer's claim.
A broker's resale is plainly foreseeable.
Consequential loss may replace the formula if provable.
That stacks the same loss.
Correct. A broker's resale is plainly foreseeable. Don't stack market damages on top of the same liability.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Broker liable to customer

q: A seed company's contract limits the farmer's remedy to "replacement of seed reported defective within 10 days of delivery." The seed's defect, low germination, can't be discovered until weeks after planting. What is the most likely result when the farmer's crop fails?
o: The farmer gets replacement seed, which the contract promised.
The farmer gets nothing, because he didn't report the defect within 10 days.
The farmer gets nothing, because seed is sold "as is" by usage of trade.
The limited remedy fails of its essential purpose.
The farmer may recover, but only if the seller acted in bad faith.
oe: Replacement seed weeks into the season is worthless; that's why the remedy fails.
Enforcing an impossible deadline would leave the farmer with no remedy at all.
Nothing in the facts shows such a usage of trade.
Correct. A remedy limited to a period that expires before a latent defect can be discovered deprives the buyer of a fair quantum of remedy and fails of its essential purpose (§ 2-719(2), cmt. 1).
Failure of essential purpose doesn't require bad faith.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Latent defect, short window

q: Elmo buys a pressure cooker from a kitchen store. He lends it to his neighbor, Telly, who uses it in Telly's own kitchen. The lid explodes off and burns Telly. The state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. Can Telly sue the store for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because anyone who may reasonably be expected to use the goods may sue under Alternative A.
No, because Alternative A reaches only the buyer's family, household, and guests.
Yes, but only if the store knew that Elmo planned to lend the cooker to Telly.
Yes, because privity is never required for a personal-injury claim under Article 2.
No, because only the person who bought the goods can ever sue for breach of warranty.
oe: That broader reach is Alternative B. Alternative A is limited to family, household, and guests.

Correct. Alternative A covers "any natural person who is in the family or household of his buyer or who is a guest in his home" who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and is injured in person. A neighbor using the cooker in his own home doesn't fit.
Alternative A doesn't turn on the seller's knowledge of a loan.
Section 2-318 defines how far privity is relaxed. Under Alternative A, Telly is outside it.
Section 2-318 extends warranties to certain non-buyers. Telly just isn't in the protected group under Alternative A.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Privity: § 2-318 Alternative A

q: A law student describes what a "sales system" does and what shapes its design. Which statement fits the course materials?
o: It requires every sale to pass through a broker.
It replaces the common law of contracts in every sale.
It applies only to continuing relationships between merchants.
It exists mainly to protect consumers from merchants.
It brings parties together and supplies terms and ways to perform and resolve disputes.
oe: Brokered sales are just one component.
The Code is supplemented by the common law (§ 1-103(b)).
It also covers isolated and consumer sales.
Consumer protection is left mostly to other statutes (§ 2-102(3)(b)).

Correct. Those are the system's four roles. Recurring themes are certainty, responsiveness, laissez-faire, simplicity, efficiency and internationalism. Systems vary by merchant status, goods (special, unique, fungible), future goods, and continuing deals.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Role of sales systems

q: Fozzie sells 500 rubber chickens to Gonzo for $8,000, payment due in 30 days. The signed contract says: "Seller may not assign its right to payment, and any attempted assignment is void." Fozzie assigns the right to payment to Muppet Bank, which sends Gonzo a signed notice telling him to pay the bank. Gonzo pays Fozzie anyway, and the bank sues Gonzo. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because the contract expressly made any attempted assignment void.
The bank wins, but Fozzie is liable to Gonzo for breaching the anti-assignment clause.
The bank wins, because a term restricting assignment of a right to payment for goods is ineffective, and after notice Gonzo could discharge his debt only by paying the bank.
The bank wins, but only if Gonzo consented to the assignment in a signed record.
Gonzo wins, because he paid the full price to the party he actually contracted with.
oe: The "void" language would matter for most rights, but § 9-406(d) makes it ineffective as to a right to payment for goods.
§ 9-406(d) provides that such an assignment is not a breach or default, so Gonzo has no claim against Fozzie for making it.
Correct. § 9-406(d) overrides the anti-assignment term for an account (a right to payment for goods sold), and under § 9-406(a) payment to the assignor after notice does not discharge the buyer.
The account debtor's consent is not required for an assignment of a right to payment.
After notification, paying the assignor does not discharge the obligor (§ 9-406(a)). Gonzo may have to pay twice and seek repayment from Fozzie.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Void clause vs. right to payment

q: Which of the following statements about the § 1-304 duty of good faith is NOT correct?
o: It cannot be disclaimed by agreement.
It applies to the performance and enforcement of every contract under the UCC.
The parties may set standards for measuring good faith if they are not manifestly unreasonable.
It creates an independent cause of action that can override an express contract term.
It does not apply to negotiations before the contract is formed.
oe: Correct statement (§ 1-302(b)).
Correct statement (§ 1-304).
Correct statement (§ 1-302(b)).
Correct: this statement is NOT correct. Good faith is a lens for interpreting and performing the agreement. It is not a stand-alone claim, and it cannot contradict express terms.
Correct statement. The duty attaches to performance and enforcement.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith: limits

q: Which pairing of excuse provisions is correct?
o: Article 2A has no excuse provisions at all.
oe: Section 2A-221 tracks § 2-613.
It has several.
Section 2A-405 tracks § 2-615.
Correct. Section 2A-221 tracks § 2-613.
Section 2A-404 tracks § 2-614.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Excuse tracking

q: Under a shipment contract, conforming goods are destroyed in transit after risk passed to the buyer. The buyer refuses to pay. What may the seller recover?
o: Only its incidental damages.
The price, but only if the seller had insured the goods.
The price, since risk had passed before the loss.
Only market damages under § 2-708(1).
Nothing, since the buyer never received the goods.
oe: The price is recoverable.
Insurance isn't a condition of the price action.
Correct. Section 2-709(1)(a). Buyer's recourse is against the carrier.
The price is available under § 2-709(1)(a).
Risk passed on tender to the carrier.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Price: goods lost after risk passed

q: Kermit contracts to sell Fozzie 100 standard steel I-beams for $20,000. Kermit then assigns "the contract" to Beaker Manufacturing, which accepts. Beaker tenders conforming I-beams. Which statement is correct?
o: Fozzie must accept and pay Beaker, but Kermit stays liable.
Fozzie may refuse Beaker's I-beams, because he contracted with Kermit.
The assignment transfers only Kermit's right to payment.
Kermit is released from all liability once Beaker accepts.
Fozzie must pay Kermit, because only rights, not duties, were transferred.
oe: Correct. § 2-210(5); Problem 6-2(c). An assignment of "the contract" assigns Kermit's rights and delegates his duties. Fozzie must accept Beaker's conforming I-beams and pay Beaker, but Kermit remains liable if Beaker fails. Fozzie may also demand adequate assurance from Beaker (§ 2-210(6)).
Standard I-beams: Fozzie has no substantial interest in Kermit personally performing.
An assignment of "the contract" also delegates the duties.
Delegation never relieves the delegator.
Both were transferred, and Fozzie pays the assignee.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Assignment of the contract

q: A seafood company tells a trailer dealer it needs refrigerated trailers to haul live lobsters in seawater tanks over long distances. The dealer recommends a model, which the company buys in reliance. The trailers keep lobsters cold but can't keep them alive. The dealer argues that hauling seafood is the ordinary use of refrigerated trailers, so only merchantability could apply. What is the best response?
o: A fitness warranty arises only if the buyer's use is unique to that buyer.
The dealer is right, because hauling seafood is the ordinary use of refrigerated trailers, so no fitness warranty can arise.
The purpose need not be unique; it need only differ from the goods' customary use, a question of fact.
A fitness warranty arises whenever the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: Uniqueness isn't required.
Ingram River rejected that argument as a matter of law.

Correct. This is Ingram River: whether the use is "particular" depends on how the goods are characterized (tank barges vs. heating-coil barges), and the use need only be sufficiently different from customary use.
Fitness turns on purpose and reliance, not merchant status.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Particular vs. ordinary purpose

q: In a deposition, Oscar admits that he orally agreed to buy 200 trash cans from Telly, although Telly claims the deal was for 300. There is no signed record. To what extent is the contract enforceable against Oscar?
o: Not at all, because there is no signed record.
Up to 250 trash cans, splitting the difference between the two claims.
Up to 300 trash cans, because Oscar admitted a contract exists.
Up to 300 trash cans, if Telly proves that quantity at trial.
None of the above.
oe: The admission exception applies (§ 2-201(3)(b)).
There is no compromise rule.
Enforcement is limited to the quantity admitted.
Even then, the exception stops at the admitted quantity.
Correct. The contract is enforceable against Oscar up to 200 trash cans, the quantity he admitted in court (§ 2-201(3)(b)). No choice states that.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Admission

q: A seller contracts to supply corrugated boxes at a fixed price. Months later, a mill fire across the region causes the price of the seller's raw paperboard to triple, so continuing at the contract price would cause heavy losses.
