The seller explains the situation and asks for a 15% increase, and the buyer agrees in an email. Later, the buyer refuses to pay the increase, arguing it got nothing new in return. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller wins only if the modification was in a writing signed by both of the parties.
The buyer wins, because the seller was already legally obligated to perform at the original price.
The buyer wins, because the seller gave no new consideration for the 15% increase.
The seller wins, because a good-faith modification is binding without consideration.
The buyer wins, because the cost increase would have excused the seller under § 2-615 anyway.
oe: Unless the contract has a no-oral-modification clause or the modified deal falls within § 2-201, no particular writing is required. An email from the buyer would likely satisfy either anyway.
That is the common-law pre-existing duty rule, which § 2-209(1) displaces.
Article 2 doesn't require consideration for a modification.

Correct. Section 2-209(1) makes modifications binding without consideration. An unforeseen market shift that makes performance unexpectedly burdensome is a legitimate commercial reason for seeking one in good faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
A cost increase alone usually doesn't excuse performance under § 2-615, but that doesn't matter when the parties agreed to modify.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good-faith modification after an unforeseen cost rise

q: A buyer pays $1,200 toward a $6,000 machine and breaches. The seller justifiably withholds and proves $300 in damages. There's no LD clause. How much goes back to the buyer?
o: $1,200, as damages are too small to count.
$400, keeping both $500 and $300.
Nothing, keeping 20%.
$900, keeping the $300 proven.
$700, as the $500 statutory amount exceeds the $300.
oe: It may keep the statutory amount.
They aren't added.
It's the smaller of the two figures.
The statutory amount needs no proof, and it's larger here.
Correct. Section 2-718(2)(b): the seller keeps the smaller of 20% ($1,200) or $500, without proof. Proven damages of $300 don't exceed that, so it keeps $500.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Deposit, seller's actual damages small

q: A buyer can't find a price quotation for the proper day at the place for tender, but has one from a nearby market a week later. Which is correct?
o: It may be used as a reasonable substitute, on fair notice.
Only a seller may offer substitute price evidence.
It may be used without giving the other side any notice.
The court must fall back on the contract price.
Market damages are unavailable without an exact price.
oe: Correct. Section 2-723(2)-(3), with proper allowance for transporting the goods. Evidence offered without notice preventing unfair surprise is inadmissible.
Either party may.
Section 2-723(3) requires notice preventing unfair surprise.
That would give no damages.
Section 2-723(2) allows a reasonable substitute.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Substitute time or place

q: A contract says: "Buyer must notify Seller of any defect within 3 days of delivery." Is this enforceable?
o: No, because notice periods cannot be varied.
Yes, if the time is not manifestly unreasonable.
Yes, because the parties agreed to the period.
No, because the UCC requires a "reasonable time."
None of the above.
oe: They can.
Correct. § 1-302(b).
Not if manifestly unreasonable.
Parties may fix a time.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fixing reasonable time

q: A steel fabricator contracts to deliver 500 tons of rebar at a fixed price. Before delivery, ordinary market forces drive the price of scrap steel up 40%, which turns the expected profit into a loss. The fabricator argues it is excused under § 2-615. What is the most likely result?
o: Excused, because a 40% jump in the cost of scrap steel makes performance commercially impracticable.
Not excused, because a rise in cost alone doesn't make performance impracticable.
Excused, but only for the part of the order it can no longer afford to fill.
Excused, as long as the fabricator gives the buyer seasonable notice of the problem.
Not excused, because § 2-615 applies only to buyers, never to sellers.
oe: A market increase is a foreseeable business risk, not an unforeseen contingency.

Correct. "Increased cost alone does not excuse performance unless the rise in cost is due to some unforeseen contingency which alters the essential nature of the performance" (§ 2-615 cmt. 4). Market fluctuation is exactly the risk a fixed-price contract allocates.
Partial excuse requires an excusing contingency that affects capacity, not just higher cost.
Notice is required for excuse but doesn't create excuse.
Section 2-615 is written for sellers.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Cost increase isn't impracticability

q: A person who is not a merchant sells goods he knows have a hidden defect. Which statement best describes his obligations?
o: He makes the implied warranty of merchantability, like any seller.
No merchantability warranty, but a duty to disclose the known defect.
He has no obligations, because he is not a merchant.
He is strictly liable for the defect, whether or not he knew of it.
None of the above.
oe: Only merchants do.
Correct. Isolated sellers aren't merchants, but must disclose known material hidden defects.
Comment 3 imposes a duty to disclose known hidden defects.
Strict liability under § 2-314 applies to merchants.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Merchant's duty to disclose

q: Waldorf contracts to sell Statler all of the standing timber on Waldorf's land. The contract says Statler will cut and haul the trees himself. Does Article 2 apply?
o: Yes, because Statler is a merchant in timber.
No, because the buyer, not the seller, will sever the timber.
No, because standing timber is part of the real estate.
Yes, but only after the timber is cut.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status never decides whether Article 2 applies (Problem 1-4).
That is the rule for minerals and structures (§ 2-107(1)), not timber.
§ 2-107(2) treats timber to be cut as goods even while it stands.
The contract is for the sale of goods from the start. § 2-107(2) applies to the contract to sell timber to be cut.

Correct. Article 2 applies, but for a reason none of the choices gives: timber to be cut is a good whether the buyer or the seller severs it (§ 2-107(2)). B states the rule for minerals and structures, not timber.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Timber: either party severs

q: A seller of kitchen appliances wants a contract clause on notice of breach. Which clause is safest?
o: Notice within 30 days after the buyer discovers or should discover the defect.
A clause stating that the seller owes no duty of notice.
Certified-mail notice within 2 days after delivery, for all defects.
Notice within 24 hours after delivery, for any defect, hidden or not.
A statement that the buyer has no remedy for hidden defects.
oe: Correct. Parties may fix a reasonable time (§§ 1-205(b), 1-302). Section 1-302(b) bars manifestly unreasonable limits, and a clause cutting off hidden defects risks §§ 2-302 and 2-719. Whether parties could dispense with notice altogether is open.
The notice duty is the buyer's, so this does nothing.
Same problem: hidden defects can't be found that fast.
That's manifestly unreasonable for hidden defects (§ 1-302(b)).
That risks §§ 2-302 and 2-719.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Contract fixing notice period

q: Which correctly describes where and how a seller tenders in the three scenarios the course uses?
o: Only by carrier, for all commercial sales.
Only after full payment has been made.
Direct, at the seller's place; by carrier under § 2-504; or via a bailee.
Only with the buyer's written consent.
Only at the buyer's place, whatever the contract says.
oe: Direct and bailee tender are also common.
Tender and payment are concurrent, absent agreement.
Correct. Direct tender: hold conforming goods at the buyer's disposition. Carrier: § 2-503(2), 2-504. Bailee: § 2-503(4). The sequence of tender, inspection, acceptance and payment can vary.
Tender needs no consent.
The default place is the seller's place of business.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Three tender scenarios

q: A distributor's contract for 50 commercial dishwashers limits the buyer's remedy to refund of the price. The limitation is printed in the same type as the rest of the contract, in paragraph 14 of 20. The buyer argues the limitation is unenforceable because it is not conspicuous. Is the buyer right?
o: Yes, unless the buyer actually read paragraph 14.
Yes, because every term that reduces a buyer's rights must be conspicuous.
Yes, because § 2-316's conspicuousness rule governs remedy limitations too.
No, because § 2-719 doesn't require a remedy limitation to be conspicuous.
No, but only because both parties are merchants.
oe: Whether the buyer read it doesn't matter to enforceability under § 2-719.
No such general rule exists. Conspicuousness is required for certain § 2-316 disclaimers only.
§ 2-316(4) sends remedy limitations to §§ 2-718 and 2-719, which have no such rule.
Correct. Unlike disclaimers of merchantability (in writing) and fitness, remedy limitations need not be conspicuous. They are tested by failure of essential purpose and unconscionability.
The answer is the same for consumers; § 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement for anyone.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Conspicuousness not required

q: Elmo agrees to buy a $10,000 used piano from Hooper's Music and pays a $3,000 deposit. The contract has no liquidated damages term. Elmo repudiates, and Hooper's justifiably withholds delivery. Hooper's promptly resells the piano for $10,000 and proves no damages. How much of the deposit must Hooper's return?
oe: That keeps 20% ($2,000). § 2-718(2)(b) uses the smaller of 20% or $500.
That figure confuses the 20% amount with the refund. The refund is the deposit less $500.
Forfeiture of the whole deposit requires a valid liquidated damages term or provable damages; Hooper's has neither.

Correct. With no liquidated damages term, the seller may keep 20% of the value of the buyer's total performance or $500, whichever is smaller (§ 2-718(2)(b)). The smaller is $500, and Hooper's proved no damages to offset, so it returns $3,000 - $500 = $2,500.
The seller may keep the smaller of 20% or $500 even without proving damages (§ 2-718(2)(b)).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Deposit: no LD term

q: A contract bars all assignments. Seller fully performs by delivering the goods, and Buyer fails to pay. Can Seller assign its right to payment?
o: No, because the contract bars all assignments of any kind.
Only after Seller first sues Buyer for the price.
Only with Buyer's written consent to the assignment.
Yes, because the right arises from Seller's full performance.
None of the above.
oe: The bar doesn't reach a right arising from full performance.
There is no such requirement.
No consent is needed.
Correct. § 2-210(2): a right arising from the assignor's full performance can be assigned despite an agreement otherwise. (§ 9-406(d) reaches the same result for a right to payment.)
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Right from full performance

q: A contract requires 10,000 widgets a month for 12 months, delivered by the 5th of each month. The April shipment arrives April 7, and the buyer accepts it without complaint. In May, the seller again delivers on the 7th and argues that the parties' course of performance has moved the deadline to the 7th. Is the seller right?
o: No, because a course of performance can never change an express term such as a delivery date.
No, because one late delivery isn't a course of performance, though it may waive that delay.
Yes, because the seller relied on the buyer's acceptance when it scheduled the May delivery.
Yes, because the buyer accepted a late delivery without complaining and so agreed to the new date.
Yes, because accepting the April delivery late modified the contract's delivery deadline.
oe: Course of performance can show a waiver or modification of a term (§ 1-303(f)). It just requires more than one occasion.

Correct. A course of performance requires repeated occasions for performance accepted or acquiesced in without objection (§ 1-303(a)). One late delivery isn't enough. Accepting it may waive that one breach. See Problem 3-5(A).
Nothing shows detrimental reliance, and reliance wouldn't create a course of performance anyway.
One acceptance doesn't show the repeated pattern § 1-303(a) requires.
Nothing suggests the parties agreed to change the deadline. Silent acceptance of one late shipment isn't a modification.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — A single occasion isn't a course of performance

q: Buyer rightfully rejects a shipment of tables that are in its possession. Which statement about Buyer's duties is correct?
o: Buyer may use the tables until Seller gets around to picking them up.
Buyer must hold them with reasonable care for Seller to remove.
Buyer must ship the tables back to Seller, at Seller's expense.
Buyer may sell the tables and keep the proceeds for itself.
None of the above.
oe: Using them would be exercising ownership, which is wrongful.
The buyer has no duty to ship them back. It need only hold them with reasonable care (or follow reasonable instructions).
Merchant buyers may resell perishables or follow instructions (§§ 2-603, 2-604), but not keep proceeds as their own.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Duties after rejection

q: After a tenant stops paying rent, a self-storage company holds a lien sale and auctions off the contents of the tenant's unit. Ernie buys a television from the unit. It later turns out the tenant had borrowed it from a friend, who reclaims it. Ernie sues the storage company for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: The storage company wins, because auctions never carry a warranty of title.
The storage company wins, because the circumstances gave Ernie reason to know it was selling only whatever rights the tenant had.
Ernie wins, because the storage company is a merchant.
Ernie wins, because the borrower's friend has only a colorable claim.
Ernie wins, because the title warranty can be excluded only by specific written language.
oe: An ordinary auctioneer's sale can carry a title warranty. It's the lien-sale circumstances that exclude it here.

Correct. Title is excluded by circumstances that give the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title itself (§ 2-312(2)). A lien sale of a defaulting tenant's goods is that kind of out-of-the-ordinary sale (cmt. 5).
Merchant status doesn't matter to the title warranty; every seller makes it unless excluded.
The friend's claim is valid, not merely colorable, and in any event the warranty was excluded.
§ 2-312(2) allows exclusion by specific language or by circumstances.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Title excluded by circumstances

q: Gonzo's rooftop solar panels generate more electricity than his house uses, and he sells the excess to the local utility through a meter. Is the electricity a "good"?
o: Yes, because Gonzo is a merchant in electricity.
No, because the utility, not Gonzo, severs the electricity.
Maybe; courts split on metered electricity.
Yes, because electricity is a movable thing once generated.
No, because electricity is a service rather than a thing.
oe: Merchant status doesn't decide whether something is a good.
Severance matters for minerals and things attached to realty (§ 2-107), not electricity.
Correct. Problem 1-1 lists excess solar electricity as "maybe": courts split on whether metered electricity is a good or a service.
The answer isn't that clear; courts split.
Some courts treat metered electricity as a good; the answer is unsettled.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Excess solar electricity

q: A defective space heater burns a buyer's garage. What is the Code's basis for recovering the loss?
o: Section 2-715(2)(a), if the seller knew about the garage.
Section 2-712, cover.
Section 2-715(2)(b), injury to property from breach of warranty.
Section 2-715(1), incidental damages.
Section 2-714(1), loss in the ordinary course.
oe: Subsection (b) applies, and it has no reason-to-know element.
Replacing a garage isn't cover of the goods.
Correct. Unlike (2)(a), subsection (b) has no "reason to know" requirement.
Property injury isn't incidental.
That doesn't reach property injury from a warranty breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Injury from breach of warranty

q: A buyer accepted a lathe for $40,000 and claims $5,000 in warranty damages. Without telling the seller why, it pays $35,000. The seller sues for $5,000. Which is the best statement?
o: The buyer should have notified the seller of its intent to deduct.
A deduction is valid only if the seller agrees.
The seller must sue for the full $40,000.
A buyer may never withhold any of the price.
The buyer's deduction bars the seller's suit.
oe: Correct. Section 2-717 requires notice. It may still raise its warranty claim as a counterclaim if it gave § 2-607(3)(a) notice.
Notice is required, not agreement.
It received $35,000.
Section 2-717 allows it on notice.
Not without proper notice.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Deduct and be sued

q: Why does § 2A-219 not follow § 2-509's "passing" model for ordinary leases?
o: Title passes to the lessee at delivery.
Lessors are always required to insure.
Both parties hold property rights for the whole term.
Leased goods can't be lost or damaged.
Merchants are excluded from Article 2A.
oe: Title stays with the lessor throughout an ordinary lease.
No statute requires it.
Correct.
They plainly can.
They aren't.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Why risk differs

q: In NIPSCO v. Carbon County Coal, an electric utility with a long-term fixed-price coal contract wanted out when it could buy power much more cheaply. What result?
o: The utility was excused because regulators wouldn't let it pass costs through.
The utility was excused by frustration of its purpose.
The utility was excused because its costs became unprofitable.
The coal company had to lower its price to market.
The utility was not excused; it bore the risk of a market drop.
oe: That didn't change the risk allocation.
The court refused to excuse it.
A fixed-price contract assigns the risk of market decreases to the buyer.
The contract price stood.
Correct. Judge Posner: a fixed-price contract assigns the risk of market decreases to the buyer, and a buyer that misforecasts the market "has only himself to blame."
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — NIPSCO

q: Which statement about reclamation is correct?
o: It measures the seller's lost expectancy.
It lets the seller seize the goods without any process.
It is available to every unpaid seller.
It is restitutionary, and it needs a court if the buyer refuses.
It applies only to perishable goods.
oe: It's restitutionary, not an expectancy measure.
It isn't self-help.
It's limited to §§ 2-507 and 2-702.
Correct. It isn't an expectancy measure and isn't self-help.
Sections 2-507 and 2-702 aren't limited by the type of goods.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Nature of reclamation

q: Lou, who isn't a merchant, sells his used mower. In the bill of sale, he writes: "This mower is merchantable." It isn't. Which is correct?
o: The promise is enforceable, as a non-merchant can expressly warrant it.
It's enforceable only if Lou had reason to know the purpose.
It's unenforceable, as "merchantable" is an opinion.
It turns Lou into a merchant for all purposes.
It's unenforceable, as only merchants make that warranty.
oe: Correct. Comment 4 to § 2-314: though no warranty is implied, a non-merchant can make an express warranty of merchantability. Express warranties aren't themselves gap fillers.
That's fitness.
It's a statement of a legal standard, which can be a warranty.
A single promise doesn't change his status.
That's the rule for the implied warranty.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Non-merchant warrants merchantability

q: Which statement about insurable interests is correct?
o: Neither has one before delivery.
Only the title holder has one.
Only the buyer has one after identification.
Only a merchant may have one.
Buyer and seller can both hold one in identified goods.
oe: Identification is enough for the buyer.
Section 2-501 says otherwise.
The seller may keep one.
Merchant status is irrelevant.
Correct. Section 2-501. After an unjustified revocation Article 2 is silent, and presumably risk returns to the seller once it takes the goods back (n.30).
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Insurable interests

q: Gonzo's signed email to Rizzo says: "Confirming you will buy 80 cases of olive oil at $40 per case." The parties actually agreed on $45 per case. Rizzo seeks to enforce the deal against Gonzo. Is the email sufficient under § 2-201(1)?
o: Yes, but the contract is enforceable only at the $40 price stated in the email, not the $45 actually agreed.
No, because it misstates the price.
No, because an email can't be signed.
No, because Rizzo did not sign it.
Yes, because a record isn't insufficient just because it misstates a term other than quantity.
oe: The statute of frauds doesn't fix the price. The parties prove the actual terms.
A misstated term other than quantity doesn't make a record insufficient.
A typed name in an email is a signature, and an email is a record.
It must be signed by the party to be charged, Gonzo.
Correct. § 2-201(1). The statute caps quantity only; the true price is proved at trial.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Misstated price

q: At a police auction of unclaimed property, Telly buys a laptop that turns out to have been stolen; the true owner reclaims it. The auction terms said nothing about title. Does Telly have a claim for breach of the warranty of title?
o: No, because the circumstances of a police auction show the seller doesn't claim title in itself.
Yes, unless the auction was run by a merchant.
No, because stolen goods are not goods.
Yes, because every seller warrants good title.
Yes, because no one said "as is."
oe: Correct. § 2-312(2): circumstances like sheriff's or police sales exclude the title warranty.
Merchant status doesn't matter here.
They are goods.
Not when circumstances show the seller doesn't claim title in itself.
"As is" wouldn't disclaim title anyway.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title: police auction

q: A buyer accepts a nonconforming shipment and doesn't revoke. Which remedy is ordinarily unavailable?
o: Incidental damages under § 2-715(1).
Cover damages under § 2-712.
Consequential damages under § 2-715(2).
Value-difference damages under § 2-714(2).
Deduction from the price under § 2-717.
oe: Available after acceptance.
Correct. Without revocation the buyer loses cancellation and cover or market damages. An installment contract may differ (§§ 2-612(3), 2-711(1)).
Available after acceptance.
Available with notice.
Available on notice to the seller.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Loses cover and market

q: Which, if any, of the following language effectively disclaims the warranty of good title?
o: "Seller disclaims any warranty of title."
"These goods are sold AS IS."
"THERE ARE NO IMPLIED WARRANTIES WITH THIS SALE."
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Specific language works.
"As is" disclaims only implied warranties under § 2-316, and the title warranty isn't one of them.
The title warranty is disclaimed only by specific language or circumstances (§ 2-312(2)).
Only A works.
A works.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer

q: A buyer took a lathe, wrongfully revoked, and returned it, and a $20,000 down payment was made. Which is correct?
o: Compute market or resale, add costs, then credit the $20,000.
No damages are available after a return of goods.
The buyer forfeits the $20,000 as a penalty.
Section 2-718(2) applies exactly as written.
The seller recovers the price and keeps the lathe.
oe: Correct. Problem 9-13. Section 2-718(2) (withheld delivery) doesn't fit neatly, but the § 1-305 result is the same.
Damages are available.
It's credited.
Delivery wasn't withheld, so it doesn't fit neatly.
That's double recovery.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — After wrongful revocation

q: After agreeing orally to buy a private collector's antique carousel horses for $75,000, Big Bird types up the terms and emails them to the collector, who never replies or signs anything. Relying on the deal, Big Bird pays a $2,000 nonrefundable deposit to a moving company and rents climate-controlled storage. The collector backs out. Can Big Bird enforce the deal?
o: No, but only because the deal was over $5,000.
No, because the collector signed nothing and no exception or estoppel theory applies.
Yes, because Big Bird's reliance on the deal would make the collector's refusal to perform a fraud on Big Bird.
Yes, because the collector's silence after the email binds the collector.
Yes, because Big Bird's typed summary is a sufficient record.
oe: The threshold is $500.
Correct. This tracks Casazza: unsigned typed terms, preparatory reliance, and no exception.
Casazza rejected that argument on similar reliance (a survey and a boat slip).
Silence binds only under the merchant's-confirmation exception, which requires both parties to be merchants.
It isn't signed by the party being charged (the collector).
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unsigned typed terms; reliance

q: A tenant asks its landlord several times over 19 months to discuss the tenant's option to buy the building. The landlord evades every request, then declares the option void because the tenant missed a technical step. Under the note case Brunswick Hills, how would a court likely view the landlord's conduct?
o: As permitted, because a party may always insist on strict compliance with the contract.
As permitted, because the tenant should have hired a lawyer.
As bad faith, because it exploited an oversight it could have fixed.
As bad faith, because a landlord owes its tenant fiduciary duties.
As permitted, because good faith applies only to negotiation.
oe: Strict compliance is usually fine, but not when the party has strung the other side along to manufacture the default.
The landlord's evasion is the problem, not the tenant's lack of counsel.
Correct. Brunswick Hills (N.J.) found bad faith in the landlord's 19 months of evasion.
Good faith is less than a fiduciary duty.
Good faith applies to performance and enforcement.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Brunswick Hills

q: Elmo obtains a guitar from Grover by fraud, giving him voidable title. Elmo then gives the guitar to Zoe as a birthday present. Zoe has no idea of the fraud. Can Grover recover the guitar from Zoe?
o: Yes, because Zoe gave no value for the guitar.
No, because Elmo had voidable title when he gave it away.
No, because Zoe received it in complete good faith.
No, because a gift counts as a "purchase" under the UCC.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Purchase" includes a gift (§ 1-201(b)(29)), but § 2-403(1) protects only a good-faith purchaser for value, so Zoe takes only Elmo's voidable title.
Voidable title can become good title only in the hands of a good-faith purchaser for value.
Good faith alone isn't enough; she must also give value.
A gift is a purchase, but it is not a purchase for value.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Title: gift from voidable-title holder

q: Kermit agrees in November to buy a new $60,000 bass boat from a marine dealer and pays a $6,000 deposit. The contract says: "If Buyer fails to complete the purchase, Seller shall retain the deposit as liquidated damages." Boats sell slowly in winter, and the dealer's expected profit on the sale was about $7,000. Kermit backs out. What is the most likely result?
o: Kermit recovers all but $500, because a seller may keep only the smaller of 20% or $500.
The dealer keeps the $6,000 and may also sue Kermit for any further lost profit.
Kermit recovers the full $6,000, because deposits can never be forfeited.
The dealer keeps the $6,000, because the amount is reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
The dealer keeps $12,000, 20% of the price, by offsetting the balance against Kermit's other accounts.
oe: That default applies only when there is no valid liquidated damages term (§ 2-718(2)(b)). Here there is one.
A valid liquidated damages clause fixes the measure of damages; the dealer can't keep it and also seek more.
Deposits can be forfeited when they reasonably liquidate the seller's damages.

Correct. Forfeiture of a down payment is frequently enforced when the amount is a reasonable liquidation (§ 2-718(1), (2)(a)). A 10% deposit, close to the expected lost profit on a hard-to-resell boat, qualifies.
Twenty percent is part of the § 2-718(2)(b) default, not an entitlement, and the clause liquidates damages at the $6,000 deposit.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Forfeited boat deposit

q: Cookie Monster chokes on a bone in a salmon fillet that a restaurant sold as "boneless." Under which approach is his claim for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability strongest?
o: The foreign-natural test, because a bone is natural to fish.
Under any test, because the restaurant is a merchant.
Neither, because food served in a restaurant is not a sale of goods.
Neither, because the restaurant was not negligent.
None of the above.
oe: Under that test (Webster), a natural bone generally defeats the claim.
Merchant status triggers the warranty but doesn't decide breach. Under the foreign-natural test (Webster), a natural bone defeats the claim.
§ 2-314(1): serving food or drink for value is a sale.
Merchantability is not negligence-based.

Correct. His claim is strongest under the reasonable-expectation test (Mexicali Rose, Schafer), because a diner can reasonably expect a fillet sold as boneless to have no bones. No choice names that test.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fish bone

q: A lessee delegates its rent duty to a new business. The lessor doesn't agree otherwise. Which is correct?
o: The delegation is void without the lessor's consent.
The lessee is released by the delegation.
The lease ends on delegation.
Only the new business is now liable.
The lessee remains liable for the rent.
oe: Consent matters for release, not validity.
Delegation doesn't release it.
Delegation doesn't end the lease.
Not without a novation.
Correct. Section 2A-303(6), compare § 2-210(1).
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Delegation

q: Which is NOT one of the four limits on a buyer's consequential damages?
o: The loss must have been caused by the breach.
The loss must not be preventable by cover or otherwise.
The seller must have had reason to know of the needs.
The buyer must have told the seller in writing of its needs.
The loss must be proved with reasonable certainty.
oe: A limit: causation.
A limit: avoidability.
A limit: foreseeability at contracting.
Correct. The test is "reason to know" at contracting, which needs no writing. The limits are causation, foreseeability, avoidability and reasonable certainty.
A limit (cmt. 4).
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Consequential elements

q: A single-delivery contract calls for 1,000 blue mugs. The seller delivers 1,000, but 20 have a slightly lighter blue glaze. The delivery deadline has passed, and the seller had no reason to think the shipment would be acceptable. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer may reject only if the lighter glaze substantially impairs the value of the whole shipment.
The buyer must give the seller a further reasonable time to cure.
The buyer must accept, because the nonconformity is insubstantial.
The buyer may reject only the 20 mugs and must keep the rest.
The buyer may reject all, accept all, or accept some commercial units and reject the rest.
oe: That's the installment-contract standard.
That applies only if the seller reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable (§ 2-508(2)).
The perfect tender rule doesn't require substantial impairment.
The buyer may also reject or accept the whole.
Correct. § 2-601. No right to cure remains: the time has passed and the seller had no reason to believe the tender would be accepted (§ 2-508).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Perfect tender

q: A drought cuts a cranberry grower's harvest in half. Cranberries from its own bogs are the agreed source in several contracts, and it also has regular customers who buy without contracts. Which statement about the grower's duties is most accurate?
o: It must fill its contract orders in full before it sells any berries to customers without contracts.
It may choose which contract buyers to supply in full and which contracts to cancel outright.
It is excused from all its contracts, because the drought was an unforeseen contingency.
It must allocate fairly, may include regular non-contract customers, and must notify buyers.
It must buy cranberries from other growers to fill every contract in full at the contract price.
oe: Section 2-615(b) permits including regular customers not under contract in the allocation.
Allocation must be fair and reasonable.
A partial failure calls for allocation, not complete excuse.

Correct. When a contingency affects only part of a seller's capacity, the seller must allocate production and deliveries among its customers fairly and reasonably, may include regular customers not then under contract, and must notify buyers seasonably (§ 2-615(b), (c)).
Where the parties agreed that the berries would come from the grower's own bogs, failure of that source can excuse the shortfall (§ 2-615 cmt. 5).
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Allocation among customers

q: Big Bird gives Snuffy a new bicycle as a birthday present. The bicycle turns out to be defective. Which law governs Snuffy's rights against Big Bird?
o: UCC Article 9, because title to the bicycle passed.
UCC Article 2, because "purchase" includes a gift.
The common law, because a gift is not a sale.
The law of wills, because the gift was gratuitous.
UCC Article 2, because a bicycle is a good.
oe: Article 9 governs security interests.
"Purchase" includes a gift (§ 1-201(b)(29)) for purposes such as § 2-403, but Article 2 governs sales, which require a price.
Correct. On the class chart, a gift of goods is governed by the common law.
The law of wills governs bequests and devises.
The type of property is only the first factor. The nature of the rights transferred matters too, and a gift is not a sale.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Gift of goods

q: Which, on its own, satisfies § 1-201(b)(23)'s definition of "insolvent"?
o: The person has been named in a lawsuit.
The person is unable to pay debts as they become due.
The person has missed a single payment.
The person has a low credit score.
The person has no cash on hand on one day.
oe: Being sued isn't part of the definition.
Correct. Also having generally ceased to pay debts in the ordinary course, or being insolvent under federal bankruptcy law (a balance-sheet test).
One missed payment isn't enough.
Credit scores aren't part of the definition.
A short-term cash gap isn't the test.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Insolvent defined

q: Gonzo's Cannon Works contracts to build and deliver 50 circus cannons to Camilla's circus over the next year. Gonzo then assigns the contract to Rizzo Rat Works, a startup Camilla has never heard of, which accepts. Camilla is worried Rizzo can't do the job. What may Camilla do?
o: Sue Gonzo immediately for damages, because a delegation is itself a breach.
Demand assurance only from Gonzo, because Rizzo owes Camilla nothing.
Demand adequate assurance from Rizzo.
Cancel the contract at once, because the delegation is an anticipatory repudiation.
Nothing, because she has no right to object to a permitted delegation.
oe: Absent a contractual ban or a substantial interest, delegation is permitted and isn't a breach.
Rizzo accepted an assignment of the contract, so it promised to perform (§ 2-210(5)), and § 2-210(6) lets Camilla demand assurance from the assignee.

Correct. Under § 2-210(6), the other party may treat an assignment that delegates performance as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and may demand assurances from the assignee, without prejudice to its rights against the assignor.
Delegating isn't repudiating. Camilla's remedy is to demand assurance, then treat a failure to give it as a repudiation (§ 2-609(4)).
Even a permitted delegation gives the other party grounds for insecurity under § 2-210(6).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegation and assurance

q: Telly buys a used e-bike from Oscar's Resale under a contract stating: "SOLD AS IS, WITH ALL FAULTS." The e-bike turns out to be stolen, and the true owner reclaims it. Telly sues Oscar's Resale. What is the most likely result?
o: Oscar's wins, because Telly could have checked the bike's ownership before buying.
Telly wins, because "as is" language does not disclaim the warranty of title.
Oscar's wins, because Telly bought used goods.
Oscar's wins, because "as is" excludes all warranties.
Telly wins, but only if Oscar's knew the bike was stolen.
oe: The buyer has no duty to investigate title; the seller warrants it.

Correct. The title warranty can be excluded only by specific language or by circumstances giving the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title (§ 2-312(2)). It isn't an "implied warranty" under § 2-316, so "as is" doesn't reach it (cmt. 6).
Every seller warrants title, whether the goods are new or used.
"As is" excludes implied warranties under § 2-316(3)(a). The title warranty isn't one of them.
The title warranty doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — "As is" and title

q: Under a shipment contract, goods conforming at tender are damaged in transit. The buyer tries to reject. Which is correct?
o: The seller must replace them at its own cost.
It fails, since the goods conformed at tender, so the price is owed.
The buyer may reject, because they arrived damaged.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613.
The carrier owes the seller the price.
oe: The seller performed.
Correct. Problem 9-14(B).
Risk had passed to the buyer.
Section 2-613 needs a loss before risk passes.
The buyer owes the price.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Transit damage, shipment contract

q: A dairy buys a pasteurizer. It tells the seller at signing that it has a contract with a school district and that any shutdown could cost that contract. The seller delivers three weeks late, and the school district ends the contract, costing $80,000 in profit. Temporary pasteurizing wasn't available at any price. The dairy also spent $2,000 trying to find one. What can it recover?
o: Only the $80,000, since costs of trying to cover aren't recoverable.
The $80,000 only if the seller expressly promised to pay it.
The $80,000, if proved with reasonable certainty, and the $2,000.
Only the $2,000, since lost profits aren't recoverable.
Nothing, since delivery was merely late.
oe: Commercially reasonable cover costs are incidental.
Reason to know is enough; no express promise is needed.
Correct. The seller had reason to know at contracting, cover wasn't possible, and the $2,000 is incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
A buyer's lost profits are consequential damages (§ 2-715(2)(a)).
Late delivery is a breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Consequential: reason to know

q: A seller repudiates a contract to sell 1,000 office chairs at $100 each. The buyer promptly and reasonably buys 1,000 comparable chairs from another supplier at $130 each. The market price at the time the buyer learned of the repudiation was $125. The buyer also spent $200 on reasonable costs of finding the substitute chairs, and it saved no expenses because of the breach. If the buyer sues for damages based on cover, how much does it recover?
oe: Correct. A buyer that covers may recover the difference between the cost of cover and the contract price, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved (§ 2-712(2)). That's ($130 - $100) x 1,000 = $30,000, plus $200 in incidental damages (§ 2-715(1)).
That uses the market price under § 2-713. A buyer that has reasonably covered measures damages by the cover price.
This leaves out the $200 of incidental damages, which a covering buyer may recover.
The buyer recovers the difference between cover and contract price, not the whole cost of cover.
This uses the market measure and also omits incidental damages.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Buyer's cover damages

q: Cal buys a boat for $40,000 under a signed contract. The seller orally promises to buy the boat back for $30,000 in a year if Cal asks. The seller refuses a year later. What is the seller's best defense?
o: The promise lacks consideration.
A seller can never agree to buy goods back.
The repurchase promise is its own $500+ sale and needs its own record.
A boat isn't a good under Article 2.
The parol evidence rule alone bars every later promise.
oe: It was part of the bargain.
Nothing bars it.
Correct. Problem 2-12: an oral repurchase promise is its own sale of goods. The signed contract doesn't satisfy § 2-201 for it, because the seller signed nothing showing a contract to buy.
Boats are goods.
The promise here is contemporaneous, but the statute of frauds is the cleaner defense.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Oral repurchase promise

q: Count von Count buys a new dishwasher from a local retailer, which bought it from a distributor, which bought it from the manufacturer. It never cleans properly. The retailer has gone out of business, so the Count sues the manufacturer for economic loss under the implied warranty of merchantability. The state's courts have abolished the vertical-privity requirement for such claims. What is the most likely result?
o: The Count may proceed only on an express warranty, because implied warranties never run past the immediate seller.
The Count loses, because § 2-318 never extends warranties to economic loss.
The Count may proceed only if he was injured in person.
The Count loses, because only the retailer made him an implied warranty.
The Count may proceed against the manufacturer even though he bought from an intermediary.
oe: Once vertical privity is abolished, implied warranties can run past the immediate seller.
§ 2-318 addresses horizontal reach; it leaves vertical privity to the courts (cmt. 3), and these courts have abolished it.
The abolition here covers economic loss. Personal injury is a § 2-318 horizontal-privity question.
Without a vertical-privity requirement, the manufacturer's implied warranty can run to the remote buyer.

Correct. Where vertical privity is abolished, a consumer may sue the remote manufacturer for economic loss on the implied warranty of merchantability even though the consumer bought from someone else in the distribution chain.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Remote manufacturer

q: A computer maker used defective circuit boards. It bears the excess cost of replacement boards, the cost of installing them, repairs to computers sold, and estimates for 3,000 computers not yet failed. Which item raises the greatest certainty problem?
o: The estimated repairs of computers that haven't failed.
The cost of installing the replacement boards.
The cost of shipping and disposing of bad boards.
Repairs to computers already sold and returned.
The excess cost of the replacement boards.
oe: Correct. Problem 7-25. Each item is tested for foreseeability and proof, and the future repairs are the most speculative. Consequentials can far exceed the price.
That's a known expense.
Those are actual costs.
Those are actual costs.
That's a known expense.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Consequential items

q: A contract for a complex industrial press requires the buyer to report any defect "within 24 hours after delivery or the claim is waived." The press can't be fully tested until at least two weeks after installation. Is the 24-hour term likely enforceable?
o: Yes, because parties may always fix the time for any act.
Yes, because the buyer could hire testers to work around the clock.
Yes, because both parties are merchants.
No, because notice periods can't be shortened by agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the time isn't manifestly unreasonable.
Testing the press takes two weeks regardless.
Merchant status doesn't save a manifestly unreasonable time.
They can, within reason.

Correct. Likely not: parties may fix a time for a "reasonable time" only if it isn't manifestly unreasonable (§ 1-302(b)), and 24 hours is unreasonable for a press that takes two weeks to test. No choice says that.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fixing a "reasonable time"

q: Gobo contracts to sell Red 100 steel beams. Gobo assigns the contract to another manufacturer, which agrees to perform but never delivers. Red sues Gobo. Gobo argues that once it delegated, it was off the hook. What is the most likely result?
o: Red wins, because delegating doesn't relieve Gobo of its duty or liability.
Red wins only if the contract prohibited Gobo from delegating its duties.
Red may sue only the manufacturer, which took over the contract and promised to perform it.
Gobo wins, because a valid delegation transfers the duty entirely to the delegate.
Gobo wins, because Red never objected when Gobo assigned the contract to the manufacturer.
oe: Correct. "No delegation of performance relieves the party delegating of any duty to perform or any liability for breach" (§ 2-210(1)). See Problem 6-2(c).
Gobo remains liable whether or not delegation was permitted.
Red may sue the delegate, but it doesn't lose its claim against Gobo.
Delegation adds a party who owes the performance but doesn't release the original party.
Red's failure to object doesn't release Gobo. Only a novation, which requires Red's agreement, would do that.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegating party stays liable

q: A seller may reclaim $10,000 of goods within 10 days after delivery to an insolvent buyer, or sue for the price. It hears the goods have dropped to $6,000 in value. Which is the best advice?
o: Sue for the price, then reclaim on loss.
Reclaim, then sue for the $4,000 difference.
Reclamation is always worth more than the price.
Reclaim by self-help, to save time.
Think first, as reclaiming excludes other remedies for those goods.
oe: The 10-day window will close.
Successful reclamation bars that.
It depends on the buyer's ability to pay.
Reclamation isn't self-help.
Correct. Section 2-702(3). If the price is collectible, it may be better; if the buyer can't pay, $6,000 of goods beats an unsecured claim.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Reclamation choice

q: A buyer receives a shipment of 100 office chairs. Which of the following would NOT be an acceptance of the chairs?
o: Telling the seller it will keep the chairs despite a defect.
Failing to reject after a reasonable chance to inspect.
Keeping the chairs for a reasonable time to inspect and test them.
Bolting the chairs to an auditorium floor after noticing torn fabric.
Reselling ten of the chairs to an employee.
oe: Acceptance under § 2-606(1)(a).
Acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b).
Correct. Possession during a reasonable inspection isn't acceptance (§ 2-606(1)).
Also an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
An act inconsistent with the seller's ownership (§ 2-606(1)(c)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Not an acceptance

q: A student is unsure how § 2-719 applies. An Official Comment seems to say something slightly different from the statute's text. How should the student proceed?
o: Ignore the purposes in § 1-103(a) as mere policy.
Read the text closely, find the definitions, read it in context; the text controls.
Follow the common law, because the Code is ambiguous.
Treat other states' cases as binding on the point.
Follow the Comment, because Comments are part of the enacted law.
oe: The text directs construction to promote those purposes.

Correct. The three rules: read it all and read it again, find the definitions, and read it in context of the Code's purposes. Comments are the most important aid but aren't law, so the enacted text controls. Other states' cases are persuasive.
Section 1-103(b) supplements only where the Code doesn't displace; start with the text.
They're persuasive, valuable for uniformity, but not binding.
Comments aren't enacted; the text controls in a conflict.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Interpreting a section

q: A seller's contract prices orders at 80% of its retail price "on the day an order is accepted." Knowing it will cut retail prices tomorrow, the seller accepts a huge order today. The buyer sues for bad faith. Which is the best statement of the issue?
o: Whether the statute of frauds bars the order.
Whether the price term is unconscionable as written.
Whether the buyer rejected the goods in time.
Whether the timing was opportunistic, within the good-faith duty.
Whether the seller breached a duty to disclose in negotiations.
oe: A signed agreement exists.
The term itself looks ordinary.
Nothing has been rejected.
Correct. Problems 3-2 and 3-3. Good faith is the argument, though the seller will say it merely used an express term.
Section 1-304 doesn't reach negotiations.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Timing to exploit a price term

q: A plumber contracts to buy $40,000 of standard pipe fittings for a sewer project he has agreed to build for the town of Microville. Before delivery, Microville cancels the project. The fittings are standard items the plumber could use on other jobs. The plumber claims he is excused because his purpose has been frustrated. What is the most likely result?
o: Excused, because the only reason he bought the fittings no longer exists.
Excused under § 2-613, because the fittings can no longer be used as he intended.
He can't raise frustration, because Article 2 doesn't recognize it.
Not excused, because losing his own customer is a risk the plumber bore.
Excused under § 2-615, because the town's cancellation of the project was unforeseen.
oe: Frustration is narrow. The loss of a downstream contract usually isn't enough, especially for standard goods.
Section 2-613 concerns casualty to identified goods, which hasn't occurred.
Article 2 is supplemented by the common law of excuse under § 1-103(b).

Correct. Frustration of purpose, a common-law doctrine that supplements Article 2 through § 1-103(b), requires that the principal purpose be substantially frustrated by an event whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption of the contract. A buyer's loss of its own customer is ordinarily a risk the buyer assumes. See Problem 6-8(a).
Section 2-615 excuses sellers, and nothing makes the plumber's performance, which is paying, impracticable.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Frustration of purpose

q: A lessee repudiates as to conforming identified goods, and the goods then burn. How does § 2A-220(2) treat the loss?
o: The lease is avoided.
The lessee bears the whole loss.
The insurer bears the loss, with no shift.
The lessor may shift the insurance shortfall to the lessee.
The lessor bears the whole loss.
oe: A breach followed by loss doesn't avoid it.
It's limited to the deficiency.
The shift covers any shortfall in coverage.
Correct. It parallels § 2-510(3).
The statute lets it shift the shortfall.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Lessee default and risk

q: A student asks why Article 2 supplies a "reasonable price" when the parties leave the price open. Which pairing is correct?
o: Gap fillers override express terms in the name of fairness.
Gap fillers are mandatory rules the parties can't vary.
Express warranties are the main example of a gap filler.
Gap fillers apply only to merchants, as a penalty.
Gap fillers apply only if a gap exists, and rest on policies like efficiency.
oe: Express terms come first; gap fillers fill gaps.
The parties can generally vary them.
Express warranties aren't gap fillers.
Most apply to all sellers.

Correct. Gap fillers apply only if the agreement, with course of performance, course of dealing and usage, leaves a gap. The policies include fairness, efficiency, majoritarian guesses, neutrality and penalty defaults.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Policies behind gap fillers

q: A buyer receives a commercial unit of six matched monitors, sold only as a set. It uses four and tries to reject the other two. Which is correct?
o: It has accepted the whole unit.
It may reject the two if they are defective.
It may reject the two and keep the four.
It has rejected all six.
It owes for only four monitors.
oe: Correct. Accepting part of a commercial unit accepts the whole (§ 2-606(2)).
Defect doesn't change the unit rule.
The set is a single commercial unit.
Using goods isn't a rejection.
It accepted the unit.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Acceptance of part

q: The contract between Rowlf's Pianos and a wood supplier says the price "includes delivery." In the lumber trade, delivery is usually billed separately. The supplier bills Rowlf for delivery anyway. Who wins?
o: Neither, because the conflict makes the price term too indefinite.
The supplier, because usage of trade supplements every contract in that trade, including this one.
Rowlf, but only if Rowlf was unaware of the usage.
The supplier, because Rowlf should have known the usage.
Rowlf, because express terms control over an inconsistent usage of trade.
oe: The express term is clear.
It supplements terms; it doesn't override them.
Rowlf wins either way.
Knowledge of the usage doesn't beat an express term.
Correct. § 1-303(e): express terms prevail over course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Express term vs. usage of trade

q: A gallery agrees to sell a specific etching to a collector, with payment due on delivery the next day. That evening, the etching's true owner, from whom it had been stolen years earlier, recovers it from the gallery by court order. The gallery argues the contract is avoided as a casualty to identified goods. What is the most likely result?
o: The collector must pay, because the etching was identified to the contract when it was made.
The gallery isn't excused, because it never had good title and so breached the title warranty.
The gallery is excused if it acted in good faith and didn't know the etching was stolen.
The contract is avoided, because the loss happened before risk passed and without the gallery's fault.
The contract is avoided under § 2-615, because performance became impossible for the gallery.
oe: The collector never received the etching, and the gallery couldn't deliver good title.

Correct. Section 2-613 covers casualty such as fire, flood, or theft, without fault of either party. A seller that never had good title can't pass it, and the reclamation reveals a breach of the § 2-312 warranty. See Problem 6-6(b).
Good faith isn't a defense to breach of the title warranty.
Recovery by the true owner exposes the seller's own title defect. It isn't a fortuitous casualty.
The impossibility comes from the seller's own lack of title, which is a risk the seller bears.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Goods reclaimed by their owner isn't a casualty

q: Which statement about the records used to satisfy § 2-201 is most accurate?
o: An unsigned writing satisfies the rule if both parties drafted it.
Only one document may be used, and it must contain every term.
Email can't satisfy the rule unless it bears a handwritten signature.
Connected writings may be read together if a signed one links them.
None of the above.
oe: The record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought.
Several papers may be read together if they are connected.
A record includes email, and a typed name is a signature.
Correct. In Casazza, the signed license could not be read with the unsigned typed terms because it never referred to the boat sale.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Several writings

q: An ordinary equipment lease says: "Lessee bears all risk of loss and must insure for Lessor's benefit." A fire destroys the goods. Which is correct?
o: The insurer bears it, whatever the lease says.
The lessor bears it, since the rule is mandatory.
The lessee bears the loss, as parties often shift risk by agreement.
The lessor bears it unless the lessee is a merchant.
The clause turns the deal into a sale.
oe: That depends on the policy.
It's a default.
Correct. Section 2A-219's default yields, and § 2A-218(5) lets the parties set insurance. Taking risk of loss alone doesn't create a security interest (§ 1-203(c)(2)).
Merchant status isn't the test.
Section 1-203(c)(2) says no.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXI · Lease performance: risk, excuse & transfers (§§ 2A-219 to 2A-221, 2A-303) — Risk with a lease clause

q: Beaker agrees to be the exclusive distributor of Honeydew Labs' safety goggles in his state. The contract says nothing about effort. What duty does § 2-306(2) impose?
o: None, because the contract is silent on effort.
Only Beaker must use best efforts to promote sales.
Both must use best efforts: Beaker to sell, Honeydew to supply.
Each party must use reasonable care, but neither must use best efforts.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-306(2) fills the gap.
The duty runs both ways.
Correct. A lawful exclusive-dealing agreement imposes best efforts on both sides unless otherwise agreed.
The standard is best efforts.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Exclusive dealing

q: A buyer pays partly with a trade-in. How does § 2-718(4) treat it?
o: It counts only for consumer buyers.
It must be returned in kind in every case.
It counts at its reasonable value or resale proceeds.
It counts at double its market value.
It isn't counted as a payment at all.
oe: Section 2-718(4) applies to any buyer.
The statute treats it as payment.
Correct. A seller who has notice of the buyer's breach before reselling must follow § 2-706.
There's no multiplier.
Section 2-718(4) counts it.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Payment in goods

q: A seller tenders all 100 bushels the contract calls for. The buyer arrives with a small truck and wants to take half today and half tomorrow. Has the seller made a proper tender?
o: Yes, provided the buyer pays for all 100 bushels in advance.
No, because the buyer has a right to take the goods in installments.
No, because the seller must reasonably accommodate the buyer's truck.
Yes, because delivery is in a single lot unless otherwise agreed.
None of the above.
oe: Payment is due on tender; prepayment is not the issue.
§ 2-307 says otherwise unless the parties agree.
The buyer must furnish suitable facilities.
Correct. Problem 4-4.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Single lot: buyer wants partial

q: Which language is sufficient to disclaim the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose if it is in a conspicuous writing?
o: A clear disclaimer of fitness printed in small type on the back of the order form.
"There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof."
An oral statement by the salesperson that "this sale has no warranties."
"Seller disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability."
None of the above.
oe: That wouldn't be conspicuous.
Correct. § 2-316(2): a fitness disclaimer must be in writing and conspicuous, but need not mention fitness.
Fitness disclaimers must be written.
That covers merchantability only.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fitness disclaimer

q: An invoice says, "Title remains with Seller until paid." The buyer, who received the goods, is in default. The seller wants them back. Which is correct?
o: It holds a security interest at most, and must follow Article 9.
It remains the owner and can sue in conversion.
It may enter by force, as owner.
The clause is void, leaving only the price.
It may reclaim only within 10 days.
oe: Correct. Sections 1-201(b)(35), 2-401(1), 9-109(a)(5). It may repossess without breach of the peace under § 9-609, if a security interest exists.
Title passes on delivery.
Breach of the peace bars that.
It's recharacterized, not void.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Title clause and repossession

q: A buyer needing parts doesn't cover after the seller repudiates, and instead shuts down its line and sues. Which is correct?
o: It may claim market damages, but avoidable consequential losses are barred.
It must wait for the performance date before any claim arises.
It may recover only the price it paid, if any.
It has no remedy, because cover is mandatory mitigation.
It may recover all its shutdown losses, because cover is optional.
oe: Correct. Section 2-712(3): failure to cover doesn't bar other remedies. But § 2-715(2)(a) limits consequential damages to losses that could not reasonably be prevented "by cover or otherwise."
A repudiation may be treated as a breach at once (§ 2-610).
Market damages under § 2-713 remain available.
Section 2-712(3): failure to cover doesn't bar other remedies.
Optional or not, § 2-715(2)(a) excludes losses preventable by cover.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Failure to cover not fatal

q: Julia buys a new SUV from a dealer. The manufacturer's warranty, which limits her remedy to repair and states in bold capitals that consequential damages are excluded, is printed only in the owner's manual in the glove box. Nothing in the sale documents mentions it, and she never sees it until weeks later. Repairs fail repeatedly. In a state following the independent approach, is the consequential-damages exclusion enforceable?
o: Yes, because under the independent approach the exclusion survives the failure of the repair remedy.
Probably not, because a limitation the buyer couldn't see until after contracting is procedurally unconscionable however clear its type.
Yes, because Julia could have asked to read the warranty before buying.
Yes, because it was printed in bold capitals.
No, because consequential-damages exclusions are never enforceable in consumer sales.
oe: It survives the failure only if it isn't unconscionable, and this one likely is.

Correct. Even under the independent approach, the exclusion falls if it's unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). A limitation available to the buyer only after she made the contract is unconscionable however conspicuous it is.
Nothing showed the warranty was available to her before signing, and that's the decisive fact.
Clear type doesn't help when the buyer had no chance to see the term before contracting.
They're enforceable unless unconscionable; only personal-injury exclusions in consumer goods are prima facie unconscionable.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Exclusion seen only after sale

q: A homeowner contracted with Anthony Pools to build a swimming pool. Services predominated, but the contract included a diving board, which was defective and injured the homeowner. Under the gravamen-of-the-claim test, what result?
o: Article 2 does not apply, because the predominant purpose of the contract was services.
Article 2 applies to the whole contract, including the construction work.
No warranty applies, because the homeowner is a consumer.
Article 2 applies to this claim, because it concerns the diving board.
None of the above.
oe: That is the predominant-purpose result. The gravamen test asks instead whether the claim concerns the goods.
The gravamen test sorts the claims. It applies Article 2 only to the claim about the goods.
Consumers get Article 2 warranties too.
Correct. In Anthony Pools (note case), the Maryland court applied the merchantability warranty to the unmerchantable diving board even though services predominated.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Gravamen test

q: A seller of specialized medical gloves delegates its duty to supply a hospital to a little-known manufacturer that the hospital has never dealt with. The contract doesn't prohibit delegation, and the hospital has no substantial interest in the original seller's personal performance. What may the hospital do?
o: Demand assurance from the original seller, but never from the new manufacturer.
Refuse all deliveries until the original seller agrees in writing to remain liable.
Nothing, because the delegation was permitted and the hospital has no substantial interest.
Cancel the contract, because delegating performance to a stranger is a breach.
Demand adequate assurance from the new manufacturer, while keeping its rights against the seller.
oe: Section 2-210(6) expressly allows a demand on the assignee.
The original seller remains liable automatically under § 2-210(1).
A permitted delegation still gives the hospital the right to demand assurance.
A permitted delegation isn't a breach.

Correct. The other party "may treat any assignment which delegates performance as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and may without prejudice to his rights against the assignor demand assurances from the assignee" (§ 2-210(6)).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegation as grounds for insecurity

q: A buyer prepays the full $50,000 price for custom shelving. The contract says, "Neither party may assign any right under this contract." Before delivery, the buyer sells its business and assigns its right to receive the shelving to the new owner. The seller refuses to deliver to the new owner. What is the most likely result?
o: Effective despite the clause, because the buyer has fully performed its side of the contract.
Ineffective, because a right to receive goods, unlike a right to payment, can never be assigned.
Ineffective, because the contract expressly prohibits either party from assigning any right.
The assignment breaches the contract, so the seller may keep the price and refuse to deliver.
Effective, but only if the seller consents, because the contract contains an anti-assignment clause.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-210(2), "a right to damages for breach of the whole contract or a right arising out of the assignor's due performance of his entire obligation can be assigned despite agreement otherwise." Having paid in full, the buyer has fully performed.
Rights to goods can be assigned, subject to § 2-210(2)'s limits.
The full-performance exception in § 2-210(2) overrides the clause.
Because the exception applies, the assignment is effective and the seller must deliver.
Consent isn't required when the exception applies.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Assignment after full performance

q: A lessor defaults with 12 months left at $2,000 a month. The lessee buys a replacement for $30,000. Market rent for an identical 12-month term is $2,300. Ignoring PV, what are direct damages?
o: Nothing, as the lessee bought.
$3,600, under the market-rent formula.
$27,600, the market rent.
$30,000, the cost of the purchase.
$6,000, the purchase less remaining rent.
oe: The market-rent formula applies.
Correct. A purchase isn't cover in a lease, so § 2A-519 applies: $300 × 12.
The lessee recovers the difference.
A purchase isn't measured as cover.
That's the Article 2 style of formula.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Cover vs. market choice

q: Uncle Traveling Matt orally agrees to buy 100 hiking packs from Cantus's Outfitters for $6,000. He pays $2,400 for 40 packs, and Cantus's accepts the payment. Cantus's then refuses to deliver any packs, and Matt sues. There's no writing, and Cantus's denies the deal in its pleadings. To what extent is the contract enforceable?
o: Not at all, because there's no writing.
Only as to the 40 packs that were paid for.
As to all 100 packs, because part performance takes the whole contract out of the statute.
As to all 100, because Cantus's accepted payment.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2-201(3)(c) makes the paid-for portion enforceable.

Correct. A contract that doesn't satisfy § 2-201(1) is enforceable "with respect to goods for which payment has been made and accepted or which have been received and accepted" (§ 2-201(3)(c)). The exception doesn't reach the other 60.
Article 2's part-performance exception is limited to the goods paid for or received.
Acceptance of payment validates only the goods covered by that payment.
One of the other choices is correct: Only as to the 40 packs that were paid for.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Part performance: only to the extent paid

q: Kermit "sells" his delivery van to Fozzie Finance for $10,000. The agreement requires Kermit to buy the van back in one year for $11,500, and Kermit keeps using the van in his business the whole time. Which law most likely governs?
o: UCC Article 2, because the agreement expressly calls the transaction a sale.
The common law, because vans are titled under state law.
UCC Article 2A, because Kermit keeps using the van.
UCC Article 9, because the transaction is in substance a secured loan.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control. A "sale" with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is in substance a loan.
Certificate-of-title rules do not change the nature of the transaction.
This is not a true lease either. Kermit is the borrower and the van secures repayment.
Correct. A sale with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is a disguised security interest, governed by Article 9, not Article 2 (§ 2-102(3)(a)).
D is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Disguised security interest

q: Seller ships goods and keeps a negotiable bill of lading to its own order until Buyer pays. Which statement about § 2-505 is correct?
o: Title stays with the seller until the buyer pays in full.
Seller's act is a breach of the shipment contract.
Risk of loss stays with the seller until payment.
The buyer loses all right to inspect before paying.
Seller in effect keeps a security interest, and inspection isn't lost.
oe: Section 2-401 limits the reservation to a security interest.
Shipment under reservation is allowed.
Section 2-509(1) says reservation doesn't change risk.
Section 2-310(b) preserves it.
Correct. Section 2-505(1) gives the seller a security interest in effect, holding the documents until paid. It doesn't take away the buyer's right to inspect before payment (§ 2-310(b)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Shipment under reservation

q: Herry buys a camera from a camera store, explaining that he needs a battery that lasts four hours for wedding shoots. The clerk recommends this model. The battery lasts one hour, which is normal for this camera. Which warranty is most clearly breached?
o: The warranty of good title and against encumbrances.
The warranty against infringement of third-party patents.
The implied warranty of merchantability under § 2-314.
The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose (§ 2-315).
None of the above.
oe: Title would be breached if the camera were stolen. Nothing suggests that.
No infringement claim here.
A one-hour battery may be normal for this camera, so it may be fit for ordinary purposes.
Correct. This is the outline's camera example: a battery that won't last the four hours the buyer needs breaches § 2-315.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Which warranty

q: A buyer orders 100 units at $10 and receives 90, which it accepts without complaint and notifies the seller of the shortage the next week. Which correctly states its position?
o: It owes $1,000, the full contract price.
It must now accept any later 10 units.
It owes $900, and may claim its loss from the shortfall.
It owes nothing, since the tender failed.
It has revoked by giving notice.
oe: It doesn't owe for what it never received.
The seller's right to cure may have ended with the contract time.

Correct. It owes the rate for goods accepted (§ 2-607(1)) and has § 2-714(1) damages for the nonconforming tender, on notice. Cover isn't available for accepted goods, but the 10 undelivered units can be treated as nondelivery under § 2-711.
It accepted the 90.
Notice of breach isn't revocation.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Short delivery accepted

q: A buyer in Denver rejects on arrival under a contract that is F.O.B. Omaha. It doesn't cover. Where is the market price taken?
o: Wherever the seller is located.
Denver, the place of arrival.
The place where the contract was signed.
Omaha, the place for tender.
The average of the Omaha and Denver prices.
oe: The seller's location isn't a § 2-713 reference point.
Correct. Section 2-713(2): place for tender, or place of arrival in the case of rejection after arrival or revocation.
The place of contracting isn't relevant.
That's the general rule, not the one after rejection on arrival.
There's no averaging rule.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Place after rejection on arrival

q: In Razor v. Hyundai, a car's repair-or-replace warranty failed of its essential purpose. What did the court hold about the separate exclusion of consequential damages?
o: It survives unless unconscionable, and here it was unconscionable.
It was valid, because consumers may waive consequential damages.
It automatically fell along with the failed remedy.
The exclusion was valid because it was in clear capital letters.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Razor adopted the independent approach, then found the exclusion unconscionable because the buyer couldn't see it before signing.
Consumer status cuts the other way, and the court found this exclusion unconscionable.
That's the dependent approach, which the court rejected.
Capitals don't help if the buyer couldn't see it.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Razor

q: To disclaim the implied warranty of merchantability under § 2-316(2), a seller must:
o: use the words "as is" and also mention fitness.
use both the words "fitness" and "merchantability."
mention merchantability and, if written, make it conspicuous.
put the disclaimer in a signed writing.
obtain the buyer's separate signature on the disclaimer.
oe: "As is" is a separate route under § 2-316(3)(a), and mentioning fitness isn't required to disclaim merchantability.
Fitness is a separate warranty.
An oral disclaimer can work.
A separate signature is required for a NOM clause on a merchant's form (§ 2-209(2)), not for a disclaimer.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Merchantability disclaimer

q: Under § 2-301, the buyer's basic obligation is to:
o: resell the goods if they are nonconforming.
transfer and deliver in accordance with the contract.
inspect the goods before accepting them.
insure the goods from the time of contracting.
accept and pay in accordance with the contract.
oe: That's a limited duty under § 2-603.
That's the seller's obligation.
Inspection is a right, not the basic duty.
No such duty exists.
Correct. The seller's obligation is to transfer and deliver.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Buyer's basic duties

q: Under § 2A-103(1)(j), which of the following is a "lease"?
o: A transfer of the right to possess and use goods for a term in return for consideration.
A sale on approval with a right of return.
A gratuitous loan of goods to a friend for a month.
A sale in which the seller retains a security interest.
A transfer of title to goods for a price paid over time.
oe: Correct. A sale, a sale on approval or return, and a retained or created security interest aren't leases. The lessor keeps a residual interest.
The definition expressly excludes sales on approval or return.
A lease requires consideration.
The definition expressly excludes the retention of a security interest.
A transfer of title for a price is a sale (§ 2-106(1)).
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Definition of a lease

q: A buyer offers a trade association's report to prove a usage. The seller objects that it had no notice of the report. Which is the proper analysis?
o: Express terms always yield to usage of trade.
Usage evidence is barred if any writing exists.
Ask if it exists, if it's admissible with notice, and if it's consistent.
Usage can be proved only by a written trade code.
Usage evidence is always admissible with no notice requirement.
oe: Under § 1-303(e), express terms prevail.
The parol evidence rule lets it explain or supplement.

Correct. Three questions: is there enough evidence of the usage; is it admissible (§ 1-303(g) notice to prevent unfair surprise, and the parol evidence rule); and is it consistent with the express terms? Such usages give meaning to, supplement and qualify terms (§ 1-303(d)).
Any competent evidence can prove it.
Section 1-303(g) requires notice.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Two questions on course evidence

q: An oil company sets the price its franchise dealers must pay for gasoline. The price is within the range competitors charge, but the dealers prove the company set it in order to drive them out of business. How do courts divide on whether the price was set in good faith under § 2-305(2)?
