o: All courts hold a price within the competitive range is in good faith.
Courts agree that § 2-305(2) doesn't apply to franchise agreements at all.
All courts hold that an improper motive always establishes bad faith in pricing.
Courts split; Mathis looked at motive, but most courts look only at the price.
None of the above.
oe: Mathis v. Exxon held otherwise.
Mathis applied it.
Shell v. HRN and Autry v. BP reject that view.

Correct. Mathis v. Exxon held that an intent to drive dealers out takes the case outside Comment 3's safe harbor, but the majority (Shell v. HRN; Autry v. BP) holds a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Mathis vs. majority

q: A contract calls for a seller to ship 2,000 cases of olive oil on a named ocean carrier from a particular port. Before shipment, that carrier goes out of business, but another reputable carrier at the same port can carry the goods on a similar schedule at a similar cost. The seller ships on the substitute carrier. Must the buyer accept the tender?
o: No, because the seller first had to try to get the original carrier to resume service.
Yes, but only if the buyer agreed in writing to the change of carrier before shipment.
No, because the contract named a specific carrier, so shipping on any other one is nonconforming.
No, because the agreed carrier's failure excuses the seller from performing at all.
Yes, because a commercially reasonable substitute carrier must be tendered and accepted.
oe: The statute asks only whether a commercially reasonable substitute is available.
Section 2-614(1) needs no agreement.
Section 2-614(1) requires acceptance of a commercially reasonable substitute.
Excuse isn't available when a reasonable substitute exists. Substitute performance is required.
Correct. Where "an agreed type of carrier becomes unavailable ... but a commercially reasonable substitute is available, such substitute performance must be tendered and accepted" (§ 2-614(1)).
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Substituted performance

q: Grover's Mill has a three-year contract to supply "all the flour required by Cookie Monster's Bakery," a single shop. Cookie assigns his rights under the contract to Mega Bakes Corp., which runs 40 bakeries and plans to fill all of their flour needs under it. Grover objects. Is the assignment effective?
o: Yes, because the contract doesn't prohibit assignment.
No, because a requirements contract lacks mutuality and so is unenforceable by any assignee.
No, because it would materially change Grover's duty and materially increase his burden.
Yes, because a buyer's right to receive goods is always freely assignable.
Yes, as long as Mega Bakes's requirements are ordered in good faith.
oe: Silence removes only the contract limit. The statutory limit on material changes in the other party's duty still applies.
Requirements contracts are enforceable (§ 2-306). The problem is the change in Grover's duty, not mutuality.

Correct. Rights can't be assigned when the assignment would materially change the other party's duty or materially increase its burden or risk (§ 2-210(2)). Swapping one shop's requirements for 40 bakeries' requirements does both (see § 2-210 cmt. 4).
It is assignable only within the § 2-210(2) limits, which this assignment exceeds.
Good faith governs quantity under § 2-306, but it doesn't cure an assignment that materially changes the seller's duty.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Requirements contract assigned

q: A contract for a commercial ice machine says: "Seller's liability for late delivery shall not exceed $5,000." The machine arrives 10 days late, and the buyer proves $1,200 in actual damages from the delay. How much can the buyer recover?
o: $5,000, unless the seller proves the buyer's actual loss was smaller.
$2,500, half the cap, as a reasonable estimate of delay damages.
Nothing, because a cap is unenforceable unless it is conspicuous.
oe: Correct. "Shall not exceed" language is a cap, a limitation of remedy under § 2-719, not liquidated damages. The buyer must prove actual damages and recovers them up to the cap.
That treats the cap as liquidated damages with a rebuttal. A cap never awards more than proven loss.
The buyer would recover $5,000 only if the clause fixed damages at that sum. A cap sets a ceiling, not an amount.
Nothing supports splitting the cap. The buyer recovers what it proves, up to $5,000.
Remedy limitations, like liquidated damages clauses, need not be conspicuous.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Cap vs. liquidated damages

q: A seller repudiates on March 1 a contract for 1,000 units at $10, for delivery June 1, F.O.B. seller's city. Prices at seller's city: March 1, $12; April 1 (a commercially reasonable time later), $13; June 1, $16. Prices at buyer's city run $1 higher. The buyer doesn't cover. Under the approach in Cosden Oil, what are direct damages?
oe: That combines the performance date with the wrong place.
That's the performance-date approach (Hess Energy).
That uses the repudiation date, a reading outside the class materials.
That wrongly uses the buyer's city, which isn't the place for tender.
Correct. Cosden uses a commercially reasonable time after repudiation: $13 minus $10 × 1,000, at the place for tender, which is the seller's city.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Market date, three prices

q: Abby, a florist, signs and sends Rosita an order: "Please send 1,000 tulip bulbs at $1 each." Rosita, who is not a merchant, never signs anything. Later Abby refuses to accept the bulbs, and Rosita sues. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Rosita can satisfy § 2-201(1) because Abby signed a sufficient record.
Rosita wins automatically, because the statute of frauds is satisfied.
Rosita loses, because Rosita herself never signed a record.
Rosita loses, because the confirmation exception requires two merchants.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Abby's signed order shows a contract for sale and states a quantity.
Satisfying the statute of frauds only opens the courthouse door. Rosita still must prove the contract.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought must sign.
Rosita doesn't need the exception. Abby's own signed record satisfies § 2-201(1).
A is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Signed by party to be charged

q: Which statement about default in a lease is correct?
o: Default can never be defined by the lease.
A lessee's remedies are all exclusive.
Only the common law defines default.
The lease and Article 2A define default, and no notice is generally due.
A party must always give notice of default.
oe: Section 2A-501(1) lets it.
They're cumulative (§ 2A-501(4)).
The agreement and the Article control.
Correct. Sections 2A-501(1), 2A-502. Remedies are cumulative, subject to § 1-305(a). Lessee's remedies are in § 2A-508, and the parties may add others.
Section 2A-502 says otherwise.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Default source

q: Article 2A is modeled on Article 2. According to the text, what single fact explains most of the differences between them?
o: Leases are governed mainly by federal law.
Leases cover only titled goods such as cars.
Article 2A was written before Article 2.
Leases are always consumer transactions.
In a lease, the lessor gets the goods back.
oe: State enactments of Article 2A govern, with some federal consumer overlay.
Article 2A covers goods generally, and its title provisions are an add-on.
Article 2A is the later statute, modeled on Article 2.
Most leases discussed in the text are commercial, and consumer status matters only for specific rules.
Correct. The study question is where Article 2A differs and why. The lessor's residual interest drives the rules on remedies, rent and repossession.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Why Article 2A differs

q: A credit seller with no security interest learns on day 15 after delivery that the buyer was insolvent on receipt. A credit seller with a perfected security interest learns the same thing the same day, after default. What can each do?
o: Both may use self-help under § 2-716.
The first may reclaim; the second must sue for the price.
Neither has a remedy against the goods.
The first is too late; the second may repossess.
Both may reclaim under § 2-702.
oe: That's a buyer's section.
That's reversed.
The secured seller has one.
Correct. Section 2-702(2)'s 10 days ran. Section 9-609 lets the secured seller repossess peaceably or by court action.
The first is out of time.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Security interest vs. reclamation

q: Telly sells his old bicycle to his neighbor Zoe at a yard sale for $40. Neither of them has ever sold a bicycle before. Does Article 2 govern the sale?
o: No, because the bicycle is used rather than new goods.
No, because the price is under the $500 threshold.
Yes, because Article 2 applies to transactions in goods.
No, because Article 2 requires at least one merchant.
Yes, but the sale must be evidenced by a writing.
oe: Used goods are still goods.
The $500 figure is the statute of frauds threshold (§ 2-201), not a limit on Article 2's scope.
Correct. Article 2 covers merchant-to-merchant, merchant-to-consumer, consumer-to-merchant, and consumer-to-consumer sales (Problem 1-4).
Article 2's scope never depends on merchant status (Problem 1-4). Merchant status matters for particular rules, such as § 2-314.
Writing goes to enforceability under § 2-201 (and this sale is under $500 anyway), not to scope.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Garage sale: scope ignores merchant status

q: A farmer agrees to sell 100 bushels of wheat to a miller. The contract doesn't say where delivery will occur. When it's made, the wheat is in the farmer's barn on the farm where he does business. Later, the farmer moves the wheat to a storage site 300 miles away and calls the miller: "Your wheat is ready. Pick it up at the storage site." Has the farmer made a proper tender?
o: Yes, because the farmer told the miller exactly where the wheat was and that it was ready.
No, because absent agreement the place for delivery is the seller's place of business.
Yes, because the seller is free to choose where to tender delivery when the contract is silent.
No, because when the contract is silent the seller must deliver the goods to the buyer's mill.
Yes, because the wheat was identified to the contract, so it could be tendered wherever it sat.
oe: Notice is necessary but doesn't make an improper place proper.

Correct. The place for delivery is the seller's place of business (§ 2-308(a)), unless the contract is for identified goods known by both parties when contracting to be elsewhere (§ 2-308(b)). The storage site wasn't known when they contracted. See Problem 4-4(a)(4).
The manner, time, and place of tender are set by the agreement and Article 2 (§ 2-503(1)), not by the seller alone.
Absent agreement, Article 2 doesn't require delivery at the buyer's place.
Identification doesn't change the place for delivery.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Tender at a different place

q: A sawmill agrees to sell its entire output of wood chips to a paper company at a fixed price. The sawmill's costs rise, so it loses money on every ton. It shuts down its chip line solely to stop those losses, though it still has plenty of logs and lumber orders. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The shutdown is a breach only if the paper company covers.
The shutdown is in good faith, because a seller need not keep operating a line that loses money on every ton.
The shutdown is fine, because output contracts set no minimum.
The shutdown is likely in bad faith, because cutting losses alone doesn't justify it.
None of the above.
oe: Cover is a remedy, not an element of breach.
Merely curtailing losses isn't a good-faith reason under § 2-306.
Good faith limits reductions.
Correct. A shutdown for lack of orders can be good faith; one merely to cut losses isn't (cmt. 2).
D is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Output: shutdown to cut losses

q: Grover agrees to buy a specific antique carousel horse from a merchant seller, to be picked up next week. Before pickup, a storm leaks through the seller's roof and the water damages the horse's paint without either party's fault. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Grover may accept the horse at the full price and also sue the seller for the cost of repainting.
Grover may avoid the contract or take the horse at a reduced price, with no further claim.
Grover must pay the full price, because the horse was identified when the contract was made.
The contract is automatically avoided, because the horse was damaged before risk passed.
None of the above.
oe: When accepting with an allowance, the buyer has no further right against the seller.

Correct. When identified goods suffer a partial casualty without fault before risk passes, the buyer may demand inspection and either avoid the contract or accept the goods "with due allowance from the contract price for the deterioration" but "without further right against the seller" (§ 2-613(b)).
Risk hadn't passed, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods (§ 2-509(3)).
Automatic avoidance applies only to a total loss (§ 2-613(a)).
One of the other choices is correct: Grover may avoid the contract or take the horse at a reduced price, with no further claim.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Partial casualty to identified goods

q: Oscar steals Telly's bicycle and sells it to Herry, who pays fair value and has no idea it was stolen. Telly finds the bicycle and sues Herry to get it back. Who wins?
o: Herry, because he is a good-faith purchaser for value.
Herry, because Oscar had voidable title.
Telly, provided he reported the theft to the police.
It depends on whether Herry had notice of Telly's interest.
None of the above.
oe: Good-faith purchase protects a buyer only from a seller with voidable title, not a thief.
A thief has void title, not voidable title.
Reporting the theft doesn't matter. A thief has void title whether or not the owner reported it.
Notice is irrelevant when the seller is a thief.
Correct. Telly wins because a thief has void title and passes nothing, even to a good-faith purchaser for value (§ 2-403(1)). C adds a condition the law doesn't impose.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Title: thief

q: A seller of used forklifts invites buyers to "look around the lot." Waldorf buys one without examining it at all. The seller never asked him to examine it. It turns out to have a cracked mast that a quick look would have revealed. The seller argues Waldorf lost his implied warranties by refusing to examine. Is the seller right?
o: No, because a buyer's examination of the goods never has any effect on implied warranties.
Yes, because a quick look at the forklift would have revealed the cracked mast to anyone.
No, because failing to inspect isn't a refusal unless the seller demanded an inspection.
Yes, because used forklifts are sold without implied warranties unless the seller gives one.
Yes, because inviting buyers to look around the lot is a demand that they examine the goods.
oe: Examination or refusal after a demand can exclude warranties as to defects that inspection ought to reveal (§ 2-316(3)(b)).
Without a demand, the buyer's failure to look doesn't exclude the warranty.
Correct. Comment 8 to § 2-316 explains that a buyer doesn't refuse to examine merely by not doing so. The seller must demand that the buyer examine the goods fully. See Problem 5-3.
Used goods sold by a merchant carry the merchantability warranty, adjusted to their age and condition.
A general invitation isn't a demand that this buyer examine these goods.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — No inspection without a demand

q: A buyer accepted goods tendered two weeks late. No warranty is involved. What is the measure?
o: The market price when learned minus the contract price.
The loss in the ordinary course of events, in any reasonable manner.
Nothing, because the buyer chose to accept the goods.
The cost of cover minus the contract price.
Value as warranted minus value as accepted.
oe: Section 2-713 doesn't apply to accepted goods.
Correct. Section 2-714(1) handles any nonconforming tender such as late or short delivery. Subsection (2) is the warranty formula.
Acceptance doesn't waive damages for late tender.
Cover isn't available for accepted goods.
That's the warranty formula; no warranty is involved.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — § 2-714(1) vs. (2)

q: Elmo and Zoe orally agree to a sale of 100 units for $1,000. Before delivery they orally agree to reduce the order to 40 units for $400. Is the modification enforceable?
o: Yes, because the contract as modified is under $500.
No, because the modification lacks new consideration.
No, because a reduction in quantity must be in a signed writing.
No, because the original contract was for $500 or more.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-4(b). § 2-209(3) asks whether the contract as modified is within § 2-201.
No consideration is needed (§ 2-209(1)).
Only if the modified contract is within the statute of frauds.
What matters is the contract as modified.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and SOF: down to $400

q: Why might a seller structure a consumer deal as a lease, according to the text?
o: An international convention preempts state lease law.
Lessees can't sue lessors for any reason.
Regulation M exempts all consumer leases.
Magnuson-Moss and lemon laws might not apply to leases.
Article 2A preempts all consumer-protection statutes.
oe: No convention governs leases of goods.
They have many remedies under Part 5.
Regulation M applies to consumer leases.

Correct. Article 2A generally defers to certificate-of-title and consumer-protection law (§§ 2A-104, 2A-105; 15 U.S.C. §§ 1667-1667f; Regulation M). No international convention governs leases of goods.
Section 2A-104 defers to them.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Other law

q: In Casazza v. Kiser, the buyer argued that the seller's acceptance of payment for a navigation software license satisfied the part-performance exception for the sale of a sailboat. Why did the court reject that argument?
o: Because the software and the boat were not a single commercial unit.
Because Article 2 does not apply to sales between individuals.
Because the software license was never signed by the seller.
Because the seller had admitted the contract in his deposition.
Because promissory estoppel is the only exception to the statute of frauds.
oe: Correct. The software was bought years after the boat and the boat was later sold without it, so part performance as to the software didn't reach the boat.
Article 2 applied even though both parties were individuals.
The license was the one document both parties did sign.
The buyer only hoped the seller would admit the deal; there was no admission.
The court rejected promissory estoppel too.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Casazza

q: Under § 2-305(2), when a contract gives one party the power to fix the price, that party must:
o: fix the lowest price on the market.
obtain the other party's approval.
fix a price no higher than its price for the prior year.
fix a price within 10% of the market price.
fix the price in good faith.
oe: Good faith doesn't require the lowest price; Comment 3 treats a posted or market price as good faith in the normal case.
Approval is not required.
There is no such cap; the test is good faith.
There is no percentage rule.
Correct. § 2-305(2). Comment 3 adds that in the normal case a posted or market price satisfies good faith.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Price set by one party

q: Seller contracts to sell Buyer 1,000 widgets at $10 each, delivery June 1. Seller fails to deliver. On June 1 the market price is $14. Buyer doesn't cover. What are Buyer's basic damages under § 2-713?
o: $10,000, the contract price, plus incidental damages.
Nothing, because Buyer chose not to cover.
$14,000, the market value of the widgets.
$4,000, plus incidental and consequential damages.
None of the above.
oe: That is the contract price.
Cover is optional.
That is the market value.
Correct. § 2-713: market price minus contract price, (14 − 10) × 1,000, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Market damages

q: Which sale allows reclamation under § 2-507 rather than § 2-702?
o: A 30-day credit sale to an insolvent buyer.
A sale for payment on delivery, by a check that bounces.
A sale on a post-dated check.
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Failed payment under a cash sale.
That's a credit term.
Only the second qualifies.
The second qualifies.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Check vs. credit

q: A signed contract for 100 steel beams at $20,000 says: "Seller may not assign this contract." Seller then assigns its right to the $20,000 payment to Sesame Bank, and the bank notifies the buyer. The buyer argues the assignment is ineffective. What is the most likely result?
o: Effective, because a ban on assigning "the contract" is read to bar only delegating the seller's duties.
Ineffective, because the contract expressly prohibits the seller from assigning it.
Ineffective, because assigning the payment materially increases the buyer's burden.
Effective, but it also delegates the seller's duty to deliver the beams to the bank.
Effective only if the buyer consents in writing to the assignment of the payment.
oe: Correct. "Unless the circumstances indicate the contrary, a prohibition of assignment of 'the contract' is to be construed as barring only the delegation to the assignee of the assignor's performance" (§ 2-210(4)). Assigning the right to payment is outside it.
Section 2-210(4) reads the clause narrowly, as a bar on delegation only.
Assigning a right to payment normally doesn't change the buyer's duty at all.
The seller assigned only the right to payment. It didn't assign the contract generally.
An assignment of rights doesn't need the other party's consent.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — "May not assign this contract" bars only delegation

q: The Count, an antiques dealer, contracts to sell Telly a specific grandfather clock, to be picked up the next week. Before pickup, lightning strikes the shop and destroys the clock. Neither party was at fault. What is the effect?
o: The Count is in breach, because a merchant seller bears the risk until receipt.
The contract is avoided, because identified goods were totally destroyed without fault before risk passed.
Telly must pay, because the clock was identified to the contract.
The Count must deliver a comparable clock.
None of the above.
oe: Risk was the Count's, but § 2-613 excuses the Count.
Correct. § 2-613(a); Problem 6-6(a).
Risk hadn't passed to Telly.
The contract was for this unique clock.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Casualty: no fault

q: While selling Kermit a used lathe, a machinery dealer says aloud: "Understand there's no warranty of merchantability on this one, and it isn't guaranteed fit for any particular job." The written contract says nothing about warranties. Which implied warranties were effectively disclaimed?
o: Fitness only, because merchantability disclaimers must be written.
Neither, because every disclaimer must be in a conspicuous writing.
Both, because the dealer clearly told Kermit about each warranty before the sale, and Kermit agreed.
Merchantability only, because a fitness disclaimer must be in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability disclaimers may be oral.
Only a written merchantability disclaimer must be conspicuous.
A fitness disclaimer must be in writing.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Oral disclaimers

q: Under a lease, Tenant may buy the property at a bargain price if Landlord refuses Tenant's request to finance improvements. Tenant knows that Landlord's manager has forgotten this clause. Tenant sends a financing request without mentioning the clause, Landlord refuses, and Tenant exercises the bargain option. Under Market Street Associates v. Frey, what is the most likely result?
o: Tenant wins, because Landlord is charged with knowing its own contract.
Tenant wins, because good faith never applies once a contract is signed.
Tenant wins, because good faith governs only the negotiation of a contract.
Tenant loses, because good faith requires Tenant to act as Landlord's fiduciary.
None of the above.
oe: Market Street rejected that view where the other side deliberately exploits a known oversight.
The duty of good faith applies to performance.
Backwards. Good faith governs performance and enforcement, not negotiation (§ 1-304).
Good faith lies between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud.

Correct. Tenant loses if it deliberately took advantage of Landlord's oversight about its contract rights when it could have corrected it at no cost. That is opportunistic "sharp dealing" in performance (Market Street). The other choices either misstate when good faith applies or overstate it as a fiduciary duty.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Market Street: after contracting

q: A restaurant receives a new dishwasher on Monday and runs it twice that day to test it. It works badly. On Tuesday it tells the seller it rejects it. Has it accepted?
o: Yes, as any use is an act of ownership.
No, as testing during a reasonable chance to inspect isn't acceptance.
Yes, as it had the machine overnight.
No, but only if it hasn't paid.
Yes, as it failed to reject at delivery.
oe: A short test is inspection.
Correct. Section 2-606(1) comes into play only after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, and inspection may include limited use (§ 2-513).
A day isn't an unreasonable time here.
Payment doesn't decide acceptance.
A reasonable time after delivery is allowed.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Inspection period and use

q: When may a lessee cancel after a default?
o: Only with 30 days' notice.
Only on substantial impairment, in every lease.
Any default, or substantial impairment if an installment lease.
Only if the goods are unique.
Only after a court order.
oe: No such period exists.
Non-installment leases don't need it.
Uniqueness isn't relevant.
It's a self-help right.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Cancelling

q: Gonzo agrees to sell Rowlf the right to drill for and remove the natural gas under Gonzo's farm. Rowlf will do all the drilling and extraction. Is this a sale of goods governed by Article 2?
o: No, because extraction rights are a service, not a sale.
Yes, because things attached to realty are goods if they can be removed.
No, because the seller will not be severing the gas.
Yes, because the parties may agree that Article 2 governs.
Yes, because natural gas becomes movable once it is extracted.
oe: It isn't a service contract. The problem is who severs the gas.
Too broad. § 2-107 treats only certain things attached to realty as goods, and minerals only when the seller severs them.
Correct. Under § 2-107(1), oil, gas, and other minerals are goods only if the seller severs them. Here the buyer extracts, so it is an interest in land (Problem 1-1).
The parties' choice of law is the last of the four factors. It cannot turn an interest in land into a sale of goods.
Gas is movable once extracted, but § 2-107(1) adds a condition for minerals: the seller must sever them.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Minerals: who severs

q: Under a contract requiring delivery of 400 lamps by June 30, a seller delivers on June 10, but 40 of the lamps have cracked shades. The buyer rightfully rejects. The seller immediately notifies the buyer that it will deliver 400 conforming lamps by June 25, and it does. Must the buyer accept them?
o: Yes, but only if the buyer agrees in writing to let the seller make a second delivery.
No, because a seller may cure only if it reasonably believed the first tender would be accepted.
No, because after a rightful rejection the buyer may cover elsewhere instead.
No, because the buyer's rightful rejection of the first delivery ended the contract.
Yes, because the seller notified the buyer and cured within the contract time.
oe: Cure under § 2-508(1) doesn't require the buyer's consent.
That condition applies to cure after the contract time expires (§ 2-508(2)), not before.
The buyer can't cover in place of a timely, proper cure. There's no uncured breach.
A rightful rejection doesn't cut off the seller's right to cure within the contract period.

Correct. When a tender is rejected as nonconforming and the time for performance hasn't expired, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of its intention to cure and then make a conforming delivery within the contract time (§ 2-508(1)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Cure before the contract time expires

q: Under § 2-314(2), which of the following is NOT one of the standards goods must meet to be merchantable?
o: They must pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.
Within the variations the agreement allows, they must be of even kind, quality, and quantity within each unit and among all units.
They must be of the highest quality the seller offers in that line of goods.
They must conform to any promises or affirmations of fact on the container or label.
They must be adequately contained, packaged, and labeled as the agreement may require.
oe: Correct. Merchantability is a floor, not a promise of top quality. The goods need only meet the minimum standards in § 2-314(2).
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Merchantable: which is NOT a standard

q: A restaurant contracts for 500 lb of swordfish at $12/lb. The seller repudiates, and the restaurant buys tuna instead at $9/lb because it's what its chef likes to cook. At the place for tender, swordfish is $15/lb when the restaurant learns of the breach. Which is correct?
o: If tuna isn't a reasonable substitute, § 2-713 gives $3/lb × 500.
The buyer forfeited its remedies by not buying swordfish.
Cover damages are negative, so it owes the seller $3/lb.
The buyer has no damages, because it paid less per pound.
Damages are $6/lb, swordfish market minus the tuna price.
oe: Correct. A purchase that isn't a reasonable substitute isn't cover, so it doesn't block market damages.
Failure to cover bars nothing (§ 2-712(3)).
The formulas never produce a claim for the seller.
That would be true only if the tuna qualified as cover.
That isn't a Code measure; tuna isn't part of the § 2-713 formula.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Non-qualifying purchase

q: Bert trades a vintage drum kit to Ernie for Ernie's used motorcycle. No money changes hands. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Article 2 applies only to whichever item is worth more.
The exchange is a gift between friends governed by the common law, because no one paid a price.
Article 2 applies, and each party is a seller of the goods it transfers.
Article 2 doesn't apply, because no price is paid in money.
None of the above.
oe: It applies to both.
Each side gives value, so it isn't a gift.
The price can be payable in goods (§ 2-304(1)).
C is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Price paid in goods

q: Two merchants sign a contract containing a valid clause that any modification must be in a signed writing. The buyer later tells the seller by phone that it may deliver two weeks late. Relying on that call, the seller cancels a rush shipping arrangement that it can't reinstate. The buyer then insists on the original date. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller wins, because the phone call was a valid modification of the delivery date.
The buyer wins, because when a contract has such a clause, a waiver must also be in writing.
The buyer wins, because the no-oral-modification clause makes the phone call irrelevant.
The seller wins, because no-oral-modification clauses can't be enforced between merchants.
The oral change can operate as a waiver, which the buyer likely can't retract now.
oe: It wasn't a valid modification because of the clause. It works only as a waiver.
Article 2 imposes no such writing requirement for a waiver.
Section 2-209(4) gives the failed modification effect as a waiver.
Between merchants, the clause is enforceable without a separate signature.

Correct. An attempted modification that doesn't satisfy a no-oral-modification clause "can operate as a waiver" (§ 2-209(4)). A waiver can be retracted only if retraction wouldn't be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance (§ 2-209(5)).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Failed modification as waiver

q: A lessor leases a forklift for two years for $20,000, and adds a one-time $500 training session. Under § 2A-102(2), how is it treated?
o: Article 2A applies, as the lease of goods predominates.
Article 2 applies, because of the training.
Only some provisions apply, as with a non-predominant hybrid.
Neither article applies.
The common law applies to the whole deal.
oe: Correct. Other law may apply to the non-goods aspects in appropriate circumstances.
It's a lease, not a sale.
That's for leases that don't predominate.
Article 2A does.
Goods predominate.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Hybrid lease predominates

q: A seller wants to be able to repossess on default. What is the simplest way?
o: An oral promise by the buyer to return the goods.
A one-sentence grant of a security interest in the goods.
A liquidated damages clause covering default.
A separate deed of trust on the goods.
A clause making the price a penalty.
oe: A security agreement generally needs a signed record or possession.
Correct. On default the secured seller may repossess peaceably or by replevin (§ 9-609).
That sets damages, not property rights.
Deeds of trust are for real property.
That wouldn't create any property right.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Creating the security interest

q: Animal's Drum Co. sells $10,000 of drum kits to a music school and assigns the right to payment to a factor, which notifies the school. The school accepts the kits, then discovers hidden defects that give it a $2,000 warranty claim against Animal's. The factor demands $10,000. How much must the school pay the factor?
o: $10,000, because the school's acceptance waived all warranty claims.
$8,000, because the school may assert its warranty claim against the factor.
$10,000, because the school must pay the assignee in full and then sue Animal's.
Nothing until Animal's repairs the drums, because the assignment suspended the school's duty to pay.
Nothing, because the goods were nonconforming when tendered.
oe: Acceptance doesn't waive warranty claims as long as the buyer gives timely notice of breach (§ 2-607(3)(a)).

Correct. An assignee steps into the assignor's shoes and takes subject to the account debtor's defenses and claims arising from the contract (see § 9-404). The school may reduce what it pays the factor by its $2,000 warranty claim.
The assignee gets no better rights than the assignor had. The school can raise its warranty claim against the factor.
The assignment didn't suspend anything. The school's duty runs to the factor, reduced by its defenses.
The school accepted the kits, so it owes the price less its damages from the nonconformity (§§ 2-607(1), 2-714).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Assignee subject to defenses

q: Broker buys 100,000 gallons at $2.50 F.O.B. New Orleans, planning to burn the oil itself and not resell it. Seller repudiates when the New Orleans market is $4.50. What is the measure?
o: The market differential, plus provable consequential loss.
Zero, since there's no resale to measure.
The lost profit on an assumed resale.
The full contract price.
Only incidental damages.
oe: Correct. With no resale to compare, the buyer's use was the expectancy.
The market differential applies.
No resale exists to measure a profit.
That isn't a buyer's measure.
More is available.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Broker's own use

q: Unless otherwise agreed, which of the following is NOT one of the seller's duties when the contract requires or authorizes it to ship goods by carrier but doesn't require delivery at a particular destination?
o: Promptly notify the buyer of the shipment.
Put the goods in the possession of a carrier.
Obtain and promptly deliver any document the buyer needs to obtain possession.
Make a contract for transportation that is reasonable given the nature of the goods.
Buy insurance covering the goods during transit for the buyer's benefit.
oe: This is required by § 2-504(c).
This is required by § 2-504(a).
This is required by § 2-504(b).
This is required by § 2-504(a).
Correct. Section 2-504 doesn't require the seller to insure. That duty arises only from a term like C.I.F. (§ 2-320).
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Seller's shipping duties: which is NOT required

q: Ernie orally agrees to buy 100 folding chairs from Bert for $2,500. Bert delivers 40 chairs, and Ernie accepts them. Ernie then refuses the rest, and Bert sues for all 100. Ernie signed nothing. What can Bert enforce?
o: Nothing, because part performance applies only to specially manufactured goods.
Nothing, because Ernie never paid.
The full contract, if Bert proves the oral deal by clear evidence.
The contract as to the 40 chairs Ernie received and accepted.
The full contract, because accepting some chairs confirms the deal.
oe: Those are separate exceptions.
Received and accepted is enough.
Stronger proof doesn't get around the statute.
Correct. § 2-201(3)(c): enforceable only for goods paid for and accepted or received and accepted.
Part performance reaches only the goods accepted.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Received and accepted

q: After accepting defective cartons, a buyer phones the seller's sales rep: "These cartons are giving us real trouble on the line." Six months later it sues. The seller says it never received notice of breach. Which is the best analysis?
o: Only filing suit gives notice.
Notice must be in writing to count.
Notice must state a claim for breach and the amount.
Notice must be sworn.
The call likely suffices if it told the seller the deal was troubled.
oe: Filing is generally too late.
No writing is required.
It needn't claim damages or state an amount.
There's no such requirement.
Correct. Comment 4 asks only that the seller know the transaction is troublesome; courts are lenient, and it must simply let the seller know. Reasonable time is a fact question.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Notice content

q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a buyer to recover consequential damages for lost profits under § 2-715(2)?
o: The loss could not reasonably have been prevented by cover or otherwise.
The loss resulted from the seller's breach.
The seller expressly agreed to be liable for consequential damages.
The seller had reason to know of the buyer's needs at the time of contracting.
None of the above.
oe: Required.
Required.
Correct. No express agreement is needed; reason to know is enough.
Required.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Consequential: limits

q: Beyond the § 2-608 analogs, what extra revocation ground does § 2A-517(2) add?
o: A lessor's default that substantially impairs the goods' value.
Any default by the lessor, however small.
Any change in market rents.
A supplier's insolvency during the lease.
A lessee's change of mind within 30 days.
oe: Correct. For example, failing to provide agreed maintenance. The lease may also add others (3).
It must substantially impair value.
Market movement isn't a default by the lessor.
A supplier's insolvency isn't a default under this lease.
A lessee can't revoke on a mere change of mind.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Revocation for lessor's default

q: In the trade of breeding show dogs, sellers customarily provide registration papers with every purebred puppy. Fozzie buys a puppy from a breeder; the contract says nothing about papers, and the breeder refuses to provide them. What is Fozzie's best claim?
o: No claim, because the contract says nothing about papers.
Breach of an implied warranty arising from usage of trade.
Breach of the warranty of title.
Breach of the warranty of fitness, because show dogs have a particular purpose.
Breach of an express warranty by description.
oe: Usage of trade fills the silence.
Correct. § 2-314(3): other implied warranties may arise from course of dealing or usage of trade (cmt. 12 uses pedigree papers as the example).
Fozzie owns the puppy. Registration papers aren't title.
Nothing shows reliance on the breeder's judgment for a particular purpose.
"Purebred" describes the dog's breeding, not paperwork.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Implied warranty from usage

q: When is a buyer most likely to accept an express disclaimer of the warranty of title?
o: When the buyer is a merchant who can investigate title.
Whenever the seller is a consumer rather than a professional dealer.
When provenance is uncertain and the price reflects that risk.
When buying new goods from an authorized dealer.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant buyers get the title warranty too; what matters is uncertain provenance reflected in the price.
Consumers still make the title warranty.
Correct. Problem 5-5.
Ordinary sales carry the warranty.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Quitclaim title

q: A landowner agrees to sell a construction company 10,000 tons of gravel from a pit on her land. Under the contract, the landowner will excavate the gravel and load it onto the company's trucks. Is the contract a sale of goods?
o: No, because contracts for minerals are always governed by real property law.
Yes, but only after the gravel is excavated.
No, because gravel is part of the real property until it's removed.
Yes, because minerals are goods when they are to be severed by the seller.
Yes, because anything removable from land is goods no matter who removes it.
oe: That's true only when the buyer is to sever them.
Section 2-107(1) characterizes the contract at the time it is made.
Section 2-107(1) treats it as goods when the seller is to sever it.
Correct. A contract for the sale of minerals "or the like" to be removed from realty is a contract for the sale of goods "if they are to be severed by the seller" (§ 2-107(1)).
For minerals and structures, it matters whether the seller or the buyer severs them (§ 2-107(1)).
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Minerals severed by the seller

q: What is the difference between excuse and risk of loss?
o: Excuse applies only to buyers, risk of loss to sellers.
Risk of loss applies only to services, excuse only to goods.
Risk of loss decides who pays damages; excuse, who absorbs the goods' value.
Excuse decides who pays damages; risk of loss, who absorbs the goods' value.
Nothing; they are two names for one doctrine.
oe: Excuse applies to sellers too.
Risk of loss is about goods.
Reversed.
Correct.
Different questions.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Excuse vs. risk of loss

q: A court orders the seller to deliver a one-of-a-kind sculpture to a buyer who has paid half. Which is correct?
o: Delay damages are unavailable once specific performance is granted.
The decree discharges the balance as a penalty for the breach.
The seller may hold the sculpture until the buyer pays interest.
The buyer owes the balance and may recover damages for the delay.
The buyer must elect between the goods and delay damages.
oe: Section 2-716(2) lets the decree include damages or other relief.
The buyer gets the goods it bargained for, not a free half.
Nothing in the Code gives the seller that right.
Correct. The unpaid price is express in § 2-502(1) and presumably true under § 2-716 (see §§ 2-607, 2-709). Delay damages rest on §§ 2-711 cmt. 1, 2-714(1), 2-715, 1-103 and 1-305.
It may have both; the decree can include damages.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Still owes the balance

q: Before selling Zoe a used boat, the seller says, "Please have it hauled out and inspected before you buy." Zoe declines. Afterward, Zoe finds a soft spot in the hull that any haul-out inspection would have revealed. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller's demand disclaimed all warranties, express and implied.
Zoe keeps the implied-warranty claim, because Zoe never actually inspected.
Zoe's claim survives unless the seller also said "as is."
Zoe keeps the claim, because the seller's demand was oral.
None of the above.
oe: It affects only implied warranties, and only for discoverable defects.
Refusing after the seller's demand counts.
The refusal is an independent ground.
The demand need not be written.

Correct. Zoe has no implied-warranty claim for that defect: when a buyer refuses to examine after the seller's demand, there is no implied warranty as to defects an examination ought to have revealed (§ 2-316(3)(b)). No choice says that.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Refusal to examine

q: Under a six-month contract requiring delivery by the 1st of each month, the buyer emails the seller in February: "No need to rush; deliveries by the 15th are fine for the rest of the contract." Relying on that email, the seller rebooks its production line and gives the 1st-to-14th slots to another customer under a new contract it can't change. In April, the buyer emails that it will now insist on delivery by May 1. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer may retract, because estoppel doesn't apply to contracts for the sale of goods.
The buyer probably can't retract, because the seller materially changed position in reliance.
The buyer may retract, because a waiver given without consideration can be withdrawn at any time.
The buyer may retract, because it gave the seller reasonable notice well before the May 1 delivery.
The seller wins, but only because the buyer's February email was a signed writing.
oe: Article 2 is supplemented by estoppel principles (§ 1-103(b)), and § 2-209(5) builds reliance into the waiver rule.

Correct. A waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract may be retracted by reasonable notice "unless the retraction would be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance on the waiver" (§ 2-209(5)).
Waivers don't require consideration. The obstacle is reliance.
Reasonable notice isn't enough when the other party has materially changed position in reliance.
The writing matters for any no-oral-modification clause, not for retraction under § 2-209(5).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Waiver retraction blocked by reliance

q: A contract for $20,000 of store display racks provides that the seller will pay $50,000 for each day of late delivery. The buyer's realistic losses from a short delay were small and easy to calculate. The racks arrive two days late, and the buyer sues for $100,000. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer recovers $100,000, because the parties agreed to the amount.
The clause is void as a penalty, and the buyer may recover its actual damages.
The court will reduce the clause to the largest amount that would be reasonable.
The buyer recovers $100,000, because the seller is a merchant.
The buyer recovers nothing, because the penalty clause voids the entire contract.
oe: Freedom of contract doesn't extend to penalties.
Correct. "A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty" (§ 2-718(1)). With the clause out, the buyer may recover ordinary Article 2 damages.
Article 2 voids an unreasonably large term instead of rewriting it.
Merchant status doesn't validate a penalty.
Only the penalty term is void.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Liquidated damages as a penalty

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Orange & Rockland factors for deciding whether a requirements increase is unreasonably disproportionate?
o: The size of the excess over the estimate.
The reason for the increase.
The seller's ability to foresee the increase.
Whether the buyer is a merchant in the goods.
The gap between the market price and the contract price.
oe: One of the five factors.
One of the factors.
One of the factors.
Correct. Merchant status is not a factor. The fifth factor is whether the market rise was fortuitous.
One of the factors.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Orange & Rockland factors

q: A seller repudiates a contract for 2,000 valves at $50 F.O.B. seller's plant. The buyer promptly buys identical valves at $58 delivered to its door. It spends $1,500 on a buyer's trip to arrange the purchase. Freight under the old contract would have cost $3,000. What are the buyer's § 2-712 damages?
oe: That ignores the incidental costs and the expenses saved.
That subtracts freight but leaves out the trip.
That adds the trip but ignores the freight saved.
Correct. ($58 minus $50) × 2,000 = $16,000, plus $1,500 incidental, minus $3,000 freight saved.
That adds the saved freight instead of subtracting it.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Cover with incidentals and savings

q: A seller sends a small parcel by air. Before delivery the buyer misses a payment, but it isn't insolvent. May the seller stop the parcel?
o: Yes, if the seller agrees to pay the carrier's charges.
Yes, since a parcel is simpler for the carrier to stop.
No, because only insolvency allows stopping a parcel.
No, because a seller can never stop goods held by a carrier.
Yes, because any breach allows stopping any shipment.
oe: Paying the charges doesn't remove the limit.
The statute's size limit points the other way.
Correct. Section 2-705(1). Insolvency allows stopping any size.
Section 2-705 allows stoppage in some cases.
The size limit applies outside insolvency.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Stopping parcels

q: Big Bird runs a commercial greenhouse. For years he has bought supplies from Oscar's Garden Wholesale, whose sales rep has toured the greenhouse and knows Big Bird grows only orchids. Big Bird phones in an order: "Send me whatever fertilizer you think is best for my plants." Oscar's sends a fertilizer that works well for most plants but is known to scorch orchids. Has Oscar's made a fitness warranty?
o: Yes, because Oscar's had reason to know both the particular purpose and Big Bird's reliance.
No, because the fertilizer works well for most plants and so was merchantable for ordinary use.
Yes, but only because Big Bird and Oscar's are both merchants dealing in garden supplies.
No, because Big Bird never told Oscar's that the fertilizer was for orchids when he ordered.
No, because a fitness warranty arises only when the seller makes some affirmation of fact.
oe: Correct. The seller need only have "reason to know" the particular purpose and the buyer's reliance (§ 2-315). Past dealings and knowledge of the buyer's business can supply it (§ 2-315 cmt. 1).
The two warranties are separate. Goods can be merchantable and still unfit for the buyer's particular purpose.
Section 2-315 applies to any seller and any buyer.
Section 2-315 doesn't require the buyer to state the purpose expressly. Reason to know is enough.
That describes an express warranty. Fitness is implied from the circumstances.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fitness: reason to know without being told

q: Which of the following is NOT a "good" under UCC § 2-105?
o: A gold coin purchased from a coin dealer for a collection.
Calves that have not yet been born.
A certificated share of Microsoft stock.
Kitchen cabinets specially manufactured for the buyer's home.
A crop of soybeans still growing in the field.
oe: It is a good. The coin is the subject of the sale, not "the money in which the price is to be paid" (Problem 1-1).
It is a good. § 2-105(1) expressly includes "the unborn young of animals."
Correct. Investment securities are excluded from "goods" (§ 2-105(1)); they are governed by Article 8.
It is a good. The definition expressly covers "specially manufactured goods."
It is a good. § 2-105(1) includes growing crops, and § 2-107(2) treats them as goods whoever severs them.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — What is a "good"

q: A dealer leases a car to Pat for family use. A state consumer statute conflicts with an Article 2A rule. Which controls?
o: Neither; federal law alone applies.
Whichever favors the lessor.
The consumer statute, under § 2A-104.
Article 2A, as the later uniform act.
The lease's choice-of-law clause.
oe: The state statute may apply.
Neither rule depends on which side it favors; § 2A-104 sets the order.
Correct. Article 2A defers to certificate-of-title and consumer-protection law.
It yields.
Section 2A-106 limits those.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Consumer protections

q: Which section pairing is correct for lessees?
o: § 2A-504 care of goods; § 2A-513 lien.
§ 2A-513 cure, with no lessee's lien at all.
oe: Section 2A-504 is liquidated damages.
Those are reversed.
Section 2A-508(5) gives one.
Those are reversed.
Correct. They track §§ 2-508, 2-603, 2-604 and 2-711(3). A purchaser from these sales takes free of lessor's or supplier's claims.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Cure and care

q: A merchant seller delivers nonconforming goods. The buyer rightfully rejects them after inspection, and they are destroyed while the seller is taking them back to its store. Who bears the risk of loss?
o: It depends on whether the seller had insurance.
The seller, because the tender was nonconforming.
The buyer, until the goods are safely returned to the seller's place of business.
The buyer, because a merchant seller's risk ends once it tenders the goods.
None of the above.
oe: The rule doesn't depend on insurance here.
Correct. § 2-510(1): when a tender so fails to conform as to give a right of rejection, risk stays with the seller until cure or acceptance.
Risk stays with the seller.
That is not the rule for a rightfully rejected tender. § 2-510(1) keeps risk on the seller until cure or acceptance.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Nonconforming goods

q: A contract between Big Bird and Snuffy's Seed Co. says: "Neither party may assign this contract." Snuffy's Seed Co. assigns to its bank the right to be paid under the contract. What is the effect of the clause?
o: It bars only delegation of Snuffy's duties.
It bars both assignment of rights and delegation of duties.
It makes the assignment to the bank void.
It bars the assignment of the right to payment.
It lets Big Bird cancel the contract for breach.
oe: Correct. § 2-210(4): unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, a prohibition on assigning "the contract" bars only the delegation of performance.
Under § 2-210(4) it bars only delegation.
To make an assignment ineffective, a clause must say something like "any attempted assignment is void," and even that can't stop an assignment of a right to payment (§ 9-406(d)).
A ban on assigning "the contract" is read narrowly.
The assignment of a right to payment isn't a breach that would justify cancellation.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — "Assign the contract" ban

q: A buyer accepts a pump warranted to deliver 100 gpm; it delivers 70. The price was $9,000 (unpaid). As warranted it's worth $10,000, and as delivered $6,000. A flooded basement caused by the shortfall did $2,000 of foreseeable, unavoidable damage. The buyer gave timely notice. What does it owe, if it deducts all it may?
oe: Correct. Value difference $4,000 plus $2,000 consequential is $6,000, deducted from the $9,000 price under § 2-717.
That leaves out the value difference.
Damages may be deducted on notice.
That uses the $10,000 warranted value as if it were the price, then adds consequentials wrongly.
That leaves out the consequential damage.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Accepted goods, full formula

q: Kermit, a novelty dealer, orally agrees to sell 600 rubber chickens to Snuffy for $3,000. Snuffy is a consumer who has never bought or sold goods of this kind. Kermit sends Snuffy a signed letter confirming the deal and its quantity. Snuffy reads it and never objects. Does § 2-201(2) make the contract enforceable against Snuffy?
o: Yes, because Snuffy failed to object within 10 days.
Yes, because the sender is a merchant.
No, because Snuffy objected too late.
No, because confirmations must be signed by both parties.
None of the above.
oe: The 10-day rule binds only a merchant recipient.
Both parties must be merchants.
Snuffy never objected, and he didn't need to. The 10-day objection rule binds only a merchant recipient.
The confirmation need only be sufficient against the sender.
Correct. § 2-201(2) applies only to a contract "between merchants." Snuffy is not a merchant, so his silence doesn't bind him, and Kermit needs a record signed by Snuffy or another exception.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Confirmation to a non-merchant

q: You represent a trucking company buying all its diesel at a price the seller sets. Which draft best protects it, within § 1-302(b)?
o: A clause saying the price is whatever the seller wishes.
A clause waiving the seller's duty of good faith.
A clause dropping any quantity term.
A clause saying a court may not review the price.
A price tied to a published index or the seller's best customer price.
oe: That gives the buyer nothing.
Good faith can't be disclaimed.
A requirements term is the quantity.
Section 2-305(2) still applies.
Correct. Problem 5-1: parties may set standards for good faith, unless manifestly unreasonable. A seller might in turn use an estimate and a minimum and maximum.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Drafting good faith and requirements

q: A long-term supply contract is repudiated, and the case comes to trial before the time for performance. Which market price do §§ 2-708 and 2-713 use?
o: The price when the aggrieved party learned of the repudiation.
The future price, as projected by experts.
The price at the time of trial.
The contract price.
The price when the contract was signed.
oe: Correct. Section 2-723(1). It matters mainly for long-term supply contracts.
That's the speculation the rule avoids.
Not the rule; § 2-723(1) looks back.
That would give zero damages.
A trial-date price isn't the statute's measure. Section 2-723(1) looks to when the party learned of the repudiation.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — § 2-723(1)

q: Gonzo accepts a used tractor warranted to have a rebuilt engine and pays the $18,000 price. The engine was never rebuilt. As warranted, the tractor would be worth $20,000; as delivered, it's worth $13,000. What are Gonzo's basic damages under § 2-714(2)?
o: Nothing, because Gonzo accepted the tractor.
$18,000, the full price.
$2,000, the value as warranted minus the price.
$7,000, the value as warranted minus the value as accepted.
$5,000, the price Gonzo paid minus the tractor's value as delivered.
oe: Acceptance doesn't bar damages, given timely notice.
Gonzo kept the tractor.
That's Gonzo's bargain, not the loss.
The measure uses value as warranted, not the price.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Accepted goods: § 2-714(2)

q: A five-year non-terminable lease of a $200,000 loader, with rent totaling $200,000, gives the lessee an option to buy at the end for $100, when the loader should be worth about $60,000. Returning it would cost the lessee about $1,500. What is the result?
o: A sale with a security interest, because $100 is nominal.
A sale, but only if the lessee in fact exercises the option.
A lease, because the option is stated in dollars.
A lease, because the term is shorter than the economic life.
A lease, because a purchase option alone never creates a security interest.
oe: Correct. $100 is less than the predictable cost of performing if the option isn't exercised (§ 1-203(d)), so § 1-203(b)(4) is met.
The test is judged at the outset (§ 1-203(e)).
Stating a fixed dollar sum doesn't make it non-nominal.
Prong (1) isn't the only route.
A nominal option meets prong (4). Section 1-203(c)(4) protects only the mere existence of an option.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Nominal: $100 option

q: Mr. Snuffleupagus takes home a $2,400 television from a store under a written deal that lets him use it for 14 days and pay only if he decides to keep it. On day 3, before he has decided, lightning strikes his house and destroys the television. Must he pay?
o: Yes, because the seller is a merchant and the buyer had already received the goods.
No, but only if he notifies the store of the loss before the 14 days run out.
No, because the risk stays with the seller until he approves the purchase.
Yes, because the television was in his possession and control when it was destroyed.
Yes, because this is a sale or return, which puts the risk on the buyer during the trial.
oe: The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) is subject to § 2-327, which keeps the risk on the seller until approval.
The risk was on the seller regardless. No notice condition applies.

Correct. When goods are delivered primarily for use and may be returned even though they conform, the deal is a sale on approval (§ 2-326(1)(a)). Risk of loss and title don't pass until the buyer accepts (§ 2-327(1)(a)), and using the goods consistently with the trial isn't acceptance.
Possession during a trial period doesn't pass the risk in a sale on approval.
A sale or return is for goods delivered primarily for resale. This TV was delivered for the buyer's own use, so it's a sale on approval.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Sale on approval

q: Animal orders a salad at a restaurant. The menu calls the olives "pitted," but Animal cracks a tooth on an olive pit. Animal sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which argument best supports the restaurant?
o: The restaurant was not negligent in preparing the salad.
Animal can sue only the olive grower, not the restaurant.
Food served in a restaurant is a service, not a sale of goods.
Pits are natural to olives, so under the foreign-natural test the salad was fit for its ordinary purpose.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability is strict liability; negligence doesn't matter.
The restaurant, a merchant seller of food, gives the warranty.
§ 2-314(1): serving food or drink for value is a sale.
Correct. That's the approach usually tied to Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (fish bones in chowder). Under the reasonable-expectation test, "pitted" would help Animal.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Food: foreign-natural test

q: A seller properly gives a carrier a timely stop order on a truckload after the buyer repudiates, with enough notice to prevent delivery. The carrier delivers anyway. What is the likely result?
o: The carrier owes nothing, because it had a bill.
The stop order was void for a truckload.
The seller must absorb the loss.
The carrier may be liable, as it had to hold as the seller directed.
The buyer owns the goods free of any claim, with no recourse.
oe: Nothing says the bill was negotiable.
A truckload qualifies.
The carrier didn't follow a proper order.
Correct. Section 2-705(3)(a)-(b): after notice enabling it to prevent delivery, it must hold and deliver as directed.
The seller still has remedies against the buyer and carrier.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Carrier ignores stop

q: In the restaurant-supply trade, sellers do not customarily season new cast-iron pans before delivery. Under three earlier contracts, however, Gonzo's Cookware always delivered seasoned pans to Miss Piggy's bistro. Their newest contract says nothing about seasoning, and Gonzo delivers unseasoned pans. Is Gonzo in breach?
o: No, because course of dealing can never add a term to a written contract.
No, because the contract's express terms say nothing about seasoning.
Yes, because of course of performance.
No, because usage of trade does not require seasoning.
Yes, because of course of dealing.
oe: It can supplement even a written contract (§ 2-202(a)).
Silence isn't a contradiction. Course of dealing supplements the terms.
Course of performance is conduct under this contract. The earlier contracts are course of dealing.
Course of dealing prevails over usage of trade (§ 1-303(e)).
Correct. Prior conduct between the parties establishes a common understanding that supplements the agreement (§ 1-303(b), (d)).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Course of dealing

q: Under an ordinary lease at $1,000 a month, the lessee accepted a truck with a warranty defect, reducing the value of its use by $150 a month. With notice, it pays $850 monthly. The lessor sues. Which is correct?
o: The deduction is proper under § 2A-508(6).
It has no right after acceptance.
It must pay full rent and sue.
It may stop paying altogether.
It may deduct only with the lessor's consent.
oe: Correct. It's an ordinary lease, so § 2A-407 doesn't apply.
Acceptance doesn't bar damages.
It may deduct on notice.
Only its damages may be deducted.
Notice is enough.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Lessee keeps goods; deducts rent

q: A buyer pays $9 a unit for goods warranted as Grade A. Grade A is worth $12 and the delivered Grade B is worth $8. What are the § 2-714(2) damages?
o: $3 a unit, the profit lost on the contract.
$9 a unit, a full refund of the price.
$1 a unit, measured from the contract price.
$12 a unit, the full warranted value.
$4 a unit, which preserves the buyer's good bargain.
oe: That doesn't fit the statute.
A refund requires revocation.
The price isn't part of the formula.
The buyer keeps goods that are worth something.
Correct. $12 minus $8. A buyer that struck a good bargain keeps it, and one that struck a bad bargain keeps that too.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Good bargain kept

q: A theater orally orders 300 custom seats embroidered with its logo from Sweetums Seating for $45,000. Before Sweetums orders any materials or begins any work, the theater calls to cancel. Sweetums sues, and the theater raises the statute of frauds. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Sweetums wins, because the exception applies whenever the buyer orders custom-made goods.
The theater wins, because Sweetums hadn't begun work before the theater canceled.
Sweetums wins, because seats embroidered with the logo aren't suitable for sale to others.
Sweetums wins, but only for the portion of the seats it could have made before trial.
The theater wins, because oral contracts for goods are never enforceable.
oe: The exception has several elements, including timing.

Correct. Section 2-201(3)(a) applies only if the seller, "before notice of repudiation is received and under circumstances which reasonably indicate that the goods are for the buyer, has made either a substantial beginning of their manufacture or commitments for their procurement."
That's one element. The seller also needs a substantial beginning before notice of repudiation.
No portion is enforceable when the exception's timing element isn't met.
Oral contracts can be enforced under the § 2-201(3) exceptions.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Specially manufactured goods: timing of repudiation

q: A student asks what happened to the 2003 amendments to Article 2. Which statement is correct?
o: They abolished the statute of frauds.
They were withdrawn, though 2022 amendments address hybrids and records.
They became law everywhere in 2003.
They replaced Article 2 with the CISG.
They restored title as Article 2's central concept.
oe: They would only have raised its threshold.

Correct. No state enacted the 2003 amendments, which would, for example, have raised the statute of frauds to $5,000. The $500 figure has been unchanged for decades. The 2022 amendments deal with hybrid transactions and records.
They were withdrawn.
The CISG is a separate treaty.
Minimizing title is one of Article 2's innovations.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Article 2's history

q: Midway through a two-year supply contract, Big Bird's supplier ships three defective loads, and Big Bird ends the contract because of them. How is Big Bird's action best classified, and what happens to Big Bird's damages claim for the defective loads?
o: Rescission; the parties are put back where they started.
Cancellation; Big Bird keeps its remedies for the breach.
Termination; Big Bird keeps only a right to a refund.
Termination; Big Bird loses its damages claim.
Cancellation; Big Bird must choose between ending the contract and suing for damages.
oe: The Code's terms here are cancellation and termination.
Correct. § 2-106(4): cancellation is ending the contract for breach, and the canceling party keeps its remedies.
It's cancellation, with full remedies.
Ending a contract for breach is cancellation.
Big Bird may do both.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Cancellation vs. termination

q: On February 1, Statler and Waldorf contract for 1,000 sacks of oats, delivery on March 15, at a price "to be agreed at delivery." On February 1, oats sell for $7 a sack. On March 15, the market price is $12 and rising. Statler tenders and demands $15. Waldorf refuses, and they never agree. Assuming they intended to be bound, what price term governs?
o: $7, the market price when the contract was made.
$15, because the seller sets the price when it is left open.
A reasonable price at the time for delivery, likely around $12.
There's no contract, because the parties never agreed on the price.
None of the above.
oe: The gap filler looks to the time for delivery, not the time of contracting.
A price left to be agreed isn't one the seller fixes.
Correct. When the price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, the price is "a reasonable price at the time for delivery" (§ 2-305(1)(b)). See Problem 4-3(a).
Section 2-305(1) saves the contract if the parties intended to be bound.
One of the other choices is correct: A reasonable price at the time for delivery, likely around $12.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Price "to be agreed"; failure to agree

q: Which is NOT a requirement of a buyer's recovery of goods under § 2-502?
o: The consumer trigger or the insolvency trigger is met.
The buyer tenders any unpaid balance of the price.
The goods must be unique.
The buyer has paid some or all of the price.
The buyer has a special property in the goods.
oe: Required: § 2-502(1)(a) or (b).
Required: "making and keeping good a tender."
Correct. Uniqueness is never a § 2-502 requirement. The buyer needs a special property (identified goods), payment of part or all of the price, a tender of any balance, and one of the two triggers.
Required.
Required: the goods must be identified.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — § 2-502 elements

q: Before buying a used box truck from a dealer, Fozzie spends an hour going over it as thoroughly as he wants. He sees obvious rust on the frame. Two weeks later, the transmission fails because of internal wear that no ordinary inspection would have revealed. The contract contains no disclaimer. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Fozzie keeps implied warranties as to the rust only, because rust is a safety defect.
Fozzie's examination excludes nothing, because there was no written disclaimer.
Fozzie's examination excludes implied warranties as to the rust, but not as to the transmission.
Fozzie's examination excludes all implied warranties.
Fozzie keeps implied warranties as to both defects, because the seller didn't demand an inspection.
oe: The test is whether the inspection ought to have revealed the defect, not how serious it is.
Section 2-316(3)(b) works without any disclaimer language.

Correct. When the buyer has examined the goods as fully as desired before contracting, there's no implied warranty "with regard to defects which an examination ought in the circumstances to have revealed" (§ 2-316(3)(b)). Hidden internal wear isn't such a defect.
An examination excludes warranties only as to defects it ought to have revealed.
A demand is needed only when the buyer refuses to inspect. Fozzie actually inspected.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Examination: patent vs. latent defects

q: Rowlf sells 50 crystal chandeliers to Camilla, F.O.B. Rowlf's warehouse. Rowlf's employees pack them loosely in thin cardboard with no padding, which falls short of what the trade expects for crystal. Rowlf hands them to a carrier and notifies Camilla. Ordinary bumps in transit shatter most of them. Who bears the loss?
o: Rowlf, because the poorly packed goods didn't conform, so the risk stayed with him.
Camilla, because in an F.O.B. seller's-warehouse contract risk passes on delivery to the carrier.
Camilla, because she can sue the carrier for damage that happened in transit.
The carrier, because goods damaged in transit are always the carrier's responsibility.
Camilla, unless the contract expressly required the seller to use special packaging.
oe: Correct. A shipment-contract seller must make a contract for transportation that is reasonable given the nature of the goods (§ 2-504(a)), and the goods themselves must be adequately packaged (§ 2-314(2)(e)). The tender didn't conform, so under § 2-510(1) the risk stayed on Rowlf. See Problem 4-7(d)(1).
Risk passes on delivery to the carrier only after a proper, conforming shipment. A defective tender keeps the risk on the seller under § 2-510(1).
The carrier isn't liable for damage caused by the shipper's own poor packing, and in any event the risk never passed.
The carrier is liable for its own fault, not for the shipper's packing failures.
Even with no packaging term, the seller must ship in a manner reasonable for the goods, and merchantability requires adequate packaging.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Improper packaging in a shipment contract

q: A utility contracts to buy all the fuel oil its plant requires at 2 cents per gallon, estimating 1 million gallons a year. When the market price rises to 6 cents, the utility starts burning oil instead of natural gas, which it had used before, so that it can sell its spare gas at a profit. Its oil requirements jump to 2.5 million gallons. What is the most likely result?
o: The utility wins, because a requirements contract lets the buyer alone decide how much it needs.
The seller wins only if the contract set a maximum quantity, since § 2-306 has no ceiling of its own.
The contract is void, because a fixed price far below the market price is unconscionable.
The seller wins, because requirements inflated to profit from the market aren't requirements in good faith.
The utility wins, because it actually burned all 2.5 million gallons at its own plant during the year.
oe: The buyer's needs must be in good faith and not unreasonably disproportionate.
Section 2-306(1) supplies the limits even without a stated maximum.
A favorable fixed price isn't unconscionable. The problem is the buyer's conduct.

Correct. Requirements must be those "as may occur in good faith" (§ 2-306(1)). Switching fuels to profit from the price difference is the kind of conduct Orange & Rockland v. Amerada Hess held to be bad faith, and the demand also far exceeds the estimate.
Actual use doesn't make requirements generated in bad faith legitimate.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: increase to exploit the market

q: After a reasonable opportunity to inspect, which of the following is NOT an acceptance?
o: The buyer tells the seller that the goods are fine.
The buyer pays for the goods before inspecting them.
The buyer says it will keep the goods despite a defect.
The buyer fails to make an effective rejection.
The buyer resells the goods to a customer.
oe: That's acceptance under § 2-606(1)(a).

Correct. Payment isn't acceptance (§ 2-512; § 2-606 lists the acts). Acceptance occurs if the buyer signifies conformity or that it will keep the goods, fails to reject effectively, or acts inconsistently with the seller's ownership.
That's acceptance under § 2-606(1)(a).
That's acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b).
That's an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership, § 2-606(1)(c).
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Acceptance acts

q: Count von Count signs a memo stating: "I agree to buy 100 wooden abacuses from Rizzo at $10 each." Rizzo claims the parties actually agreed orally to 150 abacuses. Assuming Rizzo proves the oral deal, how many abacuses can Rizzo enforce?
o: None, because Rizzo himself did not sign the memo.
150, because the memo is sufficient and Rizzo has proved the actual quantity.
100, the quantity shown in the signed memo.
125, as a compromise between the two quantities.
None, because the memo misstates the quantity agreed.
oe: The record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought, which is the Count.
The contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record (§ 2-201(1)).
Correct. The contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record (§ 2-201(1)). A record isn't insufficient because it misstates a term, but enforcement stops at the stated quantity.
There is no compromise rule.
A misstated term doesn't make the record insufficient. It caps enforcement at the stated quantity.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Quantity limit

q: Market-rent evidence for a term identical to the remaining term isn't available. Which is correct?
o: No damages may be recovered.
The original rent is used instead.
The jury sets the rent without evidence.
