Only published reports may be used.
A close substitute may be used, with allowance and notice.
oe: Substitutes are allowed (§ 2A-507(2)).
That would give nothing.
Evidence is required.
They're admissible, not exclusive.
Correct. Section 2A-507.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Market rent proof

q: A seller repudiates, and the buyer makes the goods in its own plant instead of buying them. What question does the text leave open?
o: Whether § 2-713 becomes mandatory for the buyer.
How the cost of making the goods should be measured.
Whether the seller may reject the buyer's goods.
Whether cover must come from a merchant.
Whether the buyer has breached by not buying.
oe: Nothing makes it mandatory.
Correct. Self-production may qualify, but the measure of cost (and whether overhead counts) is unsettled.
The seller has no such role.
That isn't the open question.
The buyer hasn't breached; the seller repudiated.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Making it yourself

q: After a proper stop order, the carrier incurs storage charges and rerouting costs. Who bears them?
o: The carrier, as a cost of doing business.
Seller and carrier, split equally.
The seller, who may claim them from a breaching buyer.
Nobody, since the stop order was proper.
The buyer, paying the carrier directly.
oe: The carrier follows directions at the seller's expense.
No such split exists.
Correct. Section 2-705(3)(b). It may then claim them as incidental damages from a breaching buyer (§ 2-710).
Section 2-705(3)(b) puts the costs on the seller.
The buyer isn't directly liable to the carrier.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Who pays the stoppage costs

q: Same facts, but Dana buys the car for her delivery business. Which is correct?
o: Section 2-716(3) applies automatically, since the car is identified.
She has no remedy, and she can't even get her $1,000 back.
She must first demand assurance under § 2-609 before suing.
Section 2-502 works only if the dealer became insolvent within 10 days.
Section 2-502(1)(a) still applies, since cars are consumer goods by nature.
oe: She must also be unable to cover, and similar cars are available.
She may recover the price paid under § 2-711(1).
The dealer has already repudiated, so no demand is needed.
Correct. Business goods fall outside (1)(a). Only (1)(b) is left. Otherwise she must use § 2-716, which is weak if she can cover.
The test is the purpose of this purchase, which is business.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Paid car, business use
pre: A dealer contracts to sell a specific used car for $5,000 to Dana for family use. Dana pays $1,000. The dealer, solvent, then refuses to deliver, and similar cars are easy to find. Which is Dana's strongest route to the car?

q: Rowlf contracts to sell Scooter the pumpkin crop now growing on Rowlf's farm. Scooter will harvest the pumpkins in October. Which law governs the sale?
o: Article 2 governs, but only if the crop is sold before it is planted.
Article 2 governs only if Rowlf harvests the pumpkins before delivery.
Real-property law governs until the pumpkins are harvested.
Real-property law governs, because Scooter, not Rowlf, will sever the crop.
None of the above.
oe: Timing of the sale doesn't matter. Growing crops are goods.
That is the rule for minerals and structures (§ 2-107(1)), not crops.
Growing crops are goods even while attached (§ 2-105(1)).
Who severs matters only for minerals and structures. Crops are goods whoever severs them (§ 2-107(2)).
Correct. Article 2 governs. Growing crops are goods (§ 2-105(1)), and under § 2-107(2) they are goods whether the buyer or the seller severs them. No choice says that.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Crops: either party severs

q: Under a contract for monthly deliveries, the buyer accepts one delivery that arrives a week late. What is the effect of the buyer's acceptance on its right to damages for the late delivery?
o: The buyer must reject the next delivery to preserve its claim.
It keeps its claim if it notifies the seller within a reasonable time.
The buyer waived its right to damages by accepting the delivery.
The buyer created a course of performance permitting late delivery.
None of the above.
oe: No such requirement exists.
Correct. § 2-607(2)–(3)(a); Problem 3-5(A).
Acceptance does not by itself impair any remedy for nonconformity (§ 2-607(2)).
One occasion isn't a course of performance.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — One late delivery

q: A sawmill buys a log debarker under a contract with two separate clauses: an exclusive repair-or-replace remedy and an exclusion of consequential damages. The seller's repairs fail for months, and the limited remedy fails of its essential purpose. The state's courts follow the minority (dependent) approach. The sawmill sues for profits lost during the downtime. What is the most likely result?
o: Nothing at all, because repair or replacement was the sawmill's exclusive remedy.
No lost profits, because consequential damages can never be recovered for purely commercial losses.
No lost profits, because the exclusion is tested on its own and isn't unconscionable between merchants.
Lost profits only if the exclusion clause was not printed conspicuously.
The sawmill may recover its lost profits, because under the dependent approach the exclusion falls along with the failed remedy.
oe: When an exclusive remedy fails of its essential purpose, the buyer may resort to Code remedies (§ 2-719(2)).
Lost profits are classic consequential damages (§ 2-715(2)(a)). They are excludable by agreement, but not barred by law.
That is the majority (independent) approach. This state follows the dependent approach.
§ 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement, under either approach.

Correct. Under the dependent approach, a seller that fails to deliver the limited remedy can't keep the benefit of the consequential-damages exclusion; both fall together. (The majority, independent approach would test the exclusion separately for unconscionability.)
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Dependent approach

q: Gonzo orders 5,000 T-shirts from a print shop and supplies the logo artwork himself. A company sues the print shop, claiming the logo infringes its trademark. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Gonzo must hold the print shop harmless, because he supplied the design.
The print shop wins only if it is not a merchant regularly dealing in T-shirts.
The print shop must indemnify Gonzo, because a merchant warrants goods free of infringement claims.
The print shop bears the risk, because it should have checked trademark registrations.
No one bears the risk until a court finds the trademark claim valid.
oe: Correct. A buyer who furnishes specifications must hold the seller harmless against infringement claims arising out of compliance with them (§ 2-312(3)).
Merchant status determines whether the seller gives an infringement warranty, but the buyer's hold-harmless duty applies either way.
The merchant's infringement warranty doesn't cover claims caused by the buyer's own specifications.
The statute places the risk on the buyer who supplied the design.
Under § 2-312(3) the duty to hold harmless arises from the claim; final proof of infringement isn't required first.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Infringement: buyer's design

q: Under § 2-106, what is the difference between "termination" and "cancellation"?
o: Termination preserves remedies for breach; cancellation does not.
Cancellation discharges executory duties; termination does not.
Termination is for the other side's breach; cancellation is for some other reason.
Cancellation is for the other side's breach; termination is for some other reason.
Nothing; the Code uses the two terms interchangeably.
oe: A cancelling party keeps its remedies for breach of the whole contract or unperformed balance.
Both discharge executory duties.
Reversed.
The Code defines them differently.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Termination vs. cancellation

q: A non-terminable lease runs 8 years. The goods' remaining economic life is reasonably predicted at 7 years. There is no purchase option. What is it?
o: A security interest under § 1-203(b)(1).
A question of the parties' intent.
A lease, unless the rent exceeds the value.
A lease, because there's no purchase option.
A lease, because the lessee can't buy.
oe: Correct. The term is equal to or longer than the remaining economic life.
Intent doesn't control.
Section 1-203(c)(1) makes that irrelevant.
Prong (1) needs no option.
Same point.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Term vs. economic life

q: A craft brewery supplies a regional grocery chain under an at-will arrangement with no fixed term. Encouraged by the chain's talk of a "long partnership," the brewery borrows heavily to double its capacity. Eight months later, the chain gives 90 days' notice that it is ending the arrangement, enough time to find other buyers. The brewery sues for five years of lost profits, arguing the termination was in bad faith. What is the most likely result?
o: The brewery wins, because the chain needed a good reason to terminate.
The chain wins, because termination never requires notice.
The brewery wins, because good faith bars termination before the brewery recoups its investment.
The chain wins on lost profits, because good faith doesn't override the right to end an indefinite contract on reasonable notice.
None of the above.
oe: No reason is required.
Reasonable notice is required (§ 2-309(3)).
Good faith can't override the statutory right to terminate.
Correct. This is Santa Fe Custom Shutters v. Home Depot. Claims for fraud in the inducement or inadequate notice might survive, but not five years of lost profits.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — At-will supply: heavy investment

q: A seller shipped goods under a negotiable bill to its own order, and has now indorsed and negotiated the bill to the buyer. The buyer then becomes insolvent. May the seller stop the goods?
o: Yes, if the carrier agrees.
Yes, as the seller reserved title.
No, because a parcel can't be stopped.
Yes, as insolvency allows stopping any size.
No, as negotiation of the document ended the right.
oe: The carrier's agreement doesn't restore it.
Reservation gives a security interest, and the bill is gone.
Size isn't the issue.
The right ends on negotiation.
Correct. Section 2-705(2)(d).
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Shipment under reservation and stop

q: Bunsen's lab accepts a late delivery of glassware in January without comment. In October, having said nothing to the seller in the meantime, Bunsen sues for damages caused by the delay. What is the seller's best defense?
o: The claim is barred by the four-year statute of limitations.
Bunsen should have rejected the delivery instead.
Bunsen's claim is barred because Bunsen never gave timely notice of the breach.
Bunsen waived all damages for the delay by accepting the late delivery without objecting at the time.
None of the above.
oe: Ten months is well within four years.
Bunsen could accept and still claim damages, with timely notice.
Correct. § 2-607(3)(a): a buyer who accepts must notify the seller of breach within a reasonable time after discovering it or be barred from any remedy.
Accepting goods doesn't waive damages for the breach (§ 2-607(2)).
C is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Notice after accepting a late delivery

q: When the § 1-203(b) test isn't met, a court returns to the facts under § 1-203(a). What is the real question?
o: Whether the lessor is a merchant.
Whether the parties used the word "lease."
Whether the rent equals the goods' value at signing.
Whether the lessor will likely get back goods with real value.
Whether the lessee pays the taxes and insurance.
oe: Merchant status has no role in the test.
Labels don't control.
Section 1-203(c)(1) says that alone doesn't create one.
Correct. Yes means a lease; no means a sale with a retained security interest.
Section 1-203(c)(3) says that alone doesn't create a security interest.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — The real question

q: Courts weigh freedom of contract against protecting weaker parties when they review warranty disclaimers. In which transaction are courts most likely to scrutinize a disclaimer closely?
o: A negotiated sale of commercial goods between merchants with lawyers.
A sale of new, prepackaged consumer goods to an individual.
Courts apply the same level of scrutiny to every transaction.
A sale of used goods between two merchants.
A sale of specially made commercial equipment between two merchants.
oe: Sophisticated, represented parties get the least protection.
Correct. On the continuum from freedom of contract to protection, new consumer goods sit at the protective end: the buyer can't negotiate, can't inspect what's inside, and expects the goods to work.
Courts apply § 2-316 to all sales, but how closely they review issues like conspicuousness and surprise varies with the buyer's need for protection.
Used goods and merchant parties both point toward freedom of contract.
Negotiated merchant deals for custom goods sit at the freedom-of-contract end.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — The protection continuum

q: A seller has an output contract to sell all of its factory's production of glass jars. Which reason for shutting down the factory is LEAST likely to be in good faith?
o: A fire that destroys the factory and its equipment.
A government order closing the factory for safety reasons.
A genuine lack of orders for the seller's products.
A desire to cut its losses after the market price has risen.
None of the above.
oe: A genuine casualty is not bad faith.
That is not the seller's bad faith.
A shutdown for lack of orders can be in good faith (cmt. 2).
Correct. Comment 2: a shutdown merely to curtail losses is not good faith.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Shutdown

q: How do courts generally treat § 2-607(3)(a) notice?
o: Leniently, though many still require some notice before suit.
As a requirement that binds merchants only.
Strictly, with a ten-day deadline in all cases.
As satisfied in all cases by filing the lawsuit.
As optional, at least for consumer buyers.
oe: Correct. Reasonable time is a fact question (§§ 1-205, 1-202; Golden v. Den-Mat). Content: § 2-607 cmt. 4.
Section 2-607(3)(a) applies to all buyers.
There's no fixed period; it's a reasonable time.
Filing a complaint generally isn't enough.
Consumers get more leeway, but notice isn't optional.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Courts lenient

q: A seller's form says: "Our warranties extend only to the original purchaser and to no other person." The state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. What is the effect of the clause on a household member injured by the goods?
o: It is ineffective, because a seller cannot exclude § 2-318's coverage.
It bars the claim, because the household member is not a purchaser.
It is effective, provided the clause is conspicuous.
It is effective unless the household member was a minor.
None of the above.
oe: Correct.
The seller may not exclude or limit the operation of § 2-318.
Conspicuousness doesn't help; the coverage can't be excluded.
There is no such exception.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Excluding § 2-318

q: A contract calls for "10 Model R generators from Seller's next production run." When does identification occur, absent other agreement?
o: When the buyer inspects the generators at the plant.
When the buyer pays any part of the price.
When the contract is made, as with all goods.
When title to the generators passes to the buyer.
When Seller ships, marks or otherwise designates particular generators.
oe: Inspection isn't an identification event.
Payment has no role in identification.
That rule is for goods already existing and identified.
Identification is a prerequisite to title passing (§ 2-401(1)), not the reverse.
Correct. Future goods are identified when shipped, marked or otherwise designated by the seller (§ 2-501(1)(b)). Existing, identified goods are identified at contracting.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — When identification happens

q: A seller bears the risk of loss, and the goods are destroyed before delivery without anyone's fault. If the goods were fungible wheat, not identified at contracting, what must the seller do?
o: Nothing, because the loss of the wheat excuses its performance.
Deliver the damaged wheat at a reduced price.
Tender other conforming wheat in place of the lost wheat.
Refund the price, since the contract is avoided.
None of the above.
oe: Fungible goods don't qualify for § 2-613.
Not required or allowed.
Correct. § 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract was made.
Only identified goods.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Fungible vs. identified

q: A New Orleans seller and a Louisiana buyer dispute a sale of goods. Their lawyer cites "UCC § 2-207" as if it governs. Which is the best response?
o: The UCC applies to merchants in every state regardless of enactment.
The ALI's adoption of Article 2 made it binding nationwide.
Section 2-207 applies, because every state has adopted Article 2.
The UCC is federal law, so it binds every state alike.
Louisiana never enacted Article 2, and the UCC is law only where enacted.
oe: Merchant status has no bearing on whether a state enacted the Code.
Drafting bodies can't make law; a legislature must enact it.
Louisiana is the well-known exception.
The UCC is state law, adopted state by state.

Correct. The UCC is a model code from the Uniform Law Commission and the American Law Institute. It has no force until a state enacts it, so always check the state's version. Louisiana never enacted Articles 2 or 2A.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Model code

q: After an oral agreement between two merchants, the buyer receives a signed letter from the seller: "Thank you for our discussion about the lumber. We look forward to doing business with you." The letter states no quantity. The buyer doesn't object. Can the seller use the letter to satisfy the statute of frauds against the buyer?
o: No, because a confirmation satisfies the statute only if it is signed by both of the parties.
No, because the letter doesn't indicate that a contract was made and states no quantity.
Yes, because both parties are merchants, and between merchants any signed letter will do.
Yes, because the buyer received the letter and didn't send a written objection within 10 days.
Yes, because the missing quantity term can be filled in by the parties' testimony at trial.
oe: A confirmation need be signed only by the sender.

Correct. Section 2-201(2) applies only to a confirmation that is "sufficient against the sender" under subsection (1): a signed writing that indicates a contract for sale has been made and states a quantity. See Problem 2-10(a).
Merchant status is necessary but not sufficient.
The 10-day rule applies only to a confirmation sufficient against the sender.
A writing that omits quantity can't support enforcement under § 2-201(1).
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Confirmation not sufficient against the sender

q: Which is a difference between lease acceptance and sale acceptance?
o: Section 2A-515 omits "acts inconsistent with ownership."
Acceptance doesn't oblige a lessee to pay rent.
Lessees can't accept goods at all.
A lessee may reject after it accepts.
A lessee accepts on signing the lease.
oe: Correct. Acceptance occurs by signifying conformity or that it will keep the goods, or by failing to reject. A lessee doesn't own the goods. Inspection rights exist anyway.
Section 2A-516(1) says it does.
Section 2A-515 says they do.
Section 2A-516(2) says no.
Acceptance follows a chance to inspect.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Lease acceptance

q: Which of the following is an installment contract under § 2-612?
o: A contract for one delivery with the price payable in 12 monthly parts.
A contract authorizing delivery in separate lots to be separately accepted.
A contract for one delivery of goods in a single shipment split among trucks for convenience.
Any contract that lasts more than one year.
All of the above.
oe: Paying in installments doesn't make an installment contract.
Correct. It qualifies even if it says each delivery is a separate contract. Delivery in separate lots is the test, not payment terms (p. 284 n.22).
It must require or authorize separate acceptance of lots.
Length alone doesn't matter.
Only the first choice qualifies.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Installment definition

q: Buyer pays a $1,000 deposit on a $2,000 sofa and then repudiates. The contract has no liquidated damages clause. Seller proves no damages. How much of the deposit can Buyer recover under § 2-718(2)?
o: $0, because a breaching buyer forfeits its deposit.
$1,000, because Seller proved no damages.
$600, because Seller may keep 20% of the price.
$500, because Seller may keep up to $500.
None of the above.
oe: A breaching buyer is entitled to restitution of the excess.
Seller may keep the statutory amount.
Correct. Seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price ($400) or $500, so Buyer recovers $1,000 − $400 = $600.
Seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price or $500, which here is $400.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Deposit restitution

q: A consignee under a nonnegotiable bill tells the carrier to reroute the goods. A different person, the buyer named in the sales contract but not the consignor, orders it to stop. What must the carrier do with a stop order from someone other than the consignor?
o: It need not obey anyone but the consignor.
It must surrender the bill to the buyer.
It must obey anyone claiming an interest in the goods.
It must obey whichever order it received first.
It must hold the goods for a court to decide.
oe: Correct. Section 2-705(3)(d).
That doesn't address the stop order.
Only the consignor's order binds it.
Priority of orders isn't the rule.
The statute doesn't require that.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Nonnegotiable bill

q: Uncle Deadly leaves his antique pocket watch with Big Ben's Jewelers for cleaning. Big Ben's both repairs and sells used watches. An employee mistakenly puts the watch in the display case, and Big Ben's sells it to Camilla, who buys it in good faith in the ordinary course. Uncle Deadly sues Camilla. What is the most likely result?
o: Uncle Deadly wins, because he handed over the watch only for cleaning, never for sale.
Camilla wins, because the watch was entrusted to a merchant that deals in watches.
The answer depends on whether Uncle Deadly signed a repair ticket limiting Big Ben's rights.
Uncle Deadly wins, because Big Ben's had no title to the watch and so could pass none.
Camilla wins only if Big Ben's sold the watch on purpose rather than by mistake.
oe: The conditions of the delivery don't matter. Any delivery counts as entrusting (§ 2-403(3)).

Correct. Entrusting goods to a merchant that deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer all of the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course (§ 2-403(2)). Entrusting includes any delivery for any purpose, such as repair (§ 2-403(3)).
The paperwork for the entrustment doesn't change the result.
Entrustment creates a power to transfer the entruster's rights even though the merchant has no title.
Section 2-403(2) doesn't depend on the merchant's motive.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Entrustment to a merchant

q: Which of the following statements about liquidated damages under § 2-718 is NOT correct?
o: A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty.
Nothing in § 2-718 requires the clause to be conspicuous.
The clause may state a fixed sum or a formula for computing damages.
Damages for breach by either the buyer or the seller may be liquidated in the agreement.
A clause is enforceable only if the actual harm later proves hard to measure.
oe: True. That is the last sentence of § 2-718(1).
True. Conspicuousness is a § 2-316 requirement for some disclaimers, not for liquidated damages.
True. Either form is permitted.
True. § 2-718(1) applies to "breach by either party."

Correct. This is the false statement. Difficulty of proof is one factor in judging reasonableness; it isn't a condition that the actual harm turn out hard to measure. A clause reasonable in light of anticipated harm can be enforced.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — LD rules: NOT correct

q: A contract says the statute of frauds won't apply, sets a 5-year notice-free termination right, and says reasonable time for rejection is one hour for complex machinery. Which is correct under § 1-302?
o: Only a court may set a reasonable time.
Only the statute of frauds term is enforceable.
The first fails, and the last fails as manifestly unreasonable.
None is enforceable, as Article 2 rules are mandatory.
All three are enforceable by freedom of contract.
oe: Parties may set it under § 1-302(b).
That's the one that clearly fails.

Correct. Some rules aren't variable, and the statute of frauds is one (cmt. 1). Parties may set standards unless manifestly unreasonable (§ 1-302(b)), and § 1-205 ties reasonable time to nature and purpose. Sections 2-309(3), 2-616(3), 2-718(1) and 2-719(3) are explicit limits.
Most are default rules.
Section 1-302 has limits.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Non-variable rules

q: Under § 2-306(1), which statement about the "unreasonably disproportionate" limit is correct?
o: It applies only when the buyer acts in bad faith to exploit the market.
It allows the seller to refuse any increase over the prior year's quantity.
It applies even in good faith, measured against estimates or past needs.
It applies only when the contract states an estimate of quantity.
None of the above.
oe: Orange & Rockland held it applies even when a party acts in complete good faith.
Only unreasonably disproportionate increases.
Correct. It is a limit separate from good faith, measured against any stated estimate or, if none, against normal or comparable prior requirements.
With no estimate, quantity is measured against normal or comparable prior output or requirements.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Disproportion: separate test

q: A buyer paid its first installment on June 1, the seller identified the goods on June 3, and the seller became insolvent on June 9. From what date does the ten-day period in § 2-502(1)(b) run?
o: June 1, the seller's receipt of the first installment.
The date the buyer tenders the balance of the price.
The date of the contract, whenever that was.
June 9, the date the seller became insolvent.
June 3, the date the goods were identified.
oe: Correct. The seller must become insolvent within ten days after receiving the first installment.
The tender is a separate element and doesn't set the period.
The statute keys the period to the first installment.
Insolvency must occur within the ten days; it doesn't start them.
Identification isn't the trigger for the ten days.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Timing of insolvency

q: Under § 1-103(a), the UCC must be liberally construed to promote all of the following purposes EXCEPT:
o: permitting the continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement.
simplifying, clarifying, and modernizing the law governing commercial transactions.
making the law uniform among the various jurisdictions.
protecting consumers from unfair terms in every sale of goods.
None of the above.
oe: Purpose (2).
Purpose (1).
Purpose (3).
Correct. Consumer protection isn't one of the three § 1-103(a) purposes; specific provisions (like § 2-302 and § 2-719(3)) and other consumer laws do that work.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Purposes of the UCC

q: A five-year supply contract provides: "This agreement ends automatically if Buyer closes its Wilmington store." The buyer closes that store, and the contract ends. The seller argues the buyer had to give it reasonable notice first. Is the seller right?
o: No, because closing the store was a breach, so the seller canceled the contract.
Yes, because any agreement that dispenses with notice of termination is invalid.
Yes, because every termination of a sales contract requires reasonable notice.
Yes, because the duty of good faith requires the buyer to warn the seller first.
No, because no notice is needed when the contract ends on an agreed event.
oe: Closing the store was the agreed ending event, not a breach.
A clause dispensing with notice is invalid only if its operation would be unconscionable.
Section 2-309(3) expressly excepts termination on an agreed event.
Good faith applies, but it doesn't add a notice requirement that the statute excepts.

Correct. Termination "except on the happening of an agreed event" requires reasonable notification (§ 2-309(3)). When the parties agree that a specified event ends the contract, no notice is required.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Termination on an agreed event

q: A distributor sues its supplier with a single claim: that the supplier "breached the duty of good faith" by being curt and uncooperative in meetings. The distributor doesn't point to any contract term whose performance or enforcement was affected. What is the most likely result?
o: The claim succeeds if the supplier fell below reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
The claim fails, because good faith can be disclaimed by agreement and was disclaimed here.
The claim succeeds, because every contract governed by the UCC imposes a duty of good faith.
The claim fails, because good faith doesn't create a claim apart from the contract's terms.
The claim fails, because the parties' contract didn't expressly mention good faith.
oe: Fair dealing is part of the definition of good faith (§ 1-201(b)(20)), but it still must attach to performing or enforcing a term.
Good faith can't be disclaimed (§ 1-302(b)), and nothing suggests a disclaimer.
The duty exists, but it works through specific contract obligations, not as a free-standing claim.

Correct. Every contract imposes an obligation of good faith "in its performance and enforcement" (§ 1-304). Comment 1 explains that the doctrine doesn't support an independent cause of action for failure to perform or enforce in good faith. It operates through the contract's terms.
The obligation is imposed by law in every contract. The problem is the lack of a connection to any term.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith isn't a stand-alone claim

q: Same seller, same contract, but Vega ships the full 1,000 bushels on July 16, one day late. They arrive on the date they would have arrived had they shipped on the 15th. May Marchetti reject?
o: No, because under § 2-504 a shipment problem counts only if material delay ensues.
No, because a one-day delay is cured by arrival at the normal time.
No, because no harm resulted and the buyer must show damages to reject.
Yes, because a missed shipment date is a nonconforming tender.
Yes, but only if the contract says time is of the essence.
oe: That limit covers carrier arrangements and notice, not the shipment date.
Late shipment can't be cured by the timing of arrival.
Section 2-601 requires no showing of harm.
Correct. Section 2-504's materiality limit reaches only a failure to make a proper carrier contract or to notify the buyer. It doesn't excuse a late shipment, so § 2-601 applies.
No such requirement exists under the perfect tender rule.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Late shipment under § 2-504
pre: Vega contracts to sell 1,000 bushels of Early Girl tomatoes to Marchetti, F.O.B. Vega's farm, ship by July 15. No trade usage or prior dealing bears on the point. Vega ships 990 bushels on July 14. May Marchetti reject the whole shipment?

q: An ordinary lessee accepts goods and doesn't tell the lessor about a defect for 18 months. It then sues. There's no supplier. What is the lessor's best defense?
o: A lessee can't sue on a warranty.
Acceptance bars all remedies.
No notice within a reasonable time, so the remedy is barred.
The lessor had no duty to deliver conforming goods.
The statute of limitations has run.
oe: It can.
It doesn't, with notice.
Correct. Section 2A-516(3)(a).
It did.
Four years hasn't run.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Notice in an ordinary lease

q: A store sends a customer a telescope to try at home for 14 days, with no duty to keep it. Separately, a wholesaler sends a retailer sweaters to resell, returning any unsold. A burglar takes both before acceptance or return. Who bears each loss?
o: The loss is split equally in each case.
The store bears the telescope loss; the retailer the sweaters'.
The buyers bear both, as they had possession.
The customer bears the telescope; the wholesaler the sweaters.
The sellers bear both, as neither buyer had accepted.
oe: There's no split rule.

Correct. Sections 2-326, 2-327. A sale on approval (for use): risk and title stay with the seller until acceptance. A sale or return (for resale): risk and title are with the buyer, who bears return at its own risk.
A sale on approval leaves risk with the seller.
That's reversed.
Sale or return puts risk on the buyer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Sale on approval vs. sale or return

q: A buyer accepts goods, then the market falls 30%. Which statement is correct?
o: It may cancel because market conditions have changed.
It owes the price and can't force the goods back on the seller.
It may reject if the seller happens to be a merchant.
It may reject within a reasonable time after the market falls.
It owes only the current market price of the goods.
oe: A market shift isn't a ground to cancel.
Correct. Sections 2-607(1)-(2). Losing rejection keeps a buyer from using a defect to escape a falling market.
Merchant status has no role here.
Acceptance precludes rejection (§ 2-607(2)).
It owes the contract price (§ 2-607(1)).
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Owes the price

q: A cautious lessor files a financing statement naming the parties "lessor" and "lessee." The lessee later argues the filing proves the deal is a sale. Which is correct?
o: The filing is conclusive proof of a security interest.
The filing waives the lessor's residual interest.
The filing is improper under Article 2A.
The filing shifts the risk of loss to the lessee.
The filing isn't evidence of a sale, and it perfects if one exists.
oe: Section 9-505(b): it isn't even a factor.
It waives nothing.
Section 9-505(a) allows it.
Filing has no such effect.
Correct. Section 9-505; n.3.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Protective filing

q: A consumer signs a form with a conspicuous disclaimer mentioning merchantability that fully satisfies § 2-316, for a used car with a known hidden defect. She argues unconscionability. Which statement is correct?
o: A § 2-316-compliant disclaimer can still be unconscionable.
Unconscionability applies only between merchants.
A jury decides unconscionability after hearing the evidence.
Compliance with § 2-316 always defeats an unconscionability claim.
Parties can waive § 2-302 in their contract.
oe: Correct. Section 2-302 applies mostly in consumer cases and can't be contracted away. Courts weigh matters like the price compared with value, but compliance with § 2-316 doesn't end the inquiry. The text notes some split on this point.
It arises mostly in consumer cases.
The court decides it as a matter of law.
Compliance doesn't by itself end the § 2-302 analysis.
It can't be contracted away.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionable though compliant

q: Which is NOT a purpose of the notice requirement in § 2-607(3)(a), as quoted from Aqualon?
o: To give the buyer a fresh right to reject.
To protect the seller against stale claims.
To open the way to a settlement.
To prevent surprise and let the seller suggest a fix.
To let the seller investigate and prepare its defense.
oe: Correct. The purposes are to prevent surprise and let the seller recommend a fix, let the seller investigate and prepare, open the way to settlement, and protect against stale claims. It also lets the seller preserve rights against its own supplier (Hebron).
A purpose (Aqualon).
A purpose (Aqualon).
A purpose (Aqualon).
A purpose (Aqualon).
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Purposes of notice

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors used to decide which law governs a transaction?
o: The nature of the rights being transferred.
Whether the parties are merchants.
The location of the parties.
The parties' agreement on governing law.
The type of property involved.
oe: This is the second factor (sale, lease, license, lien, gift).
Correct. Merchant status changes particular Article 2 rules, but never whether Article 2 applies (Problem 1-4).
This is the third factor (domestic or international, which can bring in the CISG).
This is the fourth factor.
This is the first factor (goods, real estate, services, intellectual property).
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Four factors

q: Under an installment contract, a buyer is late on one payment. May the seller cancel the whole contract?
o: Only with the buyer's consent to cancel.
No, never, because installment contracts can't be cancelled.
Yes, on any breach, as with a single delivery.
Yes, after 10 days without payment.
Only if the breach substantially impairs the whole contract.
oe: No consent is needed.
They can if the test is met.
Installment contracts need substantial impairment.
Section 2-612(3) sets no fixed period; it turns on substantial impairment of the whole.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Cancel an installment contract

q: Which statement about rejection is correct?
o: A rejection that is not rightful counts as an acceptance of the goods.
A rejection is effective only if the goods are in fact nonconforming.
A rejection can be effective even though it is not rightful.
A rejection is rightful whenever notice is timely.
None of the above.
oe: A wrongful but effective rejection isn't an acceptance.
That confuses effectiveness with rightfulness.

Correct. Whether the buyer had the right to reject (nonconforming tender) and whether the rejection was effective (timely, clear notice) are separate questions. A wrongful but effective rejection means no acceptance, but the buyer is in breach.
Timing goes to effectiveness; rightfulness turns on nonconformity.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Right vs. effective

q: Animal buys a new motor scooter from a dealer on May 1 and uses it without trouble for three weeks. On his next ride, the ignition shorts out and the scooter won't start. The dealer argues (1) that the scooter worked for three weeks, so it was merchantable when sold, and (2) that the dealer didn't know of any defect. Which is correct?
o: Argument (1) only.
Argument (2), but only because Animal is a consumer rather than a merchant.
Both arguments are correct.
Argument (2) only.
None of the above.
oe: Three weeks of normal use doesn't prove the scooter was free of defects at sale. A latent defect can appear later.
The buyer's status doesn't make the seller's knowledge relevant.
Neither argument is correct.
The seller's knowledge is irrelevant to an implied warranty claim.

Correct. Neither argument defeats the claim, as long as Animal can show the ignition defect existed when the scooter was sold. A latent defect can surface after weeks of normal use and can be proved circumstantially, and implied warranty liability is strict, so the seller's ignorance is irrelevant. See Problem 3-10(a).
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Defect after weeks of use; seller's knowledge

q: A distributor properly terminates an at-will supply arrangement. Before termination, the supplier shipped a load of nonconforming goods that the distributor accepted. What happens to the distributor's claim for that load?
o: It survives, because termination ends only executory duties.
It survives only if the distributor reserved it in the notice.
It becomes a claim for lost profits.
It is extinguished, because termination discharges all obligations.
None of the above.
oe: No reservation is needed.
It stays a claim for the earlier breach.
Only executory obligations.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — What survives termination

q: A candy maker buys an industrial mixer under a negotiated contract with two separate clauses: (1) an exclusive repair-or-replace remedy, and (2) a conspicuous exclusion of all consequential damages. The repair remedy fails of its essential purpose, and the candy maker sues for $90,000 in lost profits. The state follows the majority (independent) approach. What is the most likely result?
o: It may recover the lost profits, because excluding consequential damages is prima facie unconscionable.
It may recover the lost profits only if the exclusion was not conspicuous.
It may recover direct damages, but the exclusion of lost profits stands unless that clause is itself unconscionable.
It may recover nothing, because its exclusive remedy was repair or replacement.
It may recover the lost profits, because when the repair remedy fails, every limit on remedies falls with it.
oe: That presumption applies only to personal injury from consumer goods. Limiting commercial loss is not prima facie unconscionable.
§ 2-719 has no conspicuousness requirement. The test is unconscionability.

Correct. Under the independent approach, the consequential-damages exclusion is judged on its own under § 2-719(3) and survives the failure of the repair remedy unless unconscionable. Excluding commercial lost profits in a negotiated deal is not.
The failed limited remedy gives way under § 2-719(2), so direct damages are available.
That is the minority (dependent) approach. The majority tests the exclusion separately.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Independent approach: commercial loss

q: A collector agrees to sell a rare stamp collection to a dealer under a signed memo saying, "We will not be bound until we agree on a price." The dealer pays a $5,000 deposit and receives part of the collection. They never agree on a price. What is the effect?
o: A reasonable price applies, because the parties signed a memo and partly performed, showing intent to contract.
There is no contract, so each side returns what it received (or pays its value).
The dealer must pay whatever price the collector names in good faith.
The collector may keep the deposit as liquidated damages.
None of the above.
oe: They expressly intended not to be bound without an agreed price.
Nothing gave the collector the power to set the price.
There's no contract and no liquidated-damages term.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — No deal without a price

q: In which lease may a lessee deduct its damages from rent, on notice?
o: A non-consumer finance lease after acceptance.
Only a lease under $1,000.
An ordinary lease.
No lease of any kind.
Only a lease with a clause allowing it.
oe: Section 2A-407 forbids it.
Section 2A-508(6) has no dollar limit.
Correct. Section 2A-508(6), subject to § 2A-407: not in a non-consumer finance lease after acceptance.
Ordinary lessees may.
The statute itself allows it.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Deducting from rent

q: A fuel supply contract lets the seller set the monthly price but adds: "A price no higher than the published regional index plus 3 cents a gallon is conclusively in good faith." Is the clause effective?
o: Yes, because parties may set standards for good faith that are not manifestly unreasonable.
Yes, because the parties may disclaim the duty of good faith entirely, as long as they do so expressly.
No, because the duty of good faith can't be varied by agreement.
No, because price terms set by one party are void.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 1-302(b). Tying the price to an objective index is the kind of standard Problem 5-1(a) suggests.
Good faith can never be disclaimed.
It can't be disclaimed, but the parties may set standards for measuring it.
§ 2-305(2) allows a price set by one party.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Setting good-faith standards

q: On the back of a four-page purchase agreement for an industrial dishwasher, paragraph 19 of 31 reads: "Seller disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability." It's printed in the same small, plain type as every other paragraph, with no heading. The buyer never read it. The dishwasher fails in ordinary use. Is merchantability effectively disclaimed?
o: Yes, because the buyer signed the agreement and is bound by everything in it.
No, because a written disclaimer of merchantability must be conspicuous, and this one isn't.
No, because merchantability can never be disclaimed in a sale of new goods.
Yes, because both parties are businesses and should read their contracts.
Yes, because the clause expressly mentions merchantability, as § 2-316(2) requires.
oe: Signing doesn't cure the lack of conspicuousness that § 2-316(2) requires.

Correct. A term is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to have noticed it, for example through a heading in capitals or larger, contrasting type (§ 1-201(b)(10)). A clause buried in identical small print isn't conspicuous, so § 2-316(2) isn't satisfied.
It can be disclaimed by language that meets § 2-316.
Section 2-316(2) applies between merchants too.
Mentioning merchantability is necessary, but a written disclaimer must also be conspicuous.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Written disclaimer not conspicuous

q: A lease lets the lessee buy the goods at the end "at fair market value determined at that time." Under § 1-203(d), that price is:
o: Nominal, because no dollar figure is fixed.
Nominal, if the goods end up worth little.
Nominal, unless a third party appraises it.
Void for indefiniteness.
Not nominal, as a matter of statute.
oe: The statute treats such a price as not nominal.
The statute settles this for stated FMV options.
No appraisal requirement exists.
A price set by market value later is definite enough.
Correct. Consideration isn't nominal if it is stated to be fair market value determined when the option is performed.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — FMV option

q: Which of the following would satisfy the requirement that a merchant's confirmation be "sufficient against the sender" under § 2-201(2)?
o: A signed letter confirming "our widget deal" with no quantity.
A signed price quote for "widgets, quantity to be determined."
An unsigned invoice listing the goods and the price.
"This confirms our deal: 500 widgets at $10. /s/ Seller."
All of the above.
oe: Not sufficient. Quantity is the one essential term.
Not sufficient. A quote does not indicate that a contract was made, and it states no quantity.
Not sufficient. It is not signed by the sender (Problem 2-10(A)).
Correct. It is signed by the sender, indicates a contract was made, and states a quantity, so it satisfies § 2-201(1) against the sender.
Only D is sufficient.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Sufficient against the sender

q: A dealer contracts to sell a specific used car for $5,000 to Dana for family use. Dana pays $1,000. The dealer, solvent, then refuses to deliver, and similar cars are easy to find. Which is Dana's strongest route to the car?
o: Section 2-502(1)(b), because of the dealer's insolvency.
Section 2-716(3), because she cannot cover.
Section 2-716(1), because every car is unique.
Section 2-502(1)(a), on tender of the $4,000 balance.
None of them; she may only recover her $1,000.
oe: The dealer is solvent.
The facts say similar cars are easy to find.
A readily replaced used car isn't unique, and § 2-502 is the better route.
Correct. A specific existing car is identified at contracting. Dana has prepaid part, the goods are for family use, and the seller repudiated.
Section 2-502(1)(a) reaches the car itself.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Paid car, family use

q: Sweetums sells a bandstand riser to Dr. Teeth's nightclub, "F.O.B. Buyer's loading dock." The carrier arrives at the dock at 10 a.m. on a weekday, as scheduled, and tells the club the riser is ready to unload. The club's manager says the staff is busy and asks the driver to wait in the lot until the next morning. Overnight, the truck is struck by lightning and the riser is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: Sweetums, because a merchant seller bears the risk until the buyer actually receives the goods.
Sweetums, because in a destination contract risk passes only when the buyer takes the goods.
The carrier, because it agreed to keep the riser on its truck overnight.
The club, because the riser was duly tendered at the destination at a reasonable hour.
Sweetums, because the riser was still in the carrier's possession when it was destroyed.
oe: The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) applies only when goods are not shipped by carrier or held by a bailee.
The trigger is due tender at the destination, not the buyer's receipt.
The carrier's liability is a separate matter. As between seller and buyer, the risk had passed.

Correct. In a destination contract, risk passes when the goods are "duly so tendered as to enable the buyer to take delivery" there (§ 2-509(1)(b)). The carrier held the riser at the dock at a reasonable hour with notice. The club's choice not to unload doesn't keep the risk on the seller.
Who has physical possession doesn't decide it. Once due tender was made at the destination, risk passed even though the riser stayed on the truck.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Destination contract; buyer delays taking delivery

q: In a requirements contract estimated at 1,000 units, the buyer lands a huge new customer and honestly needs 8,000. In another, the buyer orders its normal 1,000 but resells half to exploit the market. Which is correct?
o: The first is disproportionate; the second is proportionate but in bad faith.
Both are valid, because the buyer alone sets requirements.
Neither contract can be enforced for lack of a quantity.
The first is valid, as honesty is the only test.
The second is valid, as the quantity matched the estimate.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-2. Section 2-306(1) needs good faith and no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to a stated estimate. Both can fail, for different reasons.
Section 2-306(1) sets limits.
Section 2-306 saves them.
Disproportion is a separate limit.
Good faith is a separate limit.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Honest but huge requirements

q: Which act by a buyer is LEAST likely to defeat an otherwise effective rejection?
o: Reselling the goods to a customer.
Installing the parts into its finished products.
Putting the goods into its regular sales inventory.
Taking possession of the goods to inspect them.
Telling the seller it will keep them anyway.
oe: Reselling generally is an act of acceptance.
That's inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
That also acts as an owner.
Correct. Merely taking possession to inspect isn't acceptance (§ 2-513). The other acts signal keeping the goods or are inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
That signifies acceptance under § 2-606(1)(a).
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Acts that defeat rejection

q: Grover buys a heat pump from a dealer. Nothing was said about a warranty during the sale. When the unit is installed, the box contains an owner's manual stating: "This unit is free from defects in materials and workmanship for one year." Eight months later the compressor fails because of a manufacturing defect. Under the approach of the Official Comments, which statement is most accurate?
o: It's only an implied warranty, because it appeared in printed materials packed with the goods.
It's a warranty only if Grover read the manual before the compressor failed.
It can be an express warranty, because a post-sale statement can modify the deal without consideration.
It can't be a warranty, because Grover gave no consideration in exchange for the promise.
It can't be a warranty, because statements made after the contract is formed are never part of the bargain.
oe: A specific promise about freedom from defects is an express affirmation, not an implied term.
Under the comment's approach, the statement becomes part of the deal as a modification. Nothing makes reading before failure the test.

Correct. Comment 7 to § 2-313 says the precise time a statement is made isn't controlling, and an affirmation made after the sale can become a modification under § 2-209, which needs no consideration. Some courts disagree, so the answer is "can be." See Problem 3-7.
Modifications under § 2-209(1) need no consideration.
Comment 7 rejects a rigid timing rule.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Statement made after the sale

q: A supply agreement of indefinite duration lets the large buyer terminate "at any time, without any notice." The small supplier, which depends on the buyer for 90% of its sales, had no power to negotiate. The buyer terminates without notice. Is the no-notice term enforceable?
o: No, if waiving notice would be unconscionable here.
Yes, because the contract was of indefinite duration.
No, because termination always requires 30 days' notice.
Yes, because parties may always waive notice.
None of the above.
oe: That's when the notice rule applies.
The standard is reasonable notice, not 30 days.
Not if waiving notice would be unconscionable.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Waiving notice of termination

q: A sale-of-goods contract contains this conspicuous clause: "THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES WHICH EXTEND BEYOND THE DESCRIPTION ON THE FACE HEREOF." The seller is a merchant, and the goods are unfit for ordinary use. Which implied warranty most clearly survives?
o: Title, because only title survives a general disclaimer.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because the clause excludes only express warranties.
Both, because the clause isn't specific enough to exclude any warranty.
Merchantability, because the clause doesn't mention merchantability.
Neither, because the clause excludes all warranties.
oe: Title is governed by § 2-312(2) and survives this clause, but the question asks which implied warranty of quality most clearly survives.
The clause is the statutory model for excluding fitness.
It's the statute's own example for fitness.

Correct. That language is the statute's example of language sufficient to exclude fitness (§ 2-316(2)). Merchantability can be excluded only by language that mentions it, or by an alternative under § 2-316(3).
It excludes fitness but not merchantability.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fitness language leaves merchantability

q: A seller orders a carrier to stop goods. What are the three questions to analyze?
o: Carrier's solvency, insurance, and merchant status.
Whether the bill is signed, the price fair, and notice written.
Seller's right, carrier's duty to obey, and who is liable.
Whether the contract is assigned, an installment, or a lease.
Whether the buyer accepted, revoked, or covered.
oe: Those aren't the stoppage questions.
Those aren't the stoppage questions.

Correct. Under § 2-705(3) the seller must give notice enabling the carrier, with reasonable diligence, to prevent delivery. The carrier then holds as directed, and the seller pays charges and damages.
Those are other topics.
Those are other topics.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Three stoppage questions

q: Snuffy has bought equipment from Big Bird's Equipment for years, and Big Bird has always delivered it to Snuffy's farm. Their new contract for a skid loader is silent on delivery. Big Bird tells Snuffy to come pick it up. Who is in breach if neither budges?
o: Snuffy, because course of dealing never fills an open term.
Big Bird, because the parties' course of dealing fills the delivery term.
Neither, because the contract is too indefinite to enforce.
Snuffy, because the default place of delivery is the seller's place of business.
None of the above.
oe: Course of dealing explains and supplements the agreement (§ 1-303(d)).
Correct. Problem 3-8(B). No gap means no gap filler.
Open terms don't defeat the contract.
The gap filler applies only if there is a gap; course of dealing fills it first.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Course of dealing fills gap

q: Under § 2-716(3), a buyer has a right of replevin for goods identified to the contract if:
o: It has paid at least part of the price for the goods.
The goods are unique, whether or not they are identified.
The court finds, in its discretion, that damages are inadequate.
The seller became insolvent within 10 days after the first payment.
It can't cover after reasonable effort, or goods shipped under reservation are paid for.
oe: Part payment is a § 2-502 element, not a replevin element.
Replevin always needs identified goods; uniqueness belongs to specific performance.
Replevin is a legal right, so the court has no such discretion.
Correct. Replevin is a legal right, so the court has no discretion once the elements are met. Prepayment is not required unless the goods were shipped under reservation.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Replevin elements

q: A court finds a clause in a consumer installment contract unconscionable. Which of the following may the court NOT do under § 2-302?
o: Limit the clause's application to avoid an unconscionable result.
Let the parties present evidence of the clause's commercial setting and purpose.
Refuse to enforce the whole contract.
Enforce the rest of the contract without the clause.
Award the buyer punitive damages for the seller's overreaching.
oe: It may.
It may.
Correct. § 2-302 lets a court refuse to enforce, strike, or limit. It is a defense, not a source of damages.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: remedies

q: A contract for machinery reads "F.A.S. the vessel Calypso, Port of Baltimore." The seller places the goods alongside the ship in the usual manner and gets a receipt from the ship's agent. A wave damages them on the dock before loading. Who bears the loss?
o: The carrier, because goods at a port are in its custody.
The buyer, because risk passed when the goods were alongside.
The buyer, but only if it had paid for the goods.
The seller, because the goods were never loaded on board.
The seller, because F.A.S. is always a destination term.
oe: The carrier hasn't taken them.

Correct. Under § 2-319(2), the seller must deliver alongside and obtain and tender a receipt. The buyer must give instructions (and failing that, it fails to cooperate). Risk passes once the seller has done so. F.O.B. vessel adds loading on board at the seller's risk.
Payment doesn't shift risk.
That describes F.O.B. vessel, not F.A.S.
It's a delivery term at the port of shipment.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — F.A.S. vessel

q: A lessor wants to know what it loses if its deal is recharacterized. Which is NOT a consequence?
o: The buyer in bankruptcy may keep the goods by paying their value.
The lessee's payments become rent deductible by the lessee.
Articles 2 and 9 replace Article 2A.
The seller, not the buyer, loses the tax ownership.
The seller must perfect, typically by filing.
oe: A true consequence.
Correct. That's what a true lease gives. Recharacterization means the buyer is tax owner and payments aren't rent. The lessor also needs perfection, and faces Article 9 and bankruptcy treatment.
A true consequence.
A true consequence.
A true consequence.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Why lessors want a true lease

q: A contract for 2,000 custom display cases says: "For each full week of delay, Seller shall pay Buyer 2% of the contract price, up to a maximum of 10%." The clause appears in ordinary type in the middle of a long paragraph. The seller argues the clause is unenforceable (1) because it states a formula rather than a dollar amount, and (2) because it isn't conspicuous. Which argument is correct?
o: Argument (1) only.
Argument (2) only.
Both (1) and (2).
Both, but only if the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: A liquidated damages clause may specify an amount or a formula for calculating damages.
Unlike a warranty disclaimer, a liquidated damages clause need not be conspicuous.
Neither argument is correct.
Merchant status doesn't matter. Formulas are permitted, and no conspicuousness rule applies to liquidated damages.

Correct. Neither argument works. A liquidated damages clause may use a formula, and § 2-718 has no conspicuousness requirement. The only question is whether the formula is reasonable under § 2-718(1).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Formula; not conspicuous

q: In Case 1, a buyer who accepted sues for breach of warranty. In Case 2, a seller sues a buyer who rejected, claiming the goods conformed. Who bears the burden of proving nonconformity or conformity?
o: Neither; the court decides without burdens.
The buyer in both cases.
The seller in both cases.
The buyer in Case 1; the seller in Case 2.
The seller in Case 1; the buyer in Case 2.
oe: Ordinary burdens apply.
In Case 2 the seller is suing.
In Case 1 the buyer bears it.
Correct. Section 2-607(4) puts it on the accepting buyer. After rejection it falls on whichever party sues.
That's reversed.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Burden, rejected vs. accepted

q: A lessee's 12-month replacement lease of a similar machine has different maintenance and insurance terms than its 36-month lease. What issue does § 2A-518 raise?
o: The new lease may not be "substantially similar."
Different terms don't matter under § 2A-518.
The lessee has no remedy at all.
The new lease is void.
The new lease must have exactly the same rent.
oe: Correct. Comments 3-7.
They go to similarity.
It still has § 2A-519.
Nothing makes it void.
The rent difference is the measure.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Substantially similar

q: Rancher gives a calf not yet born to a neighbor as a gift, and separately contracts to sell a future calf to a buyer. Which statement is correct under the UCC definitions?
o: Article 2 definitions apply to all UCC articles.
A gift can't be a "purchase" under any UCC definition.
Unborn young can be goods, and "purchase" includes taking by gift.
Animals are never goods, because they aren't manufactured.
Unborn young can't be goods until they are born.
oe: Section 1-201 applies to all articles; §§ 2-103 to 2-106 are specific to Article 2.
Section 1-201(b)(29) reaches any voluntary transaction creating an interest, including a gift.
Correct. Section 2-105(1) includes the unborn young of animals. "Purchase" in § 1-201 is broad enough to include a gift, though the protections for a good-faith purchaser also need value.
Goods are things movable at identification, manufactured or not.
Section 2-105(1) expressly includes them.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Definitions of purchase and goods

q: Under an open-price contract, a fertilizer supplier charges every customer its published list price, which tracks the market. Nothing suggests an improper motive. A buyer argues the price is too high. What is the likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because a seller-set price must equal the seller's cost plus a reasonable profit.
The buyer wins, because a seller-set price must be renegotiated each time.
The buyer wins, because open-price terms are unenforceable.
The supplier wins, because a price set by one party is never reviewable.
None of the above.
oe: No cost-plus rule exists.
§ 2-305(2) lets one party set the price.
§ 2-305 makes them enforceable.
It must be set in good faith.
Correct. The supplier wins: in the normal case, a posted price or a price in effect in the market satisfies the good-faith requirement (§ 2-305 cmt. 3). No choice says that.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Posted price safe harbor

q: A merchant seller's signed contract states, in bold capitals just above the signature line: "THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED, WITH THIS SALE." Measured against the requirements of § 2-316(2), which implied warranties does this language exclude?
o: Fitness for a particular purpose only.
Merchantability only.
Merchantability, fitness, and the warranty of title.
Both merchantability and fitness.
Neither, because the clause doesn't mention either warranty by name.
oe: Correct. Fitness may be excluded by any conspicuous writing (§ 2-316(2)). Merchantability requires language that mentions "merchantability," which this clause doesn't. (Some courts accept general language under § 2-316(3)(a), but § 2-316(2) alone doesn't.)
Merchantability can't be excluded under § 2-316(2) without mentioning it.
Title is excluded only by specific language or circumstances (§ 2-312(2)), and the clause fails for merchantability anyway.
The clause works for fitness but not merchantability under § 2-316(2), because it never mentions merchantability.
Fitness doesn't have to be named; a conspicuous writing is enough.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — General disclaimer vs. § 2-316(2)

q: Under an installment contract, a buyer fails to pay for Load 3. The seller withholds Load 4, but doesn't cancel. Is that proper?
o: Yes, as a seller may withhold on a failure to pay.
Yes, but it must first sue for Load 3.
No, unless it first cancels the whole contract.
No, because each load is a separate contract.
No, because a seller has no right to withhold.
oe: Correct. Section 2-703(a) lets it withhold as to the goods directly affected, and if the breach is of the whole, the rest. Section 2-609 and § 2-612 cmt. 6 also support suspending.
It needn't sue first.
Cancelling isn't a precondition.
It remains one contract, under § 2-612.
Section 2-703(a) gives one.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Withhold for one installment

q: A client's deal involves a sale of equipment, a lease of forklifts, a letter of credit, a bank check, and a security interest in inventory. Which pairing of transaction and UCC Article is correct?
o: Security interest in inventory: Article 7.
Letter of credit: Article 5.
Lease of forklifts: Article 9.
Bank check: Article 8.
Sale of equipment: Article 2A.
oe: Article 7 covers documents of title; Article 9 covers security interests.

Correct. Article 2 covers sales, 2A leases, 3 and 4 instruments and bank deposits, 5 letters of credit, 7 documents of title, 8 securities, 9 secured transactions, and 12 controllable electronic records.
Leases of goods fall under Article 2A; Article 9 covers security interests.
Article 8 covers investment securities; checks fall under Articles 3 and 4.
Sales of goods fall under Article 2.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — The UCC's articles

q: A signed writing is a final expression of the parties' agreement. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement contradicting a written term. Is it admissible?
o: No, unless the seller is a merchant who drafted the writing.
Yes, if the writing is only partially integrated.
No, because a final writing can't be contradicted by prior terms.
Yes, if the oral agreement was made the same day as the writing.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter.
Contradictory prior evidence is barred even for partial integrations.
Correct. § 2-202.
Contemporaneous oral contradictions are also barred.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Contradiction

q: A contract permits "up to 3% broken cookies" per carton. The cartons delivered average 2.5% broken. Are the goods conforming under § 2-106(2)?
o: No, unless the buyer inspected a sample before contracting.
Yes, because they accord with the seller's obligations under the contract.
No, because a buyer may always reject broken goods on delivery.
Yes, but only if the seller is a merchant in such goods.
No, because the perfect tender rule requires goods without any defect.
oe: Inspection of a sample isn't a condition of conformity.
Correct. Conformity is measured against the contract's obligations, not an abstract standard of perfection.
Only nonconforming goods may be rejected.
Merchant status has no role in conformity.
Perfect tender means conforming to the contract, which allowed the breakage.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Conforming defined

q: Which is NOT correct about specific performance under § 2-716(1)?
o: It may be decreed in "other proper circumstances."
The decree may include terms on price and damages.
It may be decreed where the goods are unique.
The goods must be identified to the contract.
The court keeps discretion to refuse the decree.
oe: Correct. This is the false statement. Specific performance does not need identified goods; replevin and § 2-502 do. It may be decreed where the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, it is discretionary, and the decree may set terms on price, damages or other relief.
True: the statute says "may."
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Specific performance standard

q: In a freely negotiated three-year supply contract, Kermit agreed to buy cocoa at a fixed price that matched the market at the time. Two years later, cocoa prices collapse, and the fixed price is now triple the market. Kermit argues the price term is unconscionable. What result?
o: Kermit wins if a jury finds the price shocking.
Kermit loses, because merchants can never claim unconscionability.
Kermit wins, because the term is now substantively oppressive.
Kermit wins, because a court may rewrite any price term that becomes unfair.
Kermit loses, because the term was fair when made.
oe: The court decides unconscionability as a matter of law.
Merchants can raise it, though rarely successfully.
Later events don't count. Unconscionability is judged when the contract is made.
Courts don't rewrite bargains for later market changes. Kermit bore that risk.
Correct. Unconscionability is judged at the time of contracting, and nothing here was procedurally or substantively unfair then.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: when judged

q: A $50,000 boat warranted as worth $50,000 needs a $6,000 repair. After repair it's still worth $47,000, because of a repair record. What is the best estimate of § 2-714(2) damages?
o: $6,000: only the repair cost.
$9,000: the repair plus the leftover $3,000 drop.
$47,000: the repaired value.
$3,000: only the leftover drop.
$50,000: a full refund.
oe: That ignores the remaining loss in value.
Correct. Repair cost is a proxy. If repair leaves the goods worth less than warranted, the buyer adds the leftover loss.
That's not a measure of loss.
That ignores the repair cost.
A refund needs revocation.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Repair proxy with leftover loss

q: A non-terminable 5-year lease of a machine with a 10-year life lets the lessee renew for the remaining 5 years at $1 a year. Which is correct?
o: A security interest only if renewal is exercised.
A lease, as the lessee need not renew.
A security interest, as renewal for nominal rent meets § 1-203(b)(3).
A lease, because the initial term is short.
A lease, because options never count.
oe: It's judged at the outset.
A right for nominal rent is enough; it needn't be bound.
Correct. The renewal covers the remaining economic life for nominal consideration.
Prong (3) reaches this.
Section 1-203(c)(4) protects only a bare option.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Renewal at nominal rent

q: Siebenmann sells Rogath a painting with a written warranty that it is authentic. Before the sale, Rogath hears from a museum curator (not from Siebenmann) that the painting's authenticity is doubted. The painting is a fake. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, can Rogath recover for breach of warranty?
o: Yes, but Rogath must show he relied on the warranty when buying.
No, because Rogath did not believe the warranty when he bought.
Yes, because he may have bought the warranty as insurance.
No, because Rogath waived the warranty by closing despite the doubts.
None of the above.
oe: Rogath treats the warranty as risk allocation, not as a reliance test.
The question is whether the buyer bought the seller's promise, not whether he believed it.
Correct. Rogath held that a buyer who learns doubts from a third party or from common knowledge can still enforce the warranty.
Waiver arises only when the seller himself disclosed the facts that made the warranty false.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Rogath: third-party knowledge

q: A defective space heater that Snuffy buys sets fire to the bakery next door, damaging the bakery's ovens but injuring no one. The bakery sues the heater's seller for breach of warranty. Under which § 2-318 alternative is the bakery most likely covered?
o: Alternative C, which isn't limited to personal injury.
Alternative B, because the bakery's owner is a natural person.
Alternative A, because the bakery was affected by the heater.
None, because property damage is never recoverable for breach of warranty.
Any of the three, because a seller can't exclude § 2-318.
oe: Correct. Alternative C isn't limited to personal injury.
B is limited to persons injured in person.
A covers only the buyer's family, household, and home guests, and only for personal injury.
Property damage can be a consequential loss (§ 2-715(2)(b)).
True that it can't be excluded, but the alternatives differ in whom they cover.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Privity: property damage

q: A seller tells the buyer, "Your goods are ready for pickup." Before the buyer arrives, a fire destroys them. What decides who bears the loss?
o: Whether the seller was insured.
Whether title has passed.
Whether the buyer has paid.
Whether the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: Insurance is a rationale for the rule, not the test.
Risk is not tied to title.
Payment doesn't affect risk under § 2-509(3).
Correct. Problem 4-6(b): a merchant seller bears the loss because the buyer hasn't received the goods; a non-merchant seller doesn't, because tender is complete.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Ready for pickup: merchant vs. non-merchant

q: A lessee has a lease for 12 machines delivered monthly, each separately accepted. The third is defective, but it's curable, and the lessor gives adequate assurance of cure. May the lessee reject?
o: Yes, as any nonconformity allows rejection.
Yes, unless the lessor is a merchant.
No, because leases have no rejection right.
Yes, and it may cancel the lease.
No, it must accept given adequate assurance.
oe: That's for non-installment leases.
Merchant status doesn't matter here.
They do.
Cancelling needs impairment of the whole.
Correct. Section 2A-510(1).
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Installment lease, rejection

q: For six years, under a written supply agreement with no stated end date, Statler's Hardware has bought all its padlocks from Waldorf Locks. Waldorf abruptly stops shipping, with no notice, and tells Statler it is ending the relationship. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Waldorf has no liability, because it ended the contract for a reason other than breach.
Waldorf can't end the contract, because a six-year supply relationship becomes binding indefinitely.
Waldorf is liable for all the profits Statler would have earned had the relationship continued.
Waldorf may end the deal but owed reasonable notice, so it's liable for the lack of notice.
Waldorf has no liability, because a contract with no end date isn't enforceable at all.
oe: Termination for a reason other than breach still requires reasonable notice.
Either party may terminate an indefinite contract on reasonable notice.
An indefinite contract can be terminated, so the buyer's damages are limited to the lack of notice.

Correct. A contract of indefinite duration "may be terminated at any time by either party" (§ 2-309(2)), but termination "requires that reasonable notification be received by the other party" (§ 2-309(3)). Courts limit damages to the harm from the missing notice, not the lost future of the relationship (as in Santa Fe Custom Shutters).
Indefinite-duration contracts are valid for a reasonable time (§ 2-309(2)).
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Indefinite contract ended without notice

q: A seafood distributor has supplied fish to Miss Piggy's restaurant for three years under an oral arrangement with no stated term. The distributor gives two months' notice that it will stop, explaining only that it wants to focus on grocery stores. Miss Piggy argues that the termination is invalid. Which of the following is correct?
o: It is invalid, because the statute of frauds requires written notice of termination.
It is invalid, because the distributor needs a good-faith reason that benefits both parties.
It is invalid, because a contract that has lasted three years can be ended only for cause.
It is invalid, because good faith requires the distributor to offer new terms first.
None of the above.
oe: The statute of frauds doesn't govern termination notices.
No reason is required.
Duration doesn't convert it into a for-cause arrangement.
Good faith imposes no such duty.
Correct. The termination is valid: an indefinite contract may be terminated at any time with reasonable notice, and no reason is needed (§ 2-309(2)-(3); Santa Fe). Two months is likely reasonable.
