topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — No reason needed

q: When Abby asks about a used car's history, the private seller replies, "It's never been in an accident." Abby buys it. In fact it had been in a serious crash. The seller raises three defenses: (1) the statement was oral; (2) the seller didn't intend to make a warranty and never used the word "guarantee"; and (3) Abby could have discovered the truth by having a mechanic inspect the car. Which defense, if any, is valid?
o: Defense (1) only.
Defense (2) only.
Defense (3) only.
Defenses (2) and (3).
None of the above.
oe: Express warranties don't have to be written. Oral affirmations of fact can be the basis of the bargain.
Section 2-313(2) says formal words like "warrant" or "guarantee" aren't needed, and neither is a specific intention to make a warranty.
A buyer's opportunity to inspect doesn't defeat an express warranty.
Neither defense is valid.

Correct. None of the defenses is valid. An oral, specific affirmation of fact given in response to the buyer's question can be part of the basis of the bargain (§ 2-313(1)(a)). No formal words or intent are required (§ 2-313(2)), and a buyer who could have inspected but relied on the seller's statement keeps the warranty.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Seller's three defenses to an express warranty

q: Under the 2022 amendments to Article 2, if the goods in a hybrid transaction do NOT predominate, which of the following Article 2 provisions still applies?
o: The statute of frauds for sales of goods (§ 2-201).
The battle-of-the-forms rule (§ 2-207).
The implied warranty of merchantability (§ 2-314).
The rule on modifications without consideration (§ 2-209).
None of the above.
oe: Under § 2-102(2) cmt. 5, § 2-201 does not apply when goods don't predominate.
The formation rules (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) do not apply when goods don't predominate.

Correct. Provisions that relate primarily to the goods still apply, including the warranties (§§ 2-312 to 2-318), tender and risk of loss, acceptance, rejection and cure, and the buyer's remedies for nonconforming goods.
§ 2-209 does not apply when goods don't predominate.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: what applies when goods don't predominate

q: A wholesaler's goods have a tiny defect that it would usually overlook. The market has fallen 30%, so it rejects the whole lot to buy cheaper elsewhere, and gives prompt, accurate notice. The contract is silent. What is the seller's best response?
o: The wholesaler has automatically accepted.
The rejection isn't in good faith, given the wholesaler's usual practice.
A falling market removes all right to reject.
The notice must be given within three days.
The defect must substantially impair the goods.
oe: Timely notice prevents that, even if the rejection is wrongful.

Correct. Good faith and course of dealing or performance can bar a pretextual rejection for a minor defect. Without them, perfect tender would allow it, and the text notes good faith is the main check.
A market fall doesn't remove a genuine right.
No fixed period exists.
That's the installment standard.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Rejection and market fall

q: A seller who is not a merchant sells a boat engine with a written merchantability disclaimer that is not conspicuous. Does the buyer have a merchantability claim?
o: Yes, because merchantability is implied in every sale of goods.
No, because a non-merchant makes no merchantability warranty.
No, because the written disclaimer bars the claim.
Yes, because the disclaimer is not conspicuous enough to work.
None of the above.
oe: Only merchants.
Correct. Problem 5-4. Fitness can still arise if its elements are met.
A disclaimer that isn't conspicuous wouldn't work, but the claim fails anyway: no merchantability warranty arose.
First ask whether the warranty arose at all.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Non-merchant: no merchantability

q: Miss Piggy tells a hardware-store clerk that she needs paint for the inside of her swimming pool. The clerk suggests a pool epoxy, but Miss Piggy insists, "No, I want ParisMatte Interior Eggshell, my favorite brand." She buys it, paints the pool, and the paint peels within a week. Which statement is most accurate?
o: She has a merchantability claim, because paint that peels within a week isn't fit for any purpose.
She has both claims, because the store is a merchant that deals in paint and knew her purpose.
Probably neither claim succeeds, because she didn't rely on the store and pool use isn't ordinary.
She has no claims, because implied warranties never attach to brand-name goods the buyer selects.
She has a fitness claim, because the store knew exactly why she wanted the paint when she bought it.
oe: Merchantability is measured by the goods' ordinary purposes, not by an unusual use the buyer chose.
Merchant status supports merchantability, but the paint was fit for its ordinary use, and the fitness claim fails for lack of reliance.

Correct. The fitness warranty requires the buyer's reliance on the seller's skill or judgment (§ 2-315). When the buyer insists on a particular brand, there's no reliance (§ 2-315 cmt. 5). Merchantability measures fitness for the ordinary purposes of interior paint, and pool use isn't one of them.
Brand-name goods carry implied warranties. Insisting on a brand defeats only the reliance element of fitness.
Knowledge of the purpose isn't enough. The buyer must also rely on the seller to select the goods, and she overrode the clerk.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Buyer insists on a brand: no reliance

q: A written contract might include any of the following clauses. Which one, standing alone, would most clearly bar evidence of a consistent additional term agreed to orally before signing?
o: "This Agreement is the complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the parties' agreement."
"This Agreement represents the final agreement of the parties with respect to its subject matter."
"This Agreement shall be governed by and construed under the law of the State of Delaware."
"This Agreement may not be modified or amended except by a writing signed by both parties."
"Seller disclaims all implied warranties, including the implied warranty of merchantability."
oe: Correct. A finding that the writing was intended as "a complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the agreement" is what bars consistent additional terms under § 2-202(b). See Problem 5-11.
A final writing bars contradiction, but without more it can still be supplemented by consistent additional terms.
A choice-of-law clause says nothing about integration.
That's a no-oral-modification clause. It governs later changes, not prior terms.
That's a disclaimer, not an integration clause.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Which clause creates a complete integration

q: A lessee rightfully rejects leased machines after paying $10,000 in rent and security. The lessor won't refund. What may it do?
o: Hold and dispose of them in good faith, and account for any excess.
Keep them as its own.
Repossess the lessor's other goods.
Use them for the rest of the term.
Return them, and abandon the $10,000.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-508(5) gives a security interest, subject to § 2A-527(5).
It has only a security interest.
It has no such right.
That risks acceptance.
It may hold them.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Lessee's lien and resale

q: Who bears the burden of proving breach regarding goods accepted, and after a rejection?
o: The seller in every case, since it promised conformity.
The seller after acceptance; the buyer after rejection.
The buyer in every case, including after rejection.
The buyer after acceptance; the party suing after rejection.
Neither, because burdens don't apply to warranty claims.
oe: Section 2-607(4) puts it on the buyer after acceptance.
That reverses the acceptance rule.
After rejection it depends on who sues.
Correct. Section 2-607(4) for accepted goods. After rejection, the burden falls on whichever party sues.
Ordinary burdens apply.
topic: Wk 9 · XXI · Acceptance, notice of breach & accepted-goods damages (§§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717) — Burden after acceptance

q: Prairie Dawn signs and sends a purchase order for 1,000 notebooks at $2 each to a stationery wholesaler. The wholesaler never signs anything but ships. Before the notebooks arrive, Prairie Dawn tries to cancel, arguing that the wholesaler never signed. Can the wholesaler enforce the contract against Prairie Dawn?
o: Yes, but only if the wholesaler sends a confirmation within ten days.
No, because both parties must sign a record.
No, because the goods have not yet been received and accepted.
No, because the wholesaler's shipment is not a signed record.
None of the above.
oe: No confirmation is needed.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought must sign.
That exception isn't needed when there's a signed record.
The wholesaler doesn't need a record signed by itself to enforce against Prairie Dawn.
Correct. Yes: the record need be signed only by the party against whom enforcement is sought, and Prairie Dawn signed the order. No choice says that.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Signed by the party charged

q: A seller sees one late invoice from a buyer and declares it insolvent, refusing to ship except for cash. The buyer is solvent, and has generally paid its debts. What is the risk to the seller?
o: Only a small interest penalty.
None, as a seller may always change payment terms.
None, since any late payment shows insolvency.
A wrongful demand may be its own repudiation.
The buyer may reclaim its payments.
oe: The risk is breach.
It can't, unilaterally.
A single late payment isn't insolvency.
Correct. Section 2-702(1) needs actual insolvency. One late invoice isn't enough, so the demand for cash is a change of terms; the safer route is § 2-609.
That isn't the risk here.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Insolvency and cash terms

q: Miss Piggy's contract to buy a custom gown says: "Risk of loss passes to Buyer when this contract is signed." The seller is a merchant. The gown is finished, but before Miss Piggy picks it up, it is destroyed in a fire at the seller's shop. Who bears the loss?
o: Miss Piggy, but only if the gown had been paid for.
Miss Piggy, because the parties' agreement on risk of loss controls over the default rules.
The seller, because the risk-of-loss rules are mandatory and can't be shifted by a clause in the contract.
The seller, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
None of the above.
oe: Payment doesn't matter.
They can.
That's the default, and the parties agreed otherwise.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Agreement on risk

q: A buyer argues that § 2-716(1) replaces the common-law limits on specific performance, so the court must order a hard-to-supervise delivery schedule. What is the best response?
o: The buyer must first try and fail at replevin under § 2-716(3).
Section 1-305 forbids all equitable remedies under the Code.
The word "may" keeps the remedy discretionary, so the limits presumably remain.
Section 2-716 applies only to consumer buyers, not to this buyer.
The statute lists those limits in its text, so they plainly remain.
oe: The Code doesn't set that order; the remedies are separate.
Section 1-305 sets the expectation goal and doesn't bar equity.
Correct. Damages must be inadequate, the order must not be unduly hard to enforce, and it must not cause undue hardship, unfairness or harm to the public interest.
It applies to all buyers, consumer or business.
The text doesn't list them; they survive by implication.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Common-law limits survive

q: Where the lessee cannot terminate its payment obligation, which fact does NOT by itself trigger the § 1-203(b) bright-line test?
o: An option to buy at a price above predictable market value.
The lessee may renew for the remaining economic life for nominal rent.
The original term equals the goods' remaining economic life.
The lessee may buy the goods for nominal consideration.
The lessee is bound to become the owner of the goods.
oe: Correct. That's a safe-harbor fact (§ 1-203(c)(6)). The four prongs are: term at least the remaining economic life; bound to renew for it or become owner; may renew for it, or become owner, for nominal consideration.
That's prong (3).
That's prong (1).
That's prong (4).
That's prong (2).
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Bright-line prongs

q: Fozzie agrees to buy all the bolts his widget plant requires from Kermit at a fixed price. The contract estimates 90,000 bolts a year, and Fozzie bought 90,000 in year one and 100,000 in year two. In year three, a huge new customer contract triples Fozzie's legitimate need, and he demands 300,000 bolts. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Kermit may cancel the whole contract because the demand is so far above the estimate.
Kermit must supply 300,000 bolts, but may charge the market price for the excess.
Kermit must supply all 300,000 bolts, because Fozzie's increased need is in good faith.
Kermit need supply only an amount not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
The contract is unenforceable, because it never stated a definite quantity of bolts.
oe: A disproportionate demand doesn't let the seller cancel. It need only supply a reasonable quantity.
Article 2 doesn't reprice the disproportionate excess. Kermit simply isn't obligated to supply it.
Good faith is necessary but not sufficient. The disproportion limit is separate.

Correct. A requirements quantity must be in good faith, and "no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to any stated estimate or in the absence of a stated estimate to any normal or otherwise comparable prior output or requirements may be tendered or demanded" (§ 2-306(1)). Good faith alone doesn't satisfy both limits. See Problem 4-2.
Requirements contracts are enforceable (§ 2-306(1)).
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: good faith but disproportionate

q: A utility signs a requirements contract for fuel oil at a fixed price, with estimates based on what it needs to generate electricity. The market price of oil rises far above the contract price. The utility then doubles its "requirements" so it can resell the extra oil at market prices. Under Orange & Rockland v. Amerada Hess, what result?
o: The utility wins, because a requirements buyer may order any amount.
The seller wins only if it proves the utility acted in bad faith.
The seller need not supply the excess, because it is unreasonably disproportionate.
The utility wins, because it acted in complete good faith.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-306(1) caps quantity at not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
Disproportion is a limit separate from good faith.
Correct. The court held the doubling was unreasonably disproportionate. A requirements buyer can't use the contract to speculate on the market.
The disproportion limit applies "even where one party acts with complete good faith."
C is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Orange & Rockland

q: A buyer accepts a truck with a hidden transmission defect. Before discovering it, the buyer wrecks the truck in an unrelated collision. It then learns of the defect. May it revoke?
o: Yes, but only if the seller insured the truck.
No, and it also loses all warranty claims.
No, because of a substantial change not caused by the defect.
Yes, because the defect existed at delivery.
Yes, as revocation doesn't depend on condition.
oe: Insurance isn't the test.
Warranty damages remain.
Correct. Section 2-608(2). The buyer keeps a § 2-714 claim for the defect, on notice.
The bar still applies to the collision damage.
Section 2-608(2) says otherwise.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Substantial change not caused by defect

q: What is the effect of a merger clause?
o: It conclusively establishes complete integration.
It turns a partial integration into a complete integration as a matter of law.
It bars evidence of fraud.
It bars later modifications.
None of the above.
oe: It is probative, not conclusive.
A merger clause is evidence of complete integration, not conclusive proof.
The PER never bars fraud evidence.
That's a NOM clause.

Correct. A merger clause is probative, not conclusive, evidence that the writing is a complete integration. It never bars evidence of fraud, and it says nothing about later modifications (that is a NOM clause).
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause effect

q: Which event does NOT end the seller's right to stop delivery?
o: Negotiation to the buyer of a negotiable document.
A warehouse's acknowledgment that it holds for the buyer.
The buyer's receipt of the goods.
The buyer's payment by a check that bounces.
A carrier's acknowledgment by reshipment.
oe: Ends the right: § 2-705(2)(d).
Ends the right: § 2-705(2)(b).
Ends the right: § 2-705(2)(a).

Correct. The right ends on the buyer's receipt, a non-carrier bailee's acknowledgment to the buyer, a carrier's acknowledgment by reshipment or as a warehouse, or negotiation of a negotiable document.
Ends the right: § 2-705(2)(c).
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — When the right ends

q: A year into an open-ended supply deal, a buyer gives 3 days' notice ending it. Separately, two other parties mutually agree to walk away. Which is correct?
o: The first needs reasonable notice; the second is a rescission.
The second needs a signed record in every case.
Three days is always reasonable under the Code.
Both are cancellations for breach.
The first is a rescission; the second is a termination.
oe: Correct. Section 2-309(2)-(3): an indefinite contract lasts a reasonable time, and is terminable on reasonable notice giving time to find substitutes, unless agreed otherwise and not unconscionable. Section 2-209 cmt. 3: rescission is mutual abandonment, not unilateral termination.
Not unless a term so requires (§ 2-209(2)).
It depends on the time needed to find substitutes.
Neither party breached.
That's reversed.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Rescission vs. termination

q: Abby hires Rosita's Remodeling to redo Abby's kitchen for $40,000. The contract allocates $31,000 to cabinets and appliances Rosita will supply and $9,000 to installation. The new oven Rosita supplied catches fire in its first week. Under amended § 2-102(2), how does Article 2 apply to Abby's warranty claim?
o: Article 2 applies only if Rosita is a merchant who regularly deals in ovens.
Only the Article 2 provisions that relate primarily to the goods apply.
Real-property law governs, because the oven was installed in Abby's house.
Article 2 applies to the whole transaction, because the goods predominate.
Article 2 does not apply, because a remodeling contract is a contract for services.
oe: Scope never depends on merchant status (Problem 1-4). Merchant status matters for the merchantability warranty, not for whether Article 2 governs.
That is the rule when goods do NOT predominate. Here they do, so all of Article 2 applies.
Goods are things movable at the time of identification to the contract (§ 2-105(1)). The oven was movable then.
Correct. Under amended § 2-102(2), if goods predominate in a hybrid transaction, Article 2 applies to the whole deal. An agreed price allocation (here 77% to goods) usually binds (cmt. 3).
The label doesn't decide it. This is a hybrid transaction, and the price allocation shows that the goods predominate.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: goods predominate

q: Under a § 2-207(2) clause, a hardware retailer and a farmer who buys one tractor exchange forms. Is this a deal "between merchants" under § 2-104(3)?
o: Yes, whenever one of the two parties is a merchant.
Yes, whenever the price exceeds $500.
No, because the phrase applies only to § 2-201.
No, because a farmer can never be a merchant.
Only if both are chargeable with a merchant's knowledge or skill.
oe: Both must qualify.
The price isn't relevant.
It applies wherever "between merchants" appears.
Courts have split on farmers, and practices may qualify.
Correct. Section 2-104(3) requires both parties to be chargeable with the knowledge or skill of merchants. For § 2-207, business practices are what matter, and many business people qualify.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Between merchants

q: A buyer orally agrees to buy a $200,000 sailboat, books a survey, and rents a boat slip. The seller, who never signed anything, sells to someone else. Under Casazza v. Kiser, can the buyer use promissory estoppel to enforce the oral contract?
o: No, because the buyer's reliance did not make the refusal a fraud.
Yes, because the buyer reasonably relied on the seller's promise.
No, because promissory estoppel does not apply to sales of goods.
Yes, because promissory estoppel overrides § 2-201.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The court held that promissory estoppel couldn't get around § 2-201 on these facts under any test.
Ordinary reliance was not enough.
The court analyzed the claim; it held only that this reliance wasn't enough.
Casazza held the claim failed under any test.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Promissory estoppel and § 2-201

q: Swedish Chef Supply crates and labels 500 copper pots for a restaurant under a contract that requires the restaurant to pick them up on June 1. On May 20, the restaurant repudiates. Two days later, while the seller is arranging to resell, a burst pipe ruins the pots. The seller's insurer pays 70% of their value. What is the most likely result?
o: The restaurant bears the loss only if it had insured the pots.
The seller may treat the uninsured 30% of the loss as resting on the restaurant.
The restaurant bears the entire loss, because a breaching party bears all risk of loss.
The seller bears the entire loss, because the pots were destroyed before the June 1 pickup.
The seller bears the entire loss, because risk never passed to a buyer that never took delivery.
oe: The rule looks to the seller's insurance shortfall, not the buyer's insurance.

Correct. When the buyer repudiates or breaches as to conforming goods already identified before risk has passed, the seller may treat the risk as resting on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of any deficiency in the seller's insurance (§ 2-510(3)).
The breaching buyer bears the risk only to the extent the seller's insurance falls short, and only for a commercially reasonable time.
The repudiation, not the June 1 pickup date, triggers § 2-510(3).
Section 2-510(3) shifts the uninsured part of the loss to the breaching buyer even though risk hadn't otherwise passed.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Buyer's repudiation; seller's insurance deficiency

q: A buyer that prepaid for identified goods has a right to them under § 2-502. After the seller repudiates, the buyer goes to the seller's unlocked yard at night and hauls the goods away. Which is correct?
o: It acted properly, because § 2-716(3) is a legal right and not an equitable one.
It acted properly, because no breach of the peace occurred.
It acted wrongly, because these remedies are enforced by court order.
It acted properly only if the goods were for family or household use.
It acted properly, because § 2-502 is self-executing, unlike specific performance.
oe: A legal right to replevy is still enforced through a court.
That is the Article 9 standard in § 9-609, and this buyer isn't a secured party.
Correct. All three routes to the goods need a court order. Contrast a secured party's right under § 9-609 to repossess without breach of the peace.
There's no consumer exception to the rule against self-help.
Section 2-502 also needs a court order if the seller won't deliver.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — No self-help for the goods

q: Conforming goods arrive, and the buyer promptly and clearly rejects them. What is the result?
o: Rightful and effective: the seller breached.
Wrongful but effective: no acceptance, and the buyer has breached.
No legal effect: the buyer must pay and keep the goods.
Ineffective: the buyer has accepted and owes the price.
All of the above.
oe: The goods conform, so the seller did not breach.
Correct. This is the no-right, timely-notice box. Because there's no acceptance, the seller's claim usually isn't for the price.
An effective rejection blocks acceptance.
Timely notice makes it effective.
They contradict one another.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Matrix: no right, timely

q: Before Swedish Chef buys a pizza oven, the seller tells him, "This oven reaches 900 degrees." It reaches only 650. At his deposition, the Chef admits he would probably have bought the oven anyway because the price was so good. The seller argues the statement wasn't part of the basis of the bargain because the Chef didn't rely on it. What is the most likely result under § 2-313 and its comments?
o: Probably still a warranty, because the buyer need not prove reliance on the statement.
The Chef wins only if the seller's statement was made in writing.
The seller wins, because a temperature rating is the seller's opinion, not a fact.
The seller wins, because a buyer who would have bought anyway can't show the statement was part of the bargain.
The Chef wins only if he proves the seller knew the oven couldn't reach 900 degrees.
oe: Correct. Comment 3 to § 2-313 says no particular reliance need be shown, and that "any fact which is to take such affirmations, once made, out of the agreement requires clear affirmative proof." Saying he would "probably" have bought anyway is weak proof.
Oral statements can be express warranties.
A specific, measurable temperature is an affirmation of fact.
That treats basis of the bargain as reliance. Under the comments, the burden is on the seller, and a "probably" admission is unlikely to meet it.
Knowledge of falsity is an element of fraud, not breach of warranty.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain without proof of reliance

q: A commercial bakery orders a $40,000 dough sheeter by phone after the dealer recommends that model for its volume. When the machine is delivered, the bakery's manager signs a delivery receipt. On the back, in large capitals, it says: "SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY." The machine can't keep up with the bakery's volume. Is the disclaimer effective?
o: Yes, because the disclaimer mentions merchantability and is in large capitals.
Probably not, because the contract was formed before delivery, and the receipt's disclaimer never became part of it.
No, because a disclaimer must appear on the front of a document to be effective.
Yes, because the manager signed the receipt.
Yes, but it excludes only the implied warranty of fitness.
oe: Form compliance doesn't matter if the term never became part of the contract.

Correct. Before applying § 2-316, ask whether the disclaimer is part of the contract. A disclaimer first appearing after formation is at most a proposed modification or an additional term that materially alters the deal (§ 2-207 cmt. 4). Signing a delivery receipt isn't assent to it.
Placement goes to conspicuousness. The deeper problem is that the term came after formation.
Signing a delivery receipt acknowledges delivery; it doesn't show agreement to give up warranties.
If it were part of the contract it would reach both warranties; the problem is that it isn't.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer after the deal

q: A contract calls itself a 99-year "lease" of a laptop, non-terminable, with the laptop returning at the end. What is it, and why?
o: A bailment, because laptops are personal property.
A sale, because leases can't exceed 50 years.
A lease, because the laptop returns at the end.
A lease, unless the laptop is a consumer good.
A sale, because the goods die long before the term ends.
oe: Consideration and term point to a sale.
Article 2A sets no maximum term; the point is the goods' economic life.
Nothing of value returns.
Consumer status is beside the point.
Correct. It's a lease in form only (p. 466), and the term exceeds the economic life.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — 99-year laptop

q: Where is market rent taken under § 2A-519?
o: The lessor's location, always.
The national average rent.
Wherever the goods are located.
The place for tender, or of arrival after rejection.
Wherever the lessee covered.
oe: The lessor's location isn't a reference point in § 2A-519.
A national average isn't the statutory measure; § 2A-507 allows substitutes only if needed.
That's the lessor's rule in § 2A-528.
Correct. Section 2A-519(2), matching § 2-713(2). Time is as of default.
Cover has its own measure; market rent isn't taken at the place of cover.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Market rent place

q: Under § 2-104(1), which of the following would NOT make a seller a "merchant"?
o: The seller deals in goods of the kind.
The seller once made a single sale of goods of that kind.
The seller by occupation holds itself out as having knowledge or skill about the goods.
Knowledge or skill is attributed to the seller because it employs an agent or broker who holds itself out as having that skill.
None of the above.
oe: That makes it a merchant.
Correct. An isolated sale doesn't make a seller a merchant.
That makes it a merchant (for general purposes).
That makes it a merchant.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Merchant: holding out skill

q: A lease of equipment, which the lessee can't terminate, says the lessee must buy the equipment at the end for $40,000, its predicted fair market value. Which is correct?
o: A security interest, as the lessee is bound to become the owner.
A sale only if the price is nominal.
A question for the parties' intent.
A lease, as the term is short.
A lease, since the price is fair market value.
oe: Correct. Section 1-203(b)(2). Fair value doesn't save it: there's no real residual for the lessor.
Prong (2) has no nominal element.
Intent doesn't control.
Term length isn't the issue.
FMV saves options, not obligations.
topic: Wk 12 · XXVIII · Leases: scope & lease vs. sale (§§ 2A-103, 1-203) — Bound to buy

q: Fisk buys a used car from Lonborg. Before signing, Lonborg tells him, "It's never been in an accident." The signed sales contract, which is complete and exclusive, says: "Sold AS IS. Seller makes no warranty, express or implied." Fisk later learns the car was badly damaged in a prior crash. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The oral warranty controls, because express warranties always prevail over disclaimers.
The oral statement is admissible as a consistent additional term of the agreement.
The "as is" clause is ineffective, because it didn't specifically mention merchantability.
The rule likely bars the oral warranty, but Fisk may still use the statement to prove fraud.
Fisk has no remedy at all, because he signed a contract that said "as is."
oe: Under § 2-316(1), that preference is "subject to the provisions of this Article on parol or extrinsic evidence."
It contradicts "Seller makes no warranty, express or implied," and the writing is complete and exclusive.
"As is" doesn't need to mention merchantability (§ 2-316(3)(a)), and in any event the parol evidence question turns on the writing's integration, not on the disclaimer's wording.

Correct. A prior oral warranty that contradicts a complete written disclaimer is excluded by § 2-202, and § 2-316(1) makes its express-warranty rule subject to the parol evidence rule. Evidence offered to prove fraud isn't barred, because the rule doesn't displace the law of fraud (§ 1-103(b)). See Problem 5-13.
The parol evidence rule doesn't bar a fraud claim.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Oral warranty vs. "as is" writing

q: Same facts as the family-use case, but Dana has paid nothing. Which is correct?
o: The consumer rule waives the prepayment element for her.
She has no remedy of any kind against the dealer.
Replevin applies automatically, since every used car is unique.
Section 2-502 applies, since she can still tender the whole price.
Section 2-502 is out, so she can look only to § 2-716.
oe: Section 2-502(1)(a) still requires payment of part of the price.
She still has cover or market damages.
Uniqueness isn't the replevin test, and used cars aren't all unique.
A later tender doesn't meet the element that she "has paid" part of the price.
Correct. Section 2-502 needs part or full payment. Dana is left with specific performance or replevin, so ask whether the car is unique and whether she can cover.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Unpaid car
pre: A dealer contracts to sell a specific used car for $5,000 to Dana for family use. Dana pays $1,000. The dealer, solvent, then refuses to deliver, and similar cars are easy to find. Which is Dana's strongest route to the car?

q: Which of the following UCC provisions may the parties vary by agreement?
o: The place of delivery (§ 2-308).
The scope of Article 2 (§ 2-102).
The rights of good-faith purchasers (§ 2-403).
Unconscionability (§ 2-302).
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Gap fillers like § 2-308 apply "unless otherwise agreed."
Can't be varied; parties can't contract into or out of Article 2's scope.
Can't be varied; the rights of third parties aren't the contracting parties' to bargain away.
Can't be varied by agreement (Problem 5-1(b)).
A is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Non-modifiable provisions

q: A lessee rescinds a lease for the lessor's fraud and also claims damages. The lessor says rescission bars damages. Which is correct?
o: Only a consumer may do both.
Rescission always bars damages.
Damages require affirming the lease.
Rescission doesn't bar damages under § 2A-505.
Fraud isn't recognized in leases.
oe: Section 2A-505 applies to all lessees.
The statute says otherwise.
No election is required.
Correct. Sections 2A-505(4)-(5), the analog of § 2-721.
It is.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Fraud and lease remedies

q: "F.O.B. buyer's location" means:
o: The seller pays the freight, but risk passes to the buyer when the goods are delivered to the carrier.
Risk passes to the buyer when the goods are delivered to the carrier.
The carrier bears the risk until the goods arrive.
The risk is shared equally until delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Half right. F.O.B. the destination puts both the expense and the risk of transit on the seller (§ 2-319(1)(b)).
That describes F.O.B. seller's location (a shipment contract).
As between seller and buyer, the seller bears the risk.
There's no sharing.

Correct. "F.O.B. buyer's location" makes a destination contract: the seller bears the expense and risk of getting the goods there, and risk passes when they are duly tendered at the buyer's location (§§ 2-319(1)(b), 2-509(1)(b)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — F.O.B. buyer's location

q: A buyer receives 100 cases of olive oil, opens a few, and tells the seller it will "think about it" for six months while storing them in its warehouse. Which statement best describes the buyer's position under Article 2?
o: It may accept and reject the same cases and decide later which applies.
It has rejected the goods by declining to say that it will keep them.
It must accept or reject; inaction for too long works as an acceptance.
It may hold the goods indefinitely without accepting them if it pays nothing.
It has repudiated the contract by asking for more time to decide.
oe: Section 2-607(2): acceptance precludes rejection of the goods accepted.
Rejection needs seasonable notice to the seller (§ 2-602(1)); silence or hesitation isn't notice.
Correct. A buyer can't do both (§ 2-607(2)) and can't do neither: failing to make an effective rejection after a reasonable opportunity to inspect is acceptance (§ 2-606(1)(b)).
Nonpayment doesn't stop § 2-606(1)(b) from operating once the reasonable time has passed.
Asking for time isn't a definite refusal to perform.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Accept or reject

q: At a trade show, Mahna Mahna Industries displays a model of a commercial ice machine. The model was built for the show, not taken from production stock. Its tag reads "500 lb/day." Pepe orders ten machines "same as the display model." The machines delivered produce 300 lb/day and use a cheaper compressor than the model. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No warranty arose, because Pepe saw the model and could judge its quality for himself.
The model and its tag created express warranties that the machines would match them.
No warranty arose, because only samples drawn from the actual goods create warranties.
No warranty arose, because trade-show displays are advertising, not part of the bargain.
The tag created a warranty, but the model itself created none because it wasn't for sale.
oe: Inspecting a model is how a warranty by model is formed, not a defense to one.

Correct. A model made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(c)). A model not drawn from the bulk may carry less weight than a true sample (§ 2-313 cmt. 6), but ordering "same as the display model" makes it part of the bargain, and the tag is a specific affirmation.
Section 2-313(1)(c) covers both samples and models.
Displays can create warranties when the buyer orders by reference to them.
Both the tag and the model are part of the bargain.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Model at a trade show

q: Oscar orally agrees to buy Snuffy's vintage motorcycle for $40,000. In a separate deal, Snuffy sells Oscar a $600 set of spare parts that Snuffy bought years after the motorcycle; Oscar pays for and keeps the parts. Snuffy signs only a receipt for the parts, which never mentions the motorcycle. Snuffy then sells the motorcycle to someone else. Can Oscar enforce the motorcycle deal?
o: Yes, because the signed receipt and Oscar's notes can be read together.
Yes, because Oscar paid for and accepted the parts, which counts as part performance of the overall deal.
Yes, if Oscar shows reasonable reliance under promissory estoppel.
No, because the parts aren't part of the motorcycle and no signed record covers the motorcycle.
No, because the statute of frauds does not apply between two non-merchants.
oe: Papers are read together only if they are connected. The receipt never refers to a motorcycle sale.
Part performance reaches only the goods paid for and accepted. The parts and the motorcycle aren't one commercial unit (compare the boat and software in Casazza).
Casazza held promissory estoppel couldn't get around § 2-201 on reliance like this.
Correct. As in Casazza, accepting a separately bought add-on isn't accepting the main item, and the only signed paper doesn't show a sale of the motorcycle.
It applies to any sale of goods for $500 or more, merchants or not. Oscar loses for a different reason.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Part performance: separate unit

q: A seller tells a hesitant buyer, "Don't worry, that noise is normal for this model," and the buyer accepts. It later turns out the noise means a serious internal failure, which substantially impairs the machine. Which ground best supports revocation?
o: Difficulty of discovery alone.
A reasonable assumption the defect would be cured.
Acceptance without discovery, reasonably induced by the seller's assurances.
Perfect tender.
Unconscionability.
oe: The assurances are the stronger ground.
No cure was promised; the seller denied a defect.
Correct. Section 2-608(1)(b). The buyer knew of the noise, but not the nonconformity.
Acceptance ended that.
That isn't a ground for revocation.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Assurances of seller

q: A firm in one deal sells shares of stock, licenses software, rents a warehouse building, and leaves a truck at a repair shop for a week. Which item is correctly matched to its governing law?
o: The shares of stock: Article 2, as a sale of movable things.
The truck left for repair: bailment, under the common law.
The software license: Article 2A, as a lease of goods.
The warehouse building: Article 2A, as a lease.
All four deals: Article 2, as commercial transactions.
oe: Investment securities are excluded from goods and governed by Article 8.

Correct. A bailment isn't a sale, so the common law governs. Stock falls under Article 8, licenses of intellectual property under common and federal law, and real property under real property law. Article 2 reaches none of them.
A license of IP is governed by common and federal law.
Article 2A covers goods, and a building is real property.
Article 2 covers only transactions in goods.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Other law by property type

q: After a seller's third late and defective delivery under an installment contract, which substantially impairs the value of the whole contract, the buyer writes: "We hereby terminate our agreement effective immediately." Two months later, the buyer sues for damages for the seller's breaches. The seller argues that by "terminating" the contract the buyer gave up its claims. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer keeps its claim only if its letter expressly reserved its rights to sue for damages.
The buyer keeps its claim, but only for the third delivery, which was the one that ended the contract.
The buyer keeps its claim, because ending a contract for breach preserves remedies for the breach.
The seller wins, because termination discharges all of both parties' obligations under the contract.
The seller wins, because the buyer chose to "terminate" the agreement rather than to cancel it.
oe: No express reservation is required (§ 2-720).
A cancellation for breach of the whole contract preserves remedies for the whole contract.

Correct. Putting an end to a contract "by reason of breach by the other" is cancellation, and "the cancelling party also retains any remedy for breach of the whole contract or any unperformed balance" (§ 2-106(4)). The label the buyer used doesn't control, and words of termination aren't read as a renunciation of damages claims unless that intention clearly appears (§ 2-720).
Even on termination, rights based on prior breach or performance survive (§ 2-106(3)).
Article 2 looks at the reason the contract ended, not the word used.
topic: Wk 8 · XIV · Termination — Ending for breach keeps the damages claim

q: A buyer repudiates while the goods sit on the seller's own dock. Which remedy fits?
o: Withholding delivery under § 2-703(a).
Replevin under § 2-716(3).
Cover under § 2-712.
Reclamation under § 2-702(2).
Stopping in transit under § 2-705.
oe: Correct. Withhold means the seller has the goods; stop means a carrier or bailee has them.
That's a buyer's remedy.
That's a buyer's remedy.
That's for goods already received by the buyer.
No carrier or bailee has the goods.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Withhold vs. stop

q: A coffee roaster agrees to buy all its requirements of green beans from an importer, with an estimate of 10,000 pounds a year. The roaster honestly lands a national grocery account and now needs 60,000 pounds. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The contract is void, because the roaster's needs changed.
The importer must supply 60,000 pounds, because the estimate was only a good-faith guess.
The importer must supply all 60,000 pounds, because the roaster acted in good faith.
The importer must supply 60,000 pounds but may charge the market price for the excess.
None of the above.
oe: Changed needs don't void the contract.
An estimate isn't just a guess; it limits the quantity that can be demanded.
Good faith isn't the only limit.
§ 2-306 limits quantity; it doesn't reprice the excess.

Correct. The importer need not supply a quantity unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate, even though the roaster acted in good faith. Disproportion is a separate limit (§ 2-306(1); Orange & Rockland; Problem 4-2). No choice says that.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Good faith but disproportionate

q: At an estate liquidation, Waldorf buys an antique clock under a signed bill of sale stating: "Seller transfers only whatever right, title, and interest the estate may have, and makes no warranty of title." The price is well below market because the ownership records are missing. A third party proves it owns the clock. Does Waldorf have a claim for breach of the warranty of title?
o: No, because the bill of sale specifically disclaims the warranty of title.
No, because estate and liquidation sales never carry any warranties, whatever the bill of sale says.
Yes, because the bill of sale didn't say "as is."
Yes, because the warranty of title can't be disclaimed.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-312(2). Problem 5-5: a buyer may accept such a disclaimer when provenance is uncertain and the price reflects the risk.
Circumstances alone may suffice in some sales, but here the specific language does the work.
"As is" isn't how to disclaim title.
It can, by specific language or circumstances.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer by specific language

q: A school district contracts to buy 12,000 cartons of milk a month for the school year at a fixed price. Enrollment drops 30%, and the district orders only 8,400 cartons a month. What is the dairy's position?
o: The district must take and pay for 12,000 cartons, because it agreed to a fixed quantity.
The district may cut the order but owes the dairy one month of lost profits.
The district may cut its order, because a 30% drop is not unreasonably disproportionate to the stated quantity.
The district may cut its order, because it acted in good faith.
The contract is void for mutual mistake about enrollment.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-1(a): the buyer can't cut a fixed quantity without the seller's assent.
No such rule.
Disproportion is a § 2-306 test, which doesn't apply to a fixed quantity.
Good faith limits requirements contracts. This is a fixed-quantity contract.
Enrollment risk is the kind of risk a fixed quantity allocates.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Fixed quantity

q: A seller produces a signed record that satisfies § 2-201(1). What is the effect?
o: The contract is enforceable for any quantity the seller proves.
The buyer is barred from denying that a contract was formed.
The seller wins its claim unless the buyer proves a defense.
The seller may proceed but must still prove the contract and its terms.
None of the above.
oe: Enforcement stops at the quantity shown in the record.
The buyer can still deny formation and contest the terms.
The statute of frauds says nothing about whether the contract was made or breached.
Correct. Satisfying the statute of frauds only opens the courthouse door.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Satisfying the SOF

q: Which statement most accurately distinguishes a merger clause from a no-oral-modification clause?
o: A merger clause deals with earlier agreements; a no-oral-modification clause, with later ones.
A no-oral-modification clause keeps out evidence of usage of trade; a merger clause doesn't.
A merger clause makes a contract enforceable under the statute of frauds, and a no-oral-modification clause doesn't.
A merger clause deals with later changes; a no-oral-modification clause deals with earlier agreements.
Both clauses do the same work, so a well-drafted contract needs only one of them.
oe: Correct. A merger clause is evidence that the writing is a complete integration, so it bears on the parol evidence rule (§ 2-202). A no-oral-modification clause governs later modifications (§ 2-209(2)).
Neither clause excludes usage of trade.
The statute of frauds concerns enforceability. The merger clause concerns which terms are part of the contract.
That reverses them.
They govern different points in time and different statutes.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause vs. no-oral-modification clause

q: A seller deliberately breaches because a better offer came along, and the buyer's lawyer asks for "the maximum Article 2 allows." Which statement about Article 2 remedies is correct?
o: They let the buyer recover the seller's profit on the better deal.
They aim to give the buyer the benefit of its bargain.
They treat bad faith as a separate claim under § 1-304.
They add punitive damages when the breach is deliberate.
They aim to return both parties to their pre-contract positions.
oe: Disgorgement isn't an Article 2 measure; the buyer gets its own expectancy.

Correct. Section 1-305(a) states the expectation goal. Penal damages are generally unavailable, a breach is not treated as a moral wrong, and the § 1-304 good-faith duty does not create an independent cause of action.
Good faith under § 1-304 isn't an independent cause of action.
Section 1-305(a) bars penal damages unless a provision says otherwise, and a deliberate breach isn't a wrong in itself.
That describes restitution or rescission, not the expectation goal of § 1-305(a).
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Goal of remedies

q: Lumber dealers in a region commonly accept a 2% allowance for board-length variation and adjust the price. A buyer who ordinarily follows the practice rejects a load with 1.5% variation solely because the market has fallen. Which is the seller's best response?
o: A buyer may never reject after the market falls.
Section 2-612 applies, since the buyer must show substantial impairment.
The buyer had to reject before the goods were shipped.
The buyer waived rejection by being a merchant.
Usage of trade and good faith bar rejection for this minor variation.
oe: A falling market doesn't remove a right that truly exists.
This isn't an installment contract on these facts.
Rejection follows tender.
Merchant status doesn't waive rejection.
Correct. Course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade and § 1-304 good faith can all limit rejection for minor defects. A market-driven excuse strengthens the point.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Trade limits on rejection

q: A buyer repudiates while a full truckload is in transit. The seller sends a stop order. The truck has already reached the buyer's dock and is being unloaded. Which is correct?
o: The seller couldn't stop a truckload for repudiation.
The carrier must reverse the unloading.
The seller may stop any time before payment.
The stop order is valid, but only for insolvency.
The right ended on the buyer's receipt.
oe: A truckload qualifies.
It's too late.
Receipt ends it.
Receipt ends even that.
Correct. Section 2-705(2)(a). A truckload may be stopped for repudiation, but only until receipt.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Stop order, truckload, repudiation

q: The Count buys a grandfather clock from Telly's Antiques, a retail antiques store. The Count pays the full price, and the signed sales slip says "Title passes to Buyer upon payment." Telly says, "It's yours. Leave it here in the back room and pick it up whenever you like." Two days later, before the Count comes for it, a flood destroys the store and the clock. Who bears the loss?
o: The Count, because title passed to him when he paid.
The Count, because the clock was identified to the contract when the contract was made.
The Count, because the seller tendered the clock when it said he could pick it up at any time.
Telly's Antiques, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
None of the above.
oe: Risk of loss under § 2-509 doesn't follow title. The title clause decides ownership, not who bears casualty losses.
Identification gives the buyer a special property and an insurable interest (§ 2-501). It doesn't shift the risk of loss.
Tender passes risk only when the seller is not a merchant. Telly's is a merchant, so the rule is receipt, not tender.

Correct. Under § 2-509(3), when the seller is a merchant and the goods are not shipped or held by a bailee, risk passes only on the buyer's receipt, meaning physical possession (§ 2-103(1)(c)). Passing of title and payment don't move risk; Article 2 deliberately separates risk from title.
One of the other choices is correct: Telly's Antiques, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Merchant seller; title and payment irrelevant

q: Kermit signs a contract to buy a tractor after the seller threatens to spread false rumors that would ruin Kermit's business unless Kermit signs. Article 2 says nothing about duress. What law decides whether Kermit can avoid the contract?
o: Article 2's unconscionability section, the Code's only policing doctrine.
The common law of duress, which supplements the Code.
Federal law, because a threat to ruin a business is a federal tort.
No law, because Article 2 occupies the whole field of sales of goods.
The law of the state where the tractor was made.
oe: § 2-302 is one tool, not the only one, and duress is a separate doctrine.
Correct. § 1-103(b) lists duress, coercion, fraud, mistake, and other validating and invalidating causes as supplementing the UCC.
Nothing makes this a federal question.
Article 2 doesn't displace general contract doctrines it doesn't address.
Where the goods were made doesn't choose the governing law.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Common law supplements: duress

q: Which of the following is NOT required to create an express warranty under § 2-313?
o: The seller made an affirmation of fact, a promise, a description, a sample, or a model.
The seller used a formal word such as "warrant" or "guarantee."
The statement was more than the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods.
The affirmation or promise relates to the goods.
The statement became part of the basis of the bargain.
oe: Required. One of these is the source of every express warranty.
Correct. This is not required. § 2-313(2) says formal words and a specific intention to warrant are unnecessary.
Required. Opinion, commendation, and statements of value create no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
Required. § 2-313(1)(a) covers statements that relate to the goods.
Required. Each subsection of § 2-313(1) uses the basis-of-the-bargain test.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Not required for express warranty

q: What must a notice of revocation contain?
o: A statement of the amount of the buyer's damages.
A sworn statement that the goods are defective.
No particular content, though notice must be given.
A list of every defect, or those defects are barred.
The word "revoke," or the notice is ineffective.
oe: Not required.
Not required.
Correct. Comment 5. Contrast § 2-605 for rejection.
That's § 2-605, which applies to rejection.
No magic words are needed.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Revocation notice

q: A lease states a six-year limitations period. A sale contract does too. Which is correct?
o: Both are valid.
Both are valid only for consumers.
The sale clause is invalid; the lease clause isn't barred by the statute's text.
The lease clause is invalid; the sale clause is valid.
Both are invalid.
oe: The sale clause fails.
Consumer status isn't relevant.
Correct. Section 2-725(1) bars extension. Section 2A-506(1) allows reduction and doesn't expressly bar extension (cmt.).
That's reversed.
The lease rule differs.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXII · Lessor's default & lessee's remedies (§§ 2A-508 to 2A-522) — Limitations extended

q: A seller gives an express warranty about a machine's speed. The buyer also had a particular purpose that the seller knew about and relied on. If the express warranty and the implied warranties are inconsistent, which statement is correct under § 2-317?
o: Implied warranties control, since they arise by operation of law.
A sample controls over exact specifications if the two conflict.
Express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties, except fitness.
Express warranties displace all inconsistent implied warranties, fitness included.
None of the above.
oe: The reverse, except for fitness.
Exact specifications displace an inconsistent sample (§ 2-317(a)).
Correct. § 2-317(c).
Fitness for a particular purpose is the exception.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Cumulation

q: A seller agreed to deliver equipment with payment due 15 days after delivery. Before the next shipment, the seller learns that the buyer's credit rating has been cut, that other suppliers aren't being paid on time, and that the buyer has changed banks. The seller sends a signed letter demanding adequate assurance and suspends shipment. The buyer doesn't respond for 35 days. What may the seller do?
o: Treat the buyer's silence as a repudiation only after 90 days.
Nothing more; it must resume shipping and wait to see whether the buyer pays.
Sue the buyer for the full price of all future shipments.
Treat the buyer's failure to respond as a repudiation of the contract.
None of the above.
oe: The statutory limit is 30 days.
After 30 days without adequate assurance, the seller may treat the contract as repudiated.
Repudiation opens the seller's remedies, but the price is generally recoverable only for goods accepted or in limited cases (§ 2-709).

Correct. With reasonable grounds for insecurity, a party may demand adequate assurance in a record and suspend its own performance. Failure to provide assurance within a reasonable time not exceeding 30 days after receiving a justified demand is a repudiation (§ 2-609(1), (4)). See Problem 6-3.
One of the other choices is correct: Treat the buyer's failure to respond as a repudiation of the contract.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Silence after a justified demand

q: If Sensational leased the servers to Boston rather than selling them, and Boston sublet them to Lasting, what would change?
o: Article 2 would then govern the whole deal.
Boston would become a seller of the servers.
The finance lease would become a consumer lease.
Warranties would no longer flow to Lasting.
Nothing material, because § 2A-209 covers it.
oe: Neither step is a sale.
There'd be no sale at all.
Nothing about consumer status changes.
They'd still flow.
Correct. The same result follows.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Supply lease instead of sale

q: A contract's only clause on the subject says: "This contract may not be amended except by a writing signed by both parties." The buyer offers evidence of a consistent oral term agreed before signing. Does the clause bar that evidence?
o: Yes, because it is a merger clause.
Yes, because it requires every term to be in writing.
Yes, because the clause shows the writing was meant to be complete.
No, because the clause is unenforceable.
None of the above.
oe: It's a NOM clause.
It addresses amendments only.
It speaks to future changes, not to completeness.
NOM clauses are enforceable (§ 2-209(2)).
Correct. It doesn't bar the evidence: a no-oral-modification clause governs later changes, not prior agreements (Problem 5-11, clause 4). No choice says that.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — NOM clause is not a merger clause

q: A contract calls for 12,000 tiles "delivered on one date, payment in 12 monthly installments, each month's payment a separate obligation." A second contract calls for 1,000 tiles each month for a year, and says "each delivery is a separate contract." Which is an installment contract under § 2-612?
o: Only the second, unless a court honors its label.
Only the first.
Only the second.
Both.
Neither.
oe: The statute overrides the label.
The first has a single delivery.
Correct. Delivery in separate lots to be separately accepted controls, even if each is called a separate contract. Paying in installments doesn't matter.
The first has only installment payments.
The second meets the definition despite its label.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Installment contract label

q: Big Bird and Snuffy sign an email exchange that says: "Big Bird will sell Snuffy 300 bales of hay." The email says nothing about price or delivery. Is the record sufficient under § 2-201(1)?
o: No, because an exchange of emails can't be a signed record.
Yes, but both parties must be merchants.
No, because it omits the price of the hay.
Yes, because it is signed and states a quantity.
No, because it omits the delivery date and place.
oe: A record includes email, and a typed name can be a signature.
§ 2-201(1) applies to everyone; the merchant rule is the § 2-201(2) confirmation exception.
Price can be missing or wrong. The record is not insufficient because it omits a term.
Correct. Only quantity is essential. The missing price and delivery terms are filled by the gap fillers (§§ 2-305, 2-308, 2-309).
Delivery terms are not essential to the record.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Only quantity is essential

q: Fozzie agrees to buy from Kermit "all the rubber chickens Fozzie requires" for his comedy shop. No estimate is stated. A recession hits, Fozzie's sales collapse, and his orders drop from 1,000 a month to 100. Kermit sues. Under the approach most courts take to decreases, what is the most likely result?
o: Fozzie wins, because a requirements buyer may order any amount it chooses.
Fozzie wins if the drop reflects a genuine lack of demand.
Kermit wins, because requirements contracts lack mutuality.
Kermit wins, because Fozzie must buy at least his prior average.
None of the above.
oe: Good faith limits the buyer.
Correct. § 2-306(1) measures quantity by actual requirements occurring in good faith. A genuine lack of orders can be good faith. (Some courts also apply the disproportion test to decreases.)
Requirements contracts are enforceable; the buyer's good-faith obligation supplies mutuality.
A requirements buyer isn't bound to its prior average; the quantity is its actual good-faith requirements.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: decrease in good faith

q: A lessor's agent repossesses leased equipment by persuading a low-level worker to open the gate during a shift change, with no objection from anyone. Which is correct?
o: Likely proper, if there was no violence or breach of the peace.
Improper, as a court order is always needed.
Proper only if the lessee was insolvent.
Improper, as any entry is a trespass.
Proper, even if the agent used force.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-525(3), borrowed from § 9-609.
Self-help is allowed.
Default is enough.
Trespass alone isn't a breach of the peace.
Force would be a breach.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Repossession risk

q: Which of the following factors points toward a statement being an express warranty rather than puffing?
o: The statement was general and couldn't be measured.
The statement was made orally rather than in writing.
The statement was hedged with "I think" or "probably" by the seller.
The statement was specific and answered the buyer's question.
The statement was freely volunteered by the seller.
oe: That points toward puffing.
Oral statements can be warranties, and writing is not decisive either way.
Hedged statements point toward puffing.
Correct. Those are all warranty factors on the class chart.
Volunteered statements point toward puffing; answers to the buyer's questions point toward warranty.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Factors for warranty vs. puffing

q: A grain elevator has contracts to buy 40,000 bushels of soybeans from a farm, which keeps postponing delivery. The market then shifts so that further postponement would cost the elevator heavily, the state attorney general publicly questions whether contracts like these are legal, and the farm stops returning the elevator's calls. The elevator writes demanding, as assurance, that the farm post a letter of credit for its hedging losses and sign a promise to deliver. Is the demand proper?
o: Yes, because a party may demand any assurance it wants once grounds exist.
No, because asking for a letter of credit demands more than the contract required, which is itself a repudiation.
Yes, because the grounds were reasonable and the demand wasn't unreasonable as a matter of law.
No, because grounds for insecurity must come from the farm's own conduct.
None of the above.
oe: The demand must seek only adequate assurance.
Every demand for assurance asks for more than the original promise; that alone isn't repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).

Correct. This is Top of Iowa v. Sime Farms: the inverted market, the attorney general's statement, and the farmer's silence gave reasonable grounds, and margin or a letter of credit plus a delivery promise was a permissible demand.
Grounds are objective and can come from the market or third parties.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Grounds from the market and a regulator

q: Fozzie tells a hardware-store clerk, "I need a ladder to clean the gutters on my two-story house." The clerk recommends a 24-foot extension ladder, and Fozzie buys it. The first time he uses it on his gutters, set up properly, a rung splits under his ordinary weight. Which warranty claim fits best?
o: Both, because Fozzie relied on the clerk's recommendation in choosing the ladder.
Merchantability, because reaching gutters is an ordinary use of an extension ladder.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because Fozzie told the clerk exactly how he would use it.
Neither, because the clerk only recommended the ladder and Fozzie decided to buy it.
Express warranty, because the clerk's recommendation was an affirmation of fact about it.
oe: Reliance matters only if there is a particular purpose. Here the use is ordinary.

Correct. A particular purpose is a specific use peculiar to the buyer, different from the goods' ordinary use (§ 2-315 cmt. 2). Climbing an extension ladder to reach gutters is what such ladders are for, so the claim lies under § 2-314(2)(c).
Telling the seller about an ordinary use doesn't turn it into a particular purpose.
Merchantability doesn't depend on reliance, and the store is a merchant that deals in ladders.
A bare recommendation isn't an affirmation of fact about the ladder.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Ordinary vs. particular purpose

q: Telly hires a landscaper to redesign Telly's backyard. Services make up most of the $25,000 price, but the landscaper also supplies and installs a cedar swing set, which collapses in its first week and injures Telly's child. In a state that follows the gravamen-of-the-claim test, a court would most likely:
o: Apply the Article 2 merchantability warranty, because the claim concerns the swing set.
Apply Article 2 only if the swing set made up more than half of the contract price.
Apply Article 2 to the whole contract, including claims about the landscape design.
Refuse to apply Article 2, because services predominate in the contract taken as a whole, so no part of it is a sale.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the gravamen test (Anthony Pools), the court asks whether the claim relates to the goods or the services. A defective swing set is a goods claim, so the Article 2 warranty applies even though services predominate.
That mixes in the predominance factors. The gravamen test asks what the claim is about.
The gravamen test applies Article 2 only to claims about the goods. A claim about the design would be a services claim.
That is the predominant-purpose test, which is all-or-nothing. The gravamen test looks at the claim, not the whole contract.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Gravamen of the claim

q: Lasting selects 30 servers from Sensational. Boston Finance buys them and leases them to Lasting under a valid finance lease, saying nothing about their quality. Which warranties does Boston give?
o: Infringement under § 2A-211(2).
Only the warranty against interference.
None at all, not even against interference.
Merchantability and fitness.
The supplier's express warranties, as its own.
oe: Excluded in a finance lease.
Correct. No implied warranties (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213), and no express warranties on these facts.
Section 2A-211(1) still applies.
Both are excluded in a finance lease.
They flow from the supplier under § 2A-209, not from Boston.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Lasting: Boston's warranties

q: A seller ships identified goods under reservation, keeping a negotiable bill of lading. The buyer tenders the full price. The seller refuses to release the bill because the market has risen, and identical goods are readily available. May the buyer replevy?
o: No, because the seller keeps title until paid.
Yes, but only if the goods are consumer goods.
No, because it can buy identical goods elsewhere.
No, because replevin requires the seller's insolvency.
Yes, because goods shipped under reservation are reachable on tender.
oe: The reservation gives only a security interest, and the buyer tendered payment.
The reservation route has no such limit.
That defeats only the first route, not the reservation route.
Insolvency belongs to § 2-502(1)(b).

Correct. Section 2-716(3): replevin is available for identified goods if the buyer can't cover, or if they were shipped under reservation and satisfaction of the security interest is made or tendered. The second route needs no inability to cover.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Reservation and replevin

q: Under § 1-302(b), which of the following may NOT be disclaimed by agreement?
o: The obligation of good faith.
The implied warranty of merchantability.
The place of delivery.
The time for payment.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care can't be disclaimed, though parties may set standards that aren't manifestly unreasonable.
It can be disclaimed under § 2-316.
Parties may vary the default.
Parties may vary the default.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Good faith can't be disclaimed

q: Why does § 2-705 limit stopping for reasons other than insolvency?
o: To favor foreign shipments over domestic ones.
Because carriers are public agencies.
Because of the burden stoppage puts on carriers.
To protect the buyer's credit rating.
To enforce the statute of frauds.
oe: Section 2-705 draws no line between foreign and domestic shipments.
Carriers are private businesses; the point is the burden of stopping small shipments.
Correct. Shipping under reservation (§ 2-505) gives the seller a practical alternative, in effect a security interest.
That isn't the stated reason.
The statute's limit protects carriers, not the statute-of-frauds policy of evidencing deals.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Why limits on stopping

q: A dealer lets a buyer who has signed a contract take the car for a day to test it. A storm wrecks it while it's parked at the buyer's home. A separate buyer prepaid in full for goods left at a merchant seller's yard, which are then stolen. Which is correct?
o: Title decides both cases.
Risk always stays with the seller until a final signed receipt.
Risk is shared equally in each case.
Prepayment doesn't shift risk; testing turns on the terms of the deal.
Payment always moves the risk to the buyer.
oe: Article 2 risk rules don't depend on title.
Receipt doesn't require a signature.
There's no sharing rule.
Correct. Under § 2-509(3) a merchant's risk stays until receipt, whatever was paid. Goods out for testing raise whether the buyer has "received" them and the sale-on-approval rules of § 2-327.
Risk isn't tied to payment.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Goods out for testing

q: A buyer justifiably revokes acceptance of a $60,000 truck for which it paid $60,000. It then buys a comparable truck for $63,000 and pays $500 in towing and storage for the first truck. What may it recover, setting aside any use offset?
oe: That leaves out the incidentals.
It keeps the new truck, so it doesn't recover the full cover price.
That leaves out cover and incidentals.
That leaves out the refund.
Correct. $60,000 refund, $3,000 cover differential, $500 incidental.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Lemon sold to business

q: A supply contract has a valid disclaimer of fitness and a $5,000 cap on damages. Under a finance lease the goods fail, causing the lessee $40,000 in losses. What may the lessee recover from the supplier?
o: Nothing, as it isn't a party.
$40,000 from the lessor.
Up to $5,000, on any warranty that survives.
$40,000, as it never agreed to the cap.
$5,000 from each of the supplier and the lessor.
oe: Section 2A-209 gives it the benefit.
The lessor gave no warranties.
Correct. The benefit extends subject to the warranty's terms and the supply contract, including disclaimers and limits (§ 2A-209(1)).
It takes subject to the supply contract.
The lessor isn't liable.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Supplier disclaimer flows through

q: Gobo, a consumer, signs a preprinted 12-page form to buy a refrigerator. A clause in tiny type lets the seller repossess the refrigerator if Gobo is late on any payment for any item he ever buys from the seller. Gobo had no chance to negotiate. Which statement best describes how most courts would analyze the clause under § 2-302?
o: It is enforceable, because Gobo signed the form and could have read it.
Procedural unconscionability, like tiny type, is enough by itself.
The jury decides whether the clause is unfair to Gobo.
Most courts require both procedural and substantive unconscionability.
It is unconscionable only if the refrigerator's price was also unfair.
oe: Signing doesn't defeat an unconscionability claim.
Most courts want both elements.
The court decides as a matter of law.
Correct. Some courts use a sliding scale. Here the fine print and lack of choice are procedural; the one-sided repossession term is substantive.
Price is one possible kind of substantive unfairness, not a requirement.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Procedural and substantive

q: A buyer doesn't answer a proper § 2-609 demand for 40 days. On day 41, before the seller has done anything, it provides full assurance. Is it too late?
o: No, as the repudiation may be retracted if the seller hasn't acted.
No, as it had a further 30 days to respond.
Yes, as a repudiation can never be retracted.
Yes, because 30 days is an absolute cutoff.
Yes, unless the seller agrees in writing.
oe: Correct. Comment 5 and § 2-611: the 30-day limit removes uncertainty, but the resulting repudiation can still be retracted until the aggrieved party has cancelled, materially changed position, or indicated that it considers the repudiation final.
There's no second period.
Section 2-611 allows retraction.
The cutoff is for when a repudiation occurs.
Retraction needs no consent.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Retracting after 30 days

q: A seller's contract was at $10 per unit. Market at tender is $6, and it resells a week later, in a rising market, at $8.50. Under Peace River, which is the best statement?
o: It's limited to $1.50 under every authority.
It may claim nothing, as the market rose after breach.
It must elect in its pleadings or lose both.
It may claim $5.50 by adding both.
It may claim $4 a unit, with § 1-305 the buyer's counterargument.
oe: Peace River says otherwise.
Market is at tender.
The UCC rejects election of remedies.
The measures can't be stacked.
Correct. Market damages stay available even after a resale, though a court applying § 1-305 strictly might limit it to $1.50.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale vs. Peace River

q: A hospital agrees to buy "all the surgical gloves it needs this year" from a supplier at a fixed price. Midyear, the supplier refuses to deliver, arguing that the contract is unenforceable because it states no quantity. What is the most likely result?
o: The supplier wins, because the hospital never promised to buy any minimum amount.
The supplier wins, because a contract with no stated quantity is too indefinite.
The hospital wins, but only for gloves already ordered.
The supplier wins, because requirements contracts are illusory.
None of the above.
oe: Good faith limits the buyer's requirements, which supplies mutuality.
A requirements term is a quantity term.
The contract is enforceable for the year.
§ 2-306 rejects that view.
Correct. The hospital wins: a requirements term measures quantity by the buyer's actual good-faith requirements (§ 2-306(1)), so the contract is neither indefinite nor illusory. No choice says that.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: not too indefinite

q: Under a contract calling for payment on delivery, Seller demands prepayment for the first time, without any reason for insecurity, and says it won't ship otherwise. Buyer says, "Fine, I'm cancelling," and buys elsewhere at a higher price. Who is in breach?
o: Neither, because both parties chose to walk away.
Seller, because the demand conditioned performance on a change in terms.
Buyer, because Seller only asked for a change.
Buyer, because a party must always demand assurance before cancelling.
Seller, but only if Buyer first waited 30 days.
oe: Seller's conditional refusal came first and was unjustified.

Correct. A demand for more than the contract requires, as a condition of performing, is a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2). With no grounds for insecurity, § 2-609 gives Seller no cover. Buyer may cancel and cover.
A polite request isn't a repudiation, but Seller said it won't ship otherwise.
Section 2-609 is optional when the other side has already repudiated.
The 30 days applies only to § 2-609 demands.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Who breached first

q: On the day they sign a final but not complete contract for 1,000 jackets at $50 each, the parties also sign a separate side letter giving the buyer a $5 discount per jacket. The seller argues that the side letter contradicts the contract price. Is the side letter admissible?
o: Yes, because a contemporaneous written agreement is read together with the writing.
