No, because agreements made at the same time as the writing are always excluded by the parol evidence rule.
Yes, but only if the side letter has its own merger clause.
No, because it contradicts the written price.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The Problem 5-10 chart: a contradictory contemporaneous writing is admissible against a partial integration.
Only contemporaneous oral agreements are barred from contradicting.
No such requirement.
A contemporaneous writing is read with the main writing.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Contemporaneous side letter

q: Ernie buys 500 euro notes from a currency dealer to spend on his trip to Rome. Bert buys a rare 1850 coin from a coin dealer to keep in his collection. Which of these purchases is most clearly a sale of "goods"?
o: Neither purchase.
Ernie's purchase only.
It depends entirely on whether the dealers are merchants.
Both purchases.
Bert's purchase only.
oe: The collector's coin is a good.
Currency bought to be spent as money is the weaker case. Whether it is goods depends on whether it is bought as a commodity or as money.
Whether something is a good does not turn on merchant status.
The euro notes are only "depends." Currency bought as money is arguably not goods.

Correct. The collector's coin is the subject of the sale, not the money paying the price, so it is a good (Problem 1-1). Ernie's euros are the harder case: it depends whether the currency is a commodity or money.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Money as goods

q: Under an installment contract for tomatoes, Load 1 arrives one day late with no special harm. May the buyer reject the load?
o: Yes, because a late delivery can never be cured.
No, because a buyer may never reject an installment for delay.
Probably not, because one day is unlikely to be substantial impairment.
Yes, but only if the seller received written notice in advance.
Yes, because any late tender fails to conform.
oe: Incurability alone isn't enough; impairment is also required.
A material delay can qualify.
Correct. The buyer needs substantial impairment that can't be cured, judged by the contract's normal and known purposes.
No such requirement.
That's the § 2-601 test, which § 2-612 displaces here.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Installment: rotten or one day late

q: At a bike shop, Ernie picks out a specific red bicycle on the showroom floor and signs a contract to buy it, agreeing to pick it up next week after the shop adds a bell. When is the bicycle identified to the contract?
o: When the contract is made, because it is a sale of existing goods already identified.
When Ernie pays the full price.
When the shop tenders the bicycle to Ernie.
When the shop finishes adding the bell.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-501(1)(a). Ernie also gets an insurable interest then.
Payment doesn't control identification.
Identification comes earlier.
The bicycle was already identified.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Identification

q: After a justified, effective revocation, which is NOT available to the buyer?
o: Incidental damages under § 2-715(1).
Keeping the goods and also recovering the price.
Cover damages under § 2-712.
A security interest under § 2-711(3).
Recovery of the price it has paid.
oe: Available.
Correct. That's double recovery. The buyer doesn't owe the price, may cancel, has the remedies of a buyer that rightfully rejected, and has the same duties for goods in its possession.
Available under § 2-711(1).
Available in goods it holds.
Available under § 2-711(1).
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — After revocation

q: A state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. Gina buys a blender from a store, and its blade assembly flies off. Which injured person may sue the store for breach of warranty?
o: A neighbor who borrowed the blender and was injured in his own kitchen.
A houseguest injured while making smoothies in Gina's kitchen.
A coworker injured when Gina brings the blender to an office party.
A friend whose expensive countertop was cracked, with no physical injury.
Gina's adult son, who lives across town, injured while using the blender in his own apartment.
oe: The neighbor isn't in Gina's household and wasn't a guest in her home.

Correct. Alternative A extends the seller's warranty to natural persons in the buyer's family or household and guests in the buyer's home, if it's reasonable to expect them to use or be affected by the goods and they are injured in person.
Alternative A doesn't reach people outside the buyer's family, household, or home.
Alternative A covers only injury to the person.
He isn't a member of Gina's household or a guest in her home, so Alternative A doesn't reach him.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — § 2-318 Alternative A: who's covered

q: A fabricator orders 3,000 steel bolts from a distributor. Its purchase order refers to the distributor's spec sheet, which lists a tensile strength of 150,000 psi. The bolts test at 110,000 psi. The distributor argues it never "warranted" anything and the spec sheet was just technical data. Who wins?
o: The fabricator, but only under the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
The distributor, because technical data is opinion rather than fact.
The distributor, because it never used the words "warrant" or "guarantee."
The fabricator, because the spec sheet's figures are a description of the goods that formed part of the bargain.
The distributor, because the fabricator should have tested the bolts before ordering.
oe: The better claim is express warranty. Nothing shows the fabricator relied on the distributor's skill to select the bolts.
A stated tensile strength is specific, measurable, and verifiable: classic fact.
§ 2-313(2) says no formal words or specific intent to warrant are required.

Correct. Any description made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty (§ 2-313(1)(b)). Technical specifications are descriptions (cmt. 5), and formal words like "warrant" aren't needed (§ 2-313(2)).
Express warranties don't depend on the buyer's testing. Pre-contract examination affects implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(b)).
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Spec sheet as description

q: A dealer gives a written 90-day warranty on a car and, in a conspicuous clause mentioning merchantability, disclaims all implied warranties. Which is the best statement?
o: The written warranty is void.
Implied warranties can never be disclaimed.
The clause works, because it meets § 2-316.
Magnuson-Moss bars the disclaimer, as a written warranty was given.
The clause works, unless the buyer is a merchant.
oe: Only the disclaimer fails.
They can be, outside Magnuson-Moss limits.
Federal law overrides it here.
Correct. Compliance with § 2-316 isn't always enough. Magnuson-Moss bars disclaiming implied warranties alongside a written warranty; fraud can defeat "as is"; and unconscionability remains a check.
Status isn't the point.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — When compliance isn't enough

q: A lessee pays $30,000 in advance rent for a 3-year lease, then defaults at the start, before delivery. The lessor withholds and leases the goods to another on substantially similar terms for the same rent. It proves no loss. There's no LD term. The then PV of the remaining rent is $100,000. How much goes back?
o: $10,000, as the lessor keeps 20% of then PV.
Nothing.
oe: That applies 20% to the prepayment.
The statutory retention needs no proof.
Correct. Section 2A-504(3)(b): 20% of $100,000 = $20,000 kept, so $10,000 returned, since it's not a consumer lease.
That's the consumer rule.
Restitution applies.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Prepaid rent; repossession

q: A hospital accepted 40 beds. Hidden defects later appear in 10 of them, seriously impairing those beds. May it revoke?
o: Only as to all 40 or none.
Yes, as to all 40, if any one is defective.
No, since most beds work.
No, because a hospital isn't a consumer.
Yes, as to the 10, since revocation applies to a lot or commercial unit.
oe: Partial revocation by unit is allowed.
It must be as to impaired units.
The test applies to the unit.
Revocation isn't limited to consumers.
Correct. Section 2-608(1) applies to a "lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value."
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Revoke some units

q: A bakery agrees to buy all the eggs it requires for its custard line from a farm, with an estimate of 2,000 dozen a month. Facing declining custard sales and for sound business reasons unrelated to the egg contract, the bakery discontinues the custard line, and its requirements drop to zero. The farm sues. Under the approach most courts take, what is the most likely result?
o: The farm wins, because any drop far below the estimate is unreasonably disproportionate.
The farm wins, because a requirements buyer must take at least the estimated quantity.
The bakery wins only if it gave the farm a year's notice before discontinuing the line.
The bakery likely wins, because a reduction made in good faith for business reasons isn't a breach.
The contract was never enforceable, because requirements contracts lack mutuality.
oe: Most courts don't apply the disproportion limit that strictly to good-faith decreases.
An estimate isn't a minimum, though it bears on what is disproportionate.
Section 2-306 has no fixed notice period. The test is good faith.

Correct. Most courts read § 2-306(1)'s disproportion limit mainly as a check on increases and judge reductions by good faith. A buyer that cuts its requirements for legitimate business reasons, rather than to escape a bad bargain, doesn't breach (see § 2-306 cmt. 2).
Section 2-306 and good faith supply the needed mutuality.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: good-faith drop to near zero

q: Kermit emails Fozzie: "Confirming I'll buy 40 drum kits from you at $600 each. — Kermit." Kermit typed his name; there is no handwritten signature. Fozzie sues Kermit when Kermit backs out. Is the email a sufficient record signed by Kermit?
o: Yes; an email is a record, and a typed name can sign it.
No, because § 2-201 requires a handwritten signature.
Yes, provided Fozzie also signed the email reply.
No, because an email is not a writing under § 2-201.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the 2022 amendments (and UETA elsewhere), email is a record, and a typed name adopted to authenticate it is a signature.
A typed name can be a signature.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought (Kermit) must sign.
"Record" includes electronic records.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Email as a signed record

q: On March 1, a seller tells a buyer it won't deliver the 5,000 bags of fertilizer due April 1. On March 5, the buyer buys substitute fertilizer from another supplier for the season. On March 8, the seller emails that it has changed its mind and will deliver on April 1 after all. Is the retraction effective?
o: Yes, because the buyer never told the seller that it considered the repudiation final.
Yes, but only if the seller also gives the buyer adequate assurance that it will perform.
No, because once a party repudiates, the repudiation can never be retracted.
No, because the buyer materially changed its position by covering before the retraction.
Yes, because the seller retracted before April 1, when its performance was due.
oe: Materially changing position, for example by covering, is enough on its own.
Assurance is required if demanded, but here the retraction comes too late in any event.
Section 2-611 permits retraction in the right circumstances.

Correct. A repudiating party may retract until its next performance is due "unless the aggrieved party has since the repudiation cancelled or materially changed his position or otherwise indicated that he considers the repudiation final" (§ 2-611(1)).
Timing before the due date isn't enough when the buyer has already changed position.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Retraction too late after cover

q: Which may a lessor do after default, if the lease so provides?
o: Require delivery to any place in the world.
Disable consumer goods at will.
Require assembly, and disable business goods in place.
Enter a home by force.
Sell the lessee's other property.
oe: Only a reasonably convenient place.
The right covers business goods.
Correct. The first needs the lease to say so. Rendering unusable is in the statute directly.
That's a breach of the peace.
It has no such right.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Assemble and disable

q: A buyer's lawyer reads § 2-711 as a complete list of remedies for every breach. What is wrong with that reading?
o: It covers only sellers, and buyers look to § 2-703.
It applies only when the seller has acted in bad faith.
It forces the buyer to elect one remedy at the outset.
It applies only if the buyer has already paid the price.
It is an incomplete list, and it doesn't address accepted goods.
oe: Reversed: § 2-703 is the seller's catalog.
Section 2-711 has no bad-faith trigger; repudiation, nondelivery, rejection and revocation are the triggers.
The Code doesn't impose an early election of remedies.
Payment isn't required; the refund is just one item on the list.

Correct. Section 2-711 lists cancellation, recovery of price paid, cover or market damages and, where allowed, getting the goods. It does not list everything (§ 2-714 for accepted goods sits outside it).
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — § 2-711 is incomplete

q: A signed contract for industrial lubricant says it is "the complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the agreement." The buyer offers (1) evidence of a trade usage that suppliers give 60 days' notice before discontinuing a grade, and (2) evidence that the seller orally promised before signing to give such notice. Which is admissible to supplement the contract?
o: Both.
Neither, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Only (1), because usage of trade can supplement even a complete and exclusive writing, but a prior promise cannot.
Only (2), because the promise was made specifically to this buyer.
None of the above.
oe: The prior oral promise can't supplement a complete and exclusive writing.
Usage of trade can still supplement it.
Correct. § 2-202(a) and (b); Problem 5-12(a) and (b).
It's barred by the full integration.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Complete writing: usage vs. prior promise

q: Which of the following is a consequence of identifying goods to a contract under § 2-501?
o: The buyer must pay the price immediately, before delivery.
The seller loses its insurable interest in the goods.
The risk of loss passes from the seller to the buyer.
Title to the goods passes from the seller to the buyer.
The buyer gets a special property and an insurable interest.
oe: Payment is due when and where the buyer is to receive the goods unless otherwise agreed (§ 2-310(a)). Identification doesn't accelerate payment.
The seller keeps an insurable interest as long as it has title or a security interest (§ 2-501(2)).
Risk passes under §§ 2-509 and 2-510, which don't turn on identification.
Title passes under § 2-401, usually when the seller completes physical delivery, unless otherwise agreed.
Correct. Identification gives the buyer a special property and an insurable interest (§ 2-501(1)). It's also a prerequisite for some remedies, such as replevin and § 2-613 excuse.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Effect of identification

q: Which of the following is a sale of "goods" under § 2-105?
o: A lab buys liquid nitrogen in pressurized tanks from a gas supplier.
Prairie Dawn buys a landlord's right to collect next year's rent from a tenant.
Zoe buys a promissory note payable to the seller.
Herry buys certificated shares in a closely held corporation.
All of the above.
oe: Correct. Liquids and gases are movable things, so they are goods (Problem 1-1's oxygen and isotopes).
A right to payment is a thing in action, not a movable thing.
A note is a thing in action (and an Article 3 instrument), which § 2-105(1) excludes.
Investment securities are excluded; Article 8 governs them.
Only A is a sale of goods.
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — What is a "good"

q: A seller sued for the price but the court found it could resell. What then?
o: It must start over with a new lawsuit.
It is still awarded § 2-708 damages.
It gets only incidental damages.
It gets the price less 20%.
It loses its case entirely.
oe: The same action yields § 2-708 damages.
Correct. Section 2-709(3).
Section 2-708 damages are available.
Section 2-709(3) has no such discount; it gives § 2-708 damages.
Section 2-709(3) prevents that.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Not entitled to the price

q: A seller gives a written warranty that a painting is authentic. Before closing, the seller himself tells the buyer that experts have doubted the painting's authenticity. The buyer closes anyway without saying anything to preserve its rights. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, what is the most likely result?
o: The buyer recovers, because no reliance on the warranty need be shown.
The buyer waived the breach by closing without preserving its rights.
The buyer recovers, because the warranty was in a signed writing.
The buyer recovers half its loss, since both parties knew of the doubts.
None of the above.
oe: Reliance isn't the issue; waiver is.
Correct. That is why the source of the buyer's knowledge decided Rogath, and why the case was remanded for trial on who told Rogath.
A writing doesn't stop waiver.
There is no splitting rule.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Rogath: seller's own disclosure

q: A finance lessor asks what to put in its form. Which is NOT sensible advice?
o: A waiver of setoff and defenses against the lessor and assignees.
A warranty by the lessor that the goods are fit for the lessee's purpose.
An express hell-or-high-water clause as backup.
An assignment of supplier warranties to the lessee.
A signed acceptance certificate.
oe: Sensible.

Correct. That would undo the point of a finance lease. Sensible terms: an express hell-or-high-water clause (§ 2A-407(3)), a signed acceptance certificate, waiver of setoff and defenses, a disclaimer of warranties, and assignment of supplier warranties. See Wells Fargo v. B.C.B.U.
Sensible.
Sensible.
Sensible.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Drafting for Boston

q: A farmer tells a seed dealer she needs a corn variety that will mature in her short northern growing season and asks the dealer to pick one. The dealer picks a variety, and the farmer signs a contract with a conspicuous clause: "SELLER EXCLUDES THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY." The corn is healthy but needs a longer season and doesn't mature before frost. Which claim, if any, survives?
o: Fitness for a particular purpose, because the clause excludes only merchantability.
Merchantability, because a disclaimer of merchantability is unenforceable in a sale to a farmer.
Neither, because healthy seed is merchantable.
Neither, because the clause excluded all implied warranties.
Both, because the dealer selected the seed.
oe: Correct. The clause meets § 2-316(2) for merchantability, but it doesn't purport to exclude fitness, and nothing else does. The dealer knew the purpose and the farmer relied on its selection, so § 2-315 applies.
The disclaimer satisfies § 2-316(2), so merchantability is excluded.
Being merchantable doesn't defeat a separate fitness claim.
It names only merchantability. To exclude fitness, a conspicuous writing must address it, generally or specifically.
Selection supports fitness, but merchantability was effectively disclaimed.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Merchantability disclaimed; fitness survives

q: Two parties agree on a sale of bolts at a fixed price, but never state a quantity, and nothing else supplies one. Which is correct under § 2-204(3)?
o: The seller may ship what it thinks is reasonable.
The buyer may name any quantity under § 2-311.
The contract likely fails, because the Code doesn't supply quantity.
A reasonable quantity is implied by § 2-305.
The contract is enforced at one unit.
oe: Nothing gives it that power.
Section 2-311 covers particulars of performance, not quantity.
Correct. Article 2 fills gaps in price, quality and delivery, but not quantity (apart from output and requirements). Without quantity there's no reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
Section 2-305 fills price, not quantity.
There's no such default.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Quantity not gap-filled

q: A buyer with a good ground for rejection gives notice far too late. What is the result?
o: It keeps the right to reject, because the goods don't conform.
It loses all claims against the seller automatically.
It has breached and owes § 2-708 damages.
It has accepted and owes the price, but keeps a damages claim with notice.
None of the above.
oe: Rightness doesn't cure an ineffective rejection.
The claim survives with notice.
The buyer owes the price, with an offset for its damages.
Correct. The rejection is ineffective, so acceptance results, but the seller's breach doesn't disappear.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Late rejection effect

q: A buyer accepted a machine. Three months later a hidden defect that substantially impairs the machine surfaces. Which remedy route should the buyer start with?
o: Reject the machine under § 2-601.
Recover the machine under § 2-502.
Revoke acceptance under § 2-608.
Replevy the machine under § 2-716(3).
Cover immediately under § 2-712.
oe: Acceptance precludes rejection (§ 2-607(2)), so that door is closed.
Section 2-502 also reaches goods still held by the seller.

Correct. The breach-type table: repudiation or no tender leads to § 2-711; nonconforming tender leads to rejection or § 2-714; a hidden defect after acceptance leads to § 2-608 (if its limits are met) and then § 2-711.
Replevin gets goods out of the seller's hands, and the buyer already has them.
Cover follows rejection, revocation, repudiation or nondelivery, so the buyer must revoke first.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Which track fits

q: A car dealer tells a buyer that a model is "the safest car in its class." Independent crash ratings later show it is in the middle of its class. Which statement best describes how courts treat the dealer's statement?
o: Courts split: some call it puffing, others a measurable warranty.
It is puffing, because superlatives are statements of opinion.
It is a warranty when it appears in the written contract.
It is a warranty, because a merchant dealer made it about safety.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-6 treats it as a split: superlative puffery vs. a claim that can be checked.
Some courts would call it puffing, but not all.
Writing isn't decisive.
Merchant status doesn't decide it, and courts split.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Superlatives

q: A lessor discovers its lessee is insolvent before delivery. Which is correct?
o: It may reclaim only with a court order.
It may stop only carload lots.
It must deliver, and then sue on the lease.
It may refuse to deliver, or stop the goods in transit.
It must wait 30 days before acting.
oe: The goods haven't been delivered.
Insolvency permits any size.
Section 2A-525(1) lets it refuse.
Correct. Unfinished goods: § 2A-524. Cancellation is subject to substantial impairment for installment leases.
No waiting period applies.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Before delivery

q: On March 1, Kermit sends a supplier a justified written demand for adequate assurance. The supplier ignores it. By April 10, Kermit has heard nothing. What may Kermit do?
o: Cancel only after sending a second demand.
Nothing, because Kermit must sue to compel a response.
Treat the contract as repudiated and pursue its remedies.
Treat the contract as repudiated only if the supplier also misses a delivery.
None of the above.
oe: One justified demand is enough.
Silence has a statutory consequence.
Failing to respond is itself a repudiation.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — No response within 30 days

q: Rizzo's Manufacturing builds 10,000 novelty umbrellas to a design and specifications furnished by Pepe's Party Supply. A patent holder sues both companies, claiming the umbrella design infringes its patent. As between Rizzo's and Pepe's, who bears the infringement claim?
o: Neither, until a court decides whether the patent holder's patent is valid.
Pepe's, because a buyer that furnishes the specifications must hold the seller harmless.
They split it equally, because both companies took part in making the umbrellas.
Rizzo's, because the warranty of title protects the buyer against patent claims.
Rizzo's, because a merchant manufacturer always warrants that its goods don't infringe.
oe: Allocation between the parties doesn't wait for a ruling on the patent's validity.

Correct. A merchant seller regularly dealing in goods of the kind warrants against infringement, "but a buyer who furnishes specifications to the seller must hold the seller harmless against any such claim which arises out of compliance with the specifications" (§ 2-312(3)).
Section 2-312(3) puts this claim entirely on the buyer.
The title warranty concerns ownership and liens, not patents.
The warranty against infringement doesn't cover claims arising from the buyer's own specifications.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Infringement: buyer's specifications

q: A court finds that a writing is final on the terms it covers, but not complete. A party offers (1) evidence of fraud; (2) a consistent prior oral term; (3) a contradicting prior oral term. Which may come in?
o: All three items.
Only item (1).
Items (1) and (2).
Items (1) and (3).
None of them.
oe: Item (3) is barred.
Item (2) also comes in, as the writing isn't complete.
Correct. Section 2-202 doesn't bar evidence of fraud, and consistent additional terms may supplement a partial integration. Contradiction is barred. Admitted evidence must still be believed.
Item (3) contradicts the writing.
Items (1) and (2) come in.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Classifying a writing

q: Under § 2-612(3), when may a buyer treat a default as a breach of the whole installment contract?
o: Only if the seller has become insolvent.
Only after three consecutive bad installments.
Whenever any installment is rejected.
Only with a court's prior approval.
When a default substantially impairs the value of the whole.
oe: Insolvency isn't the test.
The Code has no such count.
Rejecting one installment doesn't by itself impair the whole.
No court approval is needed.
Correct. One bad installment can be enough if it undermines the whole, and so can a pattern. Short of that the buyer may use § 2-609.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Cancel the whole

q: A Vermont glassworks agrees to make custom stained-glass panels and have them "properly crated and delivered to" a church construction site in Georgia. It crates them properly and hands them to a trucking company. The truck crashes on the highway, shattering the panels. The church refuses to pay. Who bears the loss?
o: The glassworks, because "delivered to" made this a destination contract.
The church, because "delivered to" doesn't overcome the shipment-contract presumption, so risk passed at the carrier.
The glassworks, because custom goods stay at the seller's risk until installed.
The trucking company alone, so the church owes nothing until it collects.
None of the above.
oe: "Delivered to" doesn't overcome the shipment-contract presumption.
Correct. This is Windows v. Jordan Panel (Problem 4-7(a)). The church must pay and can pursue the carrier.
No special rule for custom goods.
The buyer owes the price; its claim against the carrier is separate.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — "Delivered to" the site

q: A contract for a commercial espresso machine says, conspicuously: "SELLER'S SOLE OBLIGATION FOR DEFECTIVE GOODS IS TO REPAIR OR REPLACE THEM." It doesn't mention merchantability. The machine is defective. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The merchantability warranty still exists; the clause only limits the remedy for breaching it.
The clause is effective only if the buyer signed it separately from the rest of the contract.
The clause disclaims merchantability, because it describes the seller's only obligation.
The buyer may ignore the clause, because a limited remedy must use the word "exclusive."
The clause is void, because a clause dealing with defects must mention merchantability.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer narrows what the seller promises (§ 2-316). A remedy limitation leaves the warranty intact and restricts what the buyer recovers when it's breached (§§ 2-316(4), 2-719). This clause is a remedy limitation.
Neither § 2-316 nor § 2-719 requires a separate signature.
The clause doesn't mention merchantability and doesn't say there is no warranty. It limits the remedy.
The clause says "sole obligation," which signals an exclusive remedy (§ 2-719(1)(b)).
The mention requirement applies to disclaimers, not to remedy limitations.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Remedy limitation is not a disclaimer

q: A youth league orders 300 jerseys printed with its name, logo, and players' numbers for $6,000 by phone. After the printer has printed 120 jerseys, the league calls to cancel. The league signed nothing. Can the printer enforce the contract?
o: Yes, but only for the 120 jerseys already printed.
Yes, because the jerseys are made for the league, unsuitable for others, and substantially begun before the cancellation.
Yes, because the printer is a merchant.
No, because the printer must finish all 300 before the exception applies.
No, because the league never signed a record.
oe: § 2-201(3)(a) makes the contract enforceable, not just the part already made.
Correct. § 2-201(3)(a): specially made goods, not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course, and a substantial beginning before notice of repudiation.
Merchant status alone doesn't satisfy the statute.
A substantial beginning is enough.
An exception applies.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Specially manufactured goods

q: Big Bird hires an engineering firm to design a custom irrigation system for $50,000. The price includes $6,000 for pumps and valves the firm supplies; the rest is for design work, so goods do not predominate. Under amended § 2-102(2), which of the following would NOT apply to the transaction?
o: The rules on risk of loss for the pumps and valves.
Big Bird's right to reject nonconforming pumps.
Big Bird's remedies if the pumps are never delivered.
The statute of frauds (§ 2-201).
The implied warranty of merchantability for the pumps (§ 2-314).
oe: They apply. Tender and risk of loss relate primarily to the goods (cmt. 5).
It applies. Acceptance, rejection, and cure all relate to the goods (cmt. 5).
They apply. The buyer's remedies for nondelivery of the goods relate to the goods (cmt. 5).
Correct. Cmt. 5: when goods don't predominate, only the provisions relating primarily to the goods apply. The statute of frauds, the formation sections (§§ 2-204 to 2-207), and § 2-209 do not.
It applies. When goods don't predominate, the warranty provisions still apply to the goods (cmt. 5).
topic: Wk 1 · I · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: what doesn't apply

q: A buyer repudiates a contract for 400 units at $100, F.O.B. seller. The seller gives notice and properly resells at $85, paying $1,000 in commissions and $500 for storage, and saves $2,000 in packing it would have spent on the buyer's order. What are its § 2-706 damages?
oe: That ignores the incidentals.
That ignores the expenses saved.
That ignores both incidentals and savings.
Correct. ($100 minus $85) × 400 = $6,000, plus $1,500 incidental, minus $2,000 saved.
That adds the savings.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale math with incidentals

q: After giving proper notice of revocation, a business keeps using a machine until a replacement arrives. Which is correct?
o: The seller may then repossess by self-help.
The buyer must first post a bond.
Use is unlimited, with no offset.
Any use after revocation automatically reinstates acceptance.
Reasonable, necessary use may not undo revocation, but expect an offset.
oe: It has no such right.
There's no such requirement.
An offset is likely.
Not under the evolving majority.
Correct. Section 2-608(3) gives the rights and duties of a rejecting buyer, and courts apply Johannsen to use after revocation.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Revocation after notice but with use

q: Which right does a consumer finance lessee have that a non-consumer finance lessee lacks?
o: To reject before acceptance.
To have risk of loss stay with the lessor.
To sue the supplier.
To receive implied warranties from the lessor.
To revoke for a lessor's default that substantially impairs value.
oe: Both may.
Risk passes to any finance lessee.
Both may, through § 2A-209.
Neither gets them: the carve-out covers all finance leases.
Correct. Section 2A-517(2) excepts only non-consumer finance leases. A consumer also isn't bound by § 2A-407.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Consumer finance vs. supplier

q: Miss Piggy's Bakery has a two-year contract to buy "all the flour it requires" from a mill at a fixed $20 a bag, with an estimate of 1,000 bags a month based on its baking. Flour prices jump to $45. Miss Piggy then orders 2,500 bags a month, planning to resell the extra to other bakeries. Must the mill fill the orders?
o: No, because buying extra to resell at market is not a good-faith requirement and is disproportionate to the estimate.
No, because requirements contracts become unenforceable when the market moves.
Yes, but only at the market price for the extra bags.
Yes, because the contract states only an estimate, not a cap.
Yes, because a requirements buyer may order whatever it needs.
oe: Correct. This is Orange & Rockland: a buyer can't use a fixed-price requirements contract to speculate when the market rises.
The contract is enforceable. The excess is what's limited.
§ 2-306 doesn't reprice the excess; it limits the quantity.
The estimate is the yardstick for disproportion (§ 2-306(1)).
Only requirements that occur in good faith, and not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Requirements: buying to resell

q: Under § 2-302, which of the following is true?
o: The parties may agree that § 2-302 will not apply to their contract.
Unconscionability is a question of fact for the jury.
The court may refuse enforcement, strike the clause, or limit it.
Unconscionability is judged as of the time of the breach.
All of the above.
oe: § 2-302 cannot be contracted away (§ 1-302).
The court decides it as a matter of law.
Correct. Those are the three options in § 2-302(1), and the parties may present evidence of the commercial setting.
It is judged as of the time the contract was made.
Only C is correct.
topic: Wks 1–2 · III · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: who decides and when

q: A business buyer prepays in full for unidentified fungible goods. The seller repudiates and remains solvent. Which is the buyer's realistic position?
o: Replevin, since full payment takes the place of identification.
An automatic lien on all of the seller's inventory.
Recovery of the goods under § 2-502, since it has paid in full.
A refund and damages, since prepaying gives no right to the goods.
Specific performance as of right, since it paid in advance.
oe: Payment can't replace identification.
A lien on goods needs an Article 9 security interest, which the buyer doesn't have.
The goods aren't identified, and no § 2-502(1) trigger is met.
Correct. Without § 2-502, § 2-716 or an Article 9 security interest, the buyer can't force the goods out. It may cancel, recover the price (§ 2-711(1)) and take cover or market damages.
The remedy is discretionary, and substitutes exist for fungible goods.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Prepaying alone

q: A bank's equipment arm picks a brand and model for a customer, buys it, and leases it. Is this a finance lease?
o: No, because the lessor selected the goods.
Yes, if the lease has a hell-or-high-water clause.
No, because a bank can't be a lessor.
Yes, since banks are always finance lessors.
Yes, because the lessor acquired the goods.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-103(1)(g)(i). The lessor must not select, make or supply the goods. So the lessor here gives implied warranties if it's a merchant.
The clause doesn't define finance status.
It can be.
Status depends on the elements.

q: Boober buys a hand loom from Mokey, a weaver selling her spare equipment, for $1,800. He pays with a check and takes the loom home. The check bounces. Mokey, because a buyer who pays with a bad check gets no title at all to pass on.
Mokey, because Wembley paid $200 less than the price Boober had agreed to pay.
Wembley, because Boober had voidable title and Wembley bought in good faith for value.
None of the above.
oe: Voidable-title protection under § 2-403(1) doesn't depend on the transferor being a merchant. That's the entrustment rule.
A bad check gives the buyer voidable title, not void title.
Value doesn't have to equal the original price. Paying $1,600 is value.

Correct. A person with voidable title has power to transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value, even when the goods were delivered in exchange for a check that was later dishonored (§ 2-403(1)(b)). Mokey's remedy is against Boober.

The seller still bears whatever the buyer's insurance doesn't cover.
There is no even split. The allocation turns on the buyer's insurance coverage.

Correct. When the buyer rightfully revokes acceptance, it may treat the risk as having rested on the seller from the beginning, but only "to the extent of any deficiency in his effective insurance coverage" (§ 2-510(2)). Beaker's insurer covers $25,000, so the seller bears the $15,000 shortfall.

Rogath rejects a strict belief-in-the-truth test.

Section 2-305 displaces that rule.
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Agreement to agree

q: Grover's buyer has always paid on time, and nothing suggests any problem. Grover nonetheless writes: "Pay the full price in advance or we won't ship." Under the § 2-609 flowchart, what is the risk to Grover?
o: The buyer must prepay within 30 days or it will be in breach.
None, because a party may demand assurance whenever it chooses.
Without reasonable grounds, his demand may itself be a repudiation.
None, so long as the demand is made in writing.
None, because a mere demand for assurance cannot be a repudiation.
oe: The buyer's duty arises only after a justified demand.
Reasonable grounds for insecurity are required.
Correct. The § 2-609/§ 2-610 flowchart.
A writing is necessary, not sufficient; grounds are also required.
It is a repudiation when performance is conditioned on it.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Demand without grounds

q: A used-car dealer has one Porsche, which it sold to Ann for $50,000. She backs out, and it sells the same car to Bo the next week for $50,000. It claims lost profit. What is the likely result?
o: It recovers lost profit, as every dealer is a lost-volume seller.
It isn't a lost-volume seller, because it could not have sold both.
It recovers double profit.
It recovers lost profit, as Ann breached.
It recovers the full $50,000.
oe: It needs a supply beyond this one car.
Correct. With only one car, the second sale replaced the first. Damages are zero, apart from incidentals. Lost volume needs capacity, and profitability, to make both sales.
There's no second lost sale.
Breach alone doesn't show lost volume.
It sold the car.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lost volume vs. used goods

q: A nursery agrees to deliver 40 trees to Big Bird's yard in the nursery's own truck. The contract has no shipping or risk terms. On the way, a storm topples a tree onto the truck and destroys the cargo. Who bears the loss?
o: The nursery, but only if it was negligent.
Big Bird, because the trees had been identified to the contract.
Big Bird, because the nursery tendered the trees by loading them.
Big Bird, because the trees were delivered to a carrier.
None of the above.
oe: Risk of loss doesn't depend on fault.
Identification doesn't pass risk.
Loading its own truck isn't a tender to the buyer.
The seller's own truck isn't a carrier.
Correct. The nursery bears it. Its own truck isn't a carrier, so § 2-509(3) applies, and a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods (Problem 4-6(a)). No choice says that.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Seller's own truck

q: At a sheriff's execution sale held to satisfy a court judgment against a debtor, Gonzo buys a motorcycle that the sheriff had seized from the debtor's garage. Nothing is said about title. It turns out the motorcycle belonged to the debtor's neighbor, who reclaims it. Gonzo sues the sheriff for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo loses, because the motorcycle was used and used goods carry no title warranty.
Gonzo wins, because the sheriff never said the motorcycle was sold "as is."
Gonzo wins, because the neighbor never entrusted the motorcycle to anyone.
Gonzo loses, because the nature of a sheriff's sale disclaims the title warranty.
Gonzo wins, because every seller warrants good title unless it uses specific disclaimer language.
oe: Used goods carry the title warranty. The result turns on the nature of the sale.
"As is" wouldn't exclude title anyway. Here the circumstances do.
Entrustment would matter in a contest between Gonzo and the neighbor. The question is whether the sheriff gave a title warranty.

Correct. The title warranty can be excluded "by circumstances which give the buyer reason to know that the person selling does not claim title in himself or that he is purporting to sell only such right or title as he or a third person may have" (§ 2-312(2)). Comment 5 lists sheriffs, executors, and foreclosing lienors. See Problem 5-5(b).
Specific language is one way to exclude the warranty. Circumstances are the other.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Sheriff's sale: title disclaimed by circumstances

q: Where does § 2A-528(1) measure market rent?
o: At the place for tender.
At the place of contracting.
Wherever the lessor picks.
At the lessor's headquarters.
At the place where the goods are located.
oe: That's the lessee's rule.
Where the lease was signed has no role in § 2A-528.
The statute fixes the place.
The statute doesn't mention headquarters; it looks to the goods.
Correct. Contrast the buyer's and lessee's place-for-tender rule. Accrued unpaid rent is added.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Market rent location

q: A contract says "Buyer shall be entitled to specific performance upon any breach." The goods are ordinary. What effect does the clause have?
o: It turns the buyer's claim into a right of replevin.
It excludes every other remedy, including damages.
It is useful evidence, but the court isn't bound by it.
It is void as against the public policy of the Code.
It binds the court, because parties may vary the Code by agreement.
oe: Replevin has its own elements, and identification and inability to cover aren't waived by a clause.
A remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive (§ 2-719(1)(b)).
Correct. Section 2-716(1) says "may," and the remedy stays with the court. Draft recitals explaining why cover is hard, and add a backup such as liquidated damages or a security interest.
Nothing voids it; it's helpful, and recitals explaining why cover is hard make it stronger.
Section 1-302 lets parties vary rules between themselves, not bind a court's discretion.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Clause granting specific performance

q: A complete and exclusive contract for monthly deliveries of printer toner says nothing about delivery time. For eight months, the seller always delivered before 9 a.m., and the buyer accepted without comment. In month nine, the seller delivers at 4 p.m. Can the buyer use the earlier pattern to show what the agreement requires?
o: Yes, but only if the pattern lasted at least a year.
Yes, because course of performance can supplement it.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
No, because course of performance requires prior contracts.
None of the above.
oe: Repeated occasions with acquiescence suffice; there's no time minimum.
Course of performance can still come in.
That's course of dealing.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Course of performance supplements

q: Buyer X rejects conforming goods with prompt notice. Buyer Y accepts conforming goods and later gives notice of revocation. Sellers sue. Which is correct?
o: Both owe the price.
Neither owes the price.
Both owe only incidental damages.
X owes the price; Y owes § 2-708 damages.
X's rejection is effective, so no price action lies; Y owes the price.
oe: X never accepted.
Y accepted, and its revocation failed.
Each owes more.
That's reversed.
Correct. A wrongful rejection blocks acceptance, so the seller usually gets § 2-708 damages. A wrongful revocation has no effect, so Y still owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)).
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Wrongful revocation vs. wrongful rejection

q: A non-consumer finance lessee signs an acceptance certificate on delivery, and only later finds defects. It stops paying rent. The lessor sues. Which is the lessor's strongest argument?
o: Acceptance made the promise irrevocable and independent.
The lessee must buy the goods.
The lessee waived all claims against the supplier.
The lessor gave a warranty that was met.
The lessee has no right of rejection in any case.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-407. The lessee must keep paying and pursue the supplier through § 2A-209.
There's no such duty.
It didn't.
It gave none.
It had that right before acceptance.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Acceptance certificate

q: Prairie Dawn buys an air conditioner. The owner's manual in the box, which she reads only after installation, says the unit "is free from defects in materials and workmanship for one year." Is this statement likely part of the basis of the bargain?
o: No, because she did not read it until after the sale.
No, because she didn't negotiate any of the manual's terms.
Likely not, because it promises future performance rather than describing the unit.
Yes, because manuals and package inserts can be warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Owner's manuals and package inserts can count even if read after the sale.
Negotiation isn't required.
Express warranties can promise future performance.
Correct. Compare Problem 3-7, where the owner's manual "free of defects for one year" was likely a warranty.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Owner's manual

q: After a badly impairing installment, which act does NOT reinstate an installment contract under § 2-612(3)?
o: Rejecting the nonconforming installment with a seasonable notice of cancellation.
Accepting the installment without seasonably notifying of cancellation.
Bringing an action only as to past installments.
Demanding performance of future installments.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Reinstatement comes from accepting a nonconforming installment without seasonably notifying of cancellation, suing only on past installments, or demanding future performance.
That reinstates.
That reinstates.
That reinstates.
The first choice names the act that does not reinstate.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Reinstating the contract

q: Which correctly states the seller's position on incidental and consequential damages?
o: Both are available to an aggrieved seller.
Incidental damages yes, even if huge; consequential damages no.
Consequential damages are available to merchants.
Neither is available to an aggrieved seller.
Incidental damages are capped at the contract price.
oe: Section 1-305(a) bars consequentials.
Correct. Section 2-710 and § 1-305(a); Validsa. Nature of the loss counts, not amount: storage costs reached $293 million in Commonwealth Edison.
Merchant status doesn't matter.
Section 2-710 gives incidentals.
There's no cap: Commonwealth Edison.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Incidental, no consequential

q: Ballistics keeps running the machine until September 1, while waiting for its replacement. Which is the best assessment of that use after revocation?
o: It automatically undoes the revocation.
It's allowed only for consumer buyers.
It's likely reasonable, with an offset for the use.
It's conversion as a matter of law.
It's free of charge, with no offset.
oe: Reasonable use doesn't undo it.
Johannsen isn't limited to consumers.
Correct. Use keeps production going and mitigates.
Johannsen makes reasonableness a fact question.
Expect an offset for the value of the use.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Use until replacement

q: In a typical finance lease, which is the correct picture of the parties?
o: The supplier leases directly to the lessee and also finances the deal.
The lessee sells its goods to the lessor and keeps them.
The lessor selects the goods and takes on all quality risk.
The lessee picks the goods; a financer buys and leases them.
The lessor manufactures the goods and leases them through a dealer.
oe: That's an ordinary lease with seller financing.
That's a sale-leaseback, a different structure.
Selecting the goods defeats finance-lease status.
Correct. In form the financer is a lessor; in substance it's a lender. It wants no responsibility for quality, and the lessee looks to the supplier. The purchase is an Article 2 sale.
A lessor that makes the goods can't be a finance lessor.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Finance lease concept

q: Which pairing is correct?
o: Replevin: identified goods not required; inability to cover required.
Replevin: identified goods required; prepayment generally not required.
Specific performance: identified goods required; prepayment not required.
Section 2-502: identified goods not required; prepayment required.
None of the above.
oe: Replevin requires identified goods.
Correct. Specific performance needs neither. Replevin needs identified goods but no prepayment (unless shipped under reservation). Section 2-502 needs both.
Specific performance doesn't require identified goods.
Section 2-502 needs both identification and prepayment.
One of the other choices is correct: Replevin: identified goods required; prepayment generally not required.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Remedy comparison grid

q: A signed written contract, intended as final, states a price of $12,000 for a delivery van. The buyer offers evidence that the day before signing, the seller orally agreed to $10,000. Is the evidence admissible to prove a $10,000 price?
o: Yes, because oral agreements control over printed forms.
Yes, if the writing is only a partial integration.
No, but only if the writing has a merger clause.
No, because it would contradict a final written term.
Yes, if the buyer proves the oral deal by clear and convincing evidence.
oe: No such rule.
Even a partial integration can't be contradicted.
No merger clause is needed to bar contradiction of a final term.
Correct. § 2-202 (first clause).
The rule bars the evidence regardless of its strength.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Contradictory prior term

q: A sales rep tells a building owner that a new HVAC unit "puts out 300,000 BTUs per hour" and that "you'll be very happy with it." The brochure, which the owner skimmed, says the unit runs "under 100 decibels." Which statements are likely express warranties?
o: None of them, because the owner didn't rely on any of them.
All three, because each was made to induce the sale.
Only "300,000 BTUs per hour," because the owner barely read the brochure.
The BTU and decibel statements, but not "very happy."
Only "you'll be very happy with it," because it's a promise.
oe: No particular reliance need be shown (§ 2-313 cmt. 3).
"You'll be very happy" is puffing.
Skimming the brochure doesn't take its specific statement out of the basis of the bargain.
Correct. Problem 3-7. Specific, measurable statements are warranties; "you'll be very happy" is puffing.
That is puffing.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — HVAC statements

q: Prairie Dawn buys a pair of everyday walking shoes from a shoe store. She tells the clerk only that she wants comfortable shoes for walking around town. After a week of ordinary walking, both soles split. What is her best warranty claim?
o: Breach of the implied warranty of fitness, because she told the clerk she would walk in them.
Breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
Breach of express warranty, because the store sold them as "shoes."
None, because a week of wear proves the shoes were merchantable when sold.
None, because she didn't rely on the clerk's skill in choosing them.
oe: Walking is the ordinary purpose of shoes, not a particular one (§ 2-315 cmt. 2). That falls under merchantability.
Correct. Goods sold by a merchant must be fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used (§ 2-314(2)(c)). Walking is the customary use of shoes.
The bare word "shoes" is a weak express-warranty theory. Merchantability squarely covers this defect.
Soles splitting after a week of ordinary use is evidence of a defect at the time of sale.
Reliance matters for fitness, not merchantability. Merchantability arises from the merchant's sale alone.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Ordinary purpose

q: Two merchants are drafting a sale contract. Which of the following Article 2 rules could they NOT change by agreement?
o: The court's power under § 2-302 to refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause.
The buyer's right under § 2-513 to inspect the goods before paying for them.
The time for payment under § 2-310, which ties payment to the buyer's receipt.
When the risk of loss passes from seller to buyer under § 2-509.
The place of delivery under § 2-308, which applies when the contract doesn't say where.
oe: Correct. Parties can't contract out of a court's power to police unconscionability. The other provisions are default rules that apply "unless otherwise agreed." See Problem 5-1(b).
Section 2-513(1) applies "unless otherwise agreed."
Section 2-310 applies "unless otherwise agreed."
Section 2-509(4) says its rules are subject to contrary agreement.
Section 2-308 applies "unless otherwise agreed."
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Which rule can't be varied by agreement

q: Must a lessor give notice before re-leasing after default?
o: No, but it should if the lease may be a disguised sale.
Yes, § 2A-527 requires it.
Yes, 30 days' notice in every case.
Never, in any case at all.
Yes, but only in consumer leases.
oe: Correct. See n.16.
Article 2A doesn't.
Article 2A sets no 30-day notice rule.
A disguised sale changes the analysis.
Article 2A's silence on notice applies to all leases, consumer or not.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Notice of disposition

q: Vega contracts to sell 1,000 bushels of Early Girl tomatoes to Marchetti, F.O.B. Vega's farm, ship by July 15. No trade usage or prior dealing bears on the point. Vega ships 990 bushels on July 14. May Marchetti reject the whole shipment?
o: Yes, because the tender failed in some respect to conform to the contract.
No, because Marchetti must accept the 990 and sue for the difference.
Yes, but only if Vega cannot cure within a further reasonable time.
No, because the F.O.B. term moved all risk of shortage onto Marchetti.
No, because a 1% shortfall is not a substantial impairment of the contract.
oe: Correct. Section 2-601 is a perfect tender rule: a failure "in any respect" allows rejection of the whole, subject to good faith, trade terms and § 2-612.
Section 2-601 gives the buyer the choice to reject the whole.
Cure limits the rejection after the fact; it isn't a precondition to the right to reject.
The F.O.B. term allocates risk of loss in transit, not the seller's duty to ship the full quantity.
Substantial impairment is the installment test (§ 2-612), and this is a single-delivery contract.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Perfect tender, minor shortfall

q: A contract for 500 bales of cotton says the price "will be set by an independent appraiser chosen by Buyer." After the seller delivers, the buyer refuses to choose an appraiser. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The seller must sue to force the buyer to choose an appraiser before it can be paid.
The price is the market price for cotton on the date the contract was made.
The buyer may set any price it chooses, because it controlled the choice of appraiser.
There's no contract, because the price was never fixed by the appraiser.
The seller may treat the contract as canceled or fix a reasonable price.
oe: Article 2 gives the seller self-help options instead.
Nothing in § 2-305 uses the date of contracting.
The buyer is the party at fault and gets no such power.
Section 2-305(3) gives the innocent party options precisely because the failure was the other party's fault.

Correct. "When a price left to be fixed otherwise than by agreement of the parties fails to be fixed through fault of one party the other may at his option treat the contract as cancelled or himself fix a reasonable price" (§ 2-305(3)). See Problem 4-3(c).
topic: Wk 3 · VII · Quantity & price — Price fixed by the buyer; buyer won't act

q: Beaker, a lab-supply merchant, signs a quote form supplied by the buyer, Bunsen. A printed line on Bunsen's form, above Beaker's only signature, says the quote "will be held open for 60 days." Two weeks later, before Bunsen accepts, Beaker revokes. Was the revocation effective?
o: No, because a merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for the stated time, without any need for consideration.
No, because Bunsen relied on the quote.
No, because 60 days is within the three-month limit.
Yes, because Bunsen gave no consideration to keep the offer open, so it was an ordinary revocable offer.
Yes, because the assurance was on a form the offeree supplied and Beaker did not separately sign it.
oe: That is the general rule, but it has an exception for assurances on the offeree's form.
Nothing shows reliance, and a firm offer doesn't depend on it anyway.
The cap matters only if the firm offer is otherwise valid.
A merchant's firm offer needs no consideration. The problem is the missing separate signature.
Correct. § 2-205: an assurance on a form supplied by the offeree must be separately signed by the offeror.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Firm offer on offeree's form

q: Elmo buys a car from Grover's Autorama, a car dealership. Elmo pays in full and receives all the title documents, but leaves the car on the lot, saying he'll pick it up Monday. Over the weekend the lot floods and the car is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: Grover's Autorama, but only if Elmo had not yet paid.
Elmo, because he had all the documents he needed to take possession.
Grover's Autorama, because Elmo had not yet received the car.
Elmo, because he had paid the full price for the car.
None of the above.
oe: The result is the same whether or not Elmo paid.
That isn't the test for a merchant seller.
Correct. § 2-509(3). A merchant seller still controls the goods and can insure them (cmt. 3).
Payment doesn't shift the risk.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Merchant seller: buyer paid

q: In a regional livestock-auction trade, it is a long-standing and regularly observed practice that cattle sold at the ring carry no warranty against disease unless the auctioneer announces one. Rowlf, a rancher in that trade, buys cattle at auction. No warranty is announced and nothing is in writing. Several cattle turn out to have been sick at the time of sale. Can the seller rely on the trade usage to defeat Rowlf's merchantability claim?
o: No, because trade usage can supplement a contract but never take away rights.
No, because a merchantability disclaimer must mention merchantability.
Yes, because an implied warranty can be excluded or modified by usage of trade.
No, because any exclusion of an implied warranty must be in writing and conspicuous.
Yes, but only if Rowlf actually knew of the usage.
oe: Section 2-316(3)(c) expressly permits exclusion by trade usage.
Section 2-316(2) is subject to § 2-316(3), which supplies alternative ways to exclude, including trade usage.
Correct. Section 2-316(3)(c) lets an implied warranty be excluded or modified by course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade, with no writing or particular words.
That's required only of a written merchantability disclaimer and of a fitness disclaimer, not of exclusion by trade usage.
A usage binds parties in the trade if they are or should be aware of it (§ 1-303(d)).
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Usage of trade excludes warranties

q: A buyer repudiates a contract in a way that substantially impairs its value to the seller. Which of the following may the seller do?
o: Resort immediately to any remedy for breach.
Urge the buyer to retract while awaiting performance.
Await the buyer's performance for a commercially reasonable time.
Suspend its own performance.
All of the above.
oe: It may, without losing its other options (§ 2-610(b)).
Correct. § 2-610 lets the aggrieved party suspend its performance and either await performance for a commercially reasonable time or resort to remedies, even after urging retraction.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Options after repudiation

q: After a seller properly demands assurance in writing, the buyer promptly sends audited financial statements and a letter from its bank confirming a healthy credit line. The seller insists on an irrevocable letter of credit for the full contract amount and keeps suspending shipments when the buyer won't provide one. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller is protected, because a letter of credit is the only acceptable assurance of payment.
The seller is protected, because the party demanding assurance decides what is adequate.
The buyer is in breach, because it refused to provide the letter of credit that was demanded.
Neither party is in breach, because the contract is suspended until they agree.
The seller is likely in breach, because the buyer's assurance was adequate.
oe: Many forms of assurance can be adequate, including proof of solvency and available credit.
Adequacy is an objective commercial question, not the demanding party's choice.
Refusing an excessive demand isn't a repudiation once adequate assurance has been given.
Suspension lasts only until adequate assurance is received.

Correct. What counts as adequate assurance is judged by commercial standards (§ 2-609(2)). Once adequate assurance is given, the right to suspend ends. Demanding more than is adequate and continuing to withhold performance can itself be a repudiation. See Problem 6-3(b).
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Adequate assurance given; seller over-demands

q: A buyer of a hidden-defect machine asks how long it has to revoke. Which is correct?
o: A reasonable time after it discovers or should have discovered the ground.
Any time before the buyer files suit.
Ten days after the buyer discovers the defect.
Four years after tender of the goods.
A reasonable time after tender, and before it pays.
oe: Correct. Section 2-608(2). Comment 4 suggests it is apparently longer than rejection.
The reasonable-time limit still applies.
There's no fixed ten-day limit.
That's the limitations period.
That's closer to rejection.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Timing of revocation

q: A seller that did not resell claims § 2-708(1) damages. Which market price is used?
o: The price when the contract was made.
The price at wherever the buyer is located.
The price on the date of any later resale.
The price when the seller learned of the breach.
The price at the time and place for tender.
oe: The contract date isn't used; a fixed price already reflects that market.
Only if that is the place for tender.
A later resale has its own measure in § 2-706; § 2-708(1) looks to tender.
That resembles the buyer's rule; the seller's is tender.
Correct. Unpaid contract price minus market price, plus incidental, minus saved. Unlike § 2-713, it isn't measured when the party learned of the breach. Section 2-723(1) is an exception.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Seller market formula

q: A bank is a true finance lessor of a generator to a business lessee. It says nothing about quality. The generator is unfit. Which claim does the lessee have against the bank?
o: A statutory claim for a refund under § 2A-407.
Fitness, since it knew the lessee's purpose.
Merchantability, since a bank regularly leases equipment.
None for merchantability or fitness.
Both implied warranties, unless disclaimed in writing.
oe: Section 2A-407 runs against the lessee.
Section 2A-213 has the same carve-out.
Section 2A-212 carves out finance leases.
Correct. Sections 2A-212, 2A-213. A finance lessor may give express warranties but rarely does.
There's nothing to disclaim.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — No implied warranties

q: Under § 1-201(b)(10), which of the following would NOT ordinarily make a disclaimer conspicuous?
o: Body text in larger type than the surrounding text.
Placing it just above the signature line, in the same type as everything else.
Body text set off from the surrounding text by symbols or other marks that call attention to it.
Body text in a contrasting color from the surrounding text.
A heading in capital letters in a larger type than the surrounding text of the same or lesser size.
oe: This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
Correct. Location near the signature, without any difference in type or other attention-getting feature, isn't one of the statute's examples, and a reasonable person might not notice it.
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(B)).
This is a statutory example (§ 1-201(b)(10)(A)).
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Conspicuous: which does NOT qualify

q: Goods are destroyed in transit under a shipment contract. In a second deal, under a destination contract, fungible goods are destroyed in transit. What must each buyer or seller do?
o: Both buyers must sue their own sellers first.
The first buyer pays and claims against the carrier; the second seller must retender.
Both buyers may refuse to pay.
Both sellers are excused under § 2-613.
The first seller must retender; the second buyer must pay.
oe: Recourse is against the carrier in the first deal.

Correct. A buyer bearing transit risk still pays, then pursues the carrier (§ 2-722, § 7-309) or its insurer. Under a destination contract the seller must timely tender substitute fungible goods or be in breach.
The first buyer bears the risk.
These goods weren't identified at contracting, and risk rules apply.
That's reversed.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Buyer's recourse for transit loss

q: While negotiating to buy a used tractor from Fozzie, Gonzo realizes from Fozzie's asking price that Fozzie doesn't know the tractor's rare engine makes it worth far more. Gonzo says nothing and buys at Fozzie's price. Fozzie later claims Gonzo breached the duty of good faith. What result?
o: Gonzo wins, but only if Gonzo is a merchant.
Fozzie wins, because the tractor's true value made the price unconscionable.
Fozzie wins, because Gonzo had a duty to disclose every material fact.
Fozzie wins, because Gonzo exploited superior knowledge.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter here.
A bargain price freely set by the seller isn't unconscionable.
There's no general duty to disclose in negotiation.
Exploiting superior knowledge before contracting is allowed (Market Street).

Correct. Gonzo wins: the § 1-304 duty of good faith covers performance and enforcement, not negotiation, and Market Street allows a party to use superior knowledge before contracting. No choice says that.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith before contracting

q: Under an installment contract, a buyer may reject one nonconforming installment if:
o: the buyer can show a fall in the market price.
it fails to conform in any respect.
the seller has failed to give 30 days' written notice.
It substantially impairs that installment and can't be cured.
it substantially impairs the value of the whole contract.
oe: A market shift isn't a ground.
That's the single-delivery perfect tender rule in § 2-601.
No such notice rule exists.
Correct. Section 2-612(2). A defect in required documents also qualifies. Assurance of cure otherwise obliges the buyer to accept.
That's the test for cancelling the whole under § 2-612(3).
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Rejecting an installment

q: The buyer claims the seller fraudulently induced the contract by lying about the goods. The writing is complete and exclusive. Can the buyer introduce evidence of the fraud?
o: Yes, unless the writing contains a merger clause.
No, unless the misrepresentation itself was made in writing.
Yes, because the rule does not bar evidence of fraud.
No, because the writing is a complete and exclusive statement of the terms.
None of the above.
oe: A merger clause doesn't bar fraud evidence.
Fraud is usually oral, and the PER doesn't bar evidence of it.
Correct.
The PER does not bar evidence of fraud.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Fraud

q: Herry buys a ladder from a hardware store and lends it to a coworker, who uses it at the coworker's own home. The ladder collapses and injures the coworker. Under which § 2-318 alternative can the coworker sue the store for breach of warranty?
o: Alternative A only.
Alternative B only.
Alternatives B and C, but not A.
All three alternatives.
None of them, because the coworker isn't in privity with the store.
oe: Alternative A covers only the buyer's family, household, and guests in the buyer's home.
B covers the coworker, but so does C.

Correct. B covers any natural person who may reasonably be expected to use the goods and is injured in person; C covers any person reasonably expected to be affected who is injured. A doesn't reach a coworker at the coworker's home.
A doesn't cover the coworker.
§ 2-318 extends warranties beyond the buyer.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Privity: borrowed ladder

q: Seller sends Buyer a proposal (the offer). Buyer responds with a purchase order whose boilerplate says acceptance is "expressly limited to such terms" as appear in the purchase order. The forms differ on several terms. Under Daitom v. Pennwalt, is Buyer's purchase order an acceptance?
o: Yes, because that boilerplate does not make acceptance expressly conditional.
No, because it varies the offer's terms, so it is a counteroffer.
No, because it is expressly conditional on Seller's assent to Buyer's terms.
Yes, and Buyer's terms control because Buyer sent the last form.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Daitom (following Dorton) treated the purchase order as a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance under § 2-207(1).
§ 2-207(1) abolishes the mirror-image rule for sales of goods.
Daitom held that language like "expressly limited to such terms" is not enough. The offeree must clearly show it is unwilling to proceed unless its terms are accepted.
§ 2-207 also abolishes the "last shot" rule.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Daitom: expressly conditional

q: On May 1, a seller delivers 50 industrial fans to a buyer. Delivery wasn't due until May 20. The fans are wired for 220 volts instead of the 110 volts the contract requires, which the seller could easily fix. The buyer emails, "We reject the fans as nonconforming," without saying why. On May 25, the buyer sues for breach. Can the buyer rely on the wiring defect?
o: Yes, because the buyer gave the seller timely notice that it was rejecting the fans.
Yes, because the seller should have inspected the fans before delivering them.
No, because a wiring problem doesn't substantially impair the value of the fans.
No, because the buyer didn't state a defect the seller could have cured in time.
Yes, because under the perfect tender rule a buyer may reject for any defect at all.
oe: Notice of rejection is necessary but not sufficient. The defect must be stated when the seller could cure it.
The seller's diligence doesn't excuse the buyer's failure to particularize.
Substantial impairment matters for installments and revocation, not a single-delivery rejection. The buyer's problem is § 2-605.

Correct. A buyer's failure to state in connection with rejection a particular defect that is ascertainable by reasonable inspection bars reliance on it "where the seller could have cured it if stated seasonably" (§ 2-605(1)(a)). With time left before May 20, cure was possible (§ 2-508(1)).
Perfect tender is subject to the seller's right to cure and to the duty to particularize.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Failure to particularize a curable defect

q: At a yard sale, Bert tells a shopper that a used espresso machine "works great. I used it this morning." The shopper pays $60, and the machine fails the first time the shopper uses it. Did Bert make an express warranty?
o: No, because Bert is not a merchant.
Probably yes, because it states a fact about the machine's present condition.
Yes, because every statement a seller makes about the goods during the sale is an express warranty.
Yes, but only the implied warranty of merchantability.
No, because the sale was under $500.
oe: Any seller can make an express warranty.
Correct. Statements of present working condition are close calls from a casual seller (Petti), but "I used it this morning" makes this one specific and factual.
Opinion, commendation, and value statements aren't.
Bert isn't a merchant, and the question is about an express warranty.
The price affects the statute of frauds, not warranties.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Casual seller's statement

q: Before choosing a buyer's remedy, which question should come first?
o: Whether the buyer has already bought substitute goods.
Whether the buyer has paid any part of the purchase price.
What the contract's terms are and who breached.
Whether the seller acted in bad faith in failing to perform.
Whether the goods are unique or otherwise hard to replace.
oe: Cover matters only after a seller's breach is established, so it can't come first.
Payment matters to §§ 2-502 and 2-711(1), not to whether anyone breached.

Correct. Run the thresholds in order: the terms (agreement plus course of performance, dealing, usage and gap fillers), who breached, whether the failure is excused, and whether remedies are limited. Only then do the type of breach and the location of the goods pick the remedy.
Breach doesn't depend on motive; Article 2 doesn't treat breach as a moral wrong.
Uniqueness matters only to specific performance, well down the road.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Threshold order

q: A lessor repossesses and sells a machine without notifying the lessee. A court later holds the "lease" a security agreement. What is the risk?
o: Sections 2-706(3) and 9-611 may apply, so the sale may be defective.
There's none, as Article 2A needs no notice.
The lessee automatically owes more.
The buyer of the machine loses it.
The lessor loses title to all its leases.
oe: Correct. That's why the text advises giving notice anyway (n.16).
That's true only for a true lease.
The risk runs against the lessor.
Good-faith purchasers are generally protected.
The point is narrower.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Lessor's notice and disguised sale

q: Worried about a buyer's finances, a seller phones the buyer's purchasing manager, says it needs assurances, and stops shipping. The buyer doesn't respond. Three weeks later, the seller cancels the contract. The buyer sues. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer wins only if it can prove that it was solvent the whole time.
The seller is in a weak position, because the demand should have been made in a record.
The seller is protected, because three weeks is a reasonable time to respond to a demand.
The seller is protected, because the buyer failed to respond within a reasonable time.
The seller is protected, because reasonable grounds for insecurity justify cancellation.
oe: The seller's own procedural failure is the main problem, whatever the buyer's finances.

Correct. Section 2-609(1) lets a party with reasonable grounds "demand in a record" (in writing) adequate assurance. Some courts excuse an informal demand when it is clear, but a phone call followed by quick cancellation is risky, and the seller may itself be the breaching party.
The timing rule applies only after a proper demand.
Treating silence as repudiation depends on a justified demand made the way § 2-609 requires.
Reasonable grounds justify a demand and suspension, not immediate cancellation.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Demand made only by phone

q: A music store's invoice to Floyd describes a guitar as "1959 Gibson Les Paul Standard, original finish." The store honestly believed that was true. A year later, an appraiser shows it's a 1974 reissue. The store argues it made no warranty because (1) it never used the word "warrant" or "guarantee," and (2) it honestly believed the description. Which statement is correct?
