o: Argument (2) works, because an honest mistake about the goods isn't a breach of warranty.
Neither works, but Floyd must still prove that he relied on the invoice in deciding to buy.
Argument (1) works, because express warranties require formal words such as "warrant."
Neither works, because a description that is part of the bargain is a warranty either way.
Both arguments work, so Floyd's only remedy is a claim for fraud or misrepresentation.
oe: Warranty is strict liability. The seller's good faith is irrelevant.
Comment 3 to § 2-313 says no particular reliance need be shown for affirmations made during the bargain.
Section 2-313(2) says the opposite: no formal words are necessary.

Correct. A description of the goods creates an express warranty that the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(b)). No formal words like "warrant" or "guarantee" are needed, and the seller need not intend to make a warranty (§ 2-313(2)). Warranty liability doesn't depend on fault.
Neither argument works, and Floyd doesn't have to prove fraud.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Description; seller's good faith

q: A lessee wants to protect its supplier warranties from later changes by the lessor and supplier. Which step works best?
o: Sign the supply contract too.
Pay rent early.
Make sure the supplier receives notice of the finance lease.
Record the lease in the county.
Obtain a hell-or-high-water clause.
oe: Notice is enough.
That has no effect.
Correct. Section 2A-209(3): after notice, a modification doesn't bind the lessee.
Recording isn't the mechanism.
That favors the lessor.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Notice of finance lease

q: A dealer sold a car with a hidden frame defect. The buyer drove it for ten months, and then a mechanic discovered it, making the car unsafe. A week later the buyer notifies the dealer that she is revoking. Which is correct?
o: She may revoke only if the dealer agrees.
She can't, as she drove the car for ten months.
She can't, as revocation must come within ten days of delivery.
She may revoke, as the defect was hard to discover and she acted promptly.
She may reject the car under § 2-601.
oe: It's a notice remedy.
Use before discovery doesn't defeat revocation.
There's no fixed period.
Correct. Section 2-608(1)(b) and (2): a reasonable time runs from discovery, and the car hasn't changed apart from the defect.
Rejection ended on acceptance.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Rejection window closed, revocation open

q: A buyer's purchase order says "F.O.B. Buyer's warehouse." The seller's acknowledgment, a definite acceptance, says "F.O.B. Seller's plant." Both are merchants, and neither objects. The goods are destroyed in transit. Under the knockout rule applied in Daitom, which statement is correct?
o: The loss is split, because neither form controls.
The seller bears the loss, because the acceptance's different term is a proposal the buyer never accepted.
The buyer bears the loss, because both terms drop out and the default is a shipment contract.
The seller bears the loss, because the offer's term controls.
None of the above.
oe: The gap filler, not a split, fills the hole the conflicting terms leave.
Some courts treat different terms that way, but the question asks about the knockout rule.
Correct. The different terms cancel (cmt. 6), the gap filler applies, and a contract is presumed to be a shipment contract, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).
Under the knockout rule, neither form's term controls.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Knockout: shipping terms

q: Kermit's grain sits in a public warehouse. Kermit sells it to Fozzie and, that morning, hands Fozzie a non-negotiable warehouse receipt. The warehouse hasn't been notified. That afternoon, the warehouse burns. Who most likely bears the loss?
o: Fozzie, because Fozzie received a document of title.
Fozzie, because the grain was identified to the contract.
Kermit, because risk doesn't pass until Fozzie has had a reasonable time to present the document.
The warehouse, because it's a bailee.
Kermit, because title never passes while goods are in a warehouse.
oe: A non-negotiable document doesn't pass risk immediately.
Identification doesn't pass risk.
The question is which party bears risk.
Title can pass, and risk isn't tied to title anyway.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Bailee: non-negotiable document

q: Which of the following is required to bind a party to a usage of trade?
o: Regular observance in the trade, plus notice to the party.
The parties must have used the practice in prior contracts with each other.
The usage must be followed universally across the industry.
The party must have expressly agreed to the usage in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 1-303(c) and (g). The usage must be regularly observed in the place or trade so as to justify an expectation it will be observed, and the party must have notice of it (or be in that trade).
That describes course of dealing.
It need only be regularly observed in the place, vocation, or trade.
No express agreement is needed.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Usage of trade

q: Snuffy's Fencing receives a shipment of fence posts that fully conform to the contract. Having found a cheaper supplier, Snuffy's Fencing promptly notifies the seller that it rejects them. What is the effect?
o: The rejection is rightful, because a buyer may reject for any reason before acceptance.
It's effective but wrongful, so Snuffy's Fencing is in breach.
The rejection is rightful unless the seller can show bad faith.
The rejection is ineffective, so Snuffy's Fencing has accepted the posts.
None of the above.
oe: Only nonconforming goods may be rightfully rejected.
Correct. Rejecting conforming goods can be effective but wrongful, which is a buyer's breach (§ 2-703).
The posts conform, so the rejection is wrongful regardless.
A timely, properly notified rejection is effective even if wrongful.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Wrongful but effective rejection

q: A contract says: "Seller's sole liability for defective goods is to repair or replace them." The buyer argues that the clause is ineffective because it is not conspicuous and doesn't mention merchantability. What is the best response?
o: The clause is a remedy limitation under § 2-719, not a disclaimer, so it needn't be conspicuous or mention merchantability.
The clause is void, because parties can't limit remedies for breach of warranty.
The buyer is right, because every limit on warranty liability must satisfy § 2-316.
The clause disclaims all implied warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer removes the breach; a limitation caps damages after a breach. Remedy limits needn't be conspicuous.
§ 2-719 allows it.
§ 2-316 governs disclaimers, not remedy limits.
It limits the remedy; it doesn't disclaim warranties.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer vs. remedy limitation

q: A lost-volume lessor proves § 2A-528(2) applies. Which statement about the measure is correct?
o: It gets consequential damages.
It recovers full rent and also sells the goods.
It must give up the residual.
It's limited to market rent.
It's the PV of profit, and the lessor keeps its residual.
oe: Lessors don't.
That would overcompensate.
It keeps it.
That measure is inadequate here.
Correct. It gets the profit, with reasonable overhead, plus incidentals, and due allowance for costs reasonably incurred. The goods come back.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Lost-profit lessor, retained residual

q: A used-equipment dealer sells Gordon a 12-year-old lawn tractor for a low price. Two days later, the engine seizes during ordinary mowing. The contract has no disclaimer. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No implied warranty arises, because the tractor was sold used.
The dealer warranted that the tractor would perform as well as a new one.
The warranty applies only if the dealer knew the engine was about to fail.
No implied warranty arises, because the price was low.
The merchantability warranty applies but is measured by what's appropriate for a tractor of that age and price, and an engine that seizes in two days may still breach it.
oe: Used goods sold by a merchant still carry the warranty, though its content is reduced.
The warranty for used goods is reduced; the buyer can't expect new-goods quality.
Implied warranties are strict; the seller's knowledge of the defect is irrelevant.
Price is evidence of the quality promised, but a low price doesn't eliminate the warranty.

Correct. A merchant's sale of used goods carries a merchantability warranty with a reduced content appropriate to second-hand goods (§ 2-314 cmt. 3). Even a cheap old tractor should run for more than two days.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Used goods: reduced warranty

q: Do goods have to exist or be identified at the time of breach to be resold under § 2-706?
o: Yes, they must be identified before the breach.
No, but the seller must buy new goods to resell.
Yes, they must exist at the time of the breach.
No, and § 2-704(1) lets the seller identify them after breach.
No, but only for consumer goods.
oe: Section 2-706(2) says otherwise.
That isn't a requirement.
Section 2-706(2) says otherwise.
Correct. Section 2-706(2). With fungible goods, proving which sale replaced the contract can be hard.
Section 2-706(2) applies to all goods, not just consumer goods.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale of unidentified goods

q: Tala orders three identical drill presses for her shop. One arrives with a bent spindle, which she sees on unpacking. She keeps two, and the next day she writes the seller, "I reject the one with the bent spindle. Come get it." Which is correct?
o: Proper, as she may accept commercial units and reject the rest.
Proper, but only if the seller agrees in writing.
Improper, as she has accepted all three by unpacking them.
Improper, as she must reject all or none under one contract.
Improper, unless the defect substantially impairs the press.
oe: Correct. Section 2-601(c), assuming each press is a commercial unit. The next-day notice is seasonable, and a stated defect meets § 2-605.
No agreement is needed.
Unpacking to inspect isn't acceptance.
Section 2-601 allows partial acceptance.
Any nonconformity will do for a single-delivery contract.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Reject one, keep two

q: Hale Printing contracts for a press that Dunmore Machine will build to Hale's unique specifications. Only Dunmore can make it in under a year. The half-built press sits in Dunmore's shop, not yet marked for anyone, when Dunmore repudiates because a richer customer wants the shop time. Hale has paid nothing. What is Hale's best route to the press?
o: Damages only, because a court won't order a manufacturer to finish work.
Replevin, because the press is being built specifically for Hale.
Section 2-502, because Dunmore repudiated before finishing the press.
Self-help, because a buyer may collect goods made to its specifications.
Specific performance, because it can't cover and no identification is needed.
oe: Supervision concerns weigh against an order, but they don't bar one, and the inability to cover is strong.
Replevin needs goods identified to the contract. Nothing marked or designated this press yet, though Hale could argue identification.
Hale paid nothing, and this isn't a consumer purchase.
The buyer's routes to the goods all need a court order.
Correct. Section 2-716(1) doesn't require identified goods. The inability to get the goods elsewhere in time is the classic "other proper circumstance." The remedy is still discretionary.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Custom press, buyer can't cover

q: A signed writing is a complete and exclusive statement of the terms. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement adding a consistent term. Is it admissible?
o: No, unless the buyer is a consumer who didn't read it.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Yes, because the term doesn't contradict the writing.
Yes, if the buyer proves it by clear and convincing evidence.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer's status doesn't matter.
Correct. § 2-202(b).
Not when the writing is complete and exclusive.
The PER bars it regardless.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Complete integration

q: A seller of custom brackets sells on 15-day credit terms. It learns that the buyer's credit rating has dropped and that the buyer is paying other vendors slowly, though the buyer isn't insolvent. Which response best protects the seller without risking its own breach?
o: Stop all deliveries without explanation until the buyer's rating improves.
Cancel the contract and resell the brackets.
Send a written demand for adequate assurance, offering several acceptable forms, and suspend if commercially reasonable until it arrives.
Announce that all future deliveries will be cash on delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Suspending without a written demand risks breach.
No repudiation has occurred yet.
Correct. Problem 6-3: use § 2-609, list the grounds, offer options, and set a deadline within 30 days.
Only an insolvent buyer can be put on cash terms (§ 2-702(1)); changing credit terms unilaterally risks repudiation.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Responding to a shaky buyer

q: Which of the following is NOT required for a firm offer under § 2-205?
o: The offeree is a merchant.
The offer is in a signed record.
If the assurance is on a form supplied by the offeree, the offeror separately signs it.
The offer by its terms gives assurance that it will be held open.
The offeror is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Only the offeror must be a merchant. The offeree can be anyone.
Required.
Required in that situation (§ 2-205).
Required.
Required. § 2-205 applies only to "an offer by a merchant."
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Firm offer: who must be a merchant

q: A seller has half-finished 50 custom cabinets when the buyer repudiates. Finishing costs $10,000, and the finished cabinets would fetch $60,000 from another buyer. Unfinished, they'd bring $8,000 as scrap. The contract price was $90,000. Which step is most defensible?
o: Finish, and sue for the $90,000 price.
Abandon the goods and sue for lost profit only.
Finish, and claim $10,000 as a consequential damage.
Stop at once and sell for scrap at $8,000.
Finish, resell for $60,000, and claim $30,000 plus incidentals.
oe: The goods can be resold, so no price action.
It has a better route.
The cost is reflected in the loss, and sellers get no consequentials.
That needlessly increases the loss.
Correct. Reasonable commercial judgment under § 2-704(2): spending $10,000 to raise proceeds by $52,000 avoids loss. Section 2-706 gives contract minus resale.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Seller's mix of remedies

q: Under § 2-301, which is the seller's basic obligation?
o: To install and service the goods after they are delivered.
To accept the goods and pay according to the contract.
To transfer and deliver the goods in accordance with the contract.
To deliver goods free of any defect, whatever the contract says.
To pass title to the buyer before the price is paid.
oe: Those duties exist only if the contract adds them.
That is the buyer's half of § 2-301.
Correct. Section 2-301 also states the buyer's basic obligation: to accept and pay in accordance with the contract.
The measure is conformity to the contract, which may tolerate imperfections.
When title passes depends on § 2-401 and the agreement, not § 2-301.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Basic seller duty

q: A sunroof leaks repeatedly despite four repair visits. Fixing it requires sawing off the roof. Which is correct?
o: A leak is minor as a matter of law.
Only a tort claim remains after failed repairs.
The buyer must allow the roof repair, since it's free.
Each failure strengthens substantial impairment.
The earlier repairs waived the right to revoke.
oe: Repeated leaks aren't minor.
Contract remedies remain.
A major repair needn't be accepted.
Correct. Problem 7-26(D).
Allowing repairs doesn't waive it.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Each failed repair

q: A shipment contract for 1,000 pounds of coffee says nothing about when payment is due. The seller ships and demands payment the moment the coffee is handed to the carrier. Unless the parties agree otherwise, when must the buyer pay?
o: Whenever the seller reasonably demands.
Within 30 days of the invoice date.
When the seller hands the coffee to the carrier.
When and where the buyer receives the coffee.
Before the seller ships.
oe: No such rule.
The Code presumes no credit.
That's when risk passes in a shipment contract, not when payment is due.
Correct. § 2-310(a), even when the seller is authorized to ship.
Not the default.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — When payment is due

q: After acceptance, a non-consumer finance lessee's goods are destroyed by a flood. The lease says nothing about risk. Must it keep paying rent?
o: Yes, but at half rent.
Yes, as risk passed to it and its promise is irrevocable.
No, as a casualty ends the lease.
No, as the lessor bears the risk.
No, unless the lessor insured the goods.
oe: There's no such reduction.
Correct. Sections 2A-219(1) and 2A-407.
Section 2A-221 applies before risk passes.
Not in a finance lease.
Insurance isn't the test.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Risk in finance lease

q: A contract for a commercial espresso machine says: "Seller will repair or replace any defective component within one year." Nothing else in the contract addresses remedies. The machine's boiler is defective. Instead of a repair, the buyer sues for damages. May it do so?
o: No, unless the seller has first refused to repair the boiler.
Yes, because the remedy wasn't expressly made exclusive.
No, because a repair-or-replace clause is always the buyer's sole remedy.
No, because a remedy limitation need not be conspicuous to be enforced.
Yes, but only for consequential damages, not direct damages.
oe: Refusal matters to failure of essential purpose. Here the agreed remedy was never exclusive in the first place.

Correct. Resort to a remedy provided in the contract is optional unless the remedy is expressly agreed to be exclusive, in which case it is the sole remedy (§ 2-719(1)(b)). Exclusivity must be clearly expressed (cmt. 2).
Only an expressly exclusive remedy is the sole remedy.
True that conspicuousness isn't required, but the clause still had to be expressly exclusive to bar other remedies.
The buyer has its full range of Article 2 remedies, direct and consequential.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Remedy not expressly exclusive

q: In January, a lumber mill agrees to sell Big Bird's Builders 50 truckloads a month for the year at $300 a load, a price set when the market was weak. By June, a housing boom has pushed market prices to $500, and the mill is losing money on every load. The mill tells Big Bird it will stop shipping entirely unless Big Bird agrees to $450. Unable to find lumber elsewhere, Big Bird signs the new price, then later sues to recover the difference. What is the most likely result?
o: The mill wins, because a modification needs no consideration.
Big Bird wins, because the mill gave no new consideration.
Big Bird wins, because price increases are never valid modifications.
The mill wins, because the market shift gave it a legitimate commercial reason to ask for more, so it acted in good faith.
Big Bird wins, because the mill got the increase by threatening to breach, which is not honesty in fact.
oe: True (§ 2-209(1)), but a modification must still be sought in good faith.
§ 2-209(1) abolishes the consideration requirement.
They can be, if sought in good faith.
That satisfies only the objective part of good faith.
Correct. Like Sharon Steel in Roth Steel, the mill had an objective reason, but extracting the change with a threat to stop performing is bad faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification extracted by threat

q: Grover and a supplier trade a draft contract marked "DRAFT: FOR DISCUSSION," with blanks for price and delivery date. Neither signs it. In a later dispute, the supplier argues that the draft bars evidence of their earlier discussions. Is the supplier right?
o: Yes, because Grover had a chance to object to the draft.
No, because a draft isn't a final expression.
Yes, because the draft is a written record of the deal.
No, because unsigned writings are always inadmissible.
None of the above.
oe: The question is whether it was intended as final.
Correct. An unfinished draft is outside § 2-202.
It's not a final expression.
The draft may be admissible as evidence; it just doesn't trigger the parol evidence rule.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Draft writing

q: Ernie buys a used tandem bicycle at a garage sale run by Bert, who had bought it in good faith from a stranger. It turns out the stranger stole it, and the true owner takes it back from Ernie. Ernie sues Bert. What is the most likely result?
o: Bert wins, because he sold the bike in good faith without knowing it had been stolen.
Ernie wins, but only if he can show that Bert should have known the bike was stolen.
Bert wins, because he isn't a merchant and was only selling his own used things.
Bert wins, because by custom everything at a garage sale is sold "as is."
Ernie wins, because every seller warrants good title, whatever it knew.
oe: Warranty liability doesn't depend on knowledge or fault.
No such showing is needed.
The title warranty isn't limited to merchants.
"As is" doesn't exclude the title warranty. Only specific language or circumstances showing the seller doesn't claim title can (§ 2-312(2)).
Correct. Section 2-312(1) applies to every seller, merchant or not. The warranty is breached when the buyer doesn't get good title, and the seller's good faith is no defense.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Good-faith seller still breaches title warranty

q: Under a contract for monthly parts, Load 3 is 20% defective. The seller says it can't replace them for six weeks. The buyer's line needs them this week, as the seller knows. May the buyer reject Load 3?
o: Yes, because known needs make the impairment substantial and cure too late.
No, because an installment can never be rejected.
Yes, and it may also cancel the whole contract automatically.
No, because the seller's promise of cure obliges the buyer to accept.
Yes, because any defect in an installment allows rejection.
oe: Correct. Section 2-612(2) tests that installment against normal and specifically known purposes (cmt. 4). A six-week cure gives no adequate assurance here.
It can if the test is met.
Cancelling the whole has its own test in § 2-612(3).
The assurance must be adequate; six weeks doesn't meet the known need.
Substantial impairment is required.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Assurance and substantial impairment

q: A lessee defaults and the lessor repossesses. It then sues for all the remaining rent under § 2A-529. What is the problem?
o: A lessor can never recover rent.
It must first give notice of disposition.
It must show the lessee is insolvent.
Rent isn't available for goods repossessed or tendered back.
It must first prove lost volume.
oe: It can in some cases.
Article 2A doesn't require that.
Insolvency isn't an element.
Correct. Section 2A-529(1)(a). It's limited to § 2A-527 or § 2A-528 damages (and lost profit if lost volume).
That's a different route.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Rent after repossession

q: Fozzie buys a used food truck from a dealer. When Fozzie picks it up two days after signing, the dealer says, "By the way, the engine was rebuilt last year." It wasn't. How strong is Fozzie's claim that the statement was an express warranty?
o: Weak, because the statement came after the contract and Fozzie gave nothing new for it.
Strong, but only if the dealer knew the statement was false.
Strong, because a post-sale statement can be a warranty without new consideration.
Weak, because Fozzie couldn't have relied on it when deciding to buy.
Weak, because oral statements can't be express warranties.
oe: Consideration isn't needed for a modification (§ 2-209(1)).
Warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
Correct. § 2-313 cmt. 7.
Cmt. 7 lets a post-sale statement become part of the deal.
They can.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Statement at delivery

q: Statler sells 200 theater seats to Waldorf, "F.O.B. Statler's factory." Statler properly packs the seats, hands them to a carrier, and makes a reasonable shipping contract, but forgets to tell Waldorf the seats have shipped. An hour into the trip, the carrier's truck catches fire and the seats are destroyed. Waldorf argues he bears no risk because Statler never notified him. Who is right?
o: Statler, because missing notice matters only if it causes material delay or loss.
Waldorf, because a seller that skips any of its shipping duties keeps the risk of loss.
Neither, because the loss is split when both parties were partly responsible.
Statler, but only because both parties are merchants in the theater-seat business.
Waldorf, because under F.O.B. seller's factory, risk passes only when the buyer is notified.
oe: Correct. Prompt notice is one of the seller's shipping duties under § 2-504(c), but the last sentence of § 2-504 makes failure to notify a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss ensues. The fire had nothing to do with the missing notice, so risk passed under § 2-509(1)(a).
The UCC deliberately limits the effect of a notice failure to cases where it causes material delay or loss.
Neither party caused the fire, and Article 2 has no comparative-fault allocation of risk.
Merchant status matters under § 2-509(3), not in shipment contracts. The result would be the same for non-merchants.
Under F.O.B. place of shipment, the seller bears risk only until the goods are in the carrier's possession (§ 2-319(1)(a)). Notice isn't the trigger.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Seller fails to notify; loss not caused by it

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a liquidated damages clause from a remedy limitation?
o: They are tested the same way, for reasonableness.
An LD clause fixes the amount; a limitation caps categories of loss.
An LD clause must be conspicuous; a limitation need not be.
A limitation fixes the amount of damages in advance; an LD clause caps them.
None of the above.
oe: They have different tests.

Correct. Problem 5-9. An LD clause fixes damages in advance and is tested for reasonableness. A limitation caps or eliminates categories, the buyer still proves actual loss, and it is tested by failure of essential purpose or unconscionability.
Neither must be conspicuous.
Reversed. The LD clause sets the amount; a limitation caps or removes categories.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — LD vs. limitation

q: A seller makes 500 jerseys printed with a team's name. The team folds and refuses them. The seller tries for two months and gets no offers. It sues for the $25,000 price and wins. Then a collector offers $4,000 for all 500 before the judgment is paid. What may it do?
o: It must give the jerseys to charity.
Keep the $25,000 and the $4,000.
It loses the judgment by selling them.
Sell them, and credit the net proceeds to the judgment.
It can't sell goods held for the buyer.
oe: Nothing requires that.
That's double recovery.
It only credits the proceeds.
Correct. Section 2-709(2): the seller may resell before collection, crediting proceeds. If the buyer pays, it gets any goods not resold.
It may, before collecting.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Action for the price after failed resale

q: Which of the following is a repudiation under § 2-610?
o: Asking for more than the contract gives, without conditioning your own performance on it.
Making a written demand for adequate assurance after reasonable grounds arise.
Failing to perform when performance is due.
Expressing doubt about your ability to perform while promising to try.
Clearly indicating before performance is due that you won't perform.
oe: Not by itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
That is a right under § 2-609.
That's a breach, not an anticipatory repudiation.
A repudiation requires a clear indication you won't perform.
Correct. § 2-610.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Repudiation definition

q: Nell pays $200 down on a $2,000 piano, tagged for her at Tune Town, for her home. Before she pays the balance, Tune Town, still solvent, tells her it has decided to keep the piano for its own recital room. She tenders the $1,800. Tune Town refuses. Which is correct?
o: She may recover it only if she can't find another piano.
She is limited to a refund, since prepaying gives no right to goods.
She may recover the piano under § 2-502(1)(a).
She may recover it only if the piano is unique.
She may recover it only if Tune Town became insolvent within ten days.
oe: Inability to cover is a replevin element, not a § 2-502 element.
Prepaying alone doesn't, but here § 2-502(1)(a) adds the rest.
Correct. She has a special property, has paid part of the price, has tendered the balance, the goods are for household use, and the seller repudiated. No insolvency is needed for consumer goods.
Uniqueness matters to specific performance.
That's the (1)(b) trigger for non-consumer goods. She qualifies under (1)(a).
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Consumer prepayment, insolvent dealer

q: Elmo, a dentist, sells a used road bike to Telly through a classified ad, saying, "The frame is carbon fiber." The frame is aluminum. Telly sues for breach of express warranty, and Elmo argues that a non-merchant can't make a warranty. What result?
o: Telly wins, because any seller can make an express warranty.
Elmo wins, because Telly could have checked the frame.
Telly wins, but only under the implied warranty of merchantability.
Elmo wins, because only merchants make warranties under Article 2.
Elmo wins, because the bike is used.
oe: Correct. § 2-313 applies to every seller.
A buyer's chance to inspect doesn't erase a specific affirmation of fact.
Elmo isn't a merchant, so no merchantability warranty arises.
Only merchantability requires a merchant.
Used goods can carry express warranties.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Express warranty by a non-merchant

q: A defective motorcycle catches fire and is destroyed. May the buyer still revoke?
o: No, because revocation requires returning the goods.
No, because the goods no longer exist.
No, because the buyer's only remedy is in tort.
Yes, but only for the salvage value.
Yes, because the defect itself caused the change.
oe: Return isn't possible, and the statute doesn't demand it here.
Destruction by the defect doesn't bar revocation.
Tort isn't exclusive.
Nothing limits revocation that way.
Correct. Problem 7-26(B). Revocation mostly adds the refund; any injury is consequential.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Goods destroyed by own defect

q: On March 1, a hotel mails a sign maker an offer: "Make and deliver 50 custom brass room signs at $40 each; delivery by May 1." The offer doesn't specify how to accept. The sign maker begins making the signs but never tells the hotel. By April 10, having heard nothing, the hotel orders signs elsewhere and tells the sign maker the offer is withdrawn. The sign maker says it accepted by beginning work. What is the most likely result?
o: The sign maker wins, because the signs are specially manufactured goods made for the hotel.
The hotel may treat the offer as lapsed, because the sign maker never notified it.
The sign maker wins, because the hotel's offer was irrevocable until the May 1 delivery date.
The hotel wins, because an offer to buy goods can be accepted only by a return promise.
The sign maker wins, because beginning the requested performance is a valid acceptance.
oe: That exception concerns the statute of frauds, not whether a contract was formed.

Correct. Where the beginning of a requested performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, "an offeror who is not notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as having lapsed before acceptance" (§ 2-206(2)). Six weeks of silence on a two-month job is likely more than reasonable.
Nothing made the offer a firm offer under § 2-205.
Unless the offer says otherwise, it may be accepted in any reasonable manner (§ 2-206(1)(a)), including by beginning performance.
It can be, but § 2-206(2) adds the notice requirement.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Beginning performance without notifying the offeror

q: Which statement correctly contrasts an ordinary lease with a non-consumer finance lease?
o: Only the ordinary lessee's rent promises are irrevocable.
Risk stays with the finance lessor and passes to the ordinary lessee.
The ordinary lessee may deduct from rent; the finance lessee can't.
Revocation is freer in a finance lease.
The finance lessor gives implied warranties; the ordinary one doesn't.
oe: That's reversed.
That's reversed.
Correct. Section 2A-508(6), subject to § 2A-407. Risk of loss passes to the finance lessee and stays with the ordinary lessor, and finance-lease revocation is limited to the lessor's assurances.
It's narrower, limited to the lessor's assurances.
That's reversed.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Finance vs. ordinary contrast

q: A 12-month contract calls for monthly deliveries of 10,000 widgets by the 5th of each month. In April, May, and June the seller delivers on the 9th, and each time the buyer accepts without objection. In July, the seller again delivers on the 9th, and the buyer, without any earlier warning, rejects the shipment as late. What is the most likely result?
o: The rejection is proper, because a party who waives a term may retract the waiver at any time.
The rejection is proper, because a waiver of a contract term isn't binding without consideration.
The rejection is likely wrongful, because the buyer had to give notice before demanding strict performance.
The rejection is proper, because the written delivery date is an express term and controls over conduct.
The rejection is wrongful, because the contract has been permanently rewritten to require delivery by the 9th.
oe: Retraction requires reasonable notice in advance and isn't allowed if it would be unjust because of a material change of position.
A waiver needs no consideration.

Correct. Repeated acceptance can show waiver or modification (§ 1-303(f)). A waiver affecting an executory part of the contract can be retracted only by "reasonable notification received by the other party that strict performance will be required" (§ 2-209(5)). The buyer gave none before July.
Course of performance is relevant to show a waiver of an express term (§ 1-303(f)).
Waiver of an executory term can be retracted with reasonable notice. The more precise answer is that the buyer needed to give notice.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Repeated waivers; retraction needs notice

q: A two-page form contract between a consumer and a dealer contains a boilerplate merger clause. The consumer offers evidence of an oral side term consistent with the writing. Which statement best describes the merger clause's effect?
o: It bars evidence of fraud.
It conclusively makes the writing complete and exclusive.
It bars later modifications.
It has no effect in consumer contracts.
It is strong evidence that the writing is complete and exclusive, but not conclusive.
oe: The parol evidence rule never bars fraud evidence.
It's evidence, not a conclusive rule.
That's a NOM clause.
It's still evidence of integration.
Correct. A merger clause is probative, not conclusive, especially in a short consumer form.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause: weight

q: A contract calls for 12 monthly deliveries of 1,000 printed labels. In the fourth delivery, 50 labels are misprinted. The defect doesn't substantially impair the value of the whole contract, and the seller promptly offers to replace them within a week and assures the buyer it will. The buyer wants to reject the entire fourth delivery. May it?
o: Yes, but only if the buyer is a consumer, because merchants must accept installments that can be cured.
No, because the defect can be cured and the seller has given adequate assurance that it will cure.
No, because a buyer under an installment contract must accept every delivery and sue for damages instead.
Yes, and because one installment was defective, the buyer may also cancel the rest of the contract.
Yes, because under the perfect tender rule a buyer may reject any delivery that fails to conform in any respect.
oe: Section 2-612 applies regardless of the parties' status.
Correct. Section 2-612(2) replaces perfect tender for installments. If the nonconformity can be cured and the seller gives adequate assurance of cure, the buyer must accept the installment.
A buyer may reject an installment that is substantially impaired and can't be cured.
Cancellation of the whole requires a nonconformity that substantially impairs the value of the whole contract (§ 2-612(3)).
Section 2-601 is expressly subject to § 2-612 for installment contracts.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Installment contract; curable defect

q: A lessee defaults, with $3,000 of rent unpaid at repossession, and 10 months left at $1,000. Market rent where the goods are is $700 for a 10-month term. The lessor keeps the goods. Ignoring PV, what are damages, before incidentals?
oe: That leaves out either accrued rent or the difference.
That uses the market rent rather than the difference.
That's accrued plus all remaining rent, ignoring market value.
Correct. Accrued $3,000 plus ($1,000 minus $700) × 10 = $3,000. Section 2A-528(1).
That's all remaining rent.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Accrued rent plus market

q: Goods are stored in a warehouse, and the seller does not intend to move them. When does the risk of loss pass to the buyer if the warehouse has issued a negotiable warehouse receipt?
o: When the buyer receives the negotiable warehouse receipt.
When the buyer physically takes the goods from the warehouse.
A reasonable time after the seller tells the buyer where the goods are.
When the contract for sale is signed by both parties.
None of the above.
oe: Physical possession isn't required.
That's closer to the rule for non-negotiable documents.
Not under § 2-509(2).
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Bailee: negotiable document

q: A seller under a shipment contract forgets to tell the buyer the goods have shipped. They arrive on time and conform, but the buyer, annoyed, rejects them. Which is correct?
o: The seller has breached and owes damages.
The rejection is proper, as the tender failed in some respect.
The rejection is ineffective, as notice to the seller came too late.
The rejection is wrongful, as no material delay or loss ensued.
The rejection is proper, as risk of loss stayed with the seller.
oe: No loss resulted from the missed notice.
Section 2-504 is a specific limit on § 2-601.
Timing isn't the problem on these facts.
Correct. Failure to notify is a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss ensues (§ 2-504).
Risk isn't the issue; the goods arrived fine.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Rejection vs. shipment term

q: Gonzo buys a new $30,000 sedan from a dealer. It meets every state and federal safety standard, but a national consumer magazine rates it the lowest in its class for front-impact protection. Gonzo is badly hurt in a high-speed head-on crash and sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. What is the most likely result?
o: The dealer likely wins, because merchantability doesn't require the safest car in its class.
The dealer wins, because Gonzo was driving at high speed when the crash happened.
Gonzo wins, because a car rated lowest in its class can't pass without objection in the trade.
Gonzo wins, because serious injuries in a crash show that the car wasn't fit for driving.
The dealer wins, because complying with government safety regulations always proves merchantability.
oe: Correct. Merchantability is a minimum standard (§ 2-314(2)). A car that meets all safety regulations and is merely rated lower than its competitors can still pass without objection in the trade and be fit for ordinary driving. See Problem 3-10(d).
Speed might matter to causation, but the question is whether the car was merchantable. That turns on the minimum standard.
A low comparative rating doesn't by itself make a regulation-compliant car objectionable in the trade.
Merchantability doesn't promise that a car protects occupants in every crash.
Compliance is strong evidence, but it isn't conclusive.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Meets regulations but rated low

q: A signed purchase agreement for a commercial oven sets out the model, price, and quantity and is intended as final on those terms. It says nothing about installation and has no merger clause. The buyer offers evidence that, before signing, the seller orally agreed to install the oven at no charge. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes, but only if the writing is ambiguous about whether installation was included in the price.
No, because a prior oral agreement can never be used to add a term to a signed written contract.
Probably yes, as a consistent additional term, unless the writing was meant to be complete and exclusive.
Yes, because the parol evidence rule applies only to prior written agreements, not oral ones.
No, because free installation contradicts the price term, which was final in the writing.
oe: Article 2 doesn't require ambiguity before admitting consistent additional terms (§ 2-202 cmt. 1(c)).
Section 2-202(b) allows consistent additional terms to supplement a partial integration.

Correct. A writing that is final as to the terms it includes may be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 2-202(b)), unless it was intended as complete and exclusive. Comment 3 also excludes terms that, if agreed, would certainly have been included in the document.
It applies to prior agreements and contemporaneous oral agreements.
Silence on installation isn't a contradiction. The term adds something the writing doesn't address.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Partial integration; consistent additional term

q: Kermit repudiates a contract to buy 200 guitars at $500 each. After notifying Kermit, the seller resells them in a commercially reasonable private sale for $430 each, spending $1,000 on the resale. What may the seller recover?
oe: That's the contract price.
That subtracts the expenses instead of adding them.
That leaves out the incidental expenses.
That's the resale proceeds.
Correct. § 2-706: contract minus resale ($70 × 200 = $14,000) plus incidental damages ($1,000).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Seller's resale

q: A seller wins the price of goods it couldn't resell. What are its duties?
o: Hold them for the buyer, and credit any later resale.
Return them to the manufacturer.
Destroy them to protect the market.
Keep them and collect the price too.
Donate them and keep the tax deduction.
oe: Correct. Section 2-709(2). Paying the judgment entitles the buyer to goods not resold. That's why the price is the remedy when resale is impossible.
Nothing requires that.
Nothing allows that.
That's double recovery; paying entitles the buyer to them.
They're held for the buyer.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Holding goods for buyer

q: At an estate sale, Abby buys a table described on the price tag as an "antique oak table." It turns out to be a recent reproduction. Has the seller made an express warranty?
o: No, because the price tag was not signed by the seller.
Yes, because the description became part of the basis of the bargain.
No, because an estate seller is not a merchant.
No, because "antique" is only a matter of opinion.
None of the above.
oe: An express warranty needs no signature.
Correct. § 2-313(1)(b). "Antique," like "Queen Anne" or "Ming," is a description (Problem 3-6).
Any seller can make an express warranty by description.
Whether a table is an antique is a verifiable fact.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Description

q: Under § 2-314(2), merchantable goods must at least:
o: be fit for the particular purpose the buyer has in mind.
conform to any affirmations of fact on the label.
meet every safety rating at the top of their class.
be the highest-quality goods of their kind on the market.
All of the above.
oe: That is the § 2-315 warranty, not merchantability.
Correct. That is § 2-314(2)(f), alongside passing without objection, fair average quality, fitness for ordinary purposes, even kind and quality, and adequate packaging and labeling.
A car that meets all safety rules but rates low in crash tests is likely still merchantable (Problem 3-10).
Merchantability is a minimum standard.
Only B is a requirement.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Merchantability: requirements

q: A buyer orders a dining set (a table and six matching chairs) sold and priced as one set. One chair is defective. May the buyer keep the table and five good chairs and reject the defective chair?
o: No, because the set is one commercial unit.
Yes, because the perfect tender rule lets it reject any defect.
Yes, because the buyer may accept any units and reject the rest.
No, because the buyer must reject every item or none.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-606(2). A set sold as one is a commercial unit.
The perfect tender rule speaks of commercial units.
The buyer may accept or reject commercial units, not parts of them.
The buyer could reject the whole set.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Commercial unit

q: Under an 18-month supply contract between merchants, a buyer pays three invoices late, and the seller accepts each late payment without protest. The buyer then loses its largest customer and starts missing payments to other suppliers. The seller demands adequate assurance. The buyer argues the seller waived the right by accepting the late payments. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller may demand assurance only if the contract expressly gives it a right to do so.
The buyer wins, because the course of performance changed the payment terms to allow late payment.
The buyer wins, because a party may demand assurance only after the other side actually breaches.
The seller may demand assurance, because accepting late payments doesn't waive that right.
The seller must first reject a late payment before it can demand any assurance from the buyer.
oe: The right comes from the statute.
Even if late payment became acceptable, the new facts give fresh grounds for insecurity, and § 2-609(3) preserves the right to demand assurance.
A demand requires reasonable grounds for insecurity, not an actual breach.

Correct. "Acceptance of any improper delivery or payment does not prejudice the aggrieved party's right to demand adequate assurance of future performance" (§ 2-609(3)). Between merchants, the reasonableness of the grounds is judged by commercial standards (§ 2-609(2)).
Section 2-609(3) says the opposite.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Accepting late payments doesn't waive assurance

q: Which matches the side-by-side remedies chart on consequential damages?
o: Buyer no, seller yes, lessee no, lessor yes.
All four no.
Buyer yes, seller no, lessee yes, lessor no.
Buyer and seller yes; lessee and lessor no.
All four yes.
oe: That's reversed.
Buyers and lessees do.
Correct. Lessor's incidentals are in § 2A-530.
Sellers don't, and lessees do.
Sellers and lessors don't get them.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — No consequentials for lessors

q: A contract has a no-oral-modification clause. The seller orally agrees to a new delivery date, and the buyer later claims a waiver under § 2-209(4). The seller says the buyer never relied. How do the courts in the text divide?
o: All courts agree that reliance is irrelevant to waiver.
Section 2-209(4) itself expressly requires reliance.
All courts agree that waiver requires detrimental reliance.
Courts split on whether waiver needs detrimental reliance.
The issue arises only if the parties are consumers.
oe: Wisconsin Knife Works requires it.
The text doesn't say so; that's why courts split.
BMC doesn't require it.
Correct. Wisconsin Knife Works requires reliance, so § 2-209(2) isn't swallowed. BMC goes the other way. An attempted modification failing § 2-209(2) or (3) can operate as a waiver under § 2-209(4).
The cited cases are commercial.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Waiver and reliance split

q: What is the key doctrinal difference between replevin and specific performance under § 2-716?
o: Specific performance is available only once cover has failed.
Replevin requires prepayment; specific performance does not.
Replevin is limited to consumers; specific performance is not.
Replevin is a legal right; specific performance is discretionary.
Specific performance needs identified goods; replevin does not.
oe: The Code sets no such order, though inability to cover helps.
Neither generally requires prepayment, apart from shipment under reservation.
Both are open to all buyers.
Correct. Replevin also needs identified goods and an inability to cover; specific performance needs neither identification nor, strictly, inability to cover.
That's reversed.
topic: Wk 8 · XVII · Buyer's remedies: roadmap & getting the goods (§§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502) — Replevin vs. specific performance nature

q: A buyer accepts assorted-color binders despite seeing they are all blue, after the seller says replacements are coming. None come. Which is correct?
o: Neither applies, because the defect concerns only color.
Section 2-608(1)(a) fits, but (1)(b) doesn't.
Only rejection under § 2-601 can apply here.
Section 2-608(1)(b) fits, because the seller gave assurances.
No revocation is possible for a known defect.
oe: The kind of defect doesn't matter if value is impaired.
Correct. Problem 7-26(E).
Acceptance has already occurred.
Subsection (b) requires acceptance without discovery.
Subsection (a) covers known defects.
topic: Wk 9 · XXII · Revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608) — Visible defect

q: Tomatoes are sold by the bushel. Fifty of 1,000 bushels arrive rotten. If a bushel is a commercial unit, what may the buyer do?
o: Keep the 950 only if the seller gives written consent.
Reject the whole shipment, or accept the whole, but do nothing in between.
Reject the 50 only after giving the seller a chance to substitute.
Keep all 1,000 and deduct nothing for the rotten ones.
Keep the 950 good bushels and reject the 50 rotten ones.
oe: No consent is needed.
Section 2-601(c) adds a third option, partial acceptance by commercial units.
Rejection doesn't need a prior chance to cure.
Accepting doesn't waive damages if notice is given, so this misstates the buyer's options.
Correct. Sections 2-601(c) and 2-105(6). The buyer pays for what it keeps and has remedies for the rest.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — What counts as a commercial unit

q: Under the UCC, what is the difference between the "agreement" and the "contract"?
o: The agreement must be in writing, but the contract need not be.
The contract is the parties' bargain in fact; the agreement is the legal obligation.
The agreement includes only express terms, never course of dealing or usage of trade.
Nothing; the Code uses them interchangeably.
The agreement is the bargain in fact; the contract is the resulting legal obligation.
oe: Neither definition requires a writing.
That reverses the definitions.
The agreement includes the bargain as found in course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.
The Code defines them differently.
Correct. § 1-201(b)(3) and (b)(12). The contract can include more (gap fillers, implied warranties) or less (an unconscionable term, a term barred by the statute of frauds) than the agreement.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Agreement vs. contract

q: A non-consumer finance lessee claims the lessor fraudulently induced the lease by lying about the goods. Does § 2A-407 end that defense?
o: Yes, unless the fraud was in writing.
Yes, because fraud claims don't exist under the UCC.
Not necessarily, because fraud in the inducement might survive.
Yes, because it ends every possible defense.
No, because § 2A-407 applies only to consumers.
oe: No writing rule exists.
Section 1-103(b) preserves fraud.
Correct. Faust Printing, n.13. Express clauses remain common as backup (n.14).
Common-law defenses may survive (Faust Printing).
It excludes consumers.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Surviving defenses

q: A seller ships 200 cases of canned soup to Gonzo under a shipment contract on pallets slightly below trade standard. A train strikes the truck and destroys everything; the packing played no role. Who bears the loss?
o: Gonzo, because the packing didn't cause the loss.
The seller, because its packing breached § 2-504.
The parties split it, because both bear some fault.
The seller, because any nonconformity keeps risk on the seller.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-7(d)(2) and Windows v. Jordan Panel: the packing must cause the loss before risk shifts back.
A § 2-504 failure shifts risk only if it causes material delay or loss.
Gonzo bears no fault, and there's no splitting rule.
Not where the nonconformity didn't cause the loss.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Bad packing, unrelated loss

q: A complete and exclusive contract calls for "Grade A" maple lumber but doesn't define the term. The buyer offers evidence that in the furniture trade, "Grade A" means knot-free boards. Is the evidence admissible?
o: No, unless the court first finds that "Grade A" is ambiguous on the face of the written contract.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Yes, because usage of trade may explain the terms of even a complete and exclusive writing.
Yes, but only if the seller agrees.
None of the above.
oe: Some courts require that for other explanatory evidence, but not for usage, dealing, or performance.
Usage of trade can explain even a complete writing.
Correct. § 2-202(a). Cmt. 1(c): no prior finding of ambiguity is needed for usage evidence.
Admissibility doesn't depend on consent.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Usage explains a term

q: When may a lessor recover rent under § 2A-529?
o: Accepted goods kept by the lessee, goods lost, or goods unsalable.
Only with a liquidated damages clause.
In every default by a lessee.
Only for goods the lessor has repossessed.
Only if the lessee is insolvent.
oe: Correct. Recovery is accrued rent plus PV of remaining rent, plus incidentals, less saved.
The statute needs no clause.
Only in the listed cases.
Repossessed goods are excluded.
Insolvency isn't required.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Rent formula

q: Nora buys a blender from a retailer and gives it to her neighbor Finn, who is cut when the blade flies off. Finn sues the manufacturer. What kinds of privity are missing?
o: Vertical only, until Nora gave Finn notice of the defect.
Only horizontal, since a maker is in privity with end users.
Both vertical and horizontal privity are missing.
Only vertical, since Finn is below the maker in the chain.
Neither, since others foreseeably use the goods.
oe: Notice has nothing to do with privity.
Privity exists only between immediate links.

Correct. Vertical privity concerns a buyer suing up the chain beyond its immediate seller. Horizontal privity concerns a non-buyer injured by the goods. Finn is outside the chain, and even Nora is remote from the maker.
Finn isn't in the chain at all, so horizontal privity is also missing.
Foreseeability may extend warranties; it doesn't create privity.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Vertical or horizontal

q: Before the first of three installments is due, a manufacturer writes to the buyer: "Your design drawings were incomplete. We have revised them, but we must retool, which will add expense and some delay. We will not be able to deliver the first installment on time. We expect you to cover the extra expense. We anticipate catching up by the second installment." Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is a repudiation, because the manufacturer demands that the buyer pay the extra expense.
It is a repudiation, because the manufacturer says it won't deliver the first installment on time.
It has no legal effect, because only a formal written notice can be a repudiation.
It is a valid modification of the contract that the buyer must accept.
Probably not a repudiation, but it likely gives the buyer reasonable grounds for insecurity.
oe: An expectation of reimbursement isn't a repudiation unless performance is conditioned on it.
Announcing a delay while promising to catch up isn't a clear refusal to perform the contract, though it may breach the first installment when it comes due.
Repudiation can occur by words or conduct, and the letter at least supports insecurity.
A modification requires agreement. A one-sided letter isn't one.

Correct. A repudiation requires a clear statement or action showing a party won't perform. A mere request for a change in terms isn't one unless performance is conditioned on it (§ 2-610 cmt. 2). The letter expects reimbursement but doesn't refuse to perform without it, and its warning of delay justifies a demand for assurance under § 2-609. See Problem 6-5.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Is this letter a repudiation?

q: A signed contract between two produce merchants requires delivery of lettuce "by 12:00 noon on Friday." In the regional produce trade, "Friday delivery" customarily means any time before 5 p.m. The seller delivers at 3 p.m., and the buyer rejects as late. Who is right?
o: The seller, because usage of trade defines what the parties' words mean in their trade.
The seller, because a three-hour delay is trivial and the lettuce arrived the same day.
Neither, because the conflicting terms knock each other out and a gap filler applies.
The buyer, because an express term controls when it can't be squared with a trade usage.
The seller, because both parties are merchants in the same trade and bound by its usages.
oe: Usage can explain or supplement terms, but it can't contradict a specific express term.
Under perfect tender, a buyer may reject for any nonconformity, including time (§ 2-601).
The knockout idea applies to conflicting forms under § 2-207, not to an express term versus trade usage.

Correct. Express terms, course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade are read consistently where reasonable. Where they can't be, express terms prevail (§ 1-303(e)(1)). "By 12:00 noon" can't be read as "before 5 p.m."
Being in the trade binds them to usages, but usages still yield to express terms.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Express term beats trade usage

q: Gonzo sells 1,000 cases of bottled water stored at an independent warehouse. On Monday, the warehouse acknowledges to the buyer that it now holds the water for the buyer. On Wednesday, before the buyer picks it up, a roof collapse destroys the water. Who bears the loss?
o: Gonzo, because Gonzo is a merchant seller.
Gonzo, because the buyer hadn't yet paid.
The warehouse, because the water was in its possession.
Gonzo, because the buyer never received the water.
None of the above.
oe: The merchant rule applies only under § 2-509(3).
Payment doesn't affect risk.
The question is which party bears risk.
Receipt isn't the test for goods held by a bailee.
Correct. The buyer bears it: for goods held by a bailee without being moved, risk passes when the bailee acknowledges the buyer's right to possession (§ 2-509(2)(b)). No choice says that.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Bailee: acknowledgment

q: Statler contracts to buy $4,000 of theater seats from Waldorf's Seating. The contract says that if Statler cancels, he "shall pay Seller $40,000 as liquidated damages." Statler cancels before the seats are shipped, and Waldorf resells them with a $300 loss. What may Waldorf recover?
o: Only his actual damages, because the clause is void as a penalty.
A reduced, reasonable amount that the court sets in place of the $40,000.
Nothing, because a void penalty clause voids the entire contract.
$4,000, the full contract price, as the maximum a seller can ever liquidate.
$40,000, because Statler freely agreed to the amount.
oe: Correct. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty (§ 2-718(1)). Ten times the price bears no relation to any plausible harm, so Waldorf falls back on his ordinary remedies (e.g., § 2-706).
§ 2-718(1) declares the term void. The court doesn't rewrite it; the seller proves actual damages instead.
Only the penalty term is void. The rest of the contract, including Waldorf's ordinary remedies, survives.
No rule caps liquidated damages at the price. The question is reasonableness, and this clause fails it.
Freedom of contract stops at penalties. § 2-718(1) voids unreasonably large liquidated damages.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Penalty: unreasonably large

q: Big Bird orders crab cakes described on the menu as "all lump meat, shell-free." A sharp fragment of crab shell cuts his mouth. He sues the restaurant for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: He loses, because serving food in a restaurant is a service, not a sale of goods.
He wins only if the restaurant was negligent in preparing the crab cakes.
He wins under every test, because any injury from food proves it was unmerchantable.
Under the reasonable-expectation test he likely wins, because a diner reasonably expects "shell-free" crab cakes to have no shell.
He loses under every test, because crab shell is natural to crab.
oe: Serving food or drink for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)).
Implied warranties impose strict liability; negligence isn't required.
Under the foreign-natural test, a natural substance doesn't make food unmerchantable.

Correct. The reasonable-expectation test asks what a reasonable consumer would expect, and the menu promised no shell. Under the older foreign-natural test, shell is natural to crab and the diner would likely lose.
That is only the foreign-natural test's result. The reasonable-expectation test focuses on what the diner could expect, especially given the menu.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Food: two tests

q: Which is NOT an element of a finance lease under § 2A-103(1)(g)?
o: The lessee must be a merchant in goods of the kind.
The lessor acquires the goods in connection with the lease.
The lessee gets the supply contract before signing, or an equivalent under (iii).
The lessor doesn't select, manufacture or supply the goods.
All of the above are required.
oe: Correct. Merchant status isn't an element. Elements: the lessor doesn't select, make or supply the goods; it acquires them or the right to them in connection with the lease; and one of (iii)(A)-(D) is met.
Required.
Required in one of its forms.
Required.
The first choice isn't required.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Finance lease elements

q: Statler is selling his used pontoon boat to Waldorf. Statler says: (1) "She's the finest boat on the lake." (2) "She's worth at least $40,000." (3) "The hull is aluminum, and the motor has 300 hours on it." (4) "You'll be the envy of the marina." The motor actually has 1,900 hours. Which statement created an express warranty?
o: None, because Statler isn't a merchant.
Statement (3) only.
Statements (2) and (3).
Statements (1) and (3).
All four statements.
oe: Any seller can make an express warranty. Merchant status is irrelevant under § 2-313.

Correct. A specific, verifiable affirmation of fact about the goods is an express warranty (§ 2-313(1)(a)). Statements (1) and (4) are commendation, and statement (2) is "an affirmation merely of the value of the goods," which creates no warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
An affirmation merely of value is not a warranty under § 2-313(2).
"Finest boat on the lake" is general praise, or puffing.
Only the specific factual statement is a warranty. The others are opinion, value, or praise.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Fact vs. value vs. puffing

q: A seller argues that the buyer's $400 inspection expense isn't recoverable because the seller had no reason to know of it at contracting. What must the buyer actually show?
o: That it could not have been prevented by cover.
That the expense was caused by the breach and reasonably incurred.
That the contract expressly allowed the expense.
That the seller had reason to know of it at contracting.
That the expense exceeded a reasonable minimum.
oe: That's also part of the consequential test.
Correct. Section 2-715(1) has no foreseeability test.
Section 2-715(1) supplies it without any clause.
That's the consequential-damages test.
There's no threshold.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Incidental test

q: How can a seller stay outside § 2-706, and what is the result if it recovers market damages and later resells higher?
o: It waits 30 days; it must account.
It doesn't identify the resale; there's no accounting.
It gets the buyer's consent; it must account.
It can't stay outside; there's no accounting.
It files a notice; it pays a penalty.
oe: Neither is the rule.
Correct. See n.19.
No consent is needed, and no accounting follows.
It can, by not identifying the resale (n.19).
Neither is the rule.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Avoiding § 2-706

q: Under a 10-load contract, the buyer keeps defective Load 2 without notifying the seller of cancellation, and writes, "Please send Load 3 on time." It later tries to cancel the whole contract for the Load 2 defect. What result?
o: It can, because Load 2 was defective.
It can, but only after a 30-day wait.
It can, if it also rejects Load 3.
It can't, because cancellation is never allowed in an installment contract.
It can't, because keeping Load 2 and demanding Load 3 reinstated the contract.
oe: It reinstated the contract.
Section 2-612 sets no waiting period; the problem is reinstatement.
Load 3 hasn't been shown to be defective.
It can be allowed when the whole is substantially impaired.
Correct. Section 2-612(3): accepting without seasonably notifying of cancellation, or demanding performance of future installments, reinstates.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Installment: seller's cure offer ignored

q: Statler sells Waldorf a specific antique carriage that both know, when they contract, is stored in a barn in another county. The contract says nothing about delivery. Where is the place for delivery?
o: Waldorf's residence.
Wherever Waldorf reasonably designates.
Statler's place of business.
The barn where the carriage is stored.
The nearest carrier's terminal.
oe: Never the default.
No such rule.
That's the default only if the goods aren't known to be elsewhere.
Correct. § 2-308(b): for identified goods both parties know are elsewhere at contracting, that place is the place for delivery.
No shipment is required here.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Identified goods stored elsewhere

q: Kermit and a lumber yard trade calls and emails but never agree on every term. The yard delivers lumber, Kermit uses it, and Kermit pays half the invoice. Kermit now argues that no contract was ever formed. What is the best response?
o: No contract exists, because no one can say when the contract was made.
A contract exists only for the half of the lumber Kermit paid for.
A contract exists, because conduct can show agreement.
No contract exists, because the parties never agreed on all material terms.
No contract exists, because acceptance must mirror the offer.
oe: § 2-204(2): a contract can exist even if the moment of its making is undetermined.
That mixes in the part-performance exception to the statute of frauds. The question is formation.
Correct. § 2-204(1). Delivery, use, and partial payment show agreement.
That is the common-law view. Open terms don't defeat a UCC contract (§ 2-204(3)).
The UCC rejects the mirror-image rule.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Formation by conduct

q: Which statement about § 2-318 is correct?
o: Alternative B covers corporations for property loss.
Alternative A covers all natural persons who may be affected.
Alternative C reaches any person and, in some states, property loss.
Alternative C is the rule in most states.
All of the above.
oe: B is limited to natural persons injured in person.
That's Alternative B.

Correct. Alt. A: family, household, home guests, injury in person. Alt. B: any natural person, injury in person, implicitly abolishing vertical privity. Alt. C: any person; "injured" reaches property or economic loss in some states.
Alternative A is the majority rule.
Only the first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Alternatives compared

q: Kermit, a frog who plays banjo as a hobby, is selling his old banjo. Scooter tells him, "I play outdoor gigs on the bayou. I need one that holds its tuning in heavy humidity. Pick one for me." Kermit hands him the banjo and says, "This is the one you want." Scooter buys it. It goes badly out of tune in humid weather, though it plays fine indoors. Which claim is Scooter most likely to win?
o: Both merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.
Breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
Neither, because implied warranties arise only when the seller is a merchant.
Breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
Neither, because Scooter didn't put his needs in writing.
oe: Merchantability fails because Kermit isn't a merchant with respect to banjos.
Correct. Kermit knew Scooter's particular purpose and that Scooter was relying on Kermit's judgment to select a suitable banjo. Under § 2-315 any seller, merchant or not, can make this warranty.
That limit applies only to merchantability. The fitness warranty doesn't require a merchant seller.
Kermit isn't a merchant who deals in banjos, so no merchantability warranty arises (§ 2-314(1)). And the banjo works for ordinary indoor use.
Section 2-315 doesn't require a writing. The seller need only have reason to know the purpose and the buyer's reliance.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fitness warranty by a non-merchant

q: Why does a merchant seller keep the risk of loss until the buyer receives the goods?
o: Because title doesn't pass until the buyer receives them.
Because it still controls the goods and is likely insured.
Because the buyer usually hasn't yet paid the price.
Because merchants can spread losses across many sales.
None of the above.
oe: Title isn't the basis.
Correct. § 2-509 cmt. 3.
Payment doesn't matter.
Not the rationale. § 2-509 cmt. 3 focuses on control and insurance.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Rationale for merchant rule

q: While selling Miss Piggy a scarf, the boutique clerk says: "This looks fabulous on you." The scarf later fades in the wash. Did the clerk's statement create an express warranty?
o: No, because express warranties must be in writing.
Yes, because Miss Piggy relied on it.
No, because it is mere opinion or commendation (puffing).
No, because the clerk didn't use the words "warrant" or "guarantee."
Yes, because it was made by a merchant.
oe: Oral statements can be express warranties.
Reliance alone doesn't make a statement of opinion a warranty.
Correct. "Looks good on you" is the casebook's example of puffing (Problem 3-6). It is general, unmeasurable, and says nothing about colorfastness.
Formal words aren't required (§ 2-313(2)). The statement fails because it is opinion, not because of its wording.
Merchant status does not turn opinion into fact.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Puffing

q: A lessee's neglect ruins an engine, reducing the residual by $8,000. It also defaults, leaving $5,000 in rent damages under § 2A-528. What may the lessor recover, setting aside incidentals?
o: $13,000 only if the lease says so.
$13,000, since residual damage is in addition.
oe: It keeps its rent damages too.
The statute supplies it.
There's no offset.
Residual damage is also recoverable.
Correct. Section 2A-532: "in addition to other recovery."
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIII · Lessee's default & lessor's remedies (§§ 2A-523 to 2A-532) — Residual plus rent

q: Count's buyer pays 15 days after each delivery. Count learns the buyer's credit rating was downgraded and it changed banks. Count announces that from now on it will ship only cash on delivery. What is the risk?
o: Changing the terms on its own may be a repudiation.
None, because § 2-609 lets Count impose any new terms it chooses.
None, because a downgrade lets the seller change the credit terms.
None, because the buyer must accept COD from any seller.
The buyer may cancel only if Count fails to give 30 days' notice.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-3(a). Count should instead demand adequate assurance under § 2-609.
§ 2-609 lets Count demand assurance and suspend, not rewrite the deal.
§ 2-702(1) allows a seller to demand cash only if the buyer is insolvent.
Not so; COD isn't in the contract.
That isn't the rule.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Seller demands COD

q: A seller's lawyer wants to limit a buyer's power to reject under a single-delivery contract. Which clause best serves the client?
o: A clause waiving the seller's own duty of good faith.
A clause calling every delivery a separate contract.
A materiality standard, a cure right, and short notice periods.
A statement that the goods are sold "as is" with no time limits.
A clause adding a right to reject for any defect.
oe: Section 1-302 forbids that, and it wouldn't help.
Section 2-612 ignores such a label and it wouldn't limit rejection on one delivery.

Correct. Problems 7-12 and 7-15: a seller wants materiality, cure and short periods. A buyer of custom equipment wants clear inspection on each delivery, a right to reject without proving impairment and enough time.
"As is" addresses implied warranties, not rejection for express nonconformity.
That strengthens the buyer.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Drafting for the seller

q: Under a $5,000 contract for ten desks F.O.B. Phoenix (freight about $500), the seller repudiates. The buyer buys nothing, and drops its expansion plans because the economy has turned. Which is correct?
o: Section 2-713 at Phoenix, but no lost expansion profits.
Nothing, because the buyer did not cover.
Section 2-713, with market taken in the buyer's own city.
Section 2-713, with the $500 freight deducted.
Lost expansion profits, because the breach came first.
oe: Correct. Both prices are at Phoenix, so freight doesn't adjust. The seller will argue § 1-305 limits a buyer that never wanted the desks.
Section 2-712(3) preserves other remedies.
The place for tender is Phoenix.
Both prices are at Phoenix, so freight isn't saved under this formula.
The economy, not the breach, caused that loss.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — No purchase, dropped expansion

q: Unless otherwise agreed, how are the seller's tender of delivery and the buyer's tender of payment related?
o: Each is a condition of the other's duty to perform.
The buyer must pay before the seller must deliver.
The seller must deliver first and extend credit.
They are independent; each must perform regardless.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. §§ 2-507(1), 2-511(1): they are concurrent conditions. The seller's tender conditions the buyer's duty to accept and pay, and the buyer's tender conditions the seller's duty to deliver.
Not by default.
No credit is presumed (§ 2-310(a)).
They are conditions.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Concurrent conditions

q: Gonzo signs a contract to buy a commercial pizza oven from Animal. The contract states the model and price but says nothing about the delivery date, the place of delivery, or when payment is due. Which statement best describes the contract?
o: It is enforceable, but only by the party that did not draft it.
It is enforceable only after the parties agree on the missing terms.
It is an agreement to agree that neither party can enforce.
It is enforceable if the parties intended to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for giving a remedy.
It fails for indefiniteness, because delivery, place, and payment timing are material terms the parties never settled.
oe: No such rule exists.
The gap fillers supply them.
Intent to contract plus a basis for a remedy is enough.
Correct. § 2-204(3). Gap fillers supply the place (§ 2-308), time (§ 2-309), and payment (§ 2-310).
Under the UCC, open terms don't defeat a contract.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Open terms

q: A fully integrated written contract with a merger clause, and no no-oral-modification clause, sets delivery for June 1. One week after signing, the parties orally agree to move delivery to June 15. The buyer later offers evidence of the oral agreement. Does the parol evidence rule bar it?
o: Yes, because any modification of a written sales contract must itself be in writing.
Yes, because the merger clause makes the written contract the only evidence of the deal.
No, but only if the oral agreement was supported by new consideration.
Yes, because the oral agreement contradicts the June 1 date stated in the writing.
No, because the rule doesn't reach agreements made after the writing.
