oe: Without a no-oral-modification clause or a statute-of-frauds problem, an oral modification is effective (§ 2-209).
A merger clause speaks to prior and contemporaneous agreements, not to later changes.
Modifications need no consideration (§ 2-209(1)).
Contradiction matters only for prior or contemporaneous agreements.
Correct. Section 2-202 excludes evidence of "any prior agreement or of a contemporaneous oral agreement." A later agreement is a modification governed by § 2-209, not by the parol evidence rule.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Later oral agreement isn't barred

q: Linda buys a hair dryer for home use. The manufacturer's warranty excludes "all consequential damages of any kind." The dryer overheats and burns Linda's hand. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The exclusion is valid, because consequential damages may always be excluded.
The exclusion is void only if it was not conspicuous.
The exclusion is valid, because personal injury is governed only by tort law.
The exclusion is prima facie unconscionable as applied to Linda's personal injury.
The exclusion is conclusively void, and the seller can't offer any evidence to save it.
oe: Exclusions are allowed unless unconscionable, and § 2-719(3) presumes this one is.
Conspicuousness isn't the test; unconscionability is.
Personal injury proximately caused by a breach of warranty is consequential damage under § 2-715(2)(b).

Correct. Limiting consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). The seller may try to rebut the presumption, but it starts against the seller.
"Prima facie" means a rebuttable presumption, not a conclusive rule.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Consumer personal injury

q: Which warranty does a finance lessor give?
o: That the goods are free of infringement claims.
That the goods fit the lessee's purpose.
That the goods are merchantable.
That claims from its own acts won't disturb the leasehold.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2A-211(2) excludes finance leases.
Section 2A-213 excludes finance leases.
Section 2A-212 excludes finance leases.
Correct. Section 2A-211(1). The merchant infringement warranty in (2) doesn't apply to finance leases.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 12 · XXIX · Finance leases (§§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407) — Interference and infringement

q: After signing, a buyer says "Can you do $9 instead of $10?" and the seller says "Sure." Six weeks later the buyer wants to enforce the $9 price. Which two questions control?
o: Did the price rise, and did the market fall?
Did they agree to modify, and is the change enforceable?
Was there consideration, and was it in writing?
Was the change a waiver, and was it fair and equitable?
Is the buyer a merchant, and is the seller a merchant?
oe: Market movement bears on good faith, not on these threshold questions.
Correct. Formation rules (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) answer the first. Good faith, the statute of frauds under § 2-209(3), and any no-oral-modification clause answer the second.
Consideration isn't needed (§ 2-209(1)).
The R2d § 89 "fair and equitable" standard isn't § 2-209's test.
Merchant status matters to § 2-209(2) only.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Two questions on modification

q: How does the text treat the phrase "due credit for payments or proceeds of resale" in § 2-708(2)?
o: As barring lost-volume claims altogether.
As applying only to auction sales.
As requiring a dollar-for-dollar credit in all cases.
As limiting recovery to reliance expenses.
As a likely drafting mistake to be ignored.
oe: That's what literal application would do, wrongly.
Nothing in § 2-708(2) limits the phrase to auctions.
That would defeat the remedy for a lost-volume seller.
It says nothing like that.
Correct. Applied literally it would almost always leave a lost-volume seller with nothing, contrary to § 1-305.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Due credit

q: A seller argues, "Buyer beware: a careful buyer should have checked for itself." The seller had said the tractor's engine was rebuilt. Which is the best response?
o: Caveat emptor applies between merchants.
Section 2-313 rejects caveat emptor, making the statement a warranty.
Caveat emptor still governs sales of used goods.
A warranty arises only if the buyer pays extra for it.
The seller must prove the buyer read the warranty.
oe: The statute applies to any seller.

Correct. Section 2-313 turns representations into warranties. A warranty is a promise that a fact is true, backed by an implied promise to indemnify if it isn't. Express warranties are bargained for; implied warranties are imposed by law unless disclaimed.
Article 2 rejects it for both new and used goods.
No separate price is needed.
The seller doesn't carry that burden.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Caveat emptor rejected

q: Between merchants, after a rejection, the seller makes a written request for a full and final written statement of all defects, and the buyer lists only two of five. Which is correct?
o: The rule also covers latent defects no inspection could reveal.
The buyer may rely on all five, because the seller could not have cured.
The buyer may not rely on the other three, if ascertainable by reasonable inspection.
The rule applies only to consumer buyers.
The buyer's whole rejection becomes ineffective.
oe: It reaches only defects ascertainable by reasonable inspection.
Curability isn't required for (1)(b).
Correct. Section 2-605(1)(b). This alternative applies whether or not cure was possible.
It applies only between merchants.
The rejection stands; only the unstated defects are barred.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — § 2-605 merchants

q: A contract says "$50,000 C.I.F. Rotterdam." The goods are properly shipped from New York, the seller delivers the required documents, and the ship sinks. The buyer refuses to pay. Which is correct?
o: The buyer may inspect before paying against the documents.
The buyer must pay and look to the insurance the price covers.
The buyer pays only if a C. & F. term also appears.
The buyer needn't pay, as the goods never reached Rotterdam.
The seller bears the loss, since it bought the insurance.
oe: Payment against documents comes before inspection (§ 2-513(3)).

Correct. C.I.F. means the price includes cost, insurance and freight to the named destination, but it's a shipment contract (§ 2-320). Risk passes when the goods are put on board. C. & F. omits the insurance. The buyer pays against documents.
C. & F. is a separate term that excludes insurance.
C.I.F. is a shipment contract despite naming the destination.
The policy is for the buyer's benefit.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — C. & F. and C.I.F.

q: A contract requires monthly deliveries "by the 5th." For three months the buyer accepts deliveries on the 10th without complaint. The buyer then writes: "Going forward, we require delivery by the 5th as the contract states." The seller has not changed position in reliance. Must the seller deliver by the 5th from now on?
o: No, because the buyer waived the delivery term permanently.
No, because a waiver can be retracted only with new consideration.
No, because the course of performance permanently modified the contract.
Yes, because the buyer retracted its waiver by reasonable notice.
Yes, but the buyer must pay a fee for the change.
oe: A waiver of an executory term can be retracted.
No consideration is needed. § 2-209(5) requires only reasonable notification, absent a material change of position in reliance.
Even if a course of performance supports waiver, the express term controls going forward once the waiver is retracted.
Correct. § 2-209(5). Retraction fails only if it would be unjust because of a material change of position in reliance.
No consideration is needed to retract a waiver.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Waiver retraction

q: Which section extends lease warranties to the lessee's family and guests, and how does it differ from § 2A-209?
o: Section 2A-216, which is separate from § 2A-209.
Section 2A-216, which covers finance lessees.
Both, as the two sections state the same rule.
Neither, as lease warranties don't extend past the lessee.
Section 2A-209, which covers family members.
oe: Correct.
It covers persons affected by the goods.
They do different work.
Section 2A-216 extends them.
It covers finance lessees.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Lease third parties

q: A seller isn't required to resell after a buyer's breach. Why might it choose to anyway?
o: Market price can be hard to prove, and the resale price is known.
Resale extends the limitations period.
Resale is a precondition to suing for the price.
Resale makes consequential damages available.
Resale is the only way to recover incidental damages.
oe: Correct.
Resale has no effect on § 2-725.
The opposite: the price needs inability to resell.
Sellers never get them absent a provision.
Incidentals go with every measure.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Why resell

q: A contract for 2,000 coffee mugs is "F.O.B. Seller's plant" and says nothing about when payment is due. The seller ships the mugs and demands payment on the day of shipment. The buyer says it will pay when the mugs arrive. Who is right?
o: Neither; payment is due within a reasonable time after shipment.
The buyer, but only if it has already inspected the mugs.
The seller, because risk passed on shipment, so payment is due then too.
The seller, because under an F.O.B. shipment term delivery occurs at the seller's plant.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2-310(a) ties payment to receipt, not to a reasonable time.
Payment is due on receipt, and inspection rights are a separate matter under § 2-513.
Risk and payment are separate questions under §§ 2-509 and 2-310.
The F.O.B. term governs delivery and risk, not when payment is due.

Correct. The buyer is right, but not for any reason listed. Unless otherwise agreed, payment is due "at the time and place at which the buyer is to receive the goods even though the place of shipment is the place of delivery" (§ 2-310(a)). The buyer's separate right to inspect under § 2-513 is not a condition of that rule.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Payment due on receipt despite shipment term

q: Rosita orders 100 blue widgets from Herry "for prompt shipment." Herry is out of blue widgets, so he promptly ships 100 green widgets and the same day emails Rosita: "We're out of blue. Sending green as an accommodation." What is the effect of the shipment?
o: The shipment is an acceptance, but Herry may cure by shipping blue widgets later.
The shipment is an acceptance and a breach.
The shipment is an acceptance, and the notice modifies the contract to green widgets.
Rosita must keep the green widgets and pay for them.
None of the above.
oe: The shipment is not an acceptance at all, because Herry seasonably notified Rosita that it was only an accommodation.
That is the result without the notice.
No contract was formed, so there is nothing to modify.
Rosita may reject the counteroffer.

Correct. Because Herry seasonably notified Rosita that the green widgets were offered only as an accommodation, the shipment is not an acceptance (§ 2-206(1)(b)). It is a counteroffer that Rosita may accept or reject.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Accommodation shipment

q: In Ingram River v. Pott Industries, the seller argued that carrying and heating heavy oil was the ordinary use of barges with heating coils. How did the court respond?
o: It held that only consumer buyers can have a particular purpose for goods.
It agreed, so no fitness warranty arose for the heating coils.
It held that a fitness warranty must be stated in writing.
It held a particular purpose need not be unique, only different enough.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such rule.
The court let the fitness warranty stand.
Fitness is implied.

Correct. A particular purpose need only be sufficiently different from the customary use. Whether the goods were "tank barges" or "heating-coil barges" was a fact question, and the finding for Ingram stood.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Ingram River

q: After a seller's breach, a retailer could easily have bought the same toys from a wholesaler for slightly more, but chose not to. It lost $9,000 in holiday sales, and would have spent $400 more to buy from the wholesaler. What is the most it can recover in consequential damages?
o: $9,000, because failure to cover bars no remedy.
$8,600, the lost sales less the $400 saved.
$4,500, half, since both sides contributed.
$400, the extra cost it would have paid.
None of the above.
oe: Section 2-712(3) doesn't override the avoidability limit in § 2-715(2)(a).
The loss was avoidable, so it's barred, not merely reduced.
Article 2 has no comparative-fault split.
That's not a consequential damage; it was never incurred.
Correct. None of these is right. The $9,000 was preventable by cover, so § 2-715(2)(a) bars it entirely. The retailer may still claim market damages under § 2-713.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Loss of a sale vs. avoidable

q: After the lessor breached, a lessee rightfully rejected and sold perishable leased goods to a good-faith purchaser. Does the purchaser take free?
o: No, because a lessee can't sell leased goods.
Only for 30 days after the sale.
Yes, free of the lessor's and supplier's rights.
Only if the purchaser is a merchant.
Only if the lessor agrees to the sale.
oe: Under § 2A-511 it may.
The statute sets no time limit on the purchaser's protection.
Correct. Section 2A-511(4).
Good faith is the test.
No consent is needed.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Purchaser under § 2A-511

q: A written contract for 10,000 yards of carpet yarn says: "This document contains all the terms of the parties' agreement and is the complete and exclusive statement of their agreement." In a dispute, the buyer offers three kinds of evidence. Which is admissible to supplement the writing?
o: None of the evidence, because a merger clause bars all extrinsic evidence.
Evidence of a consistent usage of trade in the carpet industry.
Evidence of a contemporaneous oral agreement adding a consistent term.
Evidence of a prior written agreement that contradicts a term in the contract.
Evidence of a prior oral agreement adding a consistent term.
oe: A merger clause doesn't bar course of dealing, usage of trade, or course of performance.

Correct. Even a complete and exclusive writing may be explained or supplemented by course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance (§ 2-202(a)). Only subsection (b), on consistent additional terms, is cut off by complete integration. See Problem 5-12(a).
Contemporaneous oral terms are excluded just like prior ones.
Contradictory prior agreements are excluded by any final writing.
A complete and exclusive writing excludes consistent additional terms (§ 2-202(b)).
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Complete integration; trade usage still in

q: A contractor building a steel water tank for a developer hears that the developer's financing may fall through. The contractor writes that it will continue only if the developer's owner personally guarantees payment, the developer escrows the full price, or the developer sells the contractor a share of the project. Which statement best describes the demand?
o: It is improper only because it wasn't sent within 30 days of the rumors.
It is proper, because the rumors gave reasonable grounds for insecurity.
It is proper, because each option gives the developer a choice.
It is improper, because these demands go beyond adequate assurance.
None of the above.
oe: The 30 days runs for the response, not the demand.
Grounds don't justify an excessive demand.
Every option goes beyond adequate assurance.
Correct. This is PDM v. Brookhaven: demands like a personal guarantee, escrow, or an ownership stake were more than adequate assurance as a matter of law.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Excessive demand

q: A contract limits a buyer's remedy for a defective industrial dryer to "replacement of defective parts." A defect causes a fire that destroys the whole dryer. What is the buyer's best argument?
o: The clause never applies to fires.
The clause is unenforceable because it wasn't conspicuous.
The limited remedy failed of its essential purpose, so general UCC remedies are available.
The clause is a penalty.
None of the above.
oe: Nothing in the clause excludes fires.
Remedy limits needn't be conspicuous.
Correct. § 2-719(2). Replacement parts are useless when the machine is gone (Problem 5-7).
Penalty analysis applies to liquidated damages, not remedy limits.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Failure of essential purpose

q: A manufacturer sells to a retailer under a valid, conspicuous disclaimer of implied warranties. In a privity-abolished state, a consumer buys from the retailer, which gives no disclaimer. The product is unmerchantable. Whom can the consumer sue on the implied warranty?
o: The retailer, but not the manufacturer.
Only the manufacturer, as the source.
Neither, as the disclaimer binds all buyers.
The manufacturer only if the consumer is injured in person.
Both, since privity has been abolished.
oe: Correct. The manufacturer made no implied warranty, having disclaimed it. The retailer did make one. The privity rule doesn't create a warranty that never arose.
The disclaimer protects it.
The retailer made its own warranty.
The disclaimer still applies.
Abolishing privity doesn't undo a valid disclaimer.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Disclaimer up the chain

q: A consumer sues a remote manufacturer. Before any privity analysis, what should be asked first?
o: Whether the manufacturer is solvent.
Whether that manufacturer made any warranty to this buyer.
Whether the buyer has given notice to the retailer.
Whether the state adopted Alternative A, B or C.
Whether the consumer has rejected the goods.
oe: Solvency has no bearing on the warranty.
Correct. An express warranty under § 2-313, an implied warranty under § 2-314, or a warranty to the distributor or retailer that extends to the buyer. No warranty means no privity question.
That's a later question under § 2-607(3)(a).
That's the next step, once a warranty exists.
Remedies come after a breach is shown.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Ask first if a warranty exists

q: Conforming goods arrive, and the buyer gives late notice of rejection. What is the result?
o: The goods are accepted, and the buyer has a § 2-714 claim.
The goods are accepted, and the buyer owes the price.
The rejection is wrongful but effective.
The rejection is rightful and effective.
None of the above.
oe: With conforming goods there is no § 2-714 claim.
Correct. Late notice means acceptance, and no nonconformity means no offset.
Late notice makes it ineffective.
Neither is true on these facts.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 9 · XIX · Rejecting the goods; installment contracts (§§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-605, 2-612) — Matrix: no right, untimely

q: Some courts require the writing to be ambiguous before admitting explanatory evidence. Which type of explanatory evidence is admissible even without ambiguity?
o: Prior negotiations between the parties.
Contemporaneous oral statements of intent.
Prior written drafts of the contract.
Course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance.
None of the above.
oe: Some courts require ambiguity.
Some courts require ambiguity.
Some courts require ambiguity before admitting these to explain a term.
Correct. § 2-202 cmt. 1(c).
D is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — Ambiguity

q: Which statement correctly compares Article 2 and Article 2A on parol evidence and modification?
o: Article 2A has no parol evidence rule.
Section 2A-208 has a statute of frauds rule for modifications.
They match, except § 2A-208 has no analog to § 2-209(3).
A lease modification needs fresh consideration.
No-oral-modification clauses are void in leases.
oe: Section 2A-202 is one.
That's the missing § 2-209(3).
Correct. Courts resolve oral lease modifications case by case.
Section 2A-208(1): none is needed.
Section 2A-208(2) respects them.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Lease parol and modification

q: When does a seller get § 2-708(2) lost profit?
o: Only for sales to consumers.
Only if the goods are unique.
Whenever market price is below contract price.
Whenever it chooses, as a free alternative.
When market damages would leave it worse off than performance.
oe: Section 2-708(2) applies to any seller for whom the market measure is inadequate.
Uniqueness isn't required.
That's the ordinary § 2-708(1) case.
Only if § 2-708(1) is inadequate.
Correct. It's a remedy of last resort, implicitly available only if resale damages are also inadequate.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lost profit formula

q: An international contract says "F.O.B. Shanghai (Incoterms 2020)." The buyer's lawyer applies § 2-319 without more. What is the flaw?
o: Incoterms may define the term differently, and parties may adopt them.
Incoterms are federal statutes.
There is no flaw, as all shipping codes are the same.
Section 2-319 voids any reference to Incoterms.
F.O.B. can't be used for ocean shipments.
oe: Correct. Incoterms may give the same abbreviations different meanings. Parties can vary §§ 2-319 to 2-322, so the agreed definitions control.
They're private trade terms.
They can differ.
Parties can vary those sections.
Section 2-319(1)(c) covers F.O.B. vessel.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Incoterms

q: Which advertising claim is most likely an affirmation of fact rather than puffing?
o: "20,679 physicians say this brand is less irritating."
"It's toasted."
"America's favorite way to relax after a long day."
"The smoothest, mildest smoke you'll ever enjoy."
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The tobacco slides treat specific claims like this, or "immediate relief in cases of asthma," as looking like facts.
The slides treat this as puffery.
General praise.
General, unmeasurable praise.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Tobacco ads

q: A con artist tells Sweetums, a private seller, that he is the famous composer Rowlf and buys Sweetums's piano, paying with a forged cashier's check. He sells the piano the next day to Janice, who pays fair value in good faith. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Janice gets good title only if Sweetums, the original seller, was a merchant.
Janice gets good title, because deceit about identity gives voidable title, not void title.
Janice gets good title only if she bought from a merchant who deals in pianos.
Sweetums keeps title, because a sale obtained by impersonating someone else is void from the start.
Sweetums keeps title, because paying with a forged check is a crime, and criminals get no title.
oe: The seller's merchant status is irrelevant to § 2-403(1).

Correct. When goods are delivered under a transaction of purchase, the purchaser can transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value even though "the transferor was deceived as to the identity of the purchaser" (§ 2-403(1)(a)).
That's the entrustment rule. Section 2-403(1) protects good-faith purchasers from any holder of voidable title.
Section 2-403(1)(a) treats deception about identity as producing voidable, not void, title.
Even delivery "procured through fraud punishable as larcenous under the criminal law" gives voidable title (§ 2-403(1)(d)).
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Impostor

q: Big Discount's supplier contract lets Big Discount demand "whatever assurances it deems appropriate, whenever it wishes." Is this clause enforceable?
o: Yes, because the supplier agreed to it in a negotiated contract.
Yes, if the supplier is also a merchant who reviewed the clause.
No, because it sets an arbitrary rather than a reasonable standard.
Yes, because parties may vary the Code's provisions by agreement.
No, because § 2-609 sets the only standard and the parties cannot change it.
oe: Agreement alone isn't enough. Parties may define adequate assurance only by reasonable standards (§ 1-302(b)).
Not the test.
Correct. § 2-609 cmt. 6; § 1-302(b); Problem 6-4.
Arbitrary standards are not enforceable.
They may, if reasonably.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Arbitrary standard

q: A contract has a NOM clause. The seller orally assures the buyer that a late delivery date is fine, and the buyer, relying on the assurance, delays buying elsewhere. Which doctrine is LEAST likely to help the buyer avoid the NOM clause?
o: Course of performance showing waiver.
Waiver under § 2-209(4).
Estoppel under § 1-103(b).
Modification under § 2-209(1).
None of the above.
oe: A course of performance may show waiver.
Conduct can still be a waiver despite a NOM clause (Problem 3-5(C)).
Estoppel is still possible, though weak.
Correct. The NOM clause bars an unwritten modification (§ 2-209(2)). Waiver and estoppel remain possible, though the NOM clause weakens the reasonableness of reliance.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Estoppel and NOM

q: A buyer asks why it recovers nothing direct when the market falls below the contract price after a seller's repudiation. Which is the best answer?
o: The seller must always pay something after a breach, so the rule is odd.
The buyer owes the seller its savings on any later purchase.
Article 2 favors sellers over buyers in a falling market.
The contract price is irrelevant to buyers' damages.
The buyer took the risk of a falling market when it fixed the price.
oe: A breach can produce zero direct damages, though incidental and consequential claims may survive.
A buyer owes no such credit.
The rule simply reflects the expectancy, not a preference.
The contract price is part of both formulas.
Correct. If the difference is zero or negative there is no direct-damage award, but incidental and consequential damages may still be available.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Direction of formulas

q: Under § 2-511, a buyer tenders payment by personal check. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller must accept a check unless the contract says otherwise.
The seller may refuse delivery without giving the buyer time to get cash.
Payment by check is conditional and fails if the check bounces.
A check is absolute payment once the seller accepts it.
None of the above.
oe: The seller may demand legal tender.
The seller must give an extension reasonably necessary to procure legal tender.
Correct. § 2-511(2)–(3). The seller may also demand legal tender, but must give the buyer a reasonable time to get it.
It is conditional.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Check payment

q: A manufacturer limits consequential damages in a sale of a consumer chainsaw. A buyer is injured and sues; § 2-719(3) makes the limit prima facie unconscionable. What might rebut that presumption?
o: Only proof the buyer was a merchant.
A statement of the limit in capital letters.
Proof the seller acted in good faith.
Nothing, as the presumption is conclusive.
A negotiated price for risk, obvious dangers, or adequate warnings.
oe: Commercial status isn't the only way.
Conspicuousness alone doesn't rebut it.
Good faith alone doesn't rebut it.
It's a prima facie rule.
Correct. Those are the items the text notes (Problem 5-8).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Rebutting personal injury presumption

q: Grover orders 100 blue widgets from Elmo "for prompt shipment." Elmo is out of blue widgets, so he promptly ships 100 green widgets without saying anything. What is the legal effect of the shipment?
o: It accepts Grover's offer and is also a breach.
It creates no contract, because the goods do not match the order.
It is an acceptance, and the contract is for green widgets.
It is a counteroffer that Grover may accept or reject.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-206(1)(b): prompt shipment of conforming or nonconforming goods accepts an order for prompt shipment. Without notice of accommodation, the nonconforming shipment is both an acceptance and a breach.
The UCC rejects that mirror-image result for shipments.
The contract is on Grover's terms (blue widgets), so the green widgets are a breach.
That is true only if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that the shipment is an accommodation.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Accepting by shipping nonconforming goods

q: After the first lessee's default, the lessor leases the same crane to a second lessee in good faith, for value. The first lessee claims priority. Who wins?
o: Neither; the lease is void.
The first, as first in time.
The first, unless it entrusted the crane.
The second, as it takes free under § 2A-527(4).
Whoever has possession.
oe: It isn't void.
The exception applies.
Another exception, not needed here.
Correct. This is an exception to the first-in-time rule.
Possession doesn't decide this; § 2A-527(4) does.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Second lessee after breach

q: A lessee's judgment creditor levies on leased goods. Which is correct?
o: It takes subject to the lease, so it doesn't beat the lessor.
It becomes the lessee automatically.
It defeats the lessor's residual.
It takes the goods free of the lease.
It has no rights at all, even to the leasehold.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-307(1).
A levy doesn't do that.
The residual survives.
It takes subject to it.
It may reach the lessee's leasehold.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Lessee's creditors

q: Under a contract for 12 monthly deliveries of cardboard boxes, the third delivery is 2% short, and the seller promptly offers to make up the shortfall within the week. The buyer rejects the whole third delivery. Was the rejection proper?
o: Yes, because a buyer may reject any installment that is late or short.
Yes, because the perfect tender rule lets the buyer reject for any shortfall.
No, because a buyer may never reject an installment.
Yes, because the shortfall breached the whole contract.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the defect substantially impairs that installment and can't be cured.
Not in an installment contract.
It may, when the § 2-612(2) test is met.
A 2% curable shortfall doesn't substantially impair the whole.

Correct. The rejection was improper: in an installment contract, a buyer may reject an installment only if the nonconformity substantially impairs its value and can't be cured (§ 2-612(2)), and a 2% shortfall the seller offers to fix within the week fails that test. No choice says that.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Installment contract

q: A buyer loses $50,000 in sales because a seller failed to deliver parts. Identical parts were available locally the next day at a small premium, and the buyer knew it. Which is correct?
o: The lost sales are barred, because cover would have prevented them.
It recovers $50,000; § 2-712(3) says failure to cover bars nothing.
It recovers $50,000, because it gave timely notice of the breach.
It recovers half, since both sides contributed to the loss.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Section 2-715(2)(a).
That bars no remedy, but the consequential claim has its own avoidability limit.
Notice isn't the issue here.
The Code has no apportionment rule.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Avoidable loss

q: A contract for industrial pumps says: "Any action for breach must be brought within 6 months after delivery." The buyer discovers a defect and sues 10 months after delivery. What result?
o: The suit is barred, because merchants may agree to any period they like.
The suit is barred, because parties may set any limitations period.
The suit is timely, because the limitations period can never be shortened.
The suit is timely, because the period can't be cut below one year.
None of the above.
oe: The one-year floor applies to merchants too.
They can't go below one year.
It can be, to as little as one year.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Shortened limitations period

q: A boat dealer's brochure describes a used 38-foot sailboat as "seaworthy and ready for offshore passages." Snuffy buys the boat after skimming the brochure but cannot show that the statement was a major reason for buying. The boat is unfit for open water. Under the view in Keith v. Buchanan, which the casebook cites, how is a court most likely to treat the brochure statement?
o: As an express warranty, but only if Snuffy proves the statement was the main reason for buying the boat.
As an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
As an express warranty that is part of the basis of the bargain without proof of specific reliance.
As puffing, because "seaworthy" is general sales talk.
As neither, because a brochure isn't addressed to a particular buyer.
oe: Many courts (and cmt. 3) don't require proof of specific reliance.
It's an express statement, and nothing shows Snuffy relied on the dealer to pick a boat for a particular purpose.
Correct. The Keith view treats such a brochure statement as an affirmation of fact and doesn't require proof of reliance (cmt. 3).
It's a specific statement about the boat's condition.
Advertising and brochures can create express warranties.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Brochure: "seaworthy"

q: Contract: 1,000 units at $20, tender June 1, F.O.B. seller's plant. The buyer repudiates May 1. Market at the plant: May 1, $18; June 1, $15. No resale. No incidentals. What are the seller's § 2-708(1) damages?
o: Nothing, because no resale occurred.
oe: Resale isn't required.
Correct. Time and place for tender: ($20 minus $15) × 1,000. The seller's rule isn't "when learned."
That's the price.
That's the difference between the two market prices.
That uses the date of repudiation.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Market math, seller

q: Under § 1-201(b)(20), "good faith" means:
o: the duty to disclose all material facts during contract negotiations.
reasonable care, so that a party who acts negligently acts in bad faith.
honesty in fact and observance of reasonable standards of fair dealing.
honesty in fact, judged by the party's own subjective belief.
acting as a fiduciary toward the other contracting party.
oe: Good faith applies to performance and enforcement, not negotiation.
The objective prong is fair dealing, not negligence.
Correct. Good faith has a subjective prong (honesty, motive) and an objective prong (fair dealing).
That is the old subjective-only definition, which some states kept in Article 1.
Good faith in performance is not a fiduciary duty (Market Street).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith definition

q: A lease states a liquidated damages formula that fairly anticipated the lessor's loss at signing. As it happens, the lessor's actual loss is far lower. The lessee argues penalty. Which is correct?
o: The clause must also be conspicuous.
The clause stands, as only then-anticipated harm matters.
The clause fails, as actual harm controls.
The clause fails, as a formula isn't allowed.
The clause fails, unless proof of loss would be difficult.
oe: There's no such requirement.
Correct. Section 2A-504(1).
That isn't the lease test.
A formula is expressly allowed.
That's an Article 2 factor, not § 2A-504(1).
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Liquidated damages with a formula

q: Which of the following is NOT required for an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: The seller has reason to know the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment.
The seller has reason to know the particular purpose for which the goods are required.
The buyer has a particular purpose, not just the ordinary one.
The seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.
The buyer actually relies on the seller's skill or judgment.
oe: Required.
Required (§ 2-315).
Required (cmt. 2).
Correct. § 2-315 applies to any seller, though in practice it is usually a merchant.
Required.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fitness: elements

q: In January, Farmer Gonzo signs a contract to sell Camilla all the sweet corn that will be grown that summer on his north field. He plants the field in May, and the corn is harvested in August. When were the goods identified to the contract?
o: In January, when the contract was made.
In August, when the corn was harvested.
Never, because growing crops aren't goods until they're severed from the land.
When the corn is shipped or marked for Camilla.
In May, when the corn was planted and became a growing crop.
oe: Identification at contracting applies to goods that are already existing and identified. The corn didn't exist yet.
Harvest isn't the trigger under § 2-501(1)(c). Planting is.
Growing crops are goods (§§ 2-105(1), 2-107(2)).
That's the rule for other future goods under § 2-501(1)(b). Crops have their own rule.
Correct. For crops to be harvested within twelve months or the next normal harvest season, identification occurs "when the crops are planted or otherwise become growing crops" (§ 2-501(1)(c)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Identification of crops

q: Which of the following is NOT a repudiation of a contract for the sale of goods?
o: A seller's failure to tender delivery of the goods on the date its performance is due.
A seller's clear statement, a month before delivery, that it won't deliver.
A seller's statement that it will deliver only if the buyer agrees to a price increase not required by the contract.
A seller's sale to a third party of the one-of-a-kind goods it had agreed to sell to the buyer.
A buyer's failure to provide adequate assurance within 30 days after receiving a justified demand.
oe: Correct. Failing to perform when performance is due is a breach, not a repudiation. A repudiation is a party's signal before performance is due that it won't perform when required.
This is the classic anticipatory repudiation (§ 2-610).
Conditioning performance on a change in terms is a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
Conduct that makes performance impossible is a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 1).
This is a repudiation under § 2-609(4).
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — What is NOT a repudiation

q: What is the difference between the parol evidence rule and the statute of frauds?
o: The PER applies only to consumer contracts.
The PER requires a writing; the SOF bars evidence of terms.
Nothing; they are two names for the same rule.
The PER governs what evidence of terms comes in; the SOF, enforceability.
None of the above.
oe: It applies to any writing the parties intended as final.
Reversed and garbled. The SOF requires a record for enforcement; the PER bars evidence of certain terms.
They answer different questions: what evidence comes in, and whether the contract can be enforced at all.
Correct.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 6–8 · XII · Parol evidence rule — PER vs. SOF

q: Which was NOT part of the reasoning in Hyundai v. Goodin?
o: Warranties work as marketing tools.
A dealer's disclaimer would leave her without a remedy.
The dealer is the manufacturer's agent, so a contract exists.
Goods reach consumers through intermediaries.
The law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers.
oe: Part of the court's reasoning.
Part of the court's reasoning.

Correct. The court didn't treat the dealer as an agent. It relied on the erosion of privity's freedom-of-contract rationale, intermediaries in distribution, warranties as marketing tools, consumer expectations, spreading the cost of lemons, and the disclaimer gap.
Part of the court's reasoning.
Part of the court's reasoning.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Goodin reasoning

q: A seller tenders 100 widgets on June 1, ten of them defective, under a contract requiring delivery by June 30. The buyer rejects. On June 5 the seller gives notice that it will replace the ten by June 20, and offers no compensation for delay. It does so. May the buyer refuse?
o: Yes, because the seller offered no compensation.
No, but only if the buyer has not yet covered.
Yes, because only a full new tender of all 100 can be a cure.
Yes, because rejection ended the seller's rights.
No, because this is a timely, noticed cure within the contract time.
oe: No allowance is needed when time remains.
A buyer's early cover doesn't defeat cure within the time; cure stands.
Replacing the defective units can fully negate the breach.
The seller keeps its right to cure.
Correct. Section 2-508(1). Any delay damages would be small, and the buyer can't refuse a conforming cure.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Cure with a lower-priced tender

q: Buyer and seller each send confirmations of an oral deal. One says "disputes in Ohio," the other "disputes in Texas." Neither objects. Which is correct under § 2-207 comment 6?
o: The first confirmation sent controls.
Each is assumed to object, so both clauses drop out.
The contract fails for lack of agreement.
The seller's clause controls, as it's the merchant in the goods.
The last confirmation sent controls.
oe: There's no first-shot rule.

Correct. Comment 6 assumes each party objects to the other's conflicting clause. Neither becomes a term, and the Code's gap fillers govern if needed. Compare Daitom's knock-out rule for different terms.
The oral deal stands; only these clauses drop out.
No rule favors the seller.
The last-shot rule is what § 2-207 abolished.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Conflicting confirmations

q: A seller, having delivered the same substitute brand to this buyer six times without complaint, reasonably ships it again on the last day allowed. This time the buyer rejects it and demands the contract brand. The seller promptly promises it within five days and delivers. Which is correct?
o: The cure is too late, as the contract time has run.
The cure fails, as past dealings are irrelevant.
The cure is good, and the buyer waives all other claims.
The cure is good, though the buyer may claim any delay damages.
The cure fails, unless the seller paid an allowance.
oe: Section 2-508(2) extends past the contract time.
Past acceptance supports reasonable grounds.
Cure doesn't waive delay damages.
Correct. The past course gives reasonable grounds under § 2-508(2). A further reasonable time applies, and the buyer may still have delay damages (§§ 2-714(1), 2-715).
"With or without money allowance."
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Cure after shipment contract failure

q: A client wants to resell used copiers after a buyer's breach and asks for instructions. Which is sound?
o: Pick the method, give notice, tie it to the contract, sell promptly.
Don't tell the buyer anything about the resale.
Sell to the first bidder and keep no records.
Set the price above the contract price, or the sale is invalid.
Delay until the market recovers, to reduce the claim.
oe: Correct. Resell in normal channels on normal terms, at the best reasonable price, and keep records.
A private sale needs notice.
Records show the sale was reasonable.
No such requirement.
Delay may be commercially unreasonable.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale instructions

q: Which formation rule from Article 2 has NO analog in Article 2A?
o: A firm offer made by a merchant.
A contract formed in any manner showing agreement.
Open terms not defeating a contract.
Acceptance in any reasonable manner.
The battle of the forms in § 2-207.
oe: Section 2A-205 is the analog.
Section 2A-204 is the analog.
Section 2A-204(3) is the analog.
Section 2A-206(1) is the analog.
Correct. There's also no analog to § 2-206(1)(b) on prompt-shipment orders. Lessees rarely send orders, and leases are negotiated, not exchanged on forms.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — No battle of the forms

q: Under Official Comment 3 to § 2-313, what must a buyer show about reliance to recover for breach of an express warranty?
o: That the buyer's reliance on the statement was reasonable.
That the buyer relied solely on the seller's statement.
Nothing in particular; such affirmations are presumed part of the bargain.
That the buyer read the warranty before signing the contract.
None of the above.
oe: Not required by Comment 3.
Comment 3 says no particular reliance need be shown.
Correct. Courts split (reliance, no reliance, rebuttable presumption), but Comment 3 is the Code's own position.
Warranties in written contracts, and even owner's manuals read after the sale, can count.
C is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain

q: A non-merchant lessee of a camera sells it to a good-faith buyer, claiming to own it. What does the buyer get?
o: Only the leasehold the lessee had, subject to the lease.
The residual interest.
A voidable title.
Full title free of the lessor.
Nothing at all.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-305(1). Entrustment needs a merchant in such goods.
That's the lessor's.
The lessee has no title.
That needs a merchant lessee and ordinary course.
The lessee can transfer its leasehold.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Lessee sells leased goods

q: A merchant buyer's contract for laboratory freezers provides: "Seller's total liability for any claim shall not exceed the price paid for the goods." Which statement is most accurate?
o: The cap is valid only if it is conspicuous.
The cap is a liquidated damages clause and must be reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
The cap is a limitation of remedy, enforceable unless it fails of its essential purpose or is unconscionable.
Caps on damages are void in contracts for the sale of goods.
None of the above.
oe: Remedy limitations need not be conspicuous.
A cap is a limitation of remedy, not liquidated damages. It doesn't fix an amount; it sets a ceiling on proven damages.
Correct. § 2-719(1)(a) lets the parties limit or alter the measure of damages, subject to failure of essential purpose (§ 2-719(2)) and unconscionability (§ 2-302, § 2-719(3)).
§ 2-719(1)(a) expressly permits limiting the measure of damages.
C correctly states the rule.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Cap at the price

q: A buyer agreed to pay C.O.D. When the shipment arrives, the crate is visibly smashed and leaking. Must the buyer pay before inspecting?
o: No, because the nonconformity is apparent without inspection.
Yes, but the buyer may reject the goods after paying.
Yes, because C.O.D. means the buyer must pay first.
No, because a buyer may always inspect before paying, even C.O.D.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer is excused from paying here.
§ 2-512(1)(a) has an exception.
C.O.D. normally removes the pre-payment inspection right.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Pay before inspection

q: Under a contract for four quarterly installments of pumps, the seller emails that the first installment will be three weeks late but that it will catch up by the second. The buyer, who has since realized it needs only half the pumps, wants to cancel the whole contract. What is the buyer's best course?
o: Cancel the whole contract, because the buyer's reduced needs are a valid reason.
Demand assurance in writing and reserve its rights.
Do nothing and accept late delivery, because the seller promised to catch up.
Cancel the whole contract now, because any repudiation lets the buyer cancel.
None of the above.
oe: They aren't a legal ground for cancellation.
Correct. Problem 6-5: don't cancel yet; demand assurance under § 2-609 and reserve rights (§§ 2-610, 2-612).
The buyer can protect itself without giving up rights.
Canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — One late installment

q: Which of the following is a way UCC Article 2 changed the common-law rules of offer and acceptance?
o: An acceptance may be made in any reasonable manner and medium.
A merchant's signed offer can be irrevocable without consideration.
An acceptance need not mirror the offer to form a contract.
An order for prompt shipment can be accepted by shipping the goods.
All of the above.
oe: True (§ 2-206(1)(a)), but it is not the only change listed.
True (§ 2-205), but not the only change.
True (§ 2-207(1)), but not the only change.
True (§ 2-206(1)(b)), but not the only change.
Correct. The slides list all four, plus treating a written confirmation as an acceptance (§ 2-207(1)).
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — How the UCC changed offer and acceptance

q: In Roth Steel v. Sharon Steel, why was the price modification unenforceable?
o: Because Roth was not a merchant, so a stricter good-faith rule applied.
Because it was not in a writing signed by Roth.
Because it lacked consideration from Roth for the higher price.
Because Sharon extracted it by threatening to stop selling to Roth.
Because a market shift is not a legitimate reason to seek a modification.
oe: Both were merchants.
The case turned on good faith, not on a writing.
Consideration isn't needed (§ 2-209(1)).
Correct. Good faith has two parts: an objective reason and honesty in fact. Extracting the change by threatening to breach failed the subjective prong.
The court found Sharon passed the objective test: the market shift gave it a legitimate commercial reason.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Roth Steel

q: A quarry tells a pump dealer it needs a pump that can drain its pit at 80 gallons per minute and relies on the dealer to choose one. The dealer's invoice expressly warrants that the pump it selects is "rated at 50 gallons per minute." The pump delivers exactly 50 gallons per minute. The dealer argues its express warranty displaces any implied warranty. Who wins?
o: The dealer, because express warranties always displace inconsistent implied warranties.
The quarry, because express warranties don't displace the fitness warranty.
The quarry, but only under the implied warranty of merchantability.
The dealer, because the quarry should have supplied its own technical specifications.
The dealer, because the pump met its express rating, so there was no breach.
oe: § 2-317(c) makes an exception for the implied warranty of fitness.

Correct. Warranties are cumulative; when they can't be reconciled, express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties other than fitness for a particular purpose (§ 2-317(c)). The quarry's fitness claim survives.
A 50-gpm pump that pumps 50 gpm is likely fit for its ordinary purpose; the quarry's claim is fitness.
Buyer-supplied specs would defeat reliance, but here the quarry relied on the dealer's selection.
Meeting the express rating doesn't satisfy the separate fitness warranty for the quarry's 80-gallon need.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Express vs. fitness: cumulation

q: A court sees that § 2-713 would give a buyer $200,000 when its true loss was $14,500. How does the text suggest thinking about the formula?
o: As void whenever it exceeds the buyer's true loss.
As binding in every case, whatever the true loss.
As a floor, so the buyer always gets at least that.
As a tool for reaching the expectancy, in tension with § 1-305(a).
As proof of punitive damages against the seller.
oe: It isn't void; some courts apply it anyway.
Courts split, so it isn't binding in every case.
That's not the text's treatment.
Correct. The recurring patterns are a buyer that passes its extra cost to someone else (7-9) and a buyer with a fixed-price resale (7-10). Courts split on what to do.
Penal damages aren't available.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Formula vs. expectancy

q: Which is listed in the text as an open question once privity falls away?
o: Whether a warranty needs a writing.
Whether the buyer must be a natural person.
Whether notice must go to the manufacturer.
Whether goods must be movable.
Whether Article 2 applies to sales.
oe: Express warranties need no writing.
Not an open question listed; Alternative C covers any person.
Correct. Others: refund and of which price; § 2-712 or § 2-713 damages; whose knowledge tests consequentials; when limitations begin; choice of law; a distributor's duty.
Section 2-105 settles that.
Plainly it does.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Open questions

q: At a garage sale, Paulette sells Ron a lamp for $20 and tells him he can pick it up on her porch that afternoon. Paulette puts the lamp on the porch and tells Ron it's there. Before Ron arrives, a storm destroys the lamp. Who bears the loss?
o: Paulette, because Ron never took possession.
Ron, because a non-merchant's risk passes on tender of delivery.
Paulette, because she had a duty to protect the lamp.
It is shared equally between Paulette and Ron.
None of the above.
oe: Receipt is the test for merchant sellers only.
Correct. § 2-509(3). Paulette completed tender by putting the lamp at Ron's disposition and telling him.
Once tender is complete, the risk is on the buyer.
There's no splitting.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Non-merchant seller: tender

q: Bert's contract to supply Ernie's restaurant with handmade pasta says: "Neither party may assign this contract." Bert later sends the restaurant pasta made by a different pasta maker under Bert's label. The pasta is equal in quality. Ernie objects. Who is right?
o: Bert, because the clause bans only assignments of rights, and Bert assigned nothing.
Ernie, but only because handmade pasta always gives the buyer a substantial interest in the original maker.
Bert, because the substitute pasta is equal in quality and Ernie suffers no harm.
Bert, because the clause is unenforceable as a restraint on alienation.
Ernie, because a ban on assigning "the contract" is generally read to bar delegation of performance.
oe: It's the reverse. § 2-210(4) reads "assign this contract" as a bar on delegating duties, not on assigning rights.
Ernie may well have such an interest, but he doesn't need it. The contract clause alone bars the delegation.
Equal quality would matter if the contract were silent. Here the parties agreed otherwise, and § 2-210(1) honors that agreement.
Restraints on assigning rights to payment are overridden by § 9-406(d), but parties may freely bar delegation of performance.

Correct. Under § 2-210(4), a prohibition on assigning "the contract" is construed (unless the circumstances indicate otherwise) as barring only the delegation of the assignor's performance. That is exactly what Bert did.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — "Assign this contract" ban: delegation

q: Big Bird, a birdseed wholesaler, sells 1,000 sacks of seed that are stored at Snuffy's Storage, an independent warehouse. No document of title has been issued. At Big Bird's request, Snuffy's emails Cookie Monster: "We now hold the 1,000 sacks for you; come get them anytime." That evening, before Cookie Monster can arrange a truck, a fire at Snuffy's destroys the sacks. Who bears the loss?
o: Big Bird, because Cookie Monster had no reasonable time to pick up the goods.
Snuffy's, because a warehouse bears the risk of loss for goods it stores.
Cookie Monster, because risk passed when the warehouse acknowledged his right to possession.
Big Bird, because no document of title was ever issued.
Big Bird, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer physically receives the goods.
oe: The reasonable-time-to-present rule applies to a nonnegotiable document or a direction to the bailee. A bailee's acknowledgment passes risk right away.
A warehouse is liable only for its own failure of care. Between seller and buyer, the risk had passed.

Correct. When goods are held by a bailee and are to be delivered without being moved, risk passes on the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right to possession (§ 2-509(2)(b)). Snuffy's email was that acknowledgment.
A document isn't necessary. Acknowledgment by the bailee is one of the three ways risk passes under § 2-509(2).
The merchant receipt rule in § 2-509(3) doesn't govern goods held by a bailee. Section 2-509(2) does.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Goods held by bailee; acknowledgment

q: Mokey buys 20 skeins of yarn and finds the color varies slightly among the five dye lots. The variation is within what the yarn trade permits. Has the seller breached the warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because merchantable goods must be of identical color and quality.
Yes, because a merchant seller warrants uniformity among lots.
No, because the variation is within what trade usage permits.
No, because color is a matter of taste rather than quality.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-314(2)(d) allows variations permitted by the agreement.
Being a merchant triggers the warranty but doesn't mean it was breached.
Correct. Problem 3-10.
That isn't the reason. The test is whether the variation is within what the agreement, including trade usage, permits.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Yarn dye lots

q: For which goods is § 2-708(1) market price hardest to prove?
o: Wheat with published daily quotations.
Copper with daily market reports.
Crude oil traded on a commodity exchange.
Standard bolts sold by many firms.
Unique goods, like a commissioned painting.
oe: Easy: published quotations.
Easy: published quotations.
Easy: published quotations (§ 2-724).
Easy: many comparable sales.
Correct. Fungibles with published quotations are easy (§ 2-724).
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Market proof

q: Seller insists that Buyer pay for a delivery of lumber before Buyer can inspect it. The contract is silent on inspection and payment. Who is right?
o: Seller, because inspection is only allowed after acceptance.
Buyer, because it may inspect before paying unless otherwise agreed.
Buyer, provided the lumber turns out to be defective.
Seller, because payment is due on delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Inspection comes before acceptance.
Correct. § 2-513(1); Problem 4-5(a).
The right to inspect doesn't depend on a defect.
Payment is due on receipt, but the buyer may inspect before payment unless otherwise agreed.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection before payment

q: Rowlf sells pianos to Doc's Music Hall, payment due in 60 days, and assigns the right to payment to Fraggle Bank. The bank notifies Doc. Doc then discovers the pianos are defective. Which statement is correct?
o: Doc must pay the bank but keeps its defenses against it.
Doc may refuse to pay anyone until Rowlf consents to the defense.
Doc loses its defenses, because the bank took the assignment in good faith.
Doc may keep paying Rowlf until the dispute is resolved.
Doc must pay both Rowlf and the bank in full.
oe: Correct. The assignee steps into the assignor's shoes; the obligor keeps its defenses.
Doc's defenses don't depend on Rowlf's consent.
The obligor keeps its defenses against the assignee.
Once notified, the obligor must pay the assignee.
Doc pays once, to the assignee.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Notice to obligor

q: A farmer rejects a defective tractor at planting time. The dealer refuses to take it back and offers no loaner, and no rental is available. The farmer plants 400 acres with it and offers to pay for the use. Is the rejection undone?
o: No, and the farmer owes nothing for the use.
Probably not, as the use was reasonable and necessary.
Yes, as the farmer should have left the land unplanted.
Yes, as any use after rejection is an acceptance.
Yes, unless the tractor was a consumer good.
oe: An offset for the value of use is likely.
Correct. Johannsen: the seller's refusal, hardship, mitigation, lack of prejudice and any bad faith favor the farmer. It's a fact question, and an offset for use is likely.
Mitigation points the other way.
The evolving majority rejects that rule.
Johannsen isn't limited to consumers.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Use after rejection, Johannsen

q: Rosita, a dressmaker, visits a fabric wholesaler and handles a swatch cut from a bolt of silk charmeuse. She orders 300 yards "like this." The silk delivered is noticeably thinner and coarser than the swatch. The wholesaler says it never said anything about the weight or feel of the fabric. Which statement is most accurate?
o: A warranty arose, but only if the wholesaler intended the swatch to be a warranty.
Only an implied warranty of merchantability arose, because samples are covered by § 2-314.
No warranty arose, because the wholesaler made no oral or written statement about the fabric.
The wholesaler made an express warranty that the whole delivery would conform to the sample.
No warranty arose, because Rosita could have tested the fabric herself.
oe: The seller doesn't need to intend to make a warranty (§ 2-313(2)).
Samples create express warranties under § 2-313. Merchantability may also apply, but the sample warranty is the stronger claim.
A sample speaks for itself. Section 2-313(1)(c) requires no affirmation in words.

Correct. "Any sample or model which is made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the whole of the goods shall conform to the sample or model" (§ 2-313(1)(c)). No words are needed.
The buyer's chance to inspect doesn't defeat a warranty by sample.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Warranty by sample

q: Kermit agrees to sell Fozzie 100 kazoos for $500. Before delivery, Kermit's costs rise, and Fozzie agrees in a signed writing to pay $600 instead. Fozzie later refuses to pay more than $500, arguing he got nothing new in return. What result?
o: Fozzie wins, because the modification needed a new writing signed by both parties.
Fozzie wins, because Kermit gave no new consideration for the higher price.
Fozzie wins, because a modification must be made under § 2-207.
Kermit wins, provided a court finds the $600 price reasonable.
Kermit wins, because Article 2 modifications need no consideration.
oe: A writing is needed only if the statute of frauds or a NOM clause requires it, and only the party to be charged must sign.
§ 2-209(1) abolishes the consideration requirement for modifications.
§ 2-207 is about the battle of the forms, not modification.
The test is good faith and the formal requirements, not reasonableness of the price.
Correct. § 2-209(1). The modification must still be sought in good faith, and a market shift that makes performance a loss can justify asking (cmt. 2).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification: consideration

q: An auction house sells a consignor's antique desk at auction, without taking title. The desk is defective. Does the auction house owe an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because it's a merchant in antiques.
Almost certainly not, because it isn't a seller.
Yes, unless it says "as is" at the sale.
Yes, because it conducted the sale.
No, because antiques can never be merchantable.
oe: Merchant status doesn't help if it isn't the seller.
Correct. "Seller" means one who sells or contracts to sell (§ 2-103(1)(d)), and a sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)).
The first question is whether it's a seller at all.
Handling a sale isn't making it.
Used goods can carry the warranty in a proper case.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Only sellers warrant

q: A signed lease with no NOM clause is orally changed to extend the term a year. The lessor later denies the change, arguing the statute of frauds applies to it. Which is correct?
o: Article 2A has no analog to § 2-209(3), so courts decide case by case.
Modifications need consideration.
Section 2-209(3) applies directly.
Section 2A-208(3) bars all oral modifications.
Oral changes are always valid.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-208 omits the rule; the text says courts resolve this.
Section 2A-208(1) says otherwise.
Article 2 doesn't govern leases.
It's about waiver.
Courts decide; it isn't automatic.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Oral lease modification

q: An ice-cream shop buys a commercial freezer under a contract that makes repair or replacement of defective parts the exclusive remedy and also says, conspicuously, "SELLER IS NOT LIABLE FOR CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES." After six failed repair attempts, the repair remedy has failed of its essential purpose. The shop lost $18,000 of inventory and sales while the freezer was down. Under the approach in Razor v. Hyundai, can the buyer recover the $18,000?
o: Yes, because the exclusion wasn't in a separate document signed by the shop.
Yes, because a clause excluding consequential damages is always unconscionable.
Probably not, because the exclusion stands on its own unless it's unconscionable.
Yes, because the failure of the repair remedy knocks out every limitation in the contract.
No, because consequential damages are never recoverable for a breach of warranty.
oe: No separate signature is required.
Only an exclusion for personal injury from consumer goods is presumptively unconscionable.

Correct. Under the independent approach in Razor, the failure of a limited remedy under § 2-719(2) doesn't automatically knock out a separate exclusion of consequential damages, which is enforceable unless unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)). Commercial losses between businesses are rarely excluded unconscionably.
That's the dependent approach some courts take, but not the one in Razor.
Consequential damages are recoverable under § 2-715(2) unless validly excluded.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Consequential exclusion survives (Razor)

q: Buyer pays $5,000 down on a $20,000 contract. The seller doesn't deliver. Buyer covers with equivalent goods for $18,000 and spends $300 finding them. What must the seller pay?
oe: That leaves out the incidental cost.
That adds the savings as if they were damages.
That wrongly credits the seller with the $2,000 the buyer saved.
That forgets the refund.
Correct. The refund comes back under § 2-711(1), and the $300 is incidental. Cover is below contract, so no cover damages arise, and the seller gets no credit for the savings.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Refund plus nothing

q: On January 2, Gonzo's Feed & Seed, a merchant, emails Camilla a signed offer: "We will sell you 200 bags of chicken feed at $18 a bag. This offer will remain open until July 1." Camilla gives no consideration. On April 15, Gonzo's emails Camilla revoking the offer. On April 20, Camilla emails her acceptance. Is there a contract?
o: No, because irrevocability ended after three months, so the April 15 revocation worked.
Yes, because an email can't be a signed record, so the revocation had no effect.
Yes, because the offer stated that it would remain open until July 1.
No, because a firm offer is binding only if the offeree gives consideration for it.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for the time stated, "but in no event may such period of irrevocability exceed three months" (§ 2-205). After April 2, the offer became revocable, and it was revoked before Camilla accepted.
An email from a business account can be a signed record, and a revocation needs no signature.
The stated time exceeds the three-month cap, so irrevocability ended after three months.
A merchant's firm offer under § 2-205 needs no consideration.
One of the other choices is correct: No, because irrevocability ended after three months, so the April 15 revocation worked.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Firm offer longer than three months

q: A judgment creditor's lien attaches to a lessor's goods before the lease is enforceable. Which is correct?
o: The lessee takes free only if it paid rent in advance.
The lien is void against any lessee.
The lien attaches to the rent, not the goods.
The lessee takes subject to the lien.
The lessee takes free as a good-faith lessee.
oe: Advance rent has no role in § 2A-307(2); timing of the lien does.
It isn't void.
The lien attaches to the goods, and the lessee takes subject to it.
Correct. Section 2A-307(2). A lien arising after is subject to the lessee's rights, with exceptions.
Section 2A-307(2) favors the earlier lien.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Lien before lease

q: Midway through a supply contract, a seller emails: "We'd like you to pay 10% more given our rising costs." A week later, it emails again: "We will make no further deliveries unless you agree to the 10% increase." Which email is a repudiation?
o: Both, because any demand for more money is a repudiation.
Neither, because the seller had a legitimate business reason to ask for more money as its costs rose.
Only the first, because it asks for more than the contract gives.
Only the second, because it conditions further performance on terms the contract doesn't require.
None of the above.
oe: Only a demand that conditions performance is.
A good reason doesn't permit conditioning performance on new terms.
Asking alone isn't repudiation.
Correct. § 2-610 cmt. 2.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Asking vs. conditioning

q: Under a contract F.O.B. Toledo for 500 chairs at $40, the chairs arrive in Tampa badly nonconforming, and the buyer rightfully rejects them on arrival. It doesn't cover. When it learned of the breach, chairs sold for $46 in Toledo and $52 in Tampa. What are direct damages?
o: $6,000, using the Tampa price.
$26,000, the Tampa price of the chairs.
$4,500, averaging the two prices.
Nothing, since it failed to cover.
$3,000, using the Toledo price.
oe: Correct. After rejection on arrival, market is measured at the place of arrival (§ 2-713(2)): ($52 minus $40) × 500.
The buyer gets the difference, not the market value.
There's no averaging rule.
Section 2-712(3) preserves market damages.
Toledo is the place for tender, but the rejection-on-arrival rule moves the place.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Which formula after rejection

q: At Pepe's Cantina, Rizzo orders a "shredded chicken enchilada" and breaks a tooth on a one-inch chicken bone in the filling. Rizzo sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It depends on the test: a natural bone defeats the claim under the foreign-natural test, but not necessarily under the reasonable-expectation test.
Rizzo wins, but only if he proves that Pepe's kitchen staff failed to use reasonable care in preparing the filling.
Pepe's wins, because a restaurant can't be liable for a hidden bone that it didn't know about and couldn't have found.
Rizzo wins under any test, because food that injures a diner isn't fit for the ordinary purpose of being eaten.
Pepe's wins under any test, because a meal served in a restaurant is a sale of services, which Article 2 doesn't cover.
oe: Correct. Serving food for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)). Courts that use the older foreign-natural test deny recovery for natural substances. Most courts now ask what a consumer would reasonably expect, which for a shredded filling likely favors Rizzo.
Warranty liability doesn't require negligence.
Implied warranty liability is strict. The seller's knowledge is irrelevant.
The foreign-natural test could defeat the claim, and even the reasonable-expectation test turns on the facts.
Section 2-314(1) expressly treats serving food or drink for value as a sale.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Food: foreign-natural vs. reasonable expectation

q: A seller assigns its right to payment under a $20,000 contract to a bank, and the bank notifies the buyer. The buyer pays the seller anyway, and the seller disappears with the money. What is the buyer's position?
o: The buyer is discharged unless the bank sues within ten days.
The buyer owes the bank only half.
The buyer is discharged, because the bank should have collected from the seller.
The buyer is discharged, because it paid the party it contracted with.
None of the above.
oe: No such rule.
No splitting rule.
The risk of paying the wrong party after notice is on the buyer.
After notice, payment to the assignor doesn't discharge.
Correct. The buyer still owes the bank: once notified of the assignment, the obligor must pay the assignee (Problem 6-2(a)). No choice says that.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Paying the assignor after notice

q: A hardware-store clerk tells Ernie several things about a portable generator. Which is MOST likely an express warranty?
o: "It runs 12 hours on one tank at half load."
"You'll love having this when the power goes out."
"It's a great value at this price."
"I'd buy this one myself."
"This is the best generator on the market."
oe: Correct. It's specific and measurable, an affirmation of fact relating to the goods (§ 2-313(1)(a)).
Opinion and sales talk.
An affirmation of value, which § 2-313(2) excludes.
The clerk's opinion or commendation.
A general superlative: puffing.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Fact vs. puffing

q: What is the starting rule for property rights in leased goods?
o: A lessee always gets good title.
A lessor loses its residual on delivery.
Liens never attach to leased goods.
A buyer always takes free of the lease.
A transferor passes only what it has.
oe: It gets a leasehold.
It keeps it.
They can (§ 2A-306).
Only in some cases.
Correct. Lessee can transfer the leasehold, lessor the residual (§ 2A-303). Fixtures, accessions and titled goods are excluded here (n.18).
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Starting point

q: A buyer rightfully rejects office chairs, and the seller gives no instructions within a reasonable time. What are the buyer's options?
o: Nothing, because it must wait for instructions indefinitely.
Use them in its office until the seller objects.
Keep them as its own and pay nothing.
Destroy them after 30 days without instructions.
Store, reship, or sell them for the seller's account.
oe: Section 2-604 lets it act after a reasonable time.
Use risks acceptance or conversion.
A rejecting buyer doesn't acquire ownership that way.
Nothing in Article 2 allows that.
Correct. Section 2-604, with reimbursement. These steps are neither acceptance nor conversion.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Nonperishable, no instructions

q: A dealer leases used equipment under a conspicuous written clause, "LEASED AS IS." Which is correct?
o: It works only if separately signed.
It excludes implied warranties, unless circumstances show otherwise.
It's ineffective because merchantability isn't mentioned.
It excludes express warranties too.
It excludes the warranty against interference.
oe: Conspicuous and in writing is enough.
Correct. Section 2A-214(3)(a).
"As is" overrides that requirement.
It reaches implied warranties.
That needs specific language under (4).
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Disclaimer in a lease by "as is"

q: Bunsen's Brewery orders a custom brewing system for its new taproom, scheduled to open May 1. After discussing projected sales, the two merchants negotiate a clause: "Seller shall pay $500 per day of late delivery as liquidated damages." The system arrives 20 days late. The seller proves that because of slow spring traffic, the brewery's actual lost profit was only $1,500. Can the brewery recover $10,000?
o: No, because the clause was not printed in conspicuous type.
Only $1,500, because liquidated damages are always reduced to the buyer's proven loss.
Yes, because courts never review liquidated damages clauses negotiated between merchants.
Probably yes, because the amount was reasonable in light of the harm the parties anticipated when they contracted.
No, because the clause yields more than six times the actual harm and is therefore a penalty.
oe: Nothing in § 2-718 requires a liquidated damages clause to be conspicuous.
That would make liquidated damages pointless. A valid clause fixes the amount regardless of later-proven loss.
Merchant status doesn't remove the § 2-718(1) reasonableness test. An unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty even between merchants.

Correct. § 2-718(1) measures reasonableness against the anticipated or actual harm. A negotiated figure based on projected profits, where lost profits were hard to prove, is reasonable when made, even if actual harm turns out smaller.
Actual harm can be considered, but the disjunctive "anticipated or actual" lets a court enforce a clause that was reasonable when made. The stronger view enforces it here.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Anticipated vs. actual harm

q: Ace emails its buyer: "The first installment of valves will be a week late, and we expect you to cover the extra freight expenses. We'll catch up by the second installment." Is the demand for extra expenses a repudiation?
o: No, because repudiation must be in a signed writing.
Yes, because the delay notice repudiates the whole contract.
No, unless Ace makes its own performance depend on the buyer's payment.
No, because Ace is a merchant entitled to recover costs.
Yes, because Ace demanded more than the contract gives.
oe: Repudiation can be by words or conduct.
Canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract.
Correct. Problem 6-5. (The statement that installment one will be late is a definite repudiation of that installment.)
Merchant status doesn't matter.
Demanding more is not by itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Demanding more

q: In a deal between merchants, the seller's acknowledgment adds a term letting the seller cancel the entire contract if any single invoice is paid even one day late. The buyer's order said nothing on the subject, and the buyer never objects. What is the most likely status of the term?
o: It is part of the contract unless a court finds it unconscionable.
It is not part of the contract, because it would materially alter the deal.
