It is part of the contract, because both parties are merchants.
It turns the acknowledgment into a counteroffer.
It is part of the contract, because the buyer did not object within a reasonable time.
oe: The test is material alteration, not unconscionability.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(b). Cmt. 4 lists a power to cancel on any late invoice as a material alteration.
Merchant status only brings added terms within § 2-207(2); a material alteration still stays out.
An added term doesn't do that unless the acceptance is expressly conditional on assent.
Silence doesn't help a term that materially alters the contract.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Material alteration

q: Gobo agrees to sell 40 pallets of radish seed to Wembley. The contract says: "Seller will ship the goods to Buyer's warehouse, 12 Rock Road, Fraggleton." It has no F.O.B. or other delivery term. Gobo delivers the seed to a reputable carrier, makes a reasonable shipping contract, and emails Wembley the tracking details. The truck overturns and the seed is ruined. Must Wembley pay?
o: Yes, but only if Wembley had already paid for the seed before it shipped.
Yes, because risk passed when Gobo duly delivered the seed to the carrier.
No, because naming the buyer's warehouse in the contract makes it a destination contract.
No, because the carrier, not the buyer, is responsible for losses during transit.
No, because Wembley never received the seed, and risk passes only on the buyer's receipt.
oe: Payment has nothing to do with when risk passes.

Correct. Article 2 presumes a shipment contract. A "ship to" instruction only names where the goods are going; it doesn't make the seller responsible for delivering them there (§ 2-503 cmt. 5). Gobo met its § 2-504 duties, so risk passed under § 2-509(1)(a).
Naming the buyer's address doesn't create a destination contract. The seller must expressly agree to deliver at a particular destination, as with "F.O.B. buyer's warehouse."
The carrier may be liable to whoever bears the risk, but between seller and buyer the risk had passed to Wembley.
Receipt is the rule for a merchant seller in a non-shipment case under § 2-509(3). Here the goods were shipped by carrier, so § 2-509(1) applies.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — "Ship to" term is a shipment contract

q: Which of the following is a consequence of a buyer's acceptance of goods?
o: The buyer automatically waives damages for nonconformity.
The buyer may still reject the goods for any nonconformity.
The buyer must notify the seller of any breach within a reasonable time.
The seller bears the burden of proving the goods conformed.
None of the above.
oe: Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies (§ 2-607(2)).
Acceptance ends the right to reject (§ 2-607(2)).
The burden shifts to the buyer (§ 2-607(4)).
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — After acceptance

q: Telly's contract with a printer has a NOM clause. Telly casually tells the printer that a later delivery date "should be fine." Without asking for a signed change, the printer turns down other work to meet the new date. If Telly sues for late delivery, why is the printer's estoppel argument weak?
o: Estoppel is not available under the UCC.
Estoppel requires a signed record.
Estoppel requires a signed record showing the promise the printer relied on.
The NOM clause makes it less reasonable to rely on an unwritten change.
None of the above.
oe: It is. § 1-103(b) preserves estoppel.
Estoppel rests on reliance, not on a writing.
It turned down other work.
Correct. Estoppel needs reasonable, detrimental reliance. A NOM clause undercuts the reasonableness of relying on an oral change (Problem 3-5(C)).
D is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Estoppel and a NOM clause

q: A buyer in a privity-abolished state tells only the retailer of a defect, then sues the manufacturer. Under the text, what is the status of the notice issue?
o: Notice to the manufacturer is always required by statute.
Notice bars the claim.
It is open: notice to the retailer may or may not be enough.
Notice to the retailer is always enough.
Notice is unnecessary against a remote seller.
oe: Section 2-607 says "the seller."
Notice preserves it.
Correct. See pp. 338-339. A careful buyer notifies both.
Not settled.
That isn't established.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Remote seller's notice

q: Under § 2-706, a seller's resale damages equal:
o: Contract price plus lost profit on the deal.
Market minus contract, plus incidental damages.
Resale minus contract, plus incidental damages.
Contract minus resale, plus incidental, minus saved.
Contract minus resale, plus consequential damages.
oe: That isn't the formula.
That also reverses the market measure.
That reverses the formula.
Correct. Every aspect of the sale must be commercially reasonable, and it must be in good faith and reasonably identified to the broken contract.
Sellers get no consequential damages.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale formula

q: Which is the best reason for a buyer to cover even when market damages look adequate?
o: Cover converts the buyer's claim into specific performance.
Market damages are unavailable for fungible goods.
Consequential damages exclude losses that cover would have prevented.
Cover is required before the buyer can file a lawsuit.
Cover always yields more than the market measure.
oe: Cover is a damages measure.
They are easiest to prove for fungibles.
Correct. Section 2-715(2)(a). The buyer may also simply need the goods.
Section 2-712(3) says the opposite.
It can yield less, and a buyer who covers is held to it.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Why cover

q: Which is NOT correct for a public resale under § 2-706(4)?
o: The seller may never bid at the sale.
It should be held at a usual place, if one is available.
Goods not in view must be available for inspection.
Only identified goods may be sold, absent a futures market.
Notice of time and place is required, except for perishables.
oe: Correct. This is false: the seller may buy at a public sale. Otherwise it must be made at a usual place if available, on notice of time and place, of identified goods (unless a recognized futures market exists), and with goods available for inspection if not in view.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Public sale rules

q: Snuffy's buyer has always paid Snuffy on time, but Snuffy learns from the trade press that the buyer is paying its other suppliers months late. Can Snuffy have reasonable grounds for insecurity?
o: Only if the buyer is insolvent in the balance-sheet sense.
Yes, because grounds need not arise from the contract at hand.
No, because trade-press reports are unverified hearsay.
No, because the buyer is current on its contract with Snuffy.
Only if the buyer admits that it can't pay its debts.
oe: Insolvency isn't required.
Correct. Being late on other accounts is a classic ground (§ 2-609 cmt.).
Reasonable grounds are a commercial judgment, not a rule of evidence.
Grounds need not arise from this contract.
An admission isn't required.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Grounds unrelated to this contract

q: An oral two-year lease of a backhoe for $600 a month is performed: the lessee receives and accepts the backhoe and pays for three months. The lessor then demands the backhoe back. Which is correct?
o: The lease is enforceable as to goods received and accepted, for a reasonable term.
It's unenforceable, as there's no record.
It's unenforceable because $1,000 is exceeded.
It's enforceable for exactly two years in all cases.
It's enforceable because rent was paid.
oe: Correct. Sections 2A-201(4)(c) and (5). Total rent exceeds $1,000, but receipt and acceptance satisfies the exception. The term is what's reasonable, absent a record or admission.
The exception applies.
That triggers the statute, but the exception saves it.
The term rule is in (5).
Rent alone isn't the exception.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Leases and statute of frauds

q: A restaurant rightfully rejects 30 cases of imported wine and notifies the seller. Which of the following may the restaurant NOT do with the rejected wine?
o: Resell it for the seller's account if the seller gives no instructions within a reasonable time.
Hold it with reasonable care for the seller to remove.
Store it for the seller's account if the seller gives no instructions.
Serve some of it to customers while waiting for the seller.
Follow the seller's reasonable instructions for returning it.
oe: Correct. After rejection, any exercise of ownership by the buyer is wrongful against the seller (§ 2-602(2)(a)).
A merchant buyer must (§ 2-603(1)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Duties after rejection

q: Manufacturer warrants a copier "3 years from purchase" and sells it to Distributor on June 1, 2021. Distributor disclaims all warranties and sells to Retailer. Retailer warrants it for 1 year and sells to Buyer on April 1, 2022. In a privity-abolished state, the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2023. Which is correct?
o: Implied warranties can't apply after one year.
Retailer's express warranty is still running.
Manufacturer's warranty has expired on every reading.
Distributor is now liable, as Retailer's warranty has ended.
Retailer's warranty has expired; Manufacturer's three years still runs.
oe: The limitations period is four years.
It expired on April 1, 2023.
Three years from June 1, 2021 is June 1, 2024.
Its disclaimer still works.
Correct. The implied warranty needs a defect at tender and four years under § 2-725 hasn't run.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Copier chain: Nov. 2023

q: A contract reads "F.O.B. Buyer's store, Wilmington." The goods are destroyed in a fire at the carrier's terminal in Baltimore, halfway through the trip. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because this is a destination contract.
The buyer, because F.O.B. terms create shipment contracts.
The carrier, because the goods were in its terminal.
The buyer, because the seller had delivered the goods to a carrier.
None of the above.
oe: Only F.O.B. the place of shipment does.
The question is which party bears risk.
That's the shipment-contract rule.
A is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — F.O.B. buyer's city

q: A hotel chain rightfully rejects $5,000 of fresh fish after paying $1,000 down. The seller has no agent nearby and gives no instructions. The hotel sells the fish, as it must, for $3,000, with $200 of expenses. How should the proceeds be handled?
o: It keeps the $3,000 only if it covers elsewhere.
It keeps its $1,000 and expenses, with a usual commission, and remits the rest.
It remits all $3,000 and sues for the $1,000.
It keeps all $3,000, as the seller breached.
It must return the fish, not sell it.
oe: Cover has nothing to do with accounting for proceeds.
Correct. Section 2-603(2) gives reimbursement for reasonable expenses and a commission. The § 2-711(3) lien covers the prepayment.
It may first satisfy its lien and expenses.
It sells for the seller's account.
Perishables must be sold.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Merchant buyer's sale of rejected goods

q: The Count mails a written offer to buy 300 pewter figurines. The offer says nothing about how to accept. The seller accepts by text message the day the offer arrives. The Count argues that a mailed offer can be accepted only by mail. Is there a contract?
o: No, because a text message is not a signed record.
No, because acceptance must use the same medium as the offer.
Yes, but only if the seller also mails a confirmation.
Yes, because any reasonable medium of acceptance will do.
None of the above.
oe: Acceptance doesn't have to be signed; signatures matter for the statute of frauds.
The UCC rejects that rule.
No second acceptance is needed.
Correct. § 2-206(1)(a), unless the offer unambiguously says otherwise.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Medium of acceptance

q: A diner buys a sandwich at Swedish Chef's café and is injured by a piece of glass in it. Does the diner have a merchantability claim?
o: Only if the diner proves the café was negligent in preparing the sandwich.
No, because serving food is a service, not a sale.
Yes, because a sandwich with glass in it is not fit for ordinary use.
No, because the café had no way of knowing about the glass.
None of the above.
oe: Negligence is not required.
§ 2-314(1) treats serving food or drink for value as a sale.
Correct. Glass is foreign under any test.
Merchantability is strict liability.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Food served for value

q: A restaurant buys a commercial dishwasher. The seller knew the restaurant had no backup machine. The dishwasher breaks down because of a defect. Which of the following losses is a consequential damage rather than an incidental one?
o: The commission paid to a broker to find a replacement dishwasher quickly.
The cost of shipping the broken dishwasher back to the seller.
The cost of storing the dishwasher while waiting for the seller to pick it up.
The cost of having a technician inspect the dishwasher to confirm the defect.
Profits lost while the restaurant was closed for two days.
oe: Commercially reasonable charges in effecting cover are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Transportation expenses after a breach are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Expenses of care and custody of rejected goods are incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Reasonable inspection expenses are incidental damages (§ 2-715(1)).

Correct. Consequential damages include losses from the buyer's general or particular requirements that the seller had reason to know of when contracting and that the buyer couldn't reasonably prevent (§ 2-715(2)(a)).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Incidental vs. consequential damages

q: Which of the following is NOT part of the duty of good faith that the UCC imposes on every contract?
o: A duty that applies when performing the contract.
Honesty in fact in the conduct concerned.
A duty that applies when enforcing the contract.
A duty to put the other party's interests ahead of one's own.
Observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
oe: Part of it.
Part of it: the subjective prong (§ 1-201(b)(20)).
Part of it. § 1-304 covers performance and enforcement.
Correct. That's a fiduciary duty, which good faith is not.
Part of it: the objective prong.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith: elements

q: Under § 2-210, which of the following uses the terms correctly?
o: A buyer delegates its right to receive the goods.
Rights and duties are both "assigned," because the UCC uses the terms interchangeably.
A seller assigns its right to be paid and delegates its duty to deliver.
A seller delegates its right to be paid.
A buyer assigns its duty to pay.
oe: A right to receive the goods is assigned.
§ 2-210 keeps them apart: subsections (1) and (6) deal with delegation, (2) and (3) with assignment.
Correct. Rights are assigned; duties are delegated.
A right to payment is assigned, not delegated.
A duty to pay is delegated, not assigned.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Rights vs. duties

q: A lessor's lender has an unperfected security interest. A lessee, without knowledge of it, gives value and receives delivery. Which is correct?
o: The lender wins, as its interest came first.
Priority goes to whoever sues first.
The lessee loses unless it's in ordinary course.
The lease is void against the lender.
The lessee takes free under § 9-317(c).
oe: Unperfected, it loses to this lessee.
Priority isn't a race to court.
Section 9-317(c) doesn't need ordinary course.
Nothing voids it.
Correct.
topic: Wk 13 · XXXIV · Property rights in leased goods (§§ 2A-304 to 2A-308) — Unperfected security interest

q: A blueprint attached to a contract shows a beam 12 feet long; the beams delivered are 11 feet. At delivery, the seller also says, "These will last 30 years." Which statement is correct?
o: A statement after the contract can never be a warranty.
The blueprint is a description, and the later statement can be a warranty.
A blueprint is a mere opinion of the engineer.
The later statement needs new consideration to bind the seller.
A description must be in words to create a warranty.
oe: Comment 7 says it can, as a modification.
Correct. Descriptions needn't be words: specs, blueprints and past deliveries count. Under Comment 7, a statement after the deal can be a warranty as a modification needing no consideration.
A dimension is a factual description.
Section 2-209(1): none is needed.
Section 2-313 reaches any description; cmt. 5 includes technical specs.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Descriptions and post-sale statements

q: How does Article 2 treat vertical privity under Alternative A?
o: It is silent, and comment 3 leaves the chain to case law.
It abolishes vertical privity in express terms.
It requires vertical privity in express terms.
It sends the question to the Permanent Editorial Board.
It applies only to sales of services.
oe: Correct. Article 2 barely addresses privity. Alternative A speaks to horizontal privity. That's the opening Goodin used.
Alternative A doesn't address it.
It doesn't require it.
Courts decide it.
Article 2 concerns goods.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Article 2 and vertical privity

q: A seller, a buyer, a lessor and a lessee each suffer the same lost-profit loss from the other side's breach. Which can claim it as a consequential damage?
o: None of them.
The seller and the lessor.
Only the buyer.
All four.
The buyer and the lessee.
oe: Buyers and lessees can.
That's reversed.
Lessees can too.
Sellers and lessors can't.
Correct. Sections 2-715(2), 2A-520(2). Sellers and lessors get none.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Parallel: consequential damages

q: A buyer of a base-model truck at $30,000 covers with the luxury trim at $38,000 even though base models were available at $32,000. What is the likely result?
o: Nothing, since any upgrade disqualifies a purchase as cover.
About $2,000, since the seller doesn't pay for the upgrade.
$38,000, the full price of the truck.
$8,000, since cover means what the buyer actually paid.
$6,000, the premium for the luxury trim.
oe: Courts can adjust the figure or use § 2-713 instead.
Correct. Some difference in quality is fine, especially if identical goods are unavailable, but courts adjust for an upgrade.
It keeps the truck.
A reasonable substitute doesn't include an unneeded upgrade.
The buyer's expectancy was a base model; the premium isn't its loss.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Upgrade as cover

q: A copier salesperson tells an inexperienced buyer, "This model will cut your copy costs by 20%." A court asks whether this is a warranty. Which statement fits the Royal Business Machines test?
o: The test looks only at the seller's subjective intent.
Any statement by a merchant is automatically a warranty.
Reliance must be shown in writing before a warranty arises.
A warranty is likelier where the buyer is ignorant of the fact.
Sales talk is never a warranty, however specific it is.
oe: Section 2-313(2) says no specific intent is needed.
Merchant status doesn't turn opinion into fact.
No writing is required under § 2-313.

Correct. Royal's test contrasts a fact about which the buyer is ignorant with an opinion on which the buyer is expected to form its own judgment. The text questions whether relative expertise should matter.
Specific factual claims can be warranties.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Royal Business Machines

q: A contract for a $200,000 custom packaging line, drafted by the seller, says: "Liquidated damages for Seller's failure to deliver shall be $10." The seller never delivers, and the buyer suffers large provable losses. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The clause is automatically valid because the buyer could have negotiated a larger amount.
The clause must be enforced, because § 2-718 limits only clauses that are too large.
The clause is void as a penalty, because it is unreasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
The buyer may recover only $10 unless the clause was conspicuous.
It isn't a penalty, but a court may strike it as unconscionable.
oe: Opportunity to bargain is relevant to unconscionability but doesn't make the term automatically valid.
The penalty rule addresses large amounts, but unconscionability can still reach an absurdly small one.
"Penalty" describes an unreasonably large amount that punishes the breaching party. A $10 figure punishes no one.
Conspicuousness isn't the test. A conspicuous $10 clause could still be struck as unconscionable.
Correct. § 2-718(1) voids only unreasonably large amounts as penalties. Comment 1 notes that an unreasonably small amount might be stricken under the unconscionability section (§ 2-302).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Unreasonably small amount

q: Which correctly maps Article 2A warranty sections?
o: § 2A-212 express, § 2A-210 merchantability, § 2A-213 fitness.
§ 2A-210 express, § 2A-213 merchantability, § 2A-212 fitness.
§ 2A-210 express, § 2A-212 merchantability, § 2A-213 fitness.
§ 2A-211 merchantability, § 2A-212 fitness, § 2A-213 express.
§ 2A-214 express, § 2A-212 merchantability, § 2A-213 fitness.
oe: Express warranties are in § 2A-210.
Those two are reversed.
Correct. They match Article 2, except that a finance lessor gives no implied warranties.
Section 2A-211 is interference and infringement.
Section 2A-214 deals with exclusions.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Lease warranties same

q: In each contract below, the agreement says nothing about assignment or delegation. Which transfer is most likely ineffective?
o: A lumber seller assigns its right to the buyer's payment to its bank.
A buyer has its parent company pay the price on the due date.
A seller of bagged road salt has a warehouse company load and deliver the salt.
A buyer of 1,000 standard pallets, F.O.B. seller's plant, assigns its right to receive them to an affiliate that will pick them up.
A bridal designer, chosen for her signature style, hands the design and sewing of a custom gown to another shop.
oe: Assigning a right to payment almost never materially changes the buyer's duty, so it's effective (§ 2-210(2)-(3)).
Payment is payment. The seller has no substantial interest in which entity writes the check, and the buyer remains liable.
Delivering fungible goods is a classic permitted delegation. The buyer has no stake in who loads the truck.
Pickup at the seller's plant by a different company doesn't materially change the seller's duty or risk (§ 2-210(2)).
Correct. A buyer of specially made goods chosen for the maker's personal style has a substantial interest in having that maker perform, so the designer can't delegate (§ 2-210(1)).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Which transfer fails

q: Seller arrives at Buyer's farm on time with a truckload of wheat, but Buyer's bins aren't ready, so Seller can't unload. What is the legal effect?
o: Seller has failed to tender and is in breach.
Seller's tender is proper, and Buyer's delay excuses Seller's.
Buyer may reject the wheat, since it wasn't unloaded.
The contract is avoided, because neither party is at fault for the delay.
None of the above.
oe: Seller did everything required.
Correct. Problem 4-4. Buyer must furnish facilities reasonably suited to receiving the goods, and § 2-311(3) excuses the other party's delay.
The wheat conforms; nothing justifies rejection.
Nothing excuses performance entirely.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Buyer's facilities

q: A manufacturer, a lost-volume seller, loses a contract at $80,000. Variable costs it avoided are $50,000. Its CEO's salary and rent allocated to this job would be $12,000. Raw material already bought and usable elsewhere is $5,000 of the $50,000. What does § 2-708(2) yield, ignoring incidentals?
oe: It avoided the costs of producing.
That wrongly subtracts overhead.
That subtracts overhead and adds the materials.
Correct. Price minus variable costs: overhead isn't deducted. The reusable materials aren't unreimbursed reliance.
That wrongly adds the reusable materials.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Manufacturer's math, overhead

q: Rosita's Flower Shop sells its five-year-old delivery van to Telly for $9,000. The shop has never sold a vehicle before. A week later, the van's transmission fails. Did the shop give Telly an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because the van failed within a week.
No, because this is not an Article 2 transaction.
No, because the shop is not a merchant with respect to vans.
Yes, because any business that sells goods is a merchant for all purposes.
No, because implied warranties never apply to used goods.
oe: Early failure may prove breach, but only if a warranty arose in the first place.
A sale of a van is a sale of goods, squarely within Article 2.
Correct. Merchantability is implied only if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind (§ 2-314(1)). A florist selling its own van in an isolated sale isn't one (cmt. 3).
Merchant status for § 2-314 is goods-specific. Being in business generally isn't enough.
They can, with a reduced content. The problem here is that the seller isn't a merchant in vans.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Not a merchant in goods of the kind

q: A seller delivers on July 5 under a contract requiring delivery by July 1. Which is correct?
o: Late delivery is cured by a money allowance.
Late delivery can't be cured, so the buyer can only waive or settle.
Delivery within a further reasonable time always cures.
The seller may unilaterally extend the delivery date.
The buyer has no claim once the goods finally arrive.
oe: A money allowance is a settlement, not a cure.
Correct. After any other cure, the buyer may still claim delay damages (§§ 2-714(1), (3), 2-715).
Time can't be turned back; that's why lateness is incurable.
It has no such power.
Delay damages remain under §§ 2-714 and 2-715.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Late delivery incurable

q: A contract between a Chicago seller and a Boston buyer says "F.O.B. Chicago." The goods are damaged in transit through no fault of the seller. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because the goods never reached Boston.
The seller, because it chose and contracted with the carrier.
The buyer, provided it has already paid for the goods.
The buyer, because risk passed on delivery to the carrier.
None of the above.
oe: F.O.B. the seller's city is a shipment contract.
The seller's duty is to make a reasonable transport contract, not to insure the trip.
Payment is irrelevant to risk of loss.
D is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — F.O.B. seller's city

q: Kermit's purchase order offers to buy 200 chairs from Fozzie's Furniture. Fozzie's acknowledgment accepts and adds: "Interest of 1.5% per month on overdue invoices." Both are merchants, Kermit's order did not limit acceptance to its terms, and Kermit never objects. Is the interest term part of the contract?
o: No, because the term materially alters the contract.
Yes, because the acknowledgment was the last form sent.
Yes, because it is a non-material additional term and no one objected.
No, because Kermit did not sign the acknowledgment.
No, because additional terms in an acceptance are mere proposals.
oe: Interest on overdue invoices is listed in cmt. 5 as not material.
The last-shot rule is gone. The term comes in only because § 2-207(2)'s conditions are met.

Correct. § 2-207(2): between merchants an additional term becomes part of the contract unless the offer limits acceptance, the term materially alters, or objection is given. Interest on overdue invoices is a standard example of a non-material term (cmt. 5).
§ 2-207(2) does not require the offeror's signature.
That is the rule only when one of the parties is not a merchant.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Additional terms between merchants

q: Abby and a supplier sign a contract for 600 lamps to be delivered June 1. It says: "No modification is effective unless in a signed record." By phone, they agree to move delivery to June 20. On June 2, Abby sues for late delivery, arguing that the phone agreement was ineffective. What is the supplier's best argument?
o: Even if the oral change fails under the NOM clause, it can operate as a waiver of the June 1 date.
The NOM clause is unenforceable between merchants.
The phone agreement was a valid modification, because modifications need no consideration under § 2-209(1).
The parol evidence rule bars proof of the June 1 date.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-209(4): an attempted modification that fails under the NOM clause can still be a waiver.
NOM clauses are enforceable under § 2-209(2).
The NOM clause bars an unwritten modification (§ 2-209(2)).
The June 1 date is in the writing. The parol evidence rule doesn't touch later agreements anyway.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — NOM clause; failed modification as waiver

q: On May 1, a seller tells Gonzo it won't deliver the July 1 shipment. On May 10, before Gonzo has canceled, bought elsewhere, or said anything else, the seller writes that it will deliver after all. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller has retracted, which reinstates the contract.
The seller may retract only with Gonzo's consent.
The retraction works only if the seller pays damages for the delay.
The repudiation became final when it was made.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-611.
No consent is needed.
No payment is required.
It can be retracted until the next performance is due.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Retraction

q: A grocery chain rightfully rejects a delivery of 500 pounds of strawberries that arrived moldy in part. The seller has no agent or place of business in the buyer's city, and it doesn't respond to the buyer's request for instructions. The berries that are still good will spoil within a day or two. What must the buyer do?
o: Hold the strawberries until the seller picks them up, even if they spoil.
Use the good strawberries in its own stores, which is consistent with the rejection.
Destroy the strawberries, because the seller abandoned them.
Nothing, because once goods are rightfully rejected the buyer has no further obligations.
Make reasonable efforts to sell the strawberries for the seller's account.
oe: For perishables with no instructions, a merchant buyer must try to resell them.
Using the goods as its own would be an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership and could be an acceptance.
The buyer must try to salvage their value by resale.
A merchant buyer has the extra duties in § 2-603 for perishable goods.

Correct. A merchant buyer that has rightfully rejected goods in its possession, when the seller has no agent or place of business at the market of rejection, must follow the seller's reasonable instructions, and without them must make reasonable efforts to sell perishable goods for the seller's account (§ 2-603(1)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Merchant buyer's duty for perishables

q: A signed record shows that Scooter will sell Rowlf 100 piano benches for $10,000. The parties later orally agree that Scooter will deliver 110 benches for the same total price. Scooter delivers only 100, and Rowlf sues for the other 10. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The extra 10 are enforceable, because modifications need no consideration under § 2-209.
The statute of frauds likely bars the extra 10, because the writing shows only 100.
The extra 10 are enforceable, because the original signed record satisfies the statute of frauds.
The whole contract is unenforceable, because the parties modified it orally.
The extra 10 are enforceable, because the total price stayed the same after the change.
oe: The issue is the statute of frauds, not consideration.

Correct. A contract as modified within § 2-201 must satisfy it (§ 2-209(3)), and a writing doesn't support enforcement "beyond the quantity of goods shown in such writing" (§ 2-201(1)). See Problem 3-4(c).
The original writing shows 100, and it can't support enforcement of 110.
The writing still supports enforcement up to the 100 benches it shows.
The quantity limit in § 2-201(1) applies whatever the price.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Oral increase beyond the quantity in the writing

q: According to Goodin, the privity bar began as a limit on which kind of claim, and what undercut it?
o: Tort claims (Winterbottom), undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen.
Bailment claims (Winterbottom), undercut by Article 9.
Contract claims (Hadley), undercut by the Erie doctrine.
Warranty claims (Henningsen), undercut by Winterbottom.
Fraud claims (MacPherson), undercut by Magnuson-Moss.
oe: Correct. The court traced that history.
That isn't the line the court cited.
That isn't the line the court cited.
That reverses the cases.
That isn't the line the court cited.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Origins of privity

q: A dealer who regularly leases generators leases one, in an ordinary lease, with no disclaimer. The generator is defective and also infringes a patent. Which warranties did the dealer give?
o: Only non-infringement.
Fitness, but neither of these.
Only merchantability.
Merchantability and non-infringement.
Neither, unless stated expressly.
oe: Merchantability also applies.
Fitness needs a particular purpose.
A merchant lessor also warrants non-infringement.
Correct. Sections 2A-212 and 2A-211(2), since this isn't a finance lease.
They're implied.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Merchant lessor warranty

q: Which use of rejected goods is most likely to be treated as neither acceptance nor conversion?
o: A manufacturer runs rejected resin through production.
A contractor builds rejected steel into a new bridge.
A consumer keeps using a mobile home because the seller won't take it back.
A buyer lends rejected tools to a friend for a month.
A retailer sells rejected goods at a profit and keeps the proceeds.
oe: That's the classic example of what not to do.
That's inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
Correct. The evolving majority: use that is reasonable and necessary under the circumstances is neither. Walking on rejected carpet over a weekend is another safe example.
Lending is an owner's act, and it's unnecessary.
Reselling for itself is an acceptance.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Using goods after rejection

q: Lew Zealand buys a used sailboat. When he asks whether it's ready for an ocean crossing, the seller says, "She's seaworthy." On the first offshore passage, the hull leaks badly through a long-standing crack. The seller argues "seaworthy" was mere puffing. What is the most likely result?
o: The seller wins, because one-word statements are too general to be warranties.
Lew wins, because "seaworthy" asserts a fact about the boat's condition.
Lew wins, but only if the seller is a boat dealer and not a private owner.
The seller wins, because Lew could have hired a marine surveyor before he bought.
The seller wins, because the statement was about how the boat would perform in the future.
oe: Length doesn't matter. The question is whether the statement asserts a fact about the goods.
Correct. "Seaworthy" describes a specific, verifiable condition, and it was given in response to an inquiry. Those factors point toward a warranty rather than commendation. See Problem 3-5(h).
Any seller can make an express warranty.
The buyer's chance to inspect doesn't automatically defeat an express warranty.
A statement about present condition is a fact. Even promises about the goods' future performance can be warranties.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Specific condition term ("seaworthy")

q: Which is NOT an element of cover under § 2-712?
o: The buyer must act in good faith.
The goods must be in substitution for those due.
The buyer's purchase must be a reasonable one.
The buyer must find the lowest price available in the market.
The buyer must act without unreasonable delay.
oe: Required by § 2-712(1).
Required by § 2-712(1).
Required by § 2-712(1).
Correct. This isn't an element. Cover must be in good faith, without unreasonable delay, and a reasonable purchase of substitute goods. Herculean efforts to find the lowest price aren't required.
Required by § 2-712(1).
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Cover elements

q: Rowlf sells custom goods to a buyer whose credit has been downgraded and who has been paying other suppliers late. Rowlf sends a proper § 2-609 demand. The buyer replies only: "Don't worry, we'll pay." Which statement is most accurate?
o: The bare promise is adequate, since the buyer has never missed a payment to Rowlf.
Rowlf may insist on a letter of credit and refuse any other assurance.
Rowlf must ship now, because the buyer responded within 30 days.
A bare promise is likely inadequate, but real proof of solvency could suffice.
None of the above.
oe: Given these grounds, a bare promise from a shaky buyer is likely inadequate.
A letter of credit is common (Top of Iowa), but insisting only on it may be too much.
A timely reply isn't enough. It must also be adequate.
Correct. Problem 6-3(b). Adequacy depends on the party's reputation and the facts (§ 2-609 cmt. 4).
D is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Adequacy of a bare promise

q: Uncle Deadly leaves his antique pocket watch with Big Ben's Jewelers, which repairs and sells used watches, for cleaning. Big Ben's owes Camilla, a watch wholesaler, $5,000 from an earlier transaction, and it hands her Uncle Deadly's watch to reduce that debt. Camilla doesn't know the watch belongs to someone else. Who has the better claim to the watch?
o: Camilla, because accepting the watch in satisfaction of a debt is giving value for it.
Camilla, because she took the watch in good faith without knowing of anyone else's claim.
Uncle Deadly, because the entrustment rule protects only consumers who buy at retail.
Camilla, because Big Ben's is a merchant that deals in watches of that kind.
Uncle Deadly, because taking goods to satisfy a debt isn't buying in ordinary course.
oe: Value matters for good-faith purchasers under § 2-403(1). Here the question is buyer-in-ordinary-course status under § 2-403(2).
Good faith isn't enough. She must also be a buyer in ordinary course, and taking goods to satisfy a debt disqualifies her.
Merchants can be buyers in ordinary course. Camilla fails because of how she acquired the watch.
The merchant's status is necessary but not enough. The buyer must also qualify.

Correct. The entrustment power runs only to a buyer in ordinary course of business (§ 2-403(2)). The definition excludes a person who acquires goods "in total or partial satisfaction of a money debt" (§ 1-201(b)(9)).
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Entrustment: not a buyer in ordinary course

q: A grain dealer's buyer breaches in June. The dealer identifies grain to the contract after breach, and resells that grain a reasonable time later. The buyer argues the grain wasn't identified at breach. Which is correct?
o: It fails, because a dealer must sue for the price.
It counts only if the buyer consents.
It fails, because goods must be identified before breach.
It fails, because grain can't be identified.
The resale can count, as § 2-706(2) doesn't require identification at breach.
oe: Resale is an alternative.
No consent is needed.
Section 2-706(2) says otherwise.
A fungible share can be.
Correct. Section 2-704(1) lets a seller identify conforming goods in its possession or control when it learned of the breach. It must still show this was a substitute sale.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Goods not identified at breach

q: A contract says: "Buyer may not assign any rights under this agreement, and any attempted assignment is void." The seller never delivers any of the goods. The buyer assigns its claim for damages for the seller's total breach to a collection firm. Is the assignment effective?
o: Yes, but only if the seller consents after the breach occurs.
No, because the contract expressly states that any attempted assignment by the buyer is void.
Yes, because a claim for damages for breach of the whole contract is assignable despite the ban.
Yes, because anti-assignment clauses are never enforceable under Article 2.
No, because only a seller's right to payment for goods can be assigned in the face of a contractual ban.
oe: The statute makes the assignment effective without the breaching seller's consent.
The "void" language can't block this particular right. § 2-210(2) carves out claims for breach of the whole contract.
Correct. § 2-210(2) expressly allows assignment of a right to damages for breach of the whole contract, notwithstanding a contrary agreement.
They can be. A valid prohibition can make an assignment of other rights ineffective; this claim is simply an exception.
§ 9-406(d) protects rights to payment, but § 2-210(2) separately protects a claim for damages for breach of the whole contract.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Damages claim despite ban

q: What is the difference between a warranty disclaimer and a remedy limitation?
o: A disclaimer limits damages; a limitation removes the warranty.
A disclaimer means no breach; a limitation caps damages for one.
A disclaimer must be conspicuous; a limitation must be in a separate signed document.
They are the same thing, just labeled differently.
None of the above.
oe: Reversed.
Correct.
Merchantability disclaimers can be oral, and limitations need not be conspicuous or separately signed.
They work at different steps: a disclaimer goes to breach, a limitation to damages.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Disclaimer vs. limitation

q: Zoot, a saxophone importer, buys 100 saxophones from a European maker "C.I.F. Port of Baltimore." The maker loads them on a ship, buys a proper insurance policy for Zoot's benefit, pays the freight, and sends Zoot the documents. The ship sinks in a storm. Must Zoot pay the price?
o: Yes, because a C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, so risk passed on shipment.
No, because a C.I.F. contract means no arrival, no sale, and the saxophones never arrived.
No, because naming the destination port makes a C.I.F. contract a destination contract.
No, because the seller paid for insurance, which shows it kept the risk during transit.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under a C.I.F. term the price includes cost, insurance, and freight to the named destination, but the seller's obligation is to ship and to tender the documents, including insurance for the buyer's benefit (§ 2-320). Risk passes on shipment, and the buyer's protection is the insurance policy.
"No arrival, no sale" is a separate term (§ 2-324). It isn't implied by C.I.F.
C.I.F. destination is a shipment term. The named port only fixes the price components.
The seller buys insurance for the buyer's benefit precisely because the buyer bears the risk in transit.
One of the other choices is correct: Yes, because a C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, so risk passed on shipment.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — C.I.F. term

q: Miss Piggy, who owns a boutique, tells Gonzo in person: "I'll hold this gown for you at $900 until Friday." On Wednesday she sells it to someone else. Gonzo shows up Thursday ready to buy. Was Miss Piggy's offer irrevocable until Friday?
o: No, because only a signed record makes a firm offer.
Yes, because she stated a specific time.
No, because a firm offer must last at least three months.
Yes, because she is a merchant.
No, because Gonzo is not a merchant.
oe: Correct. An oral assurance is not a firm offer under § 2-205. Without consideration (an option contract), it was revocable.
Stating a time is part of the test, but the assurance must be in a signed record.
Three months is the maximum, not a minimum.
Merchant status alone is not enough. § 2-205 requires a signed record.
The offeree need not be a merchant.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Firm offer: oral promise

q: Goods are in a carrier's hands when the buyer repudiates. A truckload is involved. The buyer is solvent. Which remedies may the seller properly use now?
o: Stop delivery only.
Resell only.
Stop delivery, cancel, and then resell or claim market damages.
All of the above and consequential damages.
None of the above.
oe: It has other remedies too.
It may stop first.
Sellers get no consequentials.
The third choice is correct.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Decision path: three parties

q: A buyer rejects on June 5 under a contract with delivery by June 30. It covers on June 6 at a higher price, without giving the seller a chance to cure. The seller had given notice on June 5 that it would cure by June 20. What is the problem for the buyer?
o: It ignored the seller's right to cure, so it may have no cover claim.
Cover must be made after June 30.
There's no problem, as rejection ended the contract.
It should have revoked instead.
It waited too long to cover.
oe: Correct. Section 2-508(1). With cure available, the seller hadn't finally breached.
Not exactly; the problem is cure.
Rejection doesn't end the contract.
It rejected properly.
It covered too soon.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Rejection, cure, cover timeline

q: A contract says: "Buyer may not assign its rights under this contract." Buyer assigns its right to receive the goods anyway. What is the likely effect of the clause?
o: The assignment is void, because the clause expressly forbids it.
The contract is automatically canceled, because Buyer breached.
The clause bars only delegation, so Buyer has done nothing wrong.
The assignment is valid, and the clause has no effect at all.
The assignment is effective, but Buyer may be liable to Seller for breach.
oe: To make an assignment ineffective, the clause should say something like "any attempted assignment is void."
Nothing in § 2-210 cancels the contract.
That is how § 2-210(4) reads a ban on assigning "the contract," but this clause expressly addresses Buyer's rights.
The clause can make the assignment a breach.
Correct. Wording like "may not assign" may only make the assignment a breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Ban wording: breach vs. void

q: Between merchants, how are reasonable grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of an assurance judged?
o: By the subjective feelings of the insecure party.
According to commercial standards.
By whether the assurance includes a letter of credit.
By whether the assurance is in a notarized writing.
By the court's own sense of fairness.
oe: The test is objective.
A letter of credit is one common assurance, not the test.
No formality is required.
The Code uses commercial standards.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Commercial standards

q: The casebook cites § 2A-207 for course of performance. What do the 2026 statutes show?
o: Course of performance no longer applies to leases.
Article 2A now has a new definition in § 2A-103.
Section 2-208 now governs leases.
Section 2A-207 still governs leases.
Section 2A-207 is deleted, and § 1-303 now governs.
oe: It applies through § 1-303.
Section 1-303 controls.
Section 1-303 does.
It's reserved.
Correct. The concepts of agreement, course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade and good faith are the same.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — § 2A-207 gone

q: Under § 2-718(1), a court tests whether a liquidated damages amount is reasonable in light of all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Whether the breaching party acted willfully.
The harm the parties anticipated the breach would cause.
The difficulties of proving the loss.
The inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy.
The actual harm caused by the breach.
oe: Correct. Willfulness isn't a factor. § 2-718(1) looks only to the anticipated or actual harm, the difficulty of proving loss, and the inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy.
A statutory factor: reasonableness is judged "in the light of the anticipated or actual harm."
A statutory factor named in § 2-718(1).
A statutory factor named in § 2-718(1).
A statutory factor: the test is anticipated or actual harm.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Reasonableness factors

q: A seller repudiates a contract for copper when the price is rising. The buyer, needing the copper in two weeks, waits ten weeks hoping prices will drop. They rise further, and the buyer then buys. Which is the seller's best argument?
o: Copper is fungible, so no true cover is possible.
The buyer had to demand assurance before buying.
Any cover must occur on the repudiation date itself.
The purchase wasn't made without unreasonable delay.
The buyer's damages are capped at its down payment.
oe: Fungible goods are the easiest to cover.
Not after an unequivocal repudiation.
A reasonable time is allowed.
Correct. The delay requirement stops a buyer from speculating at the seller's expense.
No such cap exists.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Playing the market

q: Grover buys a used excavator from a dealer. A bank then sues Grover, asserting a substantial and plausible lien on the excavator. After a year of litigation, a court holds the lien invalid. Did the dealer breach the warranty of title?
o: Yes, but only if the dealer knew of the bank's claim.
No, because the court held the lien invalid, so Grover ended up with exactly the title the dealer promised.
No, because a lien isn't a defect in title.
No, because the warranty of title covers only stolen goods.
Most courts say yes, because a substantial claim breaches it even if the claim fails.
oe: The seller's knowledge isn't required.
Most courts don't require the claim to succeed.
§ 2-312(1)(b) expressly covers security interests and liens.
It also covers liens and encumbrances the buyer didn't know of (§ 2-312(1)(b)).
Correct. § 2-312 cmt. 1: the buyer shouldn't have to litigate to protect its title.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Title: colorable claim

q: A buyer repudiates a two-year monthly supply contract at month 3. Trial is at month 10. For months 4-10 the seller uses tender-date market prices. For months 11-24, which price applies?
o: The price at trial.
An expert's forecast for each later month.
The price when the seller learned of the repudiation.
The contract price.
The tender-date price for month 10.
oe: Trial-date prices aren't used; the statute looks to when the seller learned of the repudiation.
The statute replaces that.
Correct. Section 2-723(1): performance not yet due at trial.
That would give zero.
Month 10's price applies to month 10 only, not to later performance.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Long contract, seller's market

q: After months of negotiation, Rosita and a buyer sign a detailed deal for restaurant equipment that lets the buyer extend the closing date by giving written notice by May 1. The buyer forgets. Rosita, who did nothing to cause the lapse and said nothing about it, refuses to extend. The buyer claims Rosita acted in bad faith. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because good faith required Rosita to remind the buyer of the deadline.
The buyer wins, because Rosita's silence was sharp dealing like the tenant's in Market Street.
Rosita wins, because merely benefiting from the buyer's own missed deadline is not bad faith.
The buyer wins, because good faith lets a court excuse a missed deadline when the loss is great.
Rosita wins, because good faith doesn't apply to sophisticated parties.
oe: Good faith imposes no duty to be the other side's keeper.
The tenant in Market Street deliberately induced and exploited the oversight. Rosita did nothing.
Correct. Compare Vintage Rodeo: in a heavily negotiated deal, a party that simply benefits from the other side's lapse does nothing wrong. Good faith fills gaps; it doesn't rewrite express terms.
Good faith can't contradict an express term.
It applies to every contract (§ 1-304).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Benefiting from a missed deadline

q: A contract for rice says "no arrival, no sale." Through no fault of the seller, the ship sinks at sea. Which is correct under § 2-324?
o: Neither party is liable, as the seller's duty depended on arrival.
The seller has breached and owes damages.
The buyer must pay, as risk passed at shipment.
The contract becomes a C.I.F. contract.
The seller must deliver substitute rice.
oe: Correct. The term puts risk on the seller in transit, but non-arrival without the seller's fault means no breach; the contract is avoided as to those goods.
Only if the seller's fault caused the failure.
The buyer pays only if goods arrive.
Shipping terms aren't converted that way.
The term excuses delivery if goods don't arrive.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — No arrival, no sale

q: Before selling a painting to Bert, a gallery owner tells him, "This artist is about to break out. This canvas will double in value within five years." Five years later, it's worth what Bert paid. Bert sues for breach of express warranty. What is the most likely result?
o: Bert wins, because the gallery is a merchant whose expertise in art Bert relied on.
The gallery wins, because a statement of the goods' value isn't a warranty.
Bert wins, because the gallery made a specific, measurable prediction about the canvas.
Bert wins, because express warranties can cover how goods will perform in the future.
The gallery wins, because the statement was made orally rather than in writing.
oe: Expertise can make some opinions into warranties, but a market-value prediction is excluded by statute.
Correct. "An affirmation merely of the value of the goods or a statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods does not create a warranty" (§ 2-313(2)).
A prediction about market value is still an affirmation of value, and § 2-313(2) excludes it.
Warranties can cover performance of the goods themselves, but not their future market value.
Oral statements can be warranties. The problem is the content.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Prediction of value

q: A defective compressor bought by Shop A explodes and damages the machines of Shop B next door. No one is hurt. Shop B sues the seller on the warranty. In which version does Shop B most likely have a claim?
o: Alternative A, because Shop B is a neighbor.
None, in any state.
Alternative C, where "injured" may reach property damage.
All three alternatives.
Alternative B, because Shop B may be affected.
oe: A reaches family, household and home guests.
Alternative C can apply.
Correct. Alternatives A and B are limited to natural persons injured in person.
Only C fits.
B needs a natural person injured in person.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Horizontal, business loss

q: Lopez contracts to deliver 200 chairs by June 30. On June 10 she tenders 200 chairs of the wrong color, and the buyer rejects. On June 12 she notifies the buyer she will deliver the right color by June 28. What is her right?
o: She has no right, because a rejection ends the contract.
She may cure, but only with a money allowance.
She may cure only if the buyer agrees.
She may cure, because time remains and she gave seasonable notice.
She may cure only if she believed the first tender would be acceptable.
oe: Rejection refuses the tender; it doesn't end the contract.
A money allowance isn't required.
Cure here is the seller's right, not a favor.

Correct. Section 2-508(1). A conforming delivery within the contract time defeats the rejection's consequences. After rejection a seller usually offers to cure, takes the goods back and refunds, or refuses.
That's the § 2-508(2) requirement; subsection (1) has none.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Cure before the deadline

q: A seller's truck arrives with goods, and the driver demands a certified check before the buyer can open the crates. The contract has no C.O.D. term and doesn't call for payment against documents. Which is correct?
o: The seller has breached simply by asking for payment.
The buyer must pay first, because payment is due on receipt.
The buyer must pay by certified check if demanded.
The seller must first let the buyer inspect the goods.
The buyer has rejected by refusing to pay.
oe: It may ask, but must allow inspection.
Inspection comes before payment here.
Section 2-511(2): tender by any means current in the ordinary course of business is sufficient, unless the seller demands legal tender and allows time.
Correct. Section 2-503 cmt. 2: a seller demanding payment on delivery must first allow inspection, unless the deal is C.O.D., C.I.F. or against documents (§ 2-513(1), (3)).
The refusal is justified.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Seller demanding payment on delivery

q: Abby, a consumer, emails a lighting store an offer to buy a lamp. The store's email reply accepts and adds a term requiring all disputes to be arbitrated. Abby never responds. Is the arbitration clause part of the contract?
o: Yes, because the store is a merchant and the term isn't material.
No, because Abby isn't a merchant, so the term is only a proposal.
Yes, because Abby's silence is acceptance of the term.
No, because the store's reply is a counteroffer Abby never accepted.
None of the above.
oe: The § 2-207(2) rule that lets additional terms in applies only "between merchants."
Correct. § 2-207(2): additional terms are proposals, and between a merchant and a consumer they become part of the contract only if the consumer agrees.
Silence does not accept a proposal.
A definite and seasonable expression of acceptance is an acceptance even with additional terms (§ 2-207(1)).
B is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Non-merchant: proposals

q: In Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, the Coop demanded that the farmer pay margins (or post a letter of credit) and sign a promise to deliver. Why was that demand not unreasonable as a matter of law?
o: Because every demand for assurance asks for more than was promised.
Because § 2-609 lets a party demand any assurance it wants.
Because the Coop was not required to have reasonable grounds.
Because the farmer had already missed a scheduled delivery.
Because the farmer's hedge-to-arrive contracts were illegal.
oe: Correct. The court also held that grounds for insecurity are objective and need not come from the other party's own conduct (the inverted market, the Attorney General's statement, and the farmer's silence).
Demands that go too far are not adequate assurance (PDM v. Brookhaven).
Reasonable grounds are required; the Coop had them.
The farmer kept rolling delivery; the issue was future performance.
The farmer argued that; it lost.
topic: Wk 8 · XV · Insecurity & repudiation — Top of Iowa

q: According to Market Street Associates v. Frey, which of the following is permitted?
o: Exploiting your superior knowledge about the value of property before the contract is made.
Deliberately taking advantage of the other party's oversight of its contract rights during performance.
Sending deliberately ambiguous letters to keep the other side from noticing a contract clause.
Refusing to perform an express term because it has become unprofitable.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Posner drew the line between formation and performance: before contracting, a party may exploit its superior knowledge.
That is bad faith in performance.
The remand court found exactly this to be bad faith.
That is a breach, not a privilege.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Market Street: before contracting

q: A seller borrows against its rights under a supply contract, giving a bank a security interest. The buyer claims this materially changes its risk. Which is correct?
o: It releases the seller from its duties.
It isn't a material change, unless it actually delegates material performance.
It makes the bank liable to deliver.
It's void without the buyer's consent.
It's always a material change.
oe: Security doesn't discharge performance.
Correct. Section 2-210(3). A buyer is more likely than a seller to have a substantial interest in who performs.
An assignment for security doesn't delegate duties.
It's effective.
The statute says otherwise.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Security interest in contract rights

q: A seller's lost profit on the breached contract is:
o: Incidental under § 2-710.
Consequential, and so barred.
Direct, so foreseeability limits generally don't apply.
Available only with a clause in the contract.
Recoverable only with notice at contracting.
oe: It isn't an expense caused by the breach.
It comes from the breached contract itself.
Correct. It comes from the breached contract itself. Contrast a buyer's lost profits on resale, which are consequential.
The statute supplies it.
No such limit applies.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Direct, not consequential

q: A seller contracts to sell coffee "ex-ship, S.S. Marigold, Port of Newark." During unloading, while the sacks hang on the ship's tackle, a sling breaks and they fall into the harbor. Who bears the loss?
o: The carrier, as a matter of strict liability.
The seller, as risk passes only once the goods leave the tackle.
The buyer, as risk passed when the goods were loaded abroad.
The buyer, as risk passed when the ship reached port.
The seller and buyer share the loss equally.
oe: That isn't the Article 2 risk rule.
Correct. Section 2-322(2): the seller must discharge all liens and furnish a direction to deliver, and risk doesn't pass until the goods leave the ship's tackle or are otherwise properly unloaded.
Ex-ship is close to a destination term.
Arrival isn't enough under ex-ship.
Article 2 has no such split.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Ex-ship

q: A homeowner hires a renovator, who buys a range for the job, in a state that keeps vertical privity. Which step would NOT give the homeowner warranty rights against the seller?
o: Having the renovator buy as the homeowner's agent.
Having the renovator assign its warranty rights.
Having the homeowner buy the range directly.
Adding warranty language to the renovation contract alone.
Having the seller name the homeowner a beneficiary.
oe: That creates privity.
That works under § 2-210.
That creates privity.

Correct. The renovation contract can't bind the appliance seller. Better options: have the homeowner buy directly, have the renovator act as the homeowner's agent, have it assign warranty rights (§ 2-210), or get the seller to name the homeowner a beneficiary.
That works.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Renovator workaround

q: A mill waits two weeks for a crank shaft the seller failed to deliver. Which is consequential rather than incidental?
o: Profits lost while the mill sat idle.
The cost of a trip to check a substitute supplier.
Commissions paid on the cover purchase.
Storage of the rejected shaft.
Shipping to return the rejected shaft.
oe: Correct. That loss comes from the buyer's needs, not the breach itself. Incidental items include inspection, transport and care of goods, and the cost of effecting cover.
Incidental: a cost of effecting cover.
Incidental: a charge of effecting cover.
Incidental: care of rejected goods.
Incidental: transportation of rejected goods.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Classify the loss

q: Two merchants agree that if the seller fails to deliver a custom kiln, the seller "shall pay $5,000 as liquidated damages." The amount was a reasonable estimate when made. The seller never delivers, and the buyer's actual losses turn out to be $20,000. What can the buyer most likely recover?
o: $25,000, the liquidated amount plus the actual loss.
$5,000, because a valid clause fixes damages whether actual loss is higher or lower.
$20,000, because a clause that undercompensates is void as a penalty.
$20,000, because a liquidated damages clause sets only a minimum recovery.
Nothing, because the buyer must elect between liquidated and actual damages before suing.
oe: Liquidated damages replace actual damages for the covered breach; they aren't added to them.
Correct. Liquidation is a two-way bargain. A reasonable liquidated amount replaces proof of actual damages, so the buyer is held to it even when actual loss turns out larger.
A penalty is an unreasonably large amount. A reasonable estimate that turns out low isn't a penalty.
A liquidated damages clause fixes the amount; it isn't a floor.
No election requirement exists. The valid clause measures the buyer's damages.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Actual loss exceeds LD

q: Which of the following statements by a car salesperson is MOST likely to be an express warranty?
o: "This car is the best value you'll find in town this year."
"I think you'll love the way it handles on the highway."
"Trust me, you'll be very happy with this one."
"This is a great car, and you won't find a better one anywhere."
"Parts for this model are readily available locally."
oe: An affirmation of value, which § 2-313(2) excludes.
Opinion, hedged with "I think."
Puffing (compare Problem 3-7, "you'll be very happy").
General praise: puffing.
Correct. It is specific and measurable, so it is likely a warranty (Problem 3-6).
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Specific vs. general

q: Scooter Corp. buys a space heater from Fozzie's Appliance and puts it in the home office of its employee, Animal. The heater shorts out and burns Animal's garage. No one is hurt. Under which version of § 2-318 does Animal have a warranty claim against Fozzie's?
o: Alternative A only.
Alternatives A and B.
Alternatives B and C.
Alternative C only.
None of the above.
oe: Alternative A covers only natural persons in the buyer's family or household, or guests in its home, who are injured in person. Animal is an employee of a corporate buyer and suffered only property damage.
Both A and B require injury "in person." Animal suffered only property damage.
Alternative B requires personal injury, so it doesn't help Animal.
Correct. Alternative C extends warranties to any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods who is injured by the breach, and isn't limited to personal injury.
Alternative C covers Animal.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — § 2-318: property damage

q: A buyer of a custom press wants the seller to repair it. The contract says nothing about cure. Which statement is correct?
o: The buyer may force a cure under § 2-508 for any curable defect.
The seller must cure within 30 days of rejection.
Section 2-508 gives a seller a right, and imposes no duty.
The contract can't change the rules on cure.
The buyer must allow unlimited attempts at repair.
oe: That reverses the statute; cure is the seller's option.
No such duty or period exists.

Correct. That's why a buyer of custom equipment wants a clause giving it a right to demand cure (Problem 7-16). A seller may welcome such a clause as an exclusive remedy. If the breach is a failure to repair, § 2-716 might apply (p. 291 n.31).
The contract can expand or limit cure.
Cure must meet the time and notice limits of § 2-508.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — One-way right

q: A contract provides that 30 crates of tile will be delivered "C.O.D." When the truck arrives, the buyer insists on opening the crates before paying. The driver refuses. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The driver must allow inspection, because C.O.D. describes only how payment is made.
The buyer must pay, and by paying it gives up its right to inspect the tile.
The buyer may refuse to pay until it inspects, because the right to inspect can't be waived.
Once the buyer pays, it has accepted the tile and can no longer reject it.
The buyer must pay first, but paying isn't acceptance, so it can still reject.
oe: C.O.D. means payment on delivery, and § 2-513(3)(a) bars inspection before payment.
The buyer keeps the right to inspect after payment.
The right to inspect before payment applies "unless otherwise agreed," and a C.O.D. term is such an agreement.
Section 2-512(2) says payment before inspection isn't acceptance.

Correct. Under a C.O.D. term, the buyer isn't entitled to inspect before payment unless otherwise agreed (§ 2-513(3)(a)). Payment required before inspection doesn't constitute acceptance or impair the buyer's right to inspect or its remedies (§ 2-512(2)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — C.O.D.: pay first, then inspect

q: Why does § 2A-201(4)(a) say goods "specially manufactured or obtained"?
o: It reaches only goods imported from abroad.
It's a drafting error in the 2022 amendments.
It excludes lessors who manufacture goods.
It applies only to consumer leases.
It fits a lessor who buys goods for the lessee.
oe: No such limit appears.
It's deliberate.
It includes them.
Section 2A-201(4)(a) applies to all leases, consumer or not.
Correct. The added word matches how lessors acquire goods.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Specially obtained goods

q: Which set of formulas is correct?
o: Cover minus contract, and resale minus contract.
Contract minus cover, and contract minus resale.
Cover minus contract, and contract minus resale.
Contract minus cover, and resale minus contract.
None of the above.
oe: The second is reversed.
The first is reversed.
Correct. Formula direction is a classic trap.
Both are reversed.
The first choice is correct.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Formula directions

q: Under § 2-204(3), a contract for sale does not fail for indefiniteness even though one or more terms are left open if:
o: the quantity term is left open but the price is fixed.
the price and delivery terms are stated.
the parties are both merchants in goods of the kind.
the parties intended to contract and there is a basis for a remedy.
the contract is in a writing signed by both parties and states a price.
oe: The question is intent plus a basis for a remedy. A missing quantity makes a remedy harder to give, not easier.
A contract can exist with an open price (§ 2-305).
Merchant status is not required.
Correct. That is the two-part test in § 2-204(3).
A writing goes to the statute of frauds, not to indefiniteness.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Open terms

q: A seller of bolts under an installment contract misses one delivery by a day and offers replacement bolts the next morning. What is the likely result, and what should the buyer have drafted?
o: The buyer likely must accept; it should have drafted a termination trigger.
The contract is void; the buyer should have added a merger clause.
The seller may refuse further deliveries; the buyer needed a guaranty.
The buyer may reject under § 2-601 and needs no clause.
The buyer must cancel now; it should have used a sole remedy clause.
oe: Correct. Lateness can't be cured, but the installment needs substantial impairment. A pattern can justify cancelling the whole.
The contract isn't void, and a merger clause is unrelated.
Nothing supports the seller's refusal.
Section 2-612, not § 2-601, governs an installment.
It need not cancel, and that clause would cut against it.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Late bolts drafting

q: Big Bird contracts to buy 500 bags of birdseed from Snuffy, delivery at Big Bird's nest on Sesame Street. Big Bird assigns his right to the birdseed to a bird sanctuary in Alaska, which demands delivery there at the same price. Must Snuffy deliver to Alaska?
o: No, because a buyer can't assign its right to receive goods.
No, because the assignment would materially increase his burden.
Yes, because the contract does not prohibit assignment.
Yes, if the sanctuary pays the price plus any extra freight.
Yes, because contract rights are freely assignable.
oe: It can, unless the assignment materially changes the seller's duty, burden, risk, or chance of return performance.
Even without a prohibition, § 2-210(2) blocks assignments that materially change the other party's duty.
Extra payment doesn't cure the problem. The assignment materially changes Snuffy's duty and risk, so § 2-210(2) blocks it.
Not when the assignment materially changes the other party's duty.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Material change of duty

q: A box says, "Waterproof to 30 feet." A consumer buys from a retailer, and the camera floods at 10 feet. The manufacturer argues it dealt only with the retailer. Which is the best response?
o: Only personal injury can support the claim.
The box is puffery.
Privity bars every warranty claim against a manufacturer.
The statement is an express warranty, and courts may not require privity.
The retailer alone made the warranty.
oe: Economic loss can.
A specific depth is a fact.
Not for public statements in many courts.
Correct. Even privity states may not require it for a manufacturer's public claims (p. 337).
The manufacturer wrote it.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Express warranty on the box

q: Under a shipment contract the seller fails to ship on May 1, but the buyer doesn't learn this until May 9, when the goods fail to arrive. Prices move in between. Which is correct?
o: The expected arrival date always controls.
The seller may pick either date.
Which date controls is unclear, so § 2-723 should be read.
Damages are zero, because the buyer didn't know.
May 1 controls, by the express terms of § 2-713.
oe: No statute says so.
The seller gets no such choice.
Correct. The seller may breach days before the buyer learns the goods won't arrive.
Ignorance doesn't erase the breach.
Section 2-713 says "learned," and the text calls this unclear.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Shipment contract date uncertain

q: Zoe buys a new e-bike. The manufacturer's warranty, in a sealed booklet inside the box that Zoe couldn't see before paying, limits remedies to repair and excludes consequential damages in bold capitals. The motor fails, and five repair attempts never fix it. What is the most likely result?
o: The exclusion is enforceable, because it was printed in bold capitals.
Zoe is limited to more repair attempts, because the remedy was expressly exclusive.
The repair remedy hasn't failed, because the manufacturer is still trying.
The repair remedy failed of its essential purpose, and the exclusion, tested separately, is likely unconscionable because Zoe couldn't see it before buying.
The repair remedy failed, so the consequential-damages exclusion automatically falls with it.
oe: Clear type doesn't help if the buyer couldn't see the term before buying.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose gives way to general remedies (§ 2-719(2)).
Repeated failed repairs are the classic failure of essential purpose.
Correct. This tracks Razor v. Hyundai: two separate tests ("concentric walls"), and a preprinted consumer exclusion unavailable before the sale was unconscionable.
That's the dependent approach (Adams), which Razor rejected.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Hidden consumer exclusion

q: A contract requires delivery by the 5th and also says: "No waiver of any term is effective unless in writing, and accepting late performance is not a waiver." The buyer accepts several late deliveries without objection. Can the seller argue the buyer waived the delivery date?
o: Courts split on whether the anti-waiver clause can itself be waived.
No, because anti-waiver clauses are enforced exactly as written.
Yes, because anti-waiver clauses are void under the UCC.
Yes, because accepting several late deliveries is a modification.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-5(D). Some courts enforce the anti-waiver clause, while others hold the clause itself can be waived by conduct. Estoppel remains possible but weak.
Courts split.
Courts split.
Nothing suggests an agreement to modify, and conduct alone raises waiver, not modification.
A is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Anti-waiver clause

q: Rizzo sells Pepe a used outboard motor. Rizzo says: "This motor has 200 hours on it." In fact it has 2,000 hours. Rizzo never used the words "warrant" or "guarantee," and he did not intend to make a warranty. Has Rizzo made an express warranty?
o: No, because a used motor is sold without warranties.
No, because Rizzo did not intend to make a warranty.
No, because Rizzo is not a merchant in outboard motors.
Yes, because "200 hours" is a specific affirmation of fact.
No, because Rizzo did not use the word "warrant" or "guarantee."
oe: Used goods can carry express warranties.
No specific intention to make a warranty is required.
Any seller can make an express warranty. Merchant status matters for § 2-314.
Correct. "200 hours" is specific and measurable, it relates to the goods, and it became part of the basis of the bargain.
§ 2-313(2): formal words such as "warrant" or "guarantee" are not required.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — No magic words

q: Rizzo pays a lab $1,200 to test a shipment of food-grade oil, finds it contaminated, and rightfully rejects it. Who bears the cost of the test?
o: Rizzo, because the buyer always bears inspection costs.
The seller, but only if the contract says so.
Rizzo, unless the contract expressly shifts the cost.
The parties split it.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the goods conform or aren't rejected.
The Code shifts the cost without a contract term.
The Code shifts it.
No splitting rule.
Correct. The seller bears it: the buyer bears inspection costs but recovers them from the seller if the goods don't conform and are rejected (§ 2-513(2)). No choice says that.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection costs
