q: A seller holds a public auction of the buyer's goods at an unusual place, with notice of neither time nor place to the buyer. The goods aren't perishable. It sells them for far below market. What is the consequence?
o: It can't use § 2-706, but can still use § 2-708.
It must buy the goods back.
The sale is void against the purchaser.
It loses all damages.
It may use § 2-706, as notice isn't needed at auction.
oe: Correct. Notice of time and place is required for a public sale, and a usual place if available. A bad resale only loses that measure (cmt. 2).
Nothing requires that.
A good-faith purchaser takes free.
It falls back.
Notice is needed for a public sale of non-perishables.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Notice to buyer, auction

q: A consumer's spouse is hurt by a toaster. The maker's warranty, valid against the buyer, disclaims nothing but limits consequential damages. Alternative A applies. What is the best analysis?
o: The limit binds the spouse fully, because it binds the buyer.
The spouse isn't covered, because only the buyer may sue.
Only a tort claim can reach the injury.
The spouse needs vertical privity.
The spouse is covered, and the limit is prima facie unconscionable.
oe: It binds, but it's prima facie unconscionable here.
Alternative A covers family.
Warranty can.
Alternative A is about horizontal privity, and many courts have relaxed vertical.
Correct. Sections 2-318 and 2-719(3). Injury to the person from consumer goods.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Warranty, disclaimer, privity chain

q: A sales form says "ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES ARE DISCLAIMED." The goods turn out to be stolen and to infringe a patent. Which is correct?
o: Title can never be disclaimed in a sale.
The clause disclaims every warranty, including title.
The clause doesn't disclaim title; infringement is less clear.
The clause disclaims title but not infringement.
A title warranty is implied only for merchants.
oe: It can, by specific language or circumstances.
Title needs specific language.

Correct. The UCC doesn't designate the title warranty "implied" (§ 2-312 cmt. 6), and § 2-312(2) needs specific language. The noninfringement warranty arises "unless otherwise agreed," and it's unclear whether § 2-316 applies.
Title is the clearer failure of the clause.
Every seller gives it.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Title warranty isn't "implied"

q: A seller's raw-material cost doubles after contracting because of an ordinary market swing. It asks to be excused under § 2-615. Which is the best advice?
o: The seller may allocate its supply among customers.
The seller may stop performing and sue the supplier.
There's no excuse; seek a good-faith modification and draft for this.
The seller may raise its price by unilateral notice.
A doubling of cost is impracticable as a matter of law.
oe: Allocation is for a real shortage under § 2-615(b).
It must perform or face breach.
Correct. Problem 6-9. Increased cost alone isn't impracticability. Ask for a § 2-209 modification and in future draft escalation and force majeure clauses.
That would be a repudiation.
Cost alone isn't enough.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Supplier price spike

q: What must a signed record show to satisfy § 2A-201?
o: All material terms, including the rent.
A lease contract, the goods, and the lease term.
The rent and the lessor's address.
A contract and the quantity, nothing more.
A statement that the lease is final.
oe: A record may omit terms (§ 2A-201(3)).
Correct. Unlike § 2-201, it needs the term and a description, since no gap filler supplies the term.
The record need not state the rent.
That's the § 2-201 test.
Finality is a parol evidence idea.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — What the record shows

q: Under Article 2, which statement about risk of loss is correct?
o: Risk stays with the seller until the buyer takes possession.
Risk is allocated by specific rules, not by who has title.
Risk of loss passes when the buyer signs the contract.
Risk of loss passes when the buyer pays the price.
Risk of loss follows title to the goods.
oe: Not for non-merchant sellers or shipment contracts.
Correct. Risk goes to the party in control, the one likely to be insured, or the one in breach.
Signing passes neither title nor risk by itself.
Payment doesn't control.
Article 2 separates risk of loss from title.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Risk not tied to title

q: Parties never discuss delivery date, and their deal includes a usage of trade on packing. Which statement about "agreement" and "contract" under § 1-201 is correct?
o: The agreement excludes usage of trade and course of dealing.
Usage of trade is part of the contract only if written down.
The two words mean the same thing throughout the Code.
A contract can never contain more than the parties' agreement.
The agreement is the bargain in fact; the contract is the total legal obligation.
oe: The definition includes them.
It's part of the bargain in fact without a writing.
Section 1-201 defines them differently.
Gap fillers add obligations.
Correct. The agreement includes course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade. The contract adds Code gap fillers, so it can be more, or sometimes less, than the agreement.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Agreement vs. contract

q: In Daitom v. Pennwalt, the seller's offer required any suit within one year of delivery. The buyer's acceptance reserved "all of its rights and remedies available at law." How did the court resolve the conflict?
o: The seller's one-year term controlled because the seller's form was the offer.
A one-year limitations period applied as a reasonable compromise.
The buyer's term controlled because the buyer sent the last form.
Both terms dropped out, and the Code's four-year limit applied.
No contract was formed, because the forms conflicted on a material term.
oe: The court did not let the offeror's term win automatically.
Courts do not split the difference. The gap filler applies.
§ 2-207 abolished the last-shot rule.
Correct. Applying the knockout rule (§ 2-207 cmt. 6), the court let both terms drop out and filled the gap with § 2-725.
The purchase order was an acceptance under § 2-207(1), so a contract was formed.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Daitom: knockout

q: Kermit contracts to sell 200 standard steel folding chairs to Sam Eagle's convention hall. The contract says nothing about delegation. Overbooked, Kermit arranges for Rowlf, another chair dealer, to deliver 200 identical chairs on the delivery date. Sam refuses them, saying he made his deal with Kermit, not Rowlf. Is Sam entitled to refuse?
o: No, but only if Rowlf is a merchant who deals in chairs of that kind.
Yes, because a party may never delegate its duties without first obtaining the other party's consent.
Yes, because only a buyer, not a seller, may delegate contractual duties.
No, and once Rowlf tenders the chairs, Kermit is released from the contract.
No. Kermit may delegate, but he remains liable if Rowlf's chairs are nonconforming.
oe: § 2-210(1) doesn't ask whether the delegate is a merchant. It asks whether Sam has a substantial interest in having Kermit himself perform.
Consent isn't required. Delegation is the default rule for both buyers and sellers (§ 2-210(1)).
Both buyers and sellers may delegate. In fact, sellers' duties are the ones most often delegated.
Sam must take the chairs, but delegation never releases the delegator from liability for breach (§ 2-210(1)).

Correct. Absent a contrary agreement or a substantial interest in Kermit's own performance, Kermit may delegate (§ 2-210(1)). Identical standard chairs give Sam no such interest, and Kermit stays on the hook for any breach.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegating standard goods

q: Before ordering 50 bags of coffee beans described in the contract as "Colombian Supremo," Zoe's café is given a sample bag drawn from the seller's warehouse lot and agrees to buy "beans like the sample." The delivered beans are genuine Colombian Supremo but a noticeably lower grade than the sample. Is the seller in breach?
o: No, because the beans match the written contract description, which controls over any sample.
Yes, because the sample was part of the bargain, so the whole lot must conform to it.
Yes, but only if the seller is a merchant with respect to coffee.
No, because a sample creates a warranty only if the seller calls it a "guarantee."
No, because Zoe could have tested the delivered beans before accepting them.
oe: When a sample from an existing bulk and a general description conflict, the sample generally controls (§ 2-317(b)).

Correct. A sample made part of the bargain warrants that the whole of the goods will conform (§ 2-313(1)(c)). A sample drawn from an existing bulk also displaces inconsistent general words of description (§ 2-317(b)).
Express warranties, including those by sample, can be made by any seller.
No formal words are needed (§ 2-313(2)).
A chance to inspect doesn't eliminate an express warranty; Zoe may still sue for breach after acceptance.
topic: Wk 2 · V · Express warranties — Sample from the bulk

q: How should wages and utilities be treated in lost-profit math?
o: It depends on whether the sale needed extra labor.
They are always variable costs.
They are always fixed costs.
They follow their treatment on the seller's tax return.
They are excluded from the calculation entirely.
oe: Correct. Fixed costs are overhead; variable costs rise with output. Tax treatment has little bearing.
They can be fixed if the sale was small.
They can be variable if the sale needed overtime.
Tax treatment has little bearing.
They must be classified.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Fixed or variable

q: A piano store with an unlimited supply of a popular model contracts to sell one to Rowlf for $8,000. Rowlf repudiates, and the store sells that piano the next day to another customer at the same price. The store's profit on each sale is $2,000. What is the store's best measure of damages?
o: $8,000, the price under § 2-709.
Nothing, because it resold at the same price.
$4,000, double the lost profit, as a penalty for repudiation.
The contract price minus the market price.
None of the above.
oe: Price is available only in limited cases, like accepted goods.
The resale would have happened anyway, so it didn't replace Rowlf's sale.
Damages aren't punitive.
That's zero here and doesn't reflect the lost sale.
Correct. The store recovers its $2,000 lost profit under § 2-708(2): a lost-volume seller would have made both sales, so the resale doesn't make it whole. No choice says that.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Lost-volume seller

q: Under a single one-year contract, Bert has delivered pigeon feed in 50-pound sacks every week for six months, and Ernie has accepted each delivery without objection. The contract does not say what size sacks to use. Which concept best describes this pattern?
o: Waiver.
Course of dealing.
Usage of trade.
Modification.
Course of performance.
oe: A course of performance may show waiver, but the pattern itself is a course of performance.
Course of dealing is conduct in prior transactions, before this contract.
Usage of trade is an industry-wide practice, not a practice between these two parties.
A course of performance may show a modification, but nothing here suggests the parties agreed to change a term.
Correct. Repeated occasions for performance under this contract, accepted with knowledge and an opportunity to object, form a course of performance (§ 1-303(a)).
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Course of performance vs. dealing

q: How is the warranty against interference or infringement disclaimed in a lease?
o: Only by a separately signed rider.
By any oral statement before signing.
By specific, written, conspicuous language.
It can't be disclaimed in a lease.
By the words "as is."
oe: No rider is required.
A writing is needed unless circumstances show otherwise.
Correct. Section 2A-214(4). Compare § 2-312(2).
Section 2A-214(4) allows it.
"As is" reaches implied quality warranties.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Disclaiming interference

q: A contract requires Abby to tell a sign maker by March 1 which colors to use for 40 signs. Abby gives no specifications until April 15, and the sign maker couldn't start without them. Which statement is correct?
o: Abby may cancel because the signs were late.
The contract is void, because a material term (the colors) was left open and never agreed by the deadline.
The sign maker is excused for the delay and may proceed reasonably or treat Abby's failure as a breach.
The sign maker is in breach for missing the delivery date.
None of the above.
oe: Abby caused the delay.
The parties agreed Abby would specify.
Its delay was caused by Abby.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Failure to cooperate

q: A buyer that did not cover sues under § 2-713. Which market price is used?
o: The price on the contract date, at the buyer's own location.
The price when the buyer learned of the breach, at the place for tender.
The price on the first day of trial.
The price when the seller learned that it would breach.
The price at the time and place for tender.
oe: Neither the date nor the place fits § 2-713.
Correct. Section 2-713(1), plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved. The place is the place of arrival instead after rejection on arrival or revocation.
Trial date is not the measure, apart from § 2-723(1).
The buyer's knowledge controls, not the seller's.
That's the seller's rule in § 2-708(1).
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Buyer market formula

q: Herry sells 300 crates of pickles stored in Monster Cold Storage, an independent warehouse, to Prairie Dawn. At 2 p.m., Herry hands Prairie Dawn a signed letter addressed to the warehouse: "Please deliver the 300 crates to the bearer, Prairie Dawn." The warehouse hasn't been contacted. At 3 p.m., before Prairie Dawn could reasonably have reached the warehouse, an ammonia leak ruins the pickles. Who bears the loss?
o: The warehouse, because it had possession of the pickles when they were ruined.
Prairie Dawn, because the pickles were identified and held by a bailee for her.
Herry, because Prairie Dawn hadn't had a reasonable time to present the letter.
Prairie Dawn, because the warehouse would have honored the letter if she had arrived.
Prairie Dawn, because receiving a signed direction to deliver completed Herry's tender.
oe: The warehouse answers only for its own negligence. The question is which contracting party bears the loss.
Goods held by a bailee are covered by § 2-509(2), and under subsection (2)(c) a direction passes risk only after a reasonable time.

Correct. Tender by a nonnegotiable document or a direction in a record to the bailee passes risk only after the buyer has had a reasonable time to present it (§§ 2-509(2)(c), 2-503(4)(b)). One hour wasn't enough.
The risk of the bailee's failure to honor, and the risk of loss, stay on the seller until a reasonable time to present has passed.
Receipt of the direction alone isn't enough. The buyer also needs a reasonable time to present it.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Direction to bailee; reasonable time to present

q: A buyer paid $4,000 of the price and $300 in freight for goods it rightfully rejected. It also has $2,000 of cover damages. What does its § 2-711(3) security interest secure?
o: Only the $2,000 of cover damages.
All $6,300, since the seller is the party in breach.
Only the $4,000 of price paid.
The $4,000 and the $300, but not the $2,000 in cover damages.
Nothing, because a buyer has no lien on a seller's goods.
oe: That's the one item not secured.
The lien doesn't secure cover damages.
Reasonable expenses on the goods are also secured.
Correct. The lien secures price paid and expenses on the goods. Cover, market and consequential damages (and some incidentals) aren't secured.
Section 2-711(3) gives one.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Lien for rejected goods

q: A grain dealer agrees to sell a miller 1,000 bushels of No. 2 yellow corn. The contract doesn't specify a source, and the dealer hasn't set aside any corn for the miller. A fire destroys the dealer's entire warehouse inventory. Is the dealer excused?
o: No, because the corn was never identified to the contract, and other corn is available.
Yes, because losing its entire inventory makes the dealer's performance commercially impracticable.
No, but the miller must give the dealer a reasonable extra time to find replacement corn.
Yes, because risk hadn't passed to the miller, so neither party owes anything for the lost corn.
Yes, because the fire destroyed the dealer's inventory without any fault on the dealer's part.
oe: Correct. Section 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract is made. When a seller can still meet a contract for fungible goods from other sources, the loss of its own stock isn't a casualty that excuses it.
Buying replacement corn may cost more, but increased cost alone doesn't make performance impracticable (§ 2-615 cmt. 4).
Article 2 gives no automatic extension here.
The risk question asks who bears the loss of particular goods. The dealer still owes 1,000 bushels from somewhere.
Lack of fault isn't enough. The goods must have been identified when the contract was made.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Fungible goods not identified

q: Wembley is an accountant. Twice a year he sells his handmade stained-glass ornaments at a craft fair, and he has done so for years. Does Wembley give the implied warranty of merchantability on the ornaments?
o: No, because he sells ornaments only twice a year.
Yes, because he regularly sells goods of that kind.
No, because his main occupation is accounting, not crafts.
No, because handmade goods carry no implied warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Regular, recurring sales are enough.
Correct. Problem 3-9. A merchant is one who deals in goods of the kind (§ 2-104(1)), and his day job is not decisive.
His occupation doesn't stop him from also dealing in ornaments.
Handmade goods are goods.
B is correct.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Artisan at craft fair

q: A manufacturer's TV ads claim that its mower "starts on the first pull, every time." A consumer who bought from a dealer sues for breach of express warranty in a state that keeps vertical privity for implied warranties. Which is correct?
o: The dealer alone is liable for the maker's advertisement.
Privity bars this claim just as it bars an implied warranty claim.
The claim requires a personal injury.
Even a privity state may not require it for public claims.
Advertisements can never create express warranties.
oe: The maker made the statement.
Express warranties are treated more leniently (p. 337).
Economic loss can be enough.
Correct. See p. 337.
Public claims can.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Express warranty and privity

q: Which statement is a TRAP, meaning it's wrong?
o: A lessee's purchase of replacement goods is measured as cover.
A wrongful revocation has no effect.
A retained-title clause is only a security interest.
Section 2-607(3)(a) applies only to accepted goods.
A purchase that isn't a reasonable substitute isn't cover.
oe: Correct. This is the trap: a lessee's purchase falls to market rent. The rest are true: a non-substitute isn't cover, § 2-607(3)(a) applies only to accepted goods, there's no wrongful effective revocation, and a retained-title clause is only a security interest.
True.
True.
True.
True.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Trap list

q: Which is NOT a Johannsen factor for a buyer's use of goods after rejection or revocation?
o: Whether the use reasonably mitigated damages.
Prejudice to the seller from the continued use.
The seller's instructions after the buyer rejected.
Hardship to the buyer if its use had to stop.
Whether the buyer has paid the seller in full.
oe: A Johannsen factor.
A Johannsen factor.
A Johannsen factor.
A Johannsen factor.
Correct. The factors are the seller's instructions, the buyer's hardship if use stopped, whether use reasonably mitigated damages, prejudice to the seller, and the seller's bad faith.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Johannsen factors

q: Snuffy contracts to sell Big Bird 100 bushels of wheat at $4 a bushel. Snuffy tenders 95 bushels. Has Snuffy made a proper tender?
o: Yes, because a 5% shortfall is within normal variation.
Yes, because 95 bushels is substantial performance.
No, because the short quantity is a nonconforming tender.
Yes, as long as Big Bird pays for 95 bushels and no more.
No, and Snuffy has lost any right to cure the shortfall.
oe: Only variations permitted by the agreement or trade usage count, and none is stated.
Article 2 uses perfect tender, not substantial performance, for a single-delivery contract.
Correct. Problem 4-4. § 2-307 requires a single delivery, and § 2-508 may allow Snuffy to cure.
The tender itself is nonconforming.
Cure may be available within the contract time (§ 2-508).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Short quantity tender

q: Grover and Elmo orally agree that Elmo will sell Grover a used sound system for $350. Before delivery, they orally agree to add speakers and raise the price to $700. Elmo later refuses to deliver the speakers. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The modification fails without a signed record, since the new deal is $500 or more, but the $350 deal stands.
Neither deal is enforceable, because once the parties raised the price, the whole contract fell within the statute of frauds.
The original contract is discharged, so Elmo owes nothing.
The $700 deal is enforceable, because modifications need no consideration.
The modification is enforceable, because the original contract didn't need a writing.
oe: Correct. § 2-209(3) applies the statute of frauds to the contract as modified (Problem 3-4(a)). The failed modification may still operate as a waiver.
The original $350 deal survives.
A failed modification doesn't discharge the original contract.
Consideration isn't the problem. The statute of frauds is.
What matters is the contract as modified.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and the SOF

q: Which is a "consumer lease"?
o: A dealer leases a car to an individual for family use.
A neighbor who has never leased anything rents a mower to a friend.
A dealer leases a truck to an LLC for deliveries.
A dealer leases a tractor to a farmer for his business.
All of the above.
oe: Correct. Section 2A-103(1)(e): a lessor regularly leasing or selling; an individual lessee; primarily personal, family or household purpose. States may set a dollar cap.
The lessor isn't regularly engaged in leasing or selling.
The lessee isn't an individual.
The purpose is business, not personal or family.
Only the first choice fits.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Consumer lease definition

q: A contractor orders custom drainage fittings designed solely for a city stormwater project. Before delivery, the city cancels the project, and the fittings have no other use. The contractor claims it is excused. What is its best argument?
o: Casualty to identified goods under § 2-613.
Frustration of purpose, because both parties assumed the project would go forward.
Commercial impracticability under § 2-615, because the city's cancellation was an unforeseen contingency.
The statute of frauds, because the contract was oral.
None of the above.
oe: The fittings weren't destroyed.
Correct. § 1-103(b) brings in common-law frustration; § 2-615 cmt. 9 notes a buyer may be excused when a contract is tied to a specific venture (Problem 6-8(a)).
That's a seller's argument, and nothing about cost is in the facts.
Nothing says it was oral.
B is correct.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Frustration of purpose

q: A printer contracts for German press parts at $10,000. The seller repudiates. Only Japanese parts are available, at $12,000; they fit and work equally well, though they aren't what was ordered. Which is the best analysis?
o: They can't be cover, as cover must be identical.
They are likely a reasonable substitute, so cover damages are $2,000.
They are cover, and damages are the full $12,000.
They are cover, but only if the seller approves.
They can't be cover, as foreign-made goods differ in origin.
oe: Section 2-712 requires substitutes, not duplicates.
Correct. Comment 2: goods need not be identical, as long as they could reasonably replace those due. Some difference is fine, especially when identical goods aren't available.
The buyer keeps the parts.
A seller's approval isn't needed.
Origin alone doesn't matter here.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Reasonable substitute test

q: Ben buys a ladder and lends it to a coworker, who is injured at the coworker's home. Under which version of § 2-318 can the coworker claim against the seller?
o: All three alternatives.
Alternatives B and C.
None of them.
Alternative C only.
Alternative A only.
oe: Alternative A doesn't fit.
Correct. A natural person reasonably expected to use the goods and injured in person fits B and C. Alternative A is limited to family, household and home guests.
B and C both fit.
Alternative B also reaches any natural person.
The coworker isn't family, household or a home guest of the buyer.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Alternative B coworker

q: Sweetums sells a used food truck to Floyd. Before signing, Floyd learns that a bank holds a recorded security interest in the truck, and he buys anyway at a discount. The bank later repossesses the truck when Sweetums defaults on the loan. Floyd sues Sweetums for breach of the warranty of title. What is the most likely result?
o: Sweetums wins, because a security interest has nothing to do with the warranty of title.
Floyd wins, but only if the bank's security interest had not been publicly recorded.
Floyd wins, because an unpaid security interest makes title defective whatever the buyer knew.
Floyd wins, because every seller warrants that its goods are free of all liens.
Sweetums wins, because Floyd knew of the security interest when he contracted.
oe: Freedom from undisclosed security interests is part of the title warranty.
Recording doesn't decide it. Floyd's actual knowledge does.
Section 2-312(1)(b) turns on the buyer's knowledge.
The warranty excludes liens the buyer knew of when contracting.
Correct. The seller warrants that the goods will be delivered free from any security interest or lien "of which the buyer at the time of contracting has no knowledge" (§ 2-312(1)(b)). Floyd knew.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Known security interest

q: Grover's purchase order offers to buy 50 printers from Elmo's Electronics. Elmo's acknowledgment accepts and adds, in bold capitals: "SELLER DISCLAIMS THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY." Both are merchants, and Grover never responds. Is the disclaimer part of the contract?
o: No, because Grover never signed the acknowledgment.
Yes, because it was conspicuous and specifically named merchantability.
No, because a warranty disclaimer materially alters the contract.
Yes, because Grover did not object within 10 days.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-207 doesn't require the offeror's signature. The term fails because it is material.
Conspicuousness matters under § 2-316, but first the term must get into the contract under § 2-207.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(b) and cmt. 4: a clause negating standard warranties is a classic material alteration, so it does not become part of the contract even between merchants.
The 10-day objection period belongs to the merchant's confirmation exception to the statute of frauds (§ 2-201(2)).
C is correct.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Material alteration: disclaimer

q: A contract's exclusive remedy for a defective TV is "store credit." Before the buyer can use it, the retailer goes bankrupt and its stores close. What result?
o: The buyer may recover only the price it paid.
The remedy is unconscionable, so the whole contract is void.
The buyer is stuck with the credit it bargained for.
The remedy failed of its essential purpose; general remedies return.
None of the above.
oe: The general remedies return in full.
Failure of essential purpose affects the remedy, not the contract.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose doesn't bind the buyer.
Correct. Problem 5-7 (the Circuit City example). § 2-719(2).
D is correct.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Worthless store credit

q: A seller under a shipment contract properly delivers the goods to a carrier but forgets to notify the buyer of the shipment. The goods arrive on time and undamaged. May the buyer reject them?
o: No, because shipping defects don't justify rejection after arrival.
Yes, because the seller failed to obtain the proper documents.
No, because missed notice justifies rejection only if material delay or loss results.
Yes, because the seller failed to notify the buyer promptly.
None of the above.
oe: It can if material delay or loss results.
The seller's failure was notice, and it caused no harm.
Correct. § 2-504.
Failure to notify justifies rejection only if material delay or loss results.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Seller's shipment duties

q: Which of the following is true of a delegation of performance under § 2-210?
o: Absent a contrary agreement or a substantial interest, the other party's consent isn't required.
The delegating party remains liable if the delegate's performance is defective.
A delegate who never agreed to assume the duty isn't liable to the other party for failing to perform.
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: True, but not the only true statement (§ 2-210(1)).
True, but not the only true statement (§ 2-210(1)).
True, but not the only true statement. A delegate becomes bound to the obligee only by assuming the duty.
Correct. Each statement is accurate. Delegation needs no consent by default, never releases the delegator, and binds the delegate only if it assumes the duty.
Each of A, B, and C is a correct statement of the law.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegation: all true

q: Which seller is the clearest lost-volume seller?
o: A manufacturer running at full capacity.
A seller whose market has collapsed.
A dealer selling one unique used car.
An artist with a single painting.
A jobber with unlimited supply.
oe: It couldn't have made both sales.
A market collapse explains a price drop; it doesn't show the seller could have made both sales.
A single item again.
A single item means no lost volume.
Correct. The breach costs it one sale, and any resale would have happened anyway.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Jobber

q: A "lessee" with a $1 buyout on a non-terminable lease returns the goods and stops paying. The "lessor" sues under Article 2A for rent. What should be analyzed first, and why?
o: Section 2-725, since time may have run.
Section 2A-504, the liquidated damages rule.
Section 2A-529, since rent is the claim.
Section 1-203, since a $1 buyout makes it a sale and security interest.
Section 2A-407, as the lessee accepted.
oe: Classification comes first.
The deal isn't a lease.
Classification comes first.
Correct. Article 2A drops out, and Articles 2 and 9 govern, with notice and deficiency rules.
Finance status isn't the issue.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Lease or sale in a remedies problem

q: Sam Eagle's bottling plant gives Gonzo's Pump Works a 30-page specification for a custom pump: flow rate, materials, seals, and motor size. Gonzo builds the pump exactly to those specifications. In service, the pump can't keep up with the plant's actual line speed. Sam sues for breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. What is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because Sam relied on his own specifications, not on Gonzo's judgment.
Sam wins, because a pump that can't keep up with the line isn't merchantable.
Sam wins, because Gonzo is a merchant that deals in pumps and so warrants their fitness.
Sam wins, because Gonzo knew the pump would be used in a bottling plant.
Gonzo wins, because the fitness warranty never applies to specially manufactured goods.
oe: Correct. The fitness warranty requires that the buyer rely on the seller's skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods (§ 2-315). A buyer that dictates detailed specifications usually relies on its own judgment, not the seller's.
A pump built to the buyer's specifications that works as specified is likely fit for its ordinary purpose. The shortfall came from the specifications.
Merchant status matters for merchantability, not for fitness.
Knowledge of the purpose is only half the test. Reliance on the seller is also required.
Specially manufactured goods can carry a fitness warranty when the buyer relies on the seller's design.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Buyer's own specifications defeat reliance

q: Animal leaves his drum kit with a recording studio while he tours. The studio rents out equipment but doesn't sell drums. The studio sells the kit to a buyer who pays fair value in good faith. Animal sues the buyer. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because the studio is a merchant in the music business.
The buyer wins, because he was a good-faith purchaser who paid fair value for the kit.
The buyer wins, because Animal voluntarily handed over possession of the kit to the studio.
Animal wins, but only if he can prove the studio acted in bad faith.
Animal wins, because the studio doesn't deal in drums and so had no power to sell his kit.
oe: It must deal in goods of the kind sold, which here means drums.
A good-faith purchaser takes no more than the transferor had or could transfer, and the studio had neither title nor power.
Voluntary delivery to a non-dealer doesn't trigger the entrustment rule.
The studio's state of mind doesn't matter. It lacked the power to transfer.

Correct. Section 2-403(2) gives the power to transfer only to "a merchant who deals in goods of that kind." A studio that rents but doesn't sell drums doesn't qualify, and the studio had no voidable title under § 2-403(1) either.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Entrustment to a non-dealer

q: A buyer paid $20,000; a valid LD clause sets damages at $10,000. The seller justifiably withholds. How much goes back to the buyer?
o: $20,000, all of the payment.
$19,500, keeping only $500.
Nothing, as the clause covers it.
$10,000, the excess over the liquidated amount.
$16,000, keeping 20% of the payment.
oe: The valid clause counts.
That's the no-LD rule.
The excess goes back.
Correct. Section 2-718(2)(a).
That isn't a Code figure.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — With valid LD

q: A thief steals Prairie Dawn's bicycle and sells it to Crazy Harry's Cycles, a used-bike shop that buys in good faith. Crazy Harry's sells it to Herry, a good-faith buyer in the ordinary course of business. Prairie Dawn finds it and sues Herry to recover it. Who wins?
o: Herry, because two good-faith purchases in a row cut off the original owner's rights.
Herry, because Crazy Harry's bought in good faith for value and so had voidable title.
Herry, because he bought in the ordinary course from a merchant that deals in bicycles.
Prairie Dawn, because a thief gets void title, and she entrusted the bike to no one.
None of the above.
oe: The number of good-faith transfers doesn't cure a void title.
A good-faith purchaser from a thief gets nothing, so Crazy Harry's had no title to pass.
Being a buyer in ordinary course helps only under the entrustment rule, which doesn't apply to stolen goods.

Correct. A purchaser takes only the title its transferor had or had power to transfer (§ 2-403(1)). A thief has void title. The entrustment rule in § 2-403(2) protects buyers only when the owner entrusted the goods to the merchant, and Prairie Dawn didn't.
One of the other choices is correct: Prairie Dawn, because a thief gets void title, and she entrusted the bike to no one.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Thief; then merchant; then ordinary-course buyer

q: Fozzie buys a used delivery van that seems fine on a test drive. Three weeks later, a hidden crack in the engine block appears and leaves the van undrivable. Fozzie promptly notifies the dealer and returns the van. Can Fozzie revoke acceptance?
o: Yes, because the hidden defect substantially impairs the van's value and Fozzie acted promptly.
No, because used goods can't be returned.
No, because revocation is allowed only for defects the seller knew about.
No, because Fozzie accepted the van after a test drive.
Yes, because any defect, hidden or not, justifies revocation if the buyer acts within 30 days of delivery.
oe: Correct. § 2-608: a nonconformity that substantially impairs value, accepted because it was hard to discover, and revoked within a reasonable time.
No such rule.
The seller's knowledge isn't required.
Revocation exists for goods already accepted.
Revocation requires substantial impairment, not just any defect.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Revocation of acceptance

q: A seller's three buyers default. Buyer 1 accepted goods. Buyer 2 wrongfully rejected, and the seller has the goods, which are readily resalable. Buyer 3 repudiated before unique custom goods were finished, and they can't be sold to anyone. Which is correct?
o: Reclamation from all three.
Price from all three.
Damages from all three.
Price from 2; damages from 1.
Price from 1; damages from 2; price from 3 if the goods are finished.
oe: Reclamation is a narrow remedy.
Buyer 2's goods can be resold.
Buyer 1 accepted, so the price applies.
That's reversed.
Correct. Section 2-709(1)(a) for accepted goods; §§ 2-706, 2-708 for goods it can resell; § 2-709(1)(b) for identified goods it can't resell, after completing them under § 2-704(2) if reasonable.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Price vs. damages by possession

q: Herry's contract to sell 400 trophies to a youth league says: "Neither party may assign this contract." After delivering the trophies, Herry assigns his right to the $6,000 price to a finance company, which notifies the league. The league argues the assignment violates the contract. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The assignment is ineffective, because the clause expressly bars assigning the contract.
The assignment is effective only because the finance company is a merchant.
It is effective, because the clause bars only delegation, and Herry delegated nothing.
The assignment is ineffective unless the league consented in writing.
The assignment is effective, but the league may cancel the contract for Herry's breach.
oe: Under § 2-210(4) that wording reaches only delegation of duties, and Herry assigned only a right.
The assignee's status is irrelevant. The result follows from § 2-210(4) and § 9-406(d).
Correct. § 2-210(4) reads the clause as barring delegation of performance only. Herry has already performed and transferred only his right to payment, which is effective (see also § 9-406(d)).
Consent isn't required to assign a right to payment.
Assigning the right to payment doesn't breach a clause that bars only delegation, and § 9-406(d) says it isn't a default.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Ban on assigning payment rights

q: A dealer contracts to sell "a print from the limited edition." Print #10, which the dealer meant to deliver, is water-damaged. The dealer still has print #12, which is identical. Must the dealer deliver #12?
o: Yes, but the buyer must pay extra for the substitute print.
No, because the casualty avoided the contract.
Yes, unless the contract was for print #10 specifically.
No, because #10 was damaged without the dealer's fault.
No, because the buyer must accept #10 with an allowance.
oe: The price doesn't change.
Avoidance requires identified goods.
Correct. Problem 6-6(c). § 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract was made, so if the prints are interchangeable, the dealer must deliver #12.
Only if the contract was for #10 specifically.
That option exists only if #10 was identified at contracting.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Interchangeable prints

q: Rosita, a nurse, agrees to sell her personal kayak to Zoe for $700. Rosita says, "I'll have it on my driveway for you starting tomorrow at noon." That night, before noon the next day, the kayak is stolen from Rosita's locked garage without either party's fault. Zoe hasn't paid. What is the most likely result?
o: Zoe must pay, because Rosita had already told her when and where to pick up the kayak.
Rosita must deliver a comparable kayak or pay Zoe damages for nondelivery.
The loss falls on Rosita, and neither party owes the other anything further.
Zoe must pay, because a non-merchant seller passes the risk as soon as the contract is made.
The answer depends on whether Rosita is a merchant with respect to kayaks, which a court will presume she is.
oe: Notice of a future pickup time isn't tender. Tender requires the goods to be actually held at the buyer's disposition.
The contract was for this identified kayak. Its loss without fault before risk passed avoids the contract under § 2-613, so Rosita isn't in breach.

Correct. A non-merchant seller passes risk on tender (§ 2-509(3)), and tender requires putting and holding the goods at the buyer's disposition (§ 2-503(1)). That hadn't happened yet. The kayak was identified when the contract was made and was lost without fault before risk passed, so § 2-613 avoids the contract.
A non-merchant passes risk on tender, not on contracting. Rosita had not yet made the kayak available.
There is no presumption of merchant status. And even for a non-merchant, risk had not passed because there was no tender yet.
topic: Wks 4–5 · IX · Risk of loss & shipping terms — Non-merchant seller; loss before tender

q: Sam Eagle, new to the lumber business, orders 5,000 "2x4" studs from a mill. The studs delivered measure 1.5 by 3.5 inches. In the lumber trade, "2x4" universally refers to that finished size. Sam claims he expected boards a full 2 by 4 inches and had never heard of the trade practice. What is the most likely result?
o: Sam wins, because the plain, literal words of the written order control over custom.
The trade meaning controls, because a trade usage binds those engaged in the trade.
The mill wins only if it can show a prior course of dealing with Sam in the same goods.
Sam wins, because a usage of trade binds a party only if he actually knew of it.
The mill wins only if the trade meaning of "2x4" was written into the contract.
oe: Article 2 reads words in light of trade usage. A literal reading doesn't prevail over an established trade meaning.
Correct. A usage of trade in the vocation or trade in which the parties are engaged, or of which they are or should be aware, gives meaning to and supplements their agreement (§ 1-303(d)).
Usage of trade works independently of any course of dealing.
The test includes parties who are engaged in the trade or should be aware of the usage.
Usage of trade supplements the contract without being stated.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Usage binds a newcomer to the trade

q: In which is the liquidated damages test narrower, and why?
o: The lease test, which looks only to anticipated harm.
The lease test, which requires actual harm.
The sale test, which has no reasonableness limit.
The sale test, which looks only to actual harm.
Neither; the two tests are identical.
oe: Correct. Sale: anticipated or actual harm.
Section 2A-504(1) looks to then-anticipated harm, not actual harm.
It has one.
It's anticipated or actual.
They differ.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Liquidated damages test compared

q: A seller has a right to cure and offers to, but the buyer refuses. What is the result under the text?
o: The seller must then sue for specific performance.
The buyer automatically owes the full price.
The contract is cancelled automatically.
It is unclear, but it may waive the curable breach.
The buyer keeps all of its remedies intact.
oe: The Code gives no such requirement.
Nothing makes the price automatically due; the text leaves the result open.
Refusing cure doesn't cancel anything.
Correct. The text flags this as unsettled.
The refusal likely has some effect, so this overstates it.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Refusing a valid cure

q: A buyer's purchase order includes a warranty term. The seller's acknowledgment says: "Our acceptance is expressly conditional on your assent to our terms," and its terms include a disclaimer. The buyer never assents to the seller's terms, but the seller ships and the buyer pays. A dispute arises over warranties. Under § 2-207, what are the terms of the contract?
o: Whatever terms the court finds most reasonable under the circumstances.
The terms on which the writings agree, plus Article 2's gap fillers.
The seller's terms, because the buyer accepted them by paying for the goods.
The buyer's terms, because its purchase order was the offer.
There's no contract, because the writings didn't form one.
oe: Section 2-207(3) supplies the formula: the agreed terms plus Article 2's gap fillers.

Correct. An expressly conditional acceptance isn't an acceptance under § 2-207(1). The parties' conduct then establishes a contract under § 2-207(3), whose terms are those "on which the writings of the parties agree, together with any supplementary terms incorporated under any other provisions of this Act," including the implied warranties.
Paying after an expressly conditional response isn't assent to the seller's terms. Section 2-207(3) applies.
Under § 2-207(3), neither party's form controls where they differ.
Conduct recognizing the existence of a contract establishes one (§ 2-207(3)).
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Expressly conditional acceptance, then performance

q: A lessor produces an e-signed record satisfying § 2A-201. Which is correct?
o: A signed record suffices, but it doesn't prove a lease exists.
A paper writing is still required.
The record proves the lease conclusively.
An e-signature works only for consumer leases.
Satisfying the statute fixes the rent.
oe: Correct. The 2022 Amendments replaced "writing" with "record"; UETA reaches the same result elsewhere.
The 2022 Amendments replaced it with a record.
It only removes the statute's bar.
The record rule applies to all leases.
It says nothing about rent.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — 2022 record amendments

q: A commercial sales form has, in ordinary type, a liquidated damages clause and a clause limiting the buyer to repair. The buyer argues neither is conspicuous. Which is correct?
o: Only the liquidated damages clause must be conspicuous.
Neither must be conspicuous, unlike warranty disclaimers.
Only the repair clause must be conspicuous.
Both are void, as all remedy terms must be conspicuous.
Both are valid only if separately signed.
oe: Section 2-718 doesn't say that.

Correct. Sections 2-718 and 2-719 have no conspicuousness rule. Whether such clauses reach fraud or negligence claims is for other law. "Personal injury" is undefined, and a seller that validly disclaims warranties sidesteps § 2-719(3).
Section 2-719 doesn't say that.
That's the § 2-316 rule for disclaimers.
Separate signing applies in § 2-209(2) and § 2-205.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Conspicuousness of remedy clauses

q: A trade journal's price report for a commodity in an established market is offered to prove market price. Which is correct?
o: It is inadmissible hearsay.
It is conclusive evidence of the price.
It is admissible only for buyers.
It needs live testimony from the publisher.
It is admissible, and how it was prepared goes to weight.
oe: Section 2-724 makes it admissible.
The other side may attack its weight.
It's admissible for either party.
The statute requires no sponsoring witness.
Correct. Section 2-724.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Market quotations

q: Which correctly describes the final exam under the syllabus?
o: 180 minutes, with electronic supplements allowed.
120 minutes, all of it multiple choice.
180 minutes in three parts, with only the last open-book.
90 minutes of multiple choice and 90 of closed-book essay.
180 minutes, all of it open-book.
oe: Only physical copies are allowed.
That isn't the format.
Correct. It's 70% of the grade.
That isn't the format.
The first two parts are closed-book.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Exam format

q: Which exception in § 2-201 has NO counterpart in § 2A-201?
o: Specially manufactured goods.
Admission in court.
All of them have counterparts.
Goods received and accepted.
The merchant confirmation exception.
oe: Section 2A-201(4)(a) has it.
Section 2A-201(4)(b) has it.
The merchant exception doesn't.
Section 2A-201(4)(c) has it.
Correct. Such lease transactions were thought to be few (cmt.). Specially made goods, admissions, and goods received and accepted all have counterparts.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Lease SOF exceptions

q: A boat dealer, a lost-volume seller with $5,000 profit per boat, sells a boat for $50,000 and takes a $10,000 deposit. There's no LD clause. The buyer backs out, and the dealer sells that boat to another. How much must it return?
o: $8,000, as it keeps 20%.
Nothing, as a deposit is forfeited.
$9,500, keeping only the statutory $500.
$10,000, as it resold the boat.
$5,000, after offsetting its proven lost profit.
oe: The statutory rule is the smaller of 20% or $500, and proven damages replace it.
Section 2-718(2) gives restitution.
It can prove larger damages.
A lost-volume seller's resale doesn't replace the sale.
Correct. Section 2-718(3). Compare Neri v. Retail Marine. Without proof it could keep only $500.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Down payment, seller's lost profit

q: When may a seller have further time to cure after the contract time has expired?
o: Whenever the buyer has not yet paid.
Never, because cure ends when the contract time ends.
Whenever the nonconformity is minor.
When it reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable.
Whenever the buyer has already resold the goods.
oe: Payment has nothing to do with the cure right.
Section 2-508(2) expressly reaches past the contract time.
Size of the defect doesn't give extra time under § 2-508(2).
Correct. Section 2-508(2), with or without a money allowance, on seasonable notice, for a further reasonable time.
A resale suggests acceptance, not a further time to cure.
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Cure past the deadline

q: A buyer's bank is seized by regulators, and the buyer's account is frozen. Is the buyer excused from paying?
o: Yes, by frustration of purpose, since the bank failure was unforeseen.
Yes, under § 2-615, as an unforeseen contingency.
No; it must offer a commercially substantial equivalent.
No, and the seller may sue for the price at once.
Yes, because payment became impossible through no fault of the buyer.
oe: The buyer's purpose isn't frustrated; only its payment method failed.
§ 2-615 is a seller's excuse.
Correct. Problem 6-8(b); § 2-614(2).
The buyer may offer a substantial equivalent.
The buyer must provide an equivalent.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Buyer's bank seized

q: A weaver buys five lots of "Magenta No. 2" yarn from a mill. The lots differ noticeably in shade, so a blanket knit from more than one lot looks striped. The mill says the variation comes from natural differences in fiber and dyeing. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The weaver has no claim, because variation caused by natural differences in fiber is never a breach.
The weaver may have a merchantability claim, unless the variation is within what the agreement or trade allows.
The weaver has a fitness claim, because knitting single-color blankets is a particular purpose.
The weaver has a claim only if the mill gave an express warranty that every lot would match.
The weaver has no claim, because each lot, considered by itself, is of even color and merchantable.
oe: The cause of a variation isn't a defense if the goods fall outside permitted variations.

Correct. Merchantable goods must "run, within the variations permitted by the agreement, of even kind, quality and quantity within each unit and among all units involved" (§ 2-314(2)(d)). Trade usage can define the permitted variation (§ 1-303(c)).
Using yarn to knit consistent-looking goods is an ordinary purpose, and nothing shows reliance on the mill's selection.
The even-quality standard is part of the implied warranty. No express warranty is needed.
The standard applies "among all units involved," not just within each lot.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Uneven kind and quality among units

q: A contract is F.O.B. Seller's City, and the buyer is in Buyer's City. The seller repudiates. Where is the § 2-713 market price taken?
o: Any commercially reasonable place the buyer chooses.
Buyer's City, where the buyer would use the goods.
Wherever the buyer eventually covers.
Seller's City, the place for tender.
The midpoint of the route between the two cities.
oe: The statute fixes the place, subject to § 2-723(2).
The place of arrival applies only after rejection on arrival or revocation.
Cover has its own measure, and § 2-713 doesn't look there.
Correct. The F.O.B. term makes it a shipment contract, so tender occurs at Seller's City. Under F.O.B. destination the place would be the destination.
There's no midpoint rule.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Place of market price

q: Which of the following statements about the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose is NOT correct?
o: The seller must have reason to know of the particular purpose at the time of contracting.
It arises only if the seller makes an affirmation of fact about the goods.
The seller need not be a merchant.
The buyer must actually rely on the seller's skill or judgment.
A conspicuous written disclaimer can exclude it without using the word "fitness."
oe: True. Knowledge gained after contracting isn't enough.
Correct. This is the false statement. Fitness arises from the seller's reason to know of the purpose and of the buyer's reliance; an affirmation of fact is what creates an express warranty.
True. § 2-315 has no merchant requirement, though the warranty usually arises with merchants.
True. Actual reliance is required (cmt. 1).
True. § 2-316(2) requires a conspicuous writing but no particular words for fitness.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Fitness: NOT correct

q: Each of the following clauses appears in a sale contract. Which limitation is most likely unenforceable?
o: In a consumer toaster sale, a clause excluding consequential damages for personal injury.
In a consumer sale, a clause limiting the remedy to repair or replacement of defective parts.
In a merchant sale, a clause capping the seller's damages at the purchase price.
In a merchant sale of industrial equipment, a clause excluding liability for lost profits.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Limitation of consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable" (§ 2-719(3)).
Repair-or-replace remedies are expressly permitted (§ 2-719(1)(a)).
Caps on damages are generally permitted between merchants.
A limitation where the loss is commercial isn't presumptively unconscionable (§ 2-719(3)).
One of the other choices is correct: In a consumer toaster sale, a clause excluding consequential damages for personal injury.
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Consumer personal injury limitation

q: Count, a consumer, signs a merchant's preprinted sales form that includes a clause requiring all modifications to be in a signed writing. Count does not separately sign the clause. Later, the merchant and Count orally agree to change the delivery date. Is the NOM clause enforceable against Count?
o: Yes, because Count signed the form that contains it.
Yes, because the delivery date is a material term.
No, because the UCC does not enforce NOM clauses.
No, because Count did not separately sign it.
None of the above.
oe: On a form supplied by a merchant, the non-merchant must separately sign the NOM clause (§ 2-209(2)).
Materiality has nothing to do with whether the NOM clause binds Count.
The UCC reverses the common law; NOM clauses are enforceable.
D is correct.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — NOM clause and non-merchant

q: Snuffy, a farmer, contracts to sell Big Bird 100 bushels of wheat. Snuffy calls Big Bird: "The wheat is ready. Pick it up within two hours or I sell it to someone else." Is this a proper tender?
o: No, because a tender of goods must be made in writing.
Yes, because tender may be made at any time the goods are ready.
Probably not, because two hours is too short a time to hold them.
Yes, because Snuffy put the goods at Big Bird's disposition.
None of the above.
oe: Tender requires notice reasonably necessary to take delivery, not a writing.
Tender must be at a reasonable hour and for a reasonable period.
Correct. Problem 4-4. § 2-503(1)(a).
The goods must also be kept available for the period reasonably necessary for the buyer to take possession.
C is correct.
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Tender: reasonable period

q: A buyer accepted 60 of 100 units and wrongfully rejected the other 40. The seller still holds the 40, which are readily resalable. What can the seller recover?
o: The price of the 60, and damages on the 40.
The price of all 100.
Damages on all 100.
Damages on the 60 and the price of the 40.
The price of the 60 only.
oe: Correct. Section 2-709(1)(a) for goods accepted; §§ 2-706 or 2-708 for the rest.
It can resell the 40.
The 60 were accepted.
That's reversed.
It also has damages for the 40.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Price for partly accepted goods

q: A signed contract describes the goods as "one 2019 Grover-Lift forklift, in good working condition," and later says, "SOLD AS IS." The forklift doesn't run. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No warranty exists, because "good working condition" is too vague to be a warranty.
The express warranty survives, because "as is" excludes only implied warranties.
The two terms cancel each other out, so neither one applies and gap fillers govern.
The later term controls, because it appears after the description in the writing.
"As is" excludes every warranty, express or implied, so the buyer has no claim.
oe: Saying a machine works is an affirmation of fact about it.

Correct. "As is" excludes implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(a)). Words creating an express warranty and words negating it are read consistently if possible, and otherwise the negation is inoperative to the extent unreasonable (§ 2-316(1)).
Article 2 resolves this conflict in favor of the express warranty under § 2-316(1).
Placement doesn't decide it. Section 2-316(1) favors the express warranty.
Section 2-316(3)(a) is limited to implied warranties.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — "As is" vs. an express description

q: The Swedish Chef orders a set of hand-forged chef's knives from Beaker, a blacksmith whose distinctive forging technique is the reason the Chef chose him. The contract says nothing about delegation. Swamped with orders, Beaker hands the job to another smith whose knives are well regarded but made differently. May the Chef refuse the knives the other smith tenders?
o: Yes, because the Chef has a substantial interest in having Beaker himself perform.
No, because knives are goods, and § 2-210 bars delegation only in contracts for services.
No, because a party may always delegate unless the contract expressly prohibits it.
Yes, but only if the Chef first demands and fails to receive adequate assurance from the other smith.
No, because the other smith's knives are well regarded, so the Chef suffers no harm.
oe: Correct. Delegation is barred when the other party has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform or control the acts required (§ 2-210(1)). A buyer of custom goods chosen for the maker's personal skill has that interest.
§ 2-210 governs contracts for the sale of goods, and its substantial-interest limit applies to them.
Contract language is one limit, but § 2-210(1) has a second one: the other party's substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
A demand for assurance is available under § 2-210(6), but here the delegation itself is ineffective, so the Chef needn't take that step first.
The test isn't whether the substitute is competent. When the goods turn on the maker's personal skill, the buyer may insist on that maker.
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Substantial interest: custom craft

q: Buyer orders a computer by phone and pays by card. The box arrives with terms saying that keeping it for 30 days means agreeing to arbitrate. Buyer keeps it for two months. Which statement about the case law is correct?
o: Hill v. Gateway holds box terms are never part of a contract.
Section 2-207 makes all box terms part of the contract automatically.
Klocek holds keeping the goods always accepts the box terms.
Arbitration clauses can't appear in the sale of goods.
Courts split: Hill v. Gateway enforces such terms, but Klocek does not.
oe: Hill enforced them.
A consumer isn't a merchant, so additional terms remain proposals.
Klocek rejected that analysis.
Nothing bars them.

Correct. Under Hill, the vendor is master of the offer and acceptance came by keeping the goods. Klocek treats the contract as formed earlier, making the box terms proposals under § 2-207. Online, dialog-box terms bind, and hyperlinked terms bind if a reasonable buyer would notice them.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Rolling contract

q: Rita fills out a catalog order form for a $900 lamp, as the catalog invites. The seller emails a stock acknowledgment. Separately, Omar writes to a dealer, "Your $900 price is too high; I can't pay more than $700." Which is the correct analysis?
o: Rita's form is the offer; Omar's letter is an offer to pay $900.
Both are mere inquiries with no legal effect.
Rita's form is an acceptance; Omar's letter is an acceptance.
Rita's form is the offer; Omar's letter is a counteroffer.
The catalog is the offer, and Rita's form accepts it.
oe: He refused that price.
Rita's signed order is a definite offer.
Neither fits; Omar proposed a different price.
Correct. Article 2 doesn't define "offer," so R2d § 24 applies. A catalog is an invitation, and the order is the offer; an acknowledgment can accept. Omar's statement rejects and proposes new terms.
Catalogs are generally invitations to deal.
topic: Wk 1 · II · Formation — Catalog order

q: A used-car dealer sells Waldorf a 10-year-old sedan with 140,000 miles. Two months later, it needs new brake pads, a normal wear item at that age. Waldorf claims breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. What result?
o: Waldorf wins, because the dealer is a merchant for used cars.
Waldorf wins, because any repair needed within 90 days is a breach.
Waldorf wins, because a dealer's car must be fit for ordinary driving.
The dealer wins, because used goods carry no implied warranty.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status triggers the warranty but doesn't prove breach.
No such rule.
It must be fit at the level appropriate for a car of that age and mileage.
Used goods can carry the warranty.

Correct. The dealer likely wins: the merchantability warranty covers used goods only at the quality appropriate for goods of that age and use, and worn brake pads on a 140,000-mile car are normal. No choice says that.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Used goods

q: When does a seller's cause of action usually accrue?
o: When the buyer fails to pay or wrongfully rejects.
When the seller discovers the breach.
When the goods are resold.
When the contract is signed.
Six years after delivery.
oe: Correct. After repudiation the seller may wait a commercially reasonable time, but that time is uncertain. Whether § 2-725 governs a secured seller's deficiency suit is split (nn.31-32).
Knowledge doesn't matter under § 2-725(2).
Resale isn't the trigger.
A claim needs a breach.
The period is four years, and this isn't an accrual rule.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVII · Prepaying buyers, casualty & limitations (§§ 2-718(2), 2-510(3), 2-725) — Seller's claim accrual

q: Which is a difference between §§ 2-719 and 2A-503?
o: Article 2A bars consequential damages for lessees.
Article 2A expressly lets consequentials be liquidated.
Article 2A forbids limits on commercial loss.
Article 2A has no failure-of-essential-purpose rule.
Article 2A makes all remedies exclusive by default.
oe: Lessees may recover them.
Correct. Sections 2A-503(2)-(3). Article 2 implies the first and probably allows the second.
It allows them.
Section 2A-503(2) has it.
A remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive.
topic: Wk 12 · XXX · Lease formation, terms & warranties (Art. 2A Parts 1 & 2) — Express unconscionability language

q: A law firm upgrades its equipment and sells its five surplus laser printers to a local school. A tech company sues the school, claiming the printers' firmware infringes its patent. Which warranty, if any, did the law firm give the school?
o: Only the warranty of title, because the firm doesn't regularly deal in printers.
Both the warranty of title and the warranty against infringement, because every seller gives both.
The warranty against infringement only, because the claim concerns a patent.
The implied warranty of merchantability, which covers infringement claims.
No warranty at all, because the printers were used office equipment.
oe: Correct. Every seller warrants title (§ 2-312(1)), but the warranty against infringement applies only when "the seller is a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind" (§ 2-312(3)). A law firm doesn't deal in printers.
The infringement warranty requires a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind.
The law firm doesn't make the infringement warranty, though it does make the title warranty.
Merchantability requires a merchant with respect to goods of that kind, and it doesn't address infringement.
The title warranty applies to used goods.
topic: Wks 2–3 · VI · Gap fillers, implied warranties & title — Infringement warranty needs a regular dealer

q: A used-equipment dealer sells Big Bird a forklift under a signed contract that says, in large bold capitals, "SOLD AS IS." It doesn't mention merchantability or fitness. The forklift's hydraulics fail the next week. Which implied warranties, if any, did the dealer disclaim?
o: All warranties, including the warranty of title.
Only fitness, because a fitness disclaimer needn't mention fitness.
Merchantability and fitness, because "as is" excludes implied warranties.
None, because a disclaimer of merchantability must mention merchantability by name, and this one doesn't.
Merchantability only, because "as is" is about ordinary quality.
oe: "As is" doesn't disclaim title (§ 2-312(2)).
"As is" reaches both implied quality warranties.
"As is" is an exception to the magic-word rule.
It reaches fitness too.
topic: Wks 5–7 · X · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — "As is"

q: A contract for a commercial walk-in freezer makes "replacement with an identical unit" the buyer's exclusive remedy. The freezer fails in month two. The manufacturer has discontinued the model, and no identical unit exists anywhere. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer may recover only the price of a replacement part.
The contract is discharged for impracticability, so neither party owes anything.
The seller may substitute any freezer of its choosing, of whatever quality.
The buyer gets nothing, because it agreed to an exclusive remedy that can no longer be performed.
The remedy fails of its essential purpose, so ordinary UCC remedies apply.
oe: The contract promised a whole unit, and in any event the failed limit falls away.
The seller's inability to perform the agreed remedy doesn't excuse its breach of warranty.
The seller can't rewrite the agreed remedy. With replacement impossible, the Code's remedies apply.
That leaves the buyer with no remedy at all. § 2-719(2) prevents exactly that.
Correct. An exclusive remedy that can't be performed deprives the buyer of the substantial value of the bargain and fails of its essential purpose (§ 2-719(2), cmt. 1).
topic: Wks 6–7 · XI · Remedies & remedy limitations — Replacement impossible

q: A seller repudiates three months before delivery, and the buyer asks what it may do now. Which is correct?
o: Cancel, but only after waiting 30 days.
Wait for as long as it likes, at no risk.
Wait a commercially reasonable time, or treat it as a breach now.
Do nothing until the delivery date passes.
Treat the contract as void from the outset.
oe: The 30 days belongs to § 2-609.
Only a commercially reasonable time; damages avoidable after that are its own.
Correct. Section 2-610. Waiting longer than commercially reasonable risks losing damages it could have avoided.
Section 2-610 lets it act at once.
It may cancel, but repudiation doesn't void the contract.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Awaiting after repudiation

q: A seller holds specially ordered, identified goods after a buyer's breach. When may it recover the full price under § 2-709(1)(b)?
o: When reasonable efforts can't resell them at a reasonable price.
Only if the buyer has already accepted the goods.
Only after a public auction of the goods has failed.
Only if the goods are perishable.
Always, once the goods are identified to the contract.
oe: Correct. Otherwise it is limited to § 2-708 (§ 2-709(3)).
Subsection (b) is for goods not accepted.
No auction is required.
Section 2-709(1)(b) covers any identified goods that can't be resold, not just perishables.
Identification alone isn't enough; the resale condition must be met.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Price: unsalable goods

q: Sections 2-602 to 2-604 appear to speak to rightfully rejected goods. What does the text say about a buyer who wrongfully rejected but holds the goods?
o: It may resell freely and keep the proceeds.
It automatically becomes the owner of the goods.
It should still use reasonable care, and resale is probably an acceptance.
It must destroy the goods to avoid further loss.
It has no duties, because the statutes don't mention it.
oe: Its resale would probably be an acceptance.
Rejection doesn't transfer ownership.
Correct. See n.32.
Nothing requires or permits that.
The text says it should still take care (n.32).
topic: Wk 9 · XX · Cure, care of rejected goods & rejection damages (§§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604) — Wrongful rejecter

q: A buyer and a commercial lessee each breach after prepaying $20,000, and each provider justifiably withholds. The sale price is $100,000; the then PV of the lease's rent is $100,000. There are no LD terms and no proof of damages. What does each get back?
o: The buyer gets nothing; the lessee gets $19,500.
The buyer gets $19,500; the lessee gets nothing.
Each gets nothing.
Each gets $19,500.
Each gets $20,000.
oe: That's reversed.
Correct. Sale: $500 is the smaller figure. Lease: 20% of $100,000 = $20,000, which is the whole prepayment.
The buyer's retention is $500.
The commercial lessee has no $500 cap.
Each provider may keep something.
topic: Wk 14 · XXXV · Final review: integrated problems & traps — Parallel: restitution for breaching party

q: When Gonzo takes delivery of a used cabin cruiser, he sees the GPS doesn't work. The seller makes no promise to fix it, and Gonzo accepts the boat anyway. A month later, frustrated with the GPS, he tries to revoke his acceptance because of it. What is the most likely result?
o: He can't revoke, and he has no remedy of any kind, because he accepted the boat.
He may revoke only if the seller is a merchant that regularly deals in boats.
He may revoke, because a buyer may revoke within a reasonable time after delivery for any defect.
He may revoke, because a broken GPS substantially impairs the value of a cabin cruiser.
He can't revoke because of the GPS, but he may still recover damages for it.
oe: Acceptance doesn't bar a damages claim for the known defect.
The seller's merchant status doesn't control revocation.
Revocation has specific conditions under § 2-608(1), and Gonzo meets neither.
Even if it does, a buyer who accepts with knowledge and no expectation of cure can't revoke for that defect.

Correct. Acceptance with knowledge of a nonconformity can't be revoked because of it unless acceptance was on the reasonable assumption that it would be seasonably cured (§§ 2-607(2), 2-608(1)(a)). Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies for the nonconformity, but the buyer must notify the seller of the breach within a reasonable time (§ 2-607(3)(a)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · VIII · Delivery, inspection & payment — Revocation for a known defect

q: A contract has a force majeure clause excusing performance for "any labor strike." The seller's workers strike. What governs?
o: Nothing; a strike is foreseeable, so it never excuses.
The common law of impossibility, which the clause can't displace.
§ 2-615 alone, because it sets the Code's excuse standard.
The force majeure clause, because the parties' agreement controls.
Whichever rule the buyer chooses to invoke.
oe: The clause can make them excuse.
The contract controls.
The excuse rules yield to the parties' agreement.
Correct.
The clause governs.
topic: Wk 8 · XVI · Excuse from performance — Force majeure

q: Which of the following statements about assignment and delegation under UCC § 2-210 is NOT correct?
o: An assignment of "the contract" is generally both an assignment of rights and a delegation of duties.
A clause barring assignment of "the contract" is generally read to bar only the delegation of duties.
Absent a contrary agreement, a seller may delegate its duty to tender standard goods without the buyer's consent.
Once the delegate agrees to perform, the delegating seller is discharged from liability for any breach.
A seller's right to payment can generally be assigned without the buyer's consent.
oe: True. § 2-210(5) reads a general assignment of "the contract" as a delegation too, unless the language or circumstances show otherwise.
True. That is the interpretive rule of § 2-210(4), unless the circumstances indicate otherwise.
True. Delegation needs no consent unless the agreement bars it or the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance (§ 2-210(1)).

Correct. This is the false statement. No delegation relieves the delegating party of any duty to perform or any liability for breach (§ 2-210(1)); only a novation, which the other party must agree to, releases it.
True. Assigning the right to payment rarely changes the buyer's duty or risk, so it is freely assignable (§ 2-210(2)-(3)).
topic: Wk 8 · XIII · Assignment & delegation — Delegator not discharged

q: Statler's three-year supply contract with Waldorf has a buried clause: if Waldorf fails to answer any written request for volume pricing within ten days, Statler gets a 30% discount for the rest of the term. Statler learns that Waldorf's new contracts manager doesn't know the clause exists, so Statler sends a short email asking about "pricing options" without mentioning it. The manager ignores the email, and Statler claims the discount. What is Waldorf's strongest argument?
o: A party may never benefit from a clause the other side has forgotten.
Statler deliberately exploited Waldorf's known oversight during performance, which is bad faith.
The discount clause is unconscionable.
Statler's request was not in a signed record.
Good faith requires each party to act as the other's fiduciary, so Statler had to point out the discount clause.
oe: Too broad. Simply benefiting from the other side's own lapse is fine (Vintage Rodeo). Deliberately inducing and exploiting it is not.
Correct. This is Market Street: after contracting, taking advantage of a partner's oversight that you could correct at no cost is opportunistic "sharp dealing."
Nothing suggests unfairness at the time of contracting.
Nothing in the clause or the Code requires a signature here.
Market Street places good faith between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud.
topic: Wk 2 · IV · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Exploiting a partner's oversight
